Endless Legend is Amplitudes second 4X game. This time it's fantasy instead of space, but it still has the "Amplitude Spirit". By that I mean that the game looks neat, isn't too heavy on your rig, has a clean and easily accessible interface but does stuff differently than you probably would expect. While Endless Space was relatively true to the 4X space standards, Dungeon of the Endless deviated from the typical rogue-like noticeably, and now, with Endless Legend they take it even a little bit further.
At first glance Endless Legend looks like your typical hex based fantasy 4X; or it looks like it will turn into one once it is finished. You start the game with a small army on a randomly generated map and the ability to found a city. As with most other fantasy 4X games where you build your first city is important. Each city generates resources based on the hex it is build on and the 6 hexes surrounding it, which resources you want depends on the faction you play. From there on you start to explore the map with your starting army, looking for ruins to loot, roaming mobs to fight and villages to burn until you meant your first AI faction and start the typical dance of diplomacy and war.
There are also heroes in Endless Legend which can either be assigned to a city or an army. Either way they gain experience and offer boni based on their skills. An army accompanied by a hero is much stronger than one without and a city with the right hero can be pretty effective.
Like most new 4X fantasy games Endless Legend has quests, but it does it a little bit differently. Quest are not just simple "fetch x kill y" missions, they also tell a story - at least the main quest which is different for each faction - and don't just give items or dust as a reward but can also give you access to technologies you can't get otherwise. So, searching ruins for quests is something you really want to do.
Once you start exploring the map you instantly notice that there is something different: The map is divided into regions.
Regions come in different sizes and shapes but they always have a least one minor faction village and some special resources, which you can only harvest if you have a city in that region. But the most important thing about them is that there can always only be one city in each region. This doesn't only mean that whoever has a city in a region basically controls it, it also makes you really think about where you want to build your city.
Over the course of the game cities can expand. You can build boroughs in hexes adjacent to a city centre or other boroughs and thereby gain access to resources that previously where out of reach.
Endless Legend utilizes a turn based tactical combat system but doesn't give you full control over your units. At first, it is kinda weird but it has its charm and give the game a unique touch.
Each battle starts with a deployment phase where you can place your units. After that you have multiple order and action phases. During the order phase you give you units orders which they than try to fulfil during the action phase. If they can't fulfil their order, e.g. cos the tile you want the to move to is already occupied by another unit or the unit you want them is already dead or out of reach, the AI will take over and let the unit do what it thinks is best.
Another neat thing about tactical battle is that they take place on the strategic map. When two opposing armies meet a battlefield is staked out around them which means that the area where you fight actually matters. This is especially true since elevation actually matters in Endless Legend and stuff like cliffs can block your movement paths.
You should think twice before you move an army next to a cliff where you opponent could attack them from above but they have no chance of reaching them.
Endless Legend doesn't allow you to fully customize your units and heroes but you can give them equipment such as weapons, shields, armour and trinkets. In addition to items heroes have a skill tree that consist of 3 different line that are connected to each other. Which skills a hero has access to depends on its type (infantry, ranged, cavalry or flyer) and the faction you play.
Each faction only has 3 units that will always do specific things and look a certain way. Equipment won't affect their appearance much nor will it allow you to change a units role. However, there are also quite a few minor faction units which you can recruit once you assimilated a village of their faction. This allows you to add troops to your army your faction otherwise wouldn't have access to.
When it comes to diplomacy, which is also not fully implemented yet, Amplitude goes for a strange new but nonetheless interesting concept. They have a resource called influence which is needed for every diplomatic act, may it be offering peace, declaring war or assimilating a minor faction.
Every 20 turns you can also use influence to change your Empire Plan, which gives you different buffs based on what you pick. A neat little idea that helps you to adapt your global strategy a little bit.
There are 8 major factions in Endless Legend, some of them are pretty standard fantasy stuff others are rather unique and offer you a different approach to the game.
The Vaulters are you typical science guys with a dwarfish love for crossbows.
The Wild Walkers are wood elves that left the woods to start a civilisation, they are you builders.
The Broken Lords are basically Dust vampires that have to purchase population.
The Necrophases are warmongering insects that can't be at peace, ever.
The Arden Mages are masochistic mages that grow stronger the more you hurt them.
The Roving Clans are nomad traders that can't deny you access to the market place.
The Drakken try to play world police, they like diplomacy and can force treaties.
The Cultists only have one city but can convert pacified minor faction villages.
Each region in Endless Legend has 1-3 villages of a minor faction in it. Unless pacified, which can either be done by bribing the, attacking the village or doing a quest, these villages will grow and spawn armies that will roam the map and cause havoc.
Once you have a city in a region with a pacified minor faction you can assimilate that minor faction which will add population to your city, give you some small bonuses and allow you to recruit a special unit.
There are two seasons in Endless Legend: Summer and winter. In summer everything is fine, your people are happy, your cities produce resources and your units can actually move. During winter however things are different. Suddenly you produce less food and dust, your people might get a little grumpy and your units can't move as far any more.
When winter is coming and how long it lasts is somewhat random. You know vaguely when to expect it, but you can't really be sure. And the longer you play the harsher the winter.
This adds another interesting layer to the game. While Endless Legend plays like a typical 4X during summer, winter changes the rules. Suddenly it becomes a survival game, if you haven't stockpiled enough food your people might starve and if you are low on dust your might have to destroy city improvements or disband armies cos you no longer can afford them.
Warfare is also quit different during winter. Units need way more time to reach their destinations, so it's probably not a good idea to send all your armies searching ruins when winter is coming.
Well, Endless Legend has multiplayer. That's pretty much all I can say about it cos I never tried it. In my book, 4X games are meant to be played solo, on your own clock.

It's ok for a few evenings...
But seriously, where do I even start? Probably with the best advice I can give: play this in multiplayer! There are discords dedicated to finding and hosting groups, no need to hope for a reply on the steam forums or join random groups in the browser. It's so much more enjoyable, but frustrating at the same time. Learn to love fort joy, as you'll be restarting many times. It took me good ~30 groups to find someone to finish the game with. Thankfully (and sadly) first act is the best made one, and there's a lot to do there.
Main reason why I would recommend this game is not it's story, or some innovative features and approaches, but it's replayability. Even 300+ hours in I found combat enjoyable, each fight a challenge, with a chance to ♥♥♥♥ up. There are some rather clever mechanics to learn and abuse, unique skills to master, builds to optimize and routes to find.
The game is well worth your money and time, despite it's shortcomings.
Speaking of which... Don't get me wrong, there's a lot of things wrong with the game. From expected (but not liked) bugs and glitches - on my last playthrough we had at least 3 bugged quests, a bunch of issues with stuck characters and desyncs - to more serious problems.
Story is passable at best. It will not keep you awake or amaze you in the end. Sidequests are often more engaging than the main plot line.
Armor system is very restricting for the most of the game, especially on the higher difficulties. It pretty much forces you in to using only physical or magical (typically physical) damage, as you need to strip the armor before controls can be used, and controls are mandatory for the most of the game. Yes, sure eventually you can get one spell room clearing mages, but that's late game, and that's not what you will be doing most of the time. Arguably mages are gimped up to level 12, which is a good half of the game. Once again, this is highest difficulty level, but this is where it gets fun.
There is also serious lack of skills, or variety, to be precise. It's fine for first game, but later you start to notice it more. And so many skills are very situational, or subpar, so you generally use ~5 constantly and a few for utility. It's specially notable between melee classes, as a rogue, knight(2h weapons), warrior(sword and board) and metamorph will use the same warfare skills, as they are core to being a melee, and not their "subclass" variations. There are also crafted skills, combining 2 schools, but combinations are between magical and physical schools, meaning you will rarely even see them.
There is very little to do outside of combat, except preparing for combat or picking up quests before you go fight stuff for the quests. A bit lacking from a cRPG.
Several of the systems feel unfinished, lacking purpose. Crafting seems like a huge part of the game initially, but you only really craft runes and lockpicks. Potions, scrolls, food and grenades quickly become useless, even healing potions are disappointing in the endgame. Scrolls hold up the longest, but not the offensive one, only the ones that can remove status effects. NPC attitude value is a glorified discount program.
AI "cheats" a lot. No one will suspect you as an undead (or having the zombie trait) outside of combat, but once initiated, get ready to receive all the healing spells. And they will forget it immediately after. Enemies will know where exactly to move, to avoid a minefield of line of sigh obstacles and smoke blockers, just to get that single possible shot on their turn.
But all of that said, I still enjoyed the hell out of my time with the game. Sure, maybe the abysmal state of PC gaming this year and lack of good RPG games in general is partially to blame, but I think there's more to it.
I would wholeheartedly recommend this to anyone looking for a game they can immerse themselves in.

Only If is currently available cheap as free on Steam, which is awfully nice, considering that it's easily one of the most effective mindscrew video games in history. Combining the down-the-rabbit-hole insanity of The Stanley Parable with a much, much more ambitious target, Only If is absolutely worth trying for its engaging puzzles, gripping "storyline," and unorthodox level design. Admittedly, it's got more than its share of snags - Creability's grasp on 3D platforming action could use a little polish, and there were some moments where my interest in experimenting was drowned out by my urge to shake the monitor and scream at it until it told me what I was doing wrong, and while the voice acting was largely some of the most human and realistic I've heard anywhere, it occasionally was so mumbled I couldn't make out a word of it (And no subtitles either! HOW IMMERSIVE!). All in all though, there's so much done excellent here that the scrappy edges you find now and again are completely forgivable.
And did I mention it's free?
For a game I'd heard nothing about and had next-to-no expectations for, Only If is an absolute masterpiece. Get it. Get it get it get. Unless you hate curse words, as there's a lot of those. Or if you hate that NPR show Wire Tap, because the characters sound almost exactly like that show's cast. But yeah, all the rest of you?

As a classic Sonic fan, I could not avoid commenting on a game in a series I grew up with.
TL;DR Version:
It's an amazing game start to finish. It's clear this is a labor of love by the fans, for the fans that the series has desperately needed. Heartily recommended, with the caveat that the Steam version requires you to be online (for now).
-The Long Version-
At the very first moment the game is started, from the beautifully animated intro video to the title screen to the save select menu, it's evident that Christian Whitehead et al. approached this game with a healthy respect for the series' roots. After all that's where much of the development team got their pedigree, as fans making their own classic Sonic creations and rom hacks.
Story is pretty thin, as was usually the case back in the day. Robotnik / Eggman along with his new Hard Boiled Heavies find a Time Stone on Angel Island which sends all involved back through time. Players start in the well-treaded Green Hill Zone. It sets the tone for what to expect for the rest of the game, as familiar elements give way to new stage designs. Even a stage so often visited in the series as the Green Hill Zone is fresh again. The Acts are far longer than they used to be, too. While it's possible (and an achievement) to finish some stages under a minute, most will take 3 - 5, with the last couple of Acts especially approaching the 8-10 minute mark - and yeah, the 10 minute rule is still in effect.
But old stages made new isn't this game's only schtick. The dev team really flexes their muscles in brand new zones like Studiopolis and Mirage Saloon. In every case, the zones are chock-full of references to either Sega's or Sonic's past. Even the Special Stage has Sonic trying to catch a UFO which is both a reference to Sonic CD's special stage and the fact that Sega makes UFO catchers. See what they did there?
While Sonic is known for his speed, many of us who played Sonic 1 - 3 remember there were two things more prevalent than simply going fast: momentum-based platforming and multiple routes to explore. Both play a big part in Mania as how fast you might be going will provide access to specific routes not available otherwise. Navigating stages then becomes an exercise in efficiency, finding the route that will get you to the end in the fastest amount of time.
The extras in the game, unlocked from finishing the Blue Sphere special stage found on the Star Poles, are mostly minor distractions. You can unlock a stripped-down version of Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine, a Sound Garden for the game's music tracks, and No Save gameplay mods including Debug mode and the memey &Knuckles mode which gives you Knuckles as a partner, even if you're already playing as Knuckles.
All around, I'm having a really hard time finding faults to gripe about. There's of course the Denuvo controversy, which requires players to be online for no discernible reason. That aside though, I've had an amazing time playing the game. For a classic gamer like me, this was pure joy.  Really the only fault gameplay wise is that there isn't more of it. No doubt some of your favorite zones may not have made the cut for the Mania treatment, but I'm hopeful that the success of this project might open up the possibility for a sequel. I can only hope.

Sonic Mania... its been 22 years since we've had a 2D classic sonic game. Ever since we've had games that try something new each time. Adventure 1, 2, Heroes and 06 trying a 3D gameplay style consisting on different play styles for each character you play as (treasure hunting, mech shooting, team based gameplay or even ♥♥♥♥ing fishing) and then Unleashed, Colours and Generations trying to be a blend of 2D and 3D. Lost World tried to be both as well but it played quite differently. Every game that has come out has come with mixed reactions and reviews. People love it, hate it or just don't know. Do I think they're all bad games? not at all, there's just certain parts of each game that I wish they didn't have. So there's never been a sonic game thats consistently good for 22 years.
2016: Sonic Mania is announced along with Sonic Forces and everyone was hyped to see Classic Sonic back in his true gameplay, not Generations, not Sonic 4 Episode III or Sonic 5, this was Sonic as in the early 90s Sonic. 3 playable characters, Sonic, Tails and Knuckles and levels from past games. This game was also made by Christian Whitehead, who was responsible for the Sonic CD PC release and the classic Sonic game re-releases on mobile. So people were excited for the game
2017: The game was meant to come out in Spring but was delayed... then it was meant to come out in July but was delayed, then August but it was delayed again for PC users. But then it finally arrived and when I finally got to play it, I couldn't believe it. The opening like Sonic 3, the remixed Green Hill Zone theme, the Death Egg robot destroying Green Hill Zone, its a lot to take in when you first play it. Especially if you've played Sonic games for a long time and this game tries to test your knowledge of previous Sonic games with callbacks to both classic and modern games, musical references, level placement so if you remember a certain trap from the last game that featured whatever level, you're aware of it this time.
The control in this game is like the Mega-Drive/Genesis games... but improved. This isn't Generations where Sonic's spindash is overpowered and there's no need to earn speed, you need to build up momentum in this game and if you don't, you won't get anywhere, especially in later levels.
The boss battles are very easy in this game.. but that might also be because you kind of know how to beat them thanks to previous games. Although the music for each boss is great and even though we get Green Hill Zone for the 500th time, its great to hear the remixes by Tee Lopes. I can't even say what my favourite song is because they're all just that good, like Sonic 3 & Knuckles, each act has its own piece of music.
The downsides of this game... if you've never played a Sonic game before, it might be odd to you, you might like it but you also might not. All the references and callbacks it does in the game might seem really odd to you if you don't understand them. Like the mean bean machine boss battle, you might be running around Chemical Plant and suddenly be brought to that and be like "ummm... what the ♥♥♥♥?"
1 very important thing for the PC version: Denuvo.. now, people keep giving this game negative reviews for it when honestly... I've had no problems. I don't know that much about Denuvo but this game is absolutely fantastic and I don't see how Denuvo is suddenly ruining all of it.
If you've been playing Sonic games for a good long while, I suggest you play this. This is easily one of my favourite Sonic games in a long time. There's nothing I hate about this game but tbh I'd love to see some DLC to more remixed levels, or more original stages. Or perhaps other characters? but we have mods for that.
If you haven't played a Sonic game... is this a good game to start off with? yes and no. Yes because its an amazing game and is exactly how 2D Sonic should be... but no because you really won't understand all of it. This is a Sonic game made by fans for fans.
Overall, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.

Yeah. I agree with everyone that this is one of the best Sonic games ever made. The best Sonic Game since the Mega Drive days. Well yes....If you ignore 3D Blast, Adventure, Rush, Rush Adventure, Unleashed, Colours and DS Colours Generations, I heard the Advance series and Tails Adventure are pretty good and I heard that the storybook had the best portrayal of Sonic. I like modern Sonic.
Story:
I don’t much to say about the story as it’s just Eggman finds a ruby with space powers and Sonic must stop him. The ruby is mainly used as a framing device as to why you go from different zones most of the time. Which was something I was a bit disappointed in cause in Sonic 3 and Knuckles, every level had a transition on how Sonic got to the next level, and while we get a few at the start, they stop doing them after a while.
And I’m sure you are aware of the new goon squad  called the Hard Boiled Heavies and they are great. With no dialogue, they show so much personality in both their movements and how they fight like Heavy Gunner is not only a bit trigger happy and kinda incompetent in how you fight him, but he’s also a massive coward who runs the moment he doesn’t have any back-up. I’ll love to see these guys again and become recurring bosses in the series.
Gameplay:
Characters are the same as ever with Sonic’s shield powers, Knuckles being able to glide and climb walls and Tails being able to fly, and I must say, Tail’s flying attack seem to be a really effective attack.  Must be a response to the Marble Garden boss. Sonic can also unlock the insta-shield from 3 and the super peel out from CD but they’re only usable in a no save game.
Almost all the redone levels have added elements from other levels of that type like the water level has the bubble gimmick from a Game Gear game as well as the spears from Labyrinth and even some new elements like the Zip lines in Green Hill. I did notice that some levels were pretty close and I was close to the 10 minute time limit like in Lava Reef. At least it doesn’t have a “Barrel of Doom”.
The special stages in this game might be my favourite in the series, mainly since it involves you chasing after the Chaos Emeralds on a race track with blue orbs to increase you speed, rings to keep the timer going and traps to lose time. What I like about them is that they really on skill and how the course works instead of quick reflexes, looking at half-pipe. Rush was the only one with the half-pipe I liked.
And I love these boss fights. They’re as gimmicky as the bosses from CD are as satisfying to destroy if you know what you’re doing like the ones from 1,2,3, Rush Adventure and DS Colors(Maybe advance too but I haven’t played those.) A few are remakes of previous bosses or have a twist to them like the frist Eggman fight being the last Sonic 2 boss that can only be hit in the head and there are numerous hills and even his arm attack to hit him.
One boss is also a fun tribute to a spinoff game and although I spoiled myself, it was still great. And they also brought back Blue Sphere as bonus stages and if you love that Special Stage like me, then you’ll love that not only are the classics from  3&K but new ones have been made and they are both though and fun. If there’s one flaw with them is that after you win all the medals for them ,there isn’t a reason to go back to them besides them being fun.
Presentaton:
It looks great. The backgrounds look lovely, my favorite being Titanic Monach. All the redone sprites of classic enemies look nice and all the character have a noticeable amount of new frames for the cast. You can even see Eggman’s belly wobbly as he runs.
And the music. Forget about how amazing the remastered music is, although what they did Flying Battery Act 2 was amazing and I always thought Lava Reef Act 1 could’ve been a little longer but the new levels and their songs are just awe inspiring. Studiopolis is like something from CD, Press Garden reminds me of Freedom Planet, Mirage Saloon sound like a song I remember from the nineties and Titanic Monach....Holy Moly that  song screams final level more than any other Sonic game besides maybe Wing Fortress.
Verdict:
This might be my new favourite Sonic game. all it had to do for that was not screw up it’s level design to take the crown from S3&K and it has.

Imagine Civilzation V with customizable armies and quests. While unit Type A defeats unit Type B in Civilzation, here you create and customize your own army, equipping them with a variety you receive from quests and from production. While Civilization's focus isn't on combat and more on build order and adapting to the environment, Endless Legend keeps in stride with interesting land improvements and incredibly unique races to play as.
Personally, I'm a fan of the Broken Lords. They look pretty sweet, and they grow from dust - the currency like gold you'd normally use to just hurry production. As a result, you don't need to worry about food but instead need to constantly manage dust, which is now used for everything from hurrying production and gaining citizens to healing your troops on the field and improving their gear.
It's a hefty price-tag for something in alpha, but the game is very playable and has yet to crash / glitch on me. I'm honestly having more fun with this than I am in Civilization V.

(This review was done pretty much immediately after release, so things may or may not have changed since.)
I'm simply baffled by this game. I know this game is supposed to be surreal (think Stanley Parable or Kentucky Route Zero), but the game is extremely confusing and irritating to play. Walkthrough is pretty much needed, as the game doesn't give the player even an inkling of an idea when it comes to solving certain puzzles.
So you begin the game by going to a party, but your vision fades to white at the door. You wake up in a strange bed with no recollection of past events, so you set to figure out what's happened. Except you're thrown into a weird dream like world that defies logic and natural laws. And you get shouted at by a voice in a radio doing a bad Al Pacino impression.
The game looks decent enough. The game runs 60 FPS most of the time, but for some odd reason tanks to 30 and even below for no apparent reason. This kind of behavior happened in the second room of the game, but when later revisiting the room in another puzzle, the game ran at 60 FPS again. I have no idea as to why this happens, forced VSync, maybe? There seems to be only very primitive graphical controls with a handful of predetermined levels of graphical fidelity. There should be more detailed graphical options for tweaking things like texture quality, anti-aliasing, anisotropic filtering, VSync etc.
The voice acting is susceptible to very annoying changes in audio level. The two types of voices you're going to hear are the main character and a mysterious voice on the radio. The main character seems to be clearly audible most of the time, but sometimes inaudibly mumbles something for no apparent reason. While this mumbling is annoying, the radio voice is even worse. Sometimes when the radio was far away, I couldn't make sense through the low audio level, distortion and unclear voice acting, whereas scenes where the radio was closer caused some clipping. In my case it got to the point of hurting my ears at certain points, especially when the radio voice was practically in my ear. The lack of captions didn't make understanding dialogue any easier.
Controlling the character is easy enough in situations that don't require precise platforming. Unfortunately, there is some precise platforming involved in at least one section. The dimensions of how far or high the main character can jump are not really clear, and I fell to my death multiple times by either bumping my head on something or just falling short. The level layout is also very confusing, and many times I had to simply make a leap of faith to see if I could make a jump - and many times that failed. There seem to be also some invisible walls, which at least in one scenario made me think I hit a bug. The way the camera behaves can also be kind of dizzying and sickess inducing at times. Especially crouching while moving can cause some tilting (I guess roll is the correct term) that is exaggerated and very unnatural.
The worst thing about Only If is the lack of direction. As of writing this review, I've been to seven or so sections. The game gives very little to no hints at all as to what you're supposed to do. Actually, I'd go even further and say that the game even misleads you. It's difficult in a review to point out these sorts of things without spoilers, and I'd like to keep this spoiler free. I'm only going to say that the game wants the player to name a thing at one point. Also, there's a button mashing sequence that, as far as I can tell, leads only to the main characters death and a level restart.
Creating an experience that is not frustratingly obscure to the player is something I expect from any game, surreal or not. The worst challenges in this game are not just stopping and thinking about all the mechanics of a puzzle, or trial and error, or even memorizing. The challenge at its worst is truly in the realm of "guess the developer logic" type of "puzzling". I simply cannot recommend this game in it's current form.

The graphics and audio are pleasing and the game play is fairly fun. The control system has clearly been designed with future mobile support in mind which tends to make it a little bit counter intuitive; it still needs to be polished. There are also some annoying bugs that are hard to pin down, such as tooltips failing to work and so forth. All of these however are to be expected for an early access game and shouldn't discourage anyone from trying the game out.
There are, however, several key design flaws to the gameplay that lead me to not recommend getting this game while it is still in earlier access. My wife and I tried playing together and found that anything we built was most likely destroyed the next time we logged in. It was also almost impossible to find open land to build on as the world is quite crowded. In addition to the frustration of having anything you build be destroyed there are many situations that can arise in the gameplay that can prevent you from being able to play.
I logged in after having not played in two weeks and found myself inside someone's base. I can't escape the base in any way. I didn't want to try to knock down any walls as I did not want to develop a criminal record. After waiting for a long time hoping a player with access to the base would open the gate I conceded that I would have to try to knock down a wall to escape, despite not wanting a criminal record. I am unable to attack any part of the walls, however, without being quickly killed by the base's arrow towers. I am now effectively stuck in the base with no way to escape or play the game. Until these types of large design flaws are addressed I would advise against paying for this game.

I'd give this a mediocre rating, but since there isn't one, I'll lean to No.
A decent and well-thought out runner that's completely ruined by the level design (or the randomly placed seeds of it, anyway) and a color palette that keeps you constantly guessing at high speed whether you can land onto or crash into it.
It commits the worst mistake of running reflex games; You see better forward than you see up or down so it becomes a memory game of remembering what kind of level blocks have what kind of stuff ahead (you could say of course the view is mainly forward, but it's really so restricted to just forward that you can barely see anything below or above you, and the game demands you do big leaps downwards). Add to that the fact that one skill has charge-up and two of the skills have a period where you can't activate your other skill so everything you do has to be prepared in advance. It's a memory game, not a reflex game.
Plus even hitting the upper half of a corner isn't enough when the character is falling or jumping, it will just kill you. Even when you think you can just run over a gap onto the next platform, the character will stub their toe and you will die. I swear I have never seen a platformer be this petty about landing onto the edge of a platform.
It's cheap and the powerups mixing between levels are interesting, but the art design fails to grasp proper contrast to your surroundings at high speed. I wouldn't pick this up for serious play, it just stays in a rainy day-pile.

It's not a bad game overall, just bad design choices IMO.
Get it if you like runner games, since it does provide some nice challenges (in-game challenges as well).
But the casual players out there might want to pass on this one, since it will require you to memorize more than you'll be bothered to.

TIS-100 is a can be a challenging puzzle game, even for those that have some programming experience. I think this game (while not a perfect model for any esiting assembly language) is a beautiful way to get into the mindset that makes programming easier (to plan and to visualize). The limitations of the instruction set used for solving each program puzzle can be frustrating, but it's a tantalizing frustration (Ex: I know how to solve this problem in C; how can I adapt what I know there into the patterns for doing things here?). I found the game highly rewarding with the open-endedness of the puzzles.
My first solutions to each of the puzzle tended to be jury-rigged together. They work, but I can make it better. I can try to make it take fewer cycles (faster) to finish testing the instructions. I can consolidate the code so it uses fewer of the nodes MOV-ing data back and forth. I can work towards a solution that needs fewer lines of code to have a solution.  Each of these “execution nodes” holds no more than 15 lines of instructions. There were many times I could’ve solved a problem easier if I had 16 lines; it forced me to think at the problem from a different perspective. I would not describe this as an easy puzzle game. It is simple, but not easy.
This game required from me:
Overall, my playtime took under 35 hours to get a working solution to each of the 47 puzzles. Interspaced in that were 40ish hours for trying to improve some of my solutions. Recently this year, I’ve taken a personal challenge at getting “UNCONDITIONAL” (like the namesake achievement) solutions to all the puzzles. I’ve already done so the first 25 puzzles (nightmare difficulty for the SEQUENCE SORTER puzzle).
If you get this game, may you come to learn the beauty of JRO and the profane magic of JRO ANY.
It's almost like programming in assembly is fun now.

Um es einfach zu sagen, dieses Game ist fuer mich der Heilige Gral dieses Spiele Genres. Nach Heroes of Might and Magic, Civilizations X-X, AoW3, traue ich mir doch zu ein wenig Ahnung von den Games aus diesem Genre zu haben. Und das was Endless Legends bietet ist einfach nur sau gut.
Was auf jeden Fall mal raussticht hingegen zu allen anderen, es ist zu 100% im Fantasy Bereich anzutreffen. Keine Menschen, Zwerge, ... Ritter, Musketen, ... Volle Dosis Fantasy in diesem Game. Insekten Monster, Geister Kaiser und und und.
Das Gelaende Design = DER HAMMER. Hunderte verschieden Tiles, optisch sehr nett miteinander verbunden und im Gesamten sehr stimmig.
Das UI - sehr modern, ich liebe es, ist allerdings sicherlich fuer viele sehr gewohnungsbeduerftig. (Nicht fuer jeden was)
Die Darstellung der Daten ist sehr gelungen und uebersichtlich und leicht zugaenglich.
Die Strategische Tiefe des Spiels ist in meinen Augen sehr gut gelungen. Es ist ein guter Mix gefunden worden, wo man tiefer gehen sollte, und wo eher nicht. Es ist fuer meinen Geschmack zwischen Casual und Hardcore eingereit.
Die eigentlichen Staerken in meinen Augen sind Dinge wie:
Diplomatie (Man braucht Einfluss um Krieg zu erklaeren, man braucht Regions um maechtig zu sein, ...)
Kampf (Man wird nicht auf ein virtuelles generiertes Kampffeld gebaemt. Man kaempft auf dem wo man steht und was man sieht.)
Winter/Sommer (Im Winter ist das ueberleben nicht leicht und man muss sich auf seine Stadt fokusieren)
Das Questsystem (Einmalig wie ich finde)
Minion System (Von ausruestung bis ueber Skills alles dabei)
Und noch vieles mehr. Das wuerde jedoch ein Review sprengen.
Ich empfehle jedem im allgemeinen sich zumindest die Videos zu diesem Spiel anzusehen im speziellen das erste grobe Tutorial Video eines Game Testers, es zeigt das Spiel im Groben sehr gut.

New to Amplitdue's games and looking for some Pros and Cons on buying Early Access? Well heres some for you.
*** Updated as of Beta v 0.5.18 S3 ***
Pros
-An incredible amount of visual polish for an Early access game, and its only going to get better. You can zoom in far out or insanely close. Up close the details are stunning. And zooming far out gives you a ancient looking map with all the details you need.
-It's a Completely unique game. Coming from someone who enjoys the Civ series thouroughly, this game feels totally different and adds yet another delicious 4X flavor to my palate. Some things that make it different: High Ground advantadge, Adaptively Progressive Tech trees, The Market, Minor faction integration, and much more.
-Unique factions: I've played all of the major factions in complete games. This much I can tell you: If you play two factions with the same strategy it will not end well for you. Their uniqueness adds allot of immersion to the game.
Cons: (Will be updated as game progresses)
-The GUI is set up in such a way that you can easily make a mis-click with units and suffer consequences you never intended. There is a high chance this will be polished up before release.
-The economics of the game feel flat. The dissaproval systems are pretty linear and leave a little to be wanted, however there is more economic depth planned and even more will most likely be added before Early Access ends.
[This game contained many cons at EA release but these are since gone]
Endless Space problems not found in Endless Legend:
-Steamrolling combat. Endless Space suffured from this, however combat is deep and thought provoking in Endless Legend even in early access. Also, there is much less of a "Rock Paper Scissor" feel to the game
-Endless Space had a lack of Diversity. Endless Legend on the other hand is teeming with diversity.
-Immersion. From seeing heroes fight on screen, to a richly stylized GUI, to incredible artwork, Endless Legend pulls you into the game's universe and keeps you there.
Overall, this game is an incredible EA game, and a steal with the release sales. And to speak of bugs, beyond a minor one here and there, they are practically non existent.
So looking for Endless entertaiment? This is it.

**Updated 4/26/14** All Future Updates will be found in chronological order as you continue to read.
First Day Launch Review. Will update as updates come (to the best of my ability).
For those who decide to look and say TL;DR - Great game, Worth the Price, Alpha = Better than any Alpha I have played, Missing Some features and directions, but will be fixed over patches as is known to happen with Amplified Studios.
Let me start by saying, this is EASILY the best Early Access game I have seen come to Steam. It is already VERY polished for a game still in Alpha. The graphics are actually more impressive than I expected from an Alpha version. Glitches? Kept to a minimum so far, in fact, I don't think I have really seen anything that was more then a moment's annoyance.
A previous review I read said, it takes too many clicks for a unit to make an action, compared to Civ. I disagree. I select the unit, tell it to walk to the tile i want, once its there, it pops up and says "Do this action?" And I can say Yes or no. Quite simple. Attacking another unit? Select your unit and click the other one. Very simple, not tedious, not a pain, and considering how much this game LACKS in direction at its current stage, its refreshing to be given instructions to understand.
The game plays like a combination of Age of Wonders (I,II,II), Civ (Any), Fallen Enchantress and Endless Space. It takes the best part of each game, and mixes them together. Want an easy way to build you cities and manage your workers? Done. Want to have a little more control over battle but still have it streamlined so it doesn't bog down your game? Done.
The Tech tree is similar to the Endless Space Tech Tree with a few differences. Right now, you can only research the Tech of the "Age" you are in. You gain levels in "Age" by researching so many of the previous "Age's" technologies. For example, you start at the First Age and can not advance to the Second until you have researched 10 technologies. The only catch on this is, you do not need to research certain technologies to unlock more advanced ones. For example, if you do not research Age One Weapons, you can still research Age Two Weapons. I am sure this is something that will be addressed in a later patch.
I have so much more to say, but I just want to play! More updates and information to come!
**Update 4/26/14**
So now that I have some more time to expand upon things I wrote earlier, I am going to do my best to do so.
So as I have said, this game plays like a combination of a few games. Most notably it feels like Fallen Enchantress and Civilization games. Allow the following to help explain what I mean by this.
Fallen Enchantress - The biggest similarities come from how the units stack. You stack armies onto a single tile. You are also limited to how many units can be in a single stack. This is based upon your hero and your tech tree. There are roaming bands of armies (mostly made up of creatures) as well as the other empire's armies. When you initiate battle, you will also notice that it has a similar system that shows you how balanced the fight will be. It differitiates slightly from here though. You pick if you want your armies to play offensively, defensively or stay put. Then, your battle takes place on the actual hexagons of the campaign map, but it is limited to a small area. It does not go to a difference screen where the single hexagon turns out to be some huge 12x12 area inside of that single tile. This means that you can potentially start a battle in a part of the world map, knowing that they have to come through a bottleneck because of a mountain range with only one entrance. Once you start your battle, you have the opportunity to place your units in the desired hexagons prior to the fight starting. this allows you to protect your ranged by playing them behind mountains or cliffs and adds a nice level of strategy into the battle, while not becoming so tedious that you spend hours in a single battle (for example a Total War game where you might spend 10+ minutes arranging your armies perfectly). After you have placed your units, you get to choose what units target which enemy units. Then once the round starts, the action is streamlined and you are along for the ride. This helps streamline battle, but it does have rounds where you can re-adjust your strategy to ensure your victory.
*A quick note I will need to add more to later, they also allow you to upgrade/change gear on your armies just like in Fallen Enchantress. I will need to expand on this more later.
Civilation - It is similar mostly through building and placing cities. You also have control over what your population works on in each city (i.e. FIDSI - Food, Industry, Dust, Science and Influence . You build expansions on your city, utilize resources in your region and basically control your settlements expansions.
A couple quick notes I want to make here.
* You can only create one settlement in each region. Choose wisely. You *can* still use any resource in that region, even if you are not settled next to it. This mainly makes you choose wisely when it comes to the resources available in the tiles near you.
*Influence and Empire Direction - You use influence to choose the direction of your empire every 20 turns. I made the mistake (due to lack of instructions) of thinking this feature was not implemented. You do not just click the direction you wish to go, you must click and DRAG it to the marker line. I spent my first 60 turns before I realized this.
*There is no tutorial. This is not a game to learn 4x strategy on. It is still being developed. There are truly no directions and you will make mistakes or wrongful assumptions. It may frustrate you when you do so. Save often, you will appreciate when you can go back 20+ turns because you didn't fully understand the consequences of an action you took so long ago, thinking it wouldn't effect you the way it did. I am sure a tutorial will be available upon release if not sooner. If you have any questions, you may also feel free to add me and I will answer them to the best of my ability.

Okay this is a review for tree of life.
Tree of life is a game where you can build, buildings with a leveling system. Simple as that. Or is it?
I'll quickly talk about the games progression.
The first thing you may want to do is, Punch trees (Minecraft? Ark?) alot of games have this system now.
Punching trees will give you twigs, apples and eventually a log.
Punching the log will give you firewood.
With the twigs you can craft torches with E [Putting the twigs into your inventory] (this is to get your "tinkering" up and so you have a light source at the night.
Torches can also be used to light campfires (you must create one to survive and cook food)
It took me a while to figure out how to consume food... You must right click+Drag to consume the food.
From there you can figure it out.
Since the game is Multiplayer, expect to work together (if you can) or not (if you have a language barrier).
Play with friends and the progress will be alot better.
Theres also a level cap in the game. As you will have a limited amount of points you can spend. (which is kind of stupid).
Most people in this game will want to work alone (i haven't seen a single person talk within the game).

Is Run or Die a good game? At first glace it looks and sounds amazing! The pixel art style, the animations, the soundtrack - really good!  You get a nice tutorial which is easy to understand, but what that tutorial doesn't tell you is that this game will be as unfair as possible. Aside from jumping and ducking, you are given 2 skills along your run that you must use to avoid obstacles. There are 5 skills in total: Leap. Dive. Dash. Emp. Ion. They are randomly chosen for you at begging of each level and once you reach a checkpoint, they are taken away and replaced with 2 new random skills as the game speeds up. You need to constantly change your strategy each time if you plan to stay alive. Did I mention the maps are randomly generated?
The biggest complain I have is that there are almost no visual cues, everything just blends in together and you have no clue whether it's part of the background or not. For a runner game that is a huge mistake because now the challenge lies not in your reflexes, but in your ability to distinguish the obstacles.
There are so many cheap deaths in this game! It's ridiculous. Every single time you think you've got the hang of it, the game decides to throw you a curveball.  You are definitely going to die a lot. It makes it sound like a good challenge, but it's more frustrating than anything and you can find much better games than Run or Die.
I've bought it on sale and it's totally worth it. Challenging and yet making fun. 4/20

The graphics QUALITY is excellent. It's a lovely game. Lots of detail and parallax animation going on.
The graphics DESIGN is terrible. The visual cues as to what is an obstacle and what isn't are inconsistent to the point I think this is a bad game as a result. A darker shade sometimes means something is in the background, and sometimes it means nothing at all. All the crap moving in parallax makes it even harder to see, and there's a lot of borderline trolling with deliberately obscured obstacles.
The gameplay is fine on the surface, but falls apart on deeper inspection. The levels seem to be based on what random powers you get, and vary too much in difficulty versus progression. Dash, ion, and leap are mechanically the fairest. Dive and emp are more annoying and require too much rote memorization. Dive by its nature requires moving into previously hidden places and the forced jump before using it is annoying.
Emp levels are by far the worst. They're full of hard to see lasers that often blend into the background tinting, lasers concealed by objects or interior walls, lasers that double as trip traps, and the lasers are often spaced to kill you with the emp's overlong cooldown. Emp is also the only power that simply by using it obscures the very obstacles that you are trying to avoid.
I prefer runner gameplay to focus on when it's appropriate to jump or use a special move. I don't prefer it to be trying to distinguish what wall will kill me. Nor do I like trying to get a feel for five different power cooldowns that are randomized every minute. Canabalt does not have this problem.
Highly Recommended !

I really like this game, still there are some issues.
+Realism
+Cool Graphics
+Extremely detailed maps,objects,people
+Fun Multiplayer with a lot of mods (+CO-OP CAMPAIGN)
+A huge variety of weapons, vehicles and troopers
+Map Editor
-The game is heavy (for your device)
-AI is not really smart (not exactly your opponents the AI, but the soldiers themselves
-Lack of animations (animation for steady-look around/interact with weapon etc.)
-Lack of voice acting- the campaign advicer does not talk, only subtitles and the phrases that the soldiers use are really annoying and not many
-A lot of glitches that can ruin you the game like:
-If a car with a mounted weapon (highly used vehicle) is empty and you want somebody just on the gun you need 3 soldiers-first enters and goes to the driver seat, second becomes the sergaent of the car and the third goes on the gun and then you mount off the 1st and the 2nd
-If you have a damaged vehicle which has no crew in it and you want to repair it-the vehicle moves by vibrating and slowly going on a random position, so if you put an e.g. engineer to repair it and he sits by the vehicle, he soon gets glitched in it's hitbox and killed by the vibration even if the vehicle is moving in other direction (shortly the vehicle kills the repear time very often)
-There is melee fighting but it is extremely stupid. They have knives which are only for throwing and do nothing
-There isn't enough information about the squads you are purchasing e.g. it says Defensive Squad, yeah but what does it do, what men does it contain? It really has one medic which is extremely important and I think a machine gunner with the rest being just normal soldiers.
Now those issues seem little, but if you play the game you will see they will bug you out.
I still recommend the game, I had real fun while playing it and really enjoyed the AI opponents in skirmish. If you have a friend to play with, I highly recommend to play the cooperative campaign as it is real fun.

2. Creating a local/online skirmish has so little options and is tucked away in the bottom left corner of the screen while the rest of the screen is cluttered with stuff... Literally I have to squint at my 32" desktop screen to try and select the few options when setting up a game.
3. You cant change the draw distance in game. This means that all you know is that there are some units over there but you have to scroll over to the area to see what it is. Not to mention that you can't change this in the settings...
4. It has workshop support but is so hard to use and navigate to activate the mods that its not worth it. For some reason in the lastest version that I just played you have to go to settings and then click on the "mods" tab, then move the mods you want to activate from the deactivated list to activated list and hit accept...? Not to mention the settings button is hard to see because the main menus is so cluttered...
Now Good things about the game:
1. AI are smart and very fun to play against
2. The cover system works and you can send units to take cover in buildings
3. Everything is highly detailed!!
4. The unit UI makes sense because it is exactly like 'Men of War'
5. The campaign is fun. Not anything revolutionary but fun.
In short, game play is your typical RTS and most RTSs are fun but if you hate cluttered UIs or main menus then gl hf dd.

This is less of a review and more of a preview of what you can expect from this game. I know that steam says I barely played EL - that's because I've been playtesting this game for several months before release. As such, I'm also inherently biased so take that into account.
Why should you buy this game? The short answer is - if you have any doubts, don't buy it. Wait for the full release and then do your research and see if it's the kind of game that you will enjoy :)
Personally though, I think that EL stands strong among other 4X games. It feels fresh and unique in many areas where 4X were starting to get stale. There's a lot to talk about so I'll just go over some of the bigger features:
Firstly, the city management aspect. Like in most 4Xs once you make a city you can grow it, make improvements, train troops, gather food, industry, science, dust/gold and influence (FIDSI in short). But population works differently - you assign your workers (you population) to specific areas like food generation or influence generation. The amount of population working on that is multiplied by various bonuses (but it's at least *3) and then other various other bonuses are also added to the amount of FIDSI you can generate. This gives you a lot of control over what your city does (more so then in civ where you're much more dependent on the tiles around your city).
Secondly, empire management. Every 20 turns you (and all other players) choose your "empire plan" which will define how you play for the next 20 turns. You need influence to invest into your empire plan - the more influence you invest, the better. You also have more options in empire plan as you enter new eras.
Another use for influence is in diplomacy - all diplomatic actions (closing borders, declaring war,  etc) require some influence. You can also spend influence to improve your influence with AIs. Right now however, this aspect of the game only has basic functionality because there's no multi (yet) and the AI is fairly dumb (for now).
Additionally, the tech is non-linear, meaning that you have free control over which tech you want to go for next. There are no prerequisites to anything. However, you have to choose what you research wisely as technology gets progressively more expensive. The only limitation are the eras. Basically, in order to unlock tech from next era, you need at least 10 tech from previous era.
Thirdly, army management. There are 5 main unit types in the game: infantry, ranged units, support units, cavalry and flying units. Each faction has access to 3 unit templates (+the settlers) which you can then customize to decent extend. For example, you can equip your infantry with weapons that will help you fight cavalry - which normally is a good counter to infantry.
Because each race can only use 3 basic templates (in as many versions as they want of course, I'm just talking about the infantry/support/etc kind of templates), you also have to rely on assimilating minor factions into your empire. Minor factions will grant you an empire bonus and give access to their unique unit templates. This allows you to make up for the fact that you don't natively have access to certain unit type. For example, the Wild Walkers faction has no access to flyers so they can assimilate Khazanji minor faction to gain access to Demons - a new flying unit template. There are of course limitations to how many races you can assimilate.
Fourthly, the battles. They're quite unique since they're played on world map (like in civ) but are little skirmishes by themselves (like in AoW3 but you have less control). Each battle starts with a deployment phase and planning phase (during which you give your units orders). Then, the battle kicks in and you watch how your units duke it out. After a while you get the opportunity to change your orders around if you so choose. You also have to remember that there's elevation in this game - attacking from high ground will give you a decisive advantage while using cliffs can lead to some Hot Gates scenarios. The battles still have ways to go, true, but they're quite enjoyable already, even in alpha state.
Lastly, the world. Auriga (the planet you play on) looks gorgeous and I wouldn't hesitate saying that it's one of the best looking 4X games (if not the best). Aside from great visuals, there are numerous things to discover on Auriga - there are many anomalies (special tiles that are usually very good), ruins to explore (they are persistent btw), minor faciton villages,  and a huge amount of various biomes. Plus the standard - resource deposits and so on.
Also, let's not forget about quests. Each faction has a storyline expressed via a quest system. Every player is given a set of quests that they can complete for rewards (completing all of them will win you the game but that's not implemented yet). Aside from these main quests, you can also gain various side quests from minor factions, ruins and so on. The quests are quite interesting and make the game feel more alive, they also let you discover the lore of the game.
In general, I do recommend this game but encourage you to do some more research first. Especially if you plan buying it in its alpha state.
Also, this review is mostly a quote from a wall of text I wrote on the forums once. Just FYI ;)

From the creators of Endless Space comes a hybrid sci-fi/fantasy strategy game set on one world.  So far it's still in early access and it blows me away how good this game is.  Very polished for the stage it is in.  It continues to evolve the combat system from Endless Space where you don't micromanage each unit, but give broad orders to your army.  Some of the game concepts aren't clear when you first begin playing; for instance how far you should place cities to maximize land use, or how terrain affects the borders of your cities.  Not all is lost, however, as you have the option of razing your cities to effectively move the city, though this slows down your empire's progress.
Some of the unit actions seem a bit more complicated than they need to be.  In Civ you're used to right clicking on a goody hut and everything is taken care of.  In Endless Legend you place your army next to the "goody hut" and then click on the action you wish your army to do, and then click again on the "goody hut".  This makes the task take three times as many clicks as needed and gets cumbersome after a short while.
The tech tree is interesting, though a bit light imo.  It follows the path system set by Endless Space with a few changes.  You are not limited to which tech you wish to research except by which phase of the game you're in, which they call "Age".  There are 6 seperate Tech Trees, one for each Age.  There are no paths between the techs currently, though I hope they change that, and it is not quite clear how to advance to the next age.  It just sort of happens as you play.
The units do not feel complete or unique yet.  They have different animations and icons, but I have yet to see a reason to bring along a support type unit with an army instead of all infantry or ranged, besides terrain.  Which leads to the next thing I'd like to talk about.  When you initiate combat the camera pans out a bit and uses the terrain of the world map as the battle field, with both height and types of terrain that affect how units move about the fight.  You can place the units initially, but after the fight starts you have no more control.  This makes ranged units very powerful, as you can place one on a cliff and it will plink away at a melee unit while it travels around the hexagon to reach the ranged unit.
Overall I do reccomend the game for fans of Endless Space and Civilization type games.  If micromanaging units is a must, stay away.

It’s been years since I’ve enjoyed a game this much! I don’t see myself getting bored any time soon. It’s like the Harvest Moon online that I always dreamed of. Between farming, fishing, building, lockpicking, crafting, levelling, always being in need of resources, and always needing to find food to eat, I find my attention pulled constantly in different directions, and always having 10 things on my list that I need to get done as I build my base and level my character. To me, that’s the mark of a well-thought out game. Plus the stealing, plundering, and pvp elements of the game add an element of danger that motivates you to keep on fortifying those walls and securing your base.
With the latest patch, many pvp’ers are complaining that the game punishes them too severely (by instituting skill loss depending on your criminal level), but I personally think the developers have done a nice job of allowing pvp and theft while yet keeping the game from being an endless griefer fest.

If you’re looking for a hardcore pvp game, this probably isn’t it (just look at the visuals!). This is more of a grindy survival sandbox. I’d compare it to the old Runescape, but without quests and with more survival elements. Some people have said the game is not solo friendly, but I have been playing solo and am doing just fine so far. Love it!

I say this in a partially joking manner, but i do actually agree with this. Enough of that though, i`d say this game is very good for what it is, and in general, for a few reasons.
First, this game has a ton of content. Its based from like 12 planets, with maybe 15 - 20 missions per planet, that you trace along following different story missions and quests. Its expansive enough as is, but then there`s the idea of doing things like gaining new weapons and frames, which requires exploring and following new quest lines. Theres alerts and new battles daily, and even a 4v4 arena mode for those that want it. Now, there`s even a free roam map that adds even more hours that you can spend in this game. Its one of the biggest games ive seen, which is quite a statement for a free game.
The gameplay is stellar, probably the best part. The idea is that of a 3rd person shooter, mixed with these hack and slash melee weapons, performed by ninjas, in space, and it`s just pure fun. You can play as you wish, running into the fray with a hammer and smashing your enemies to pieces, having a team based tactical shootout, or sneaking past enemies like you were never there at all, it supports so many styles. This is furthered by getting other warframes with unique abilities to invent new ways to get at your goals, and an intriguing mod system that allows you to alter your frame even more. It`s got a lovely parkour system as well, turning the whole game into a playground. It seems built just for fun, because it is.
The lore as well, for those that enjoy a good story, is decent. Its hard to track at some points, but intriguing and unique. Ill dive into it further with more hours.
On a side note, im writing this as i have 13.2 hrs on record. I would like to inform everyone that i am mainly a xbox player, so my time here is ill informed. I probably have a hundred easy right now, and like i said i havent even beaten through what you could consider the "main story" yet.
The game does have negatives, as do all video games. I believe it lacks direction, as i didnt even fully understand how mod polarities worked until a month ago. It has some janky hitboxes, and i find it a little difficult to gain headhots sometimes. Theres also quite a bit of grind if you wish to gain certain items and complete certain quests, but i enjoy grinding so its not a big deal to me.
All in all, with the excellent gameplay that extends for hours to days on end, constantly expanding and changing, with amazing gameplay and exciting multiplayer coop, i can`t believe this game is free.

Oblivion is a beautiful open-world fantasy role playing game, one part atmospheric walking simulator, and one part a hero's journey that you can play with extraordinary freedom. Awesomenauts is a platformer MOBA where the objective of the game is to destroy your enemy's drill core. You do this by assembling a team of 3 players to kill heroes, break turrets and hit the enemy drill core. Each game lasts no more than 10-30 minutes. The game looked fun and was fun to play the first few times but the thrill dies off. It is not a traditional MOBA like Dota2 or League of Legends, so expect less strategy and more "shootiness".
Gameplay-wise, you choose from an assortment of heroes, each with their unique play style. However, they tend to fall into 2 major categories, melee and range. You go around killing droids and heroes to collect Solar and spend them on upgrades to improve your hero. Each hero you kill gives you 30 Solar and each droid gives 5 Solar. If you run around picking up the white cubes, you can get an additional 1 Solar per white cube. Each hero has some special movement ability which can range from flying in the air, levitation, high jumping or double jumping.
Conclusion, I was an early supporter for the way Ronmino decided to make it buy-to-play. However, I am disappointed by their decision to go Free To Play and resort to the Pay To Win procedure. Many heroes are locked behind the paywall and the early supporters get a major ♥♥♥♥ you with the most common reason given as, "Why the ♥♥♥♥ should Ronmino give early supporters the heroes?".
October 2017 : I am very disappointed with the way Awesomenauts played out. After supporting it as a buy-to-play game, Ronmino decided to do a 180 degree ♥♥♥♥ you to their original supporters and made the game free to play. However, in doing so, they added 12 characters that cost $5.50-$6.50 per character to play. This is not what I signed up to support and that's why I'm giving them the negative review.

This is one of the few games I've purchased solely based on hype.  I never knew of this series prior to hearing about the amazing reception this game received.  I have not been disappointed.  It's not perfect, but some of its flaws stick out simply because it shines with the quality of any big budget release which makes it easy to forget Larian stuck to the type of game big publishers didn't want to see.  Rather than change their game into an action RPG they stuck with what they wanted to make, and that is an amazing thing to see.
The game is not perfect.  Steam Cloud in particular tends to cause several moments of severe lag after saving once there are a lot of save files.  The inventory system could use some major improvements as well to allow dealing with multiple items at once. The controller mode also lacks some of the options available for the keyboard and mouse, and in order to switch modes the player has to exit all the way to the title screen, which due to the very limited inventory interface in controller mode I find it worth doing when sorting through tons of loot to sell.  More on a neutral point, the game expects the player to know the mechanics which may make the beginning portion of the game extremely punishingly difficult depending on which classes are chosen.
There are some things that may catch players off guard if they are unfamiliar with games like this, as I was.  It's important to realize there is no such thing as "grinding" in this game and that all resources are finite and that each and every encounter is relevant to some quest or another.  There is more enough experience and cash to complete the game (especially if the player resorts to thievery), but there is no such thing as grinding encounters for money and experience.  As such, there is no such thing as a "side quest" and the player is expected to thoroughly explore the world.  Each and every player level counts, especially when higher in level, and gear stats inflate very quickly.  Most status effects do not apply until the related type of armor (magical or physical) is gone, so taking advantage of that and checking which type of armor is weaker is essential if playing a team that can deal both types of damage.  Positioning is critical and the player absolutely must know how to break the team apart and position them prior to battle.  There is so much freedom in this that it's possible to trivialize many if not most encounters if you want to play particularly dirty.  That isn't a negative thing in my opinion, but it's important to keep in mind if something seems like a brick wall.  They player absolutely should remember that there are robust saving options, including increasing the number of quicksave and autosave slots.  The game gives incredible freedom, and choosing what to say or what to do may have significant consequences.  In many cases if one character burns bridges with an NPC another character can try talking instead, but in other cases saying the wrong thing will have dire consequences.
Overall I think the game is amazing and it's easily one of my favorites now.  I love how much freedom the player has and how wildly different events can unfold depending on what the player says or does.  One thing I often forget about is the narrator, who I think does an amazing job.  Once I got the hang of the battle system it became one of my favorites.  The way armor works in this game is very different, but I think it's a creative approach and it ceased to be frustrating once I learned to best make use of my party.  It's possible to min/max one type of damage to get around the armor system, but it's not necessary to do so as long as the player constantly pays attention and examines foes before deciding a plan of action in battle.
It may seem too difficult at first, but it simply has a high learning curve and once the systems are understood and the player knows the game will let you run off to places you aren't yet ready for it's not nearly as punishing as it may seem at first, in my opinion.
I am dozens of hours in and not even half way through the game yet.  I'm sure not every player need dilly dally as much as I have, but the game has exceeded my expectations.  There are some quest glitches but that goes hand in hand with any RPG that presents so much choice, and the game is still being patched (though it is not unfinished).  It's easy for me to forget Larian didn't have a gargantuan publisher helping to fund the game.  I highly recommend the game.

Honestly, used to be wary of any and all turn-based combat games. I tried Dragon-Age Inquisition and Origin and came out with a bad experience with both. With this game, The insane amount of freedom in being able to grab almost any item and think outside of the box to accomplish the same task took me by pleasant surprise. And the In-depth combat that made me think about every possiblity of action possible where life and death felt real at any moment if I took the wrong action. Even the possibility to escape if I felt I was getting in over my head was such an alien thought to me that I don't ever remember taking that option until it was too late. Of course I learned the hard way about the autosave feature, but I hope to do a run through with this game where I don't use it at all, and that prospect actually has me excited for my next playthrough to discover what else is hidden in the land of Rivellon.
In short, being someone who normally stays away from turn-based rpg games, I whole-heartedly recommend this game to anyone who's willing to try story-based rpgs who wants a taste of a deep combat system with a truer sense of choice, and some good surprises, along with some laughs and curses along the way.

There isn't much to Mount your Friends. It's a quirky competitive game where you use physics and sticky hands and feet to climb and fling yourself to the top of the tower made up of all the other players. Every player mounting the tower makes it taller until eventually someone wins. It's really simple, well polished, but really fun to play with friends.
Solo content is available but it's not too interesting and without enemy AI, it's mostly challenges such as climb one of several given obstacle courses. Multiplayer is the preferred choice if you can grab some friends to play with. You'll be hard pressed at times to find anyone else hosting a public game. Customization is also an option, you can use some of the preset stuff to customize your team or import your own images for the body and head. This is a really cool feature that me and my friends have been abusing to import ridiculous looking characters into our game. The downside is they don't work in multiplayer, only you can see them unless you share the exact same picture with everyone else you're playing with. I'm hoping the devs patch something in to fix this but until then, the best solution is packing everything all your friends are using into a zip file on dropbox and just pass it around to all your friends.
Multiplayer has 2 Gameplay modes and 2 Variable Weather Effects that change the gameplay. Vertical climb is a simple climb to the top of the growing tower of friends. Horizontal is the same but the tower must extend to the right of the screen instead of the top. These two games modes are accompanied by Space and Storm weather effects which change the physics somewhat to challenge you. Space gives you low gravity, which makes jumping and flinging yourself around easier, but also more dangerous. Flinging yourself too far on Horizontal can lead to falling into the pit below and instantly losing, while in Vertical, you can accidentally fling yourself off the tower which spells doom for most situation. Storm halts your progress by always pushing you to the left in a windy storm. This makes it hard for everyone to move or climb and flinging yourself is a lot harder.
Overall it's quick and easy fun, you can kill time playing it or have a game night with friends, flinging off of Bill Nye in a Bra to achieve your victory. While the Single player content is lacklustre, Multiplayer is fun and worth the money if you have friends to play it with.
At £4 it's an easy purchase, unless you really need that £3.99 Whopper Meal.

The game says it's "skill based" combat. It's not. If it were, the combat would make sense more than 90% of the time. It doesn't.
Pros: Swords and stuff
Cons:
The weapon stats are completely wrong. The reach stat is irrelevant, since you can abuse the game mechanics and over reach a spear with a short sword. The speed stat is completely wrong, as several weapons with the same speed are not at all the same speed once you use them, see all weapons for Knight and Vanguard. The damage stat is irrelevant because the only mechanic that matters in combat is the block mechanic.
Archers can headshot you and because of the block mechanic, still go toe to toe with you in a 1v1 weilding a dagger because plate armor, a shield, and a long sword are nothing if that dagger "blocks" even the tip of your sword. At no point does armor, shields, armor type, weapon size, or weapon speed matter so long as you click block at the right moment.
The health difference between chain mail and plate armor is almost nonexistent, but the speed difference is insane.
A war hammer the size of a large child can be deflected by a dagger.
The "footwork" mechanics are not footwork. People spin 360 degrees and insta kill you with what long term players call "footwork", but on your screen they won't be looking at you, and their sword won't even be by you.
Team modes suck, everyone team kills, and has no idea they can't do wide swings that deal damage equally to friends and foes when surrounded by friends.
You're told in the first part of the tutorial you can bypass sheilds on the side, but 99% of the time when you swing behind the shield and onto the guy, he gets a block and free stab onto your flank.
Past the low level servers, it's all vets that play and I have yet to get into a game that isn't block spam and 360 degree spin kills. If you bring this up in the chat, they kick you.
I would not buy this game again, even for $5. You shouldn't buy this game. The weapons make no sense, the combat makes so sense, weight and speed in combat are irrelevant, momentum is irrelevant, armor type and thickness is irrelevant, attack type is largely irrelevant, and there is only one good game mode.  Waste of money, waste of time.

Run or Die is a fast paced Endless Runner that focuses on movement based abilities (and a huge Ion Cannon)! Players must make decisions in the blink of an eye in order to make their way through a hazardous city environment where every run is different!
‘Run or Die’ features simple mechanics, but ones that ultimately reward timing, trial and error, and replaying. It’s more a game of memory and reaction, rather than overall skill. I can personally see the appeal of such an endless runner, but I was hoping for something deeper.
: The skill system is slightly lackluster and the small amount of abilities limits the gameplay for me, but it works for the concept.
: 6/10
The controls for ‘Run or Die’ are…odd. The main issue is that at different moments in the game the controls will change along with your abilities, making you have to adjust to a different scheme for two buttons. It doesn’t sound like much, but the change is jarring for a fast-paced game.
: Simple, but oddly set up and the changes in-game add a needless amount of difficulty.
: 5/10
‘Run or Die’ thankfully offers a nice soundtrack that accentuates the game well, and it’s probably my favourite part of the game. It’s something we’ve all heard, but it’s much better than most games.
: Not terribly original, but fitting and of above-average quality.
: 8.5/10
As was stated above, the difficulty in the game comes from the odd control switches and the timing with things, which is not my preferred way of dealing with a game’s challenge.
: A type of difficulty that appeals to a certain section of games, but isn’t very deep or extensive.
: 7/10
The game doesn’t offer any upgrade systems, currency, or anything like that. I suppose there’s a certain amount of replayability based on competing with friends or a self-interest in short-term goals, but I don’t feel like there’s enough content to justify more than a few hours of gameplay.
: Different game modes spice up a down-to-earth endless runner that provides a small amount of replay value.
: 6/10
‘Run or Die’ is a nice endless runner with a decent amount of replayability, but nothing game-changing. I found myself wanting more than just randomly generated maps, but for the price you can’t go wrong with what the game has to offer at all.
