F2P?:
I tried to get my friends playing that goofy but enjoyable game, i hate how people claim it to be "pay to win", honestly, among the wave of F2P games available on the market, this shines abit, why? Because it really isn't, while the game does offer you to pay for weapons or equipment so you can unlock the whole game at once, no bought piece is any better than the original version, something that makes the game even less F2P is the fact that you earn points for new items VERY fast, you don't even need 24 to have the majority of the huge available armory, the game simply gives you tokens and you choose what you want, you can unlock a certain playstyle or upgrades fast, also paying makes the game feel even more cheap, the fact that you bought all the items leaves you nothing to work for, i enjoyed earning tokens.
Gameplay:
Its quite simple and sometimes basic, but the huge variety of customizable gameplay styles and upgrades make up for that, the smallest things like choosing one attachment over the over will have penalties and advantages.
Unlike other free "basic" shooters, this one shines through chaos, because of the huge amount of gameplay styles and classes, you can prepared for something but not all, while the game encourages aggressive gameplay, things change when you realise that you often have to escape situations.
Also, the game has a relaxing factor, its nice to grab a beer and enjoy the chaos, no gameplay feels really predictable and you will find when starting the game getting a huge amount of surprise deaths and kills, this game rewards cunning over skill, the most ruthless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the map will usually have a much more dominating presence than the guy that is so skilled that he could headshot people that are using the kite or hook out of panic.
Community and Developers:
Terrible, the game has been abandoned by the developers, leaving the game often quite buggy and sometimes network problems (not so much present like other F2P games that have full support) and the Community itself mostly just focuses on Deathmatch despite multiple gameplay mode, none of them are really bad so i don't know how that happened.
Conclusion:
It is (or better was) a game with high potentional, the chaotic, hilarious style and gameplay makes it very enjoyable once you start getting used to the game, it does have alot of things other Developers should learn from, although the fact the Devs gave this game up does not make it as enjoyable as it could have been.

Pros:
-Graphics are clean and lacking in glitches
-Jack Keane with a beard looks kinda like one of the Beatles
-A few exciting set-pieces
-Contains four delicious banana recipies
-Depending on your choices, certain puzzles WILL change. Characters actually acknowledge the alternate order of actions.
-"What the hell? Where did I get this sponge?"
-Dream sequences are imaginative.
Cons:
-You often end up doing things and combining items without knowing why. This isn't always because the puzzles are overly obtuse but because the game routinly let's you START solving a later puzzle before you can FINISH it.
-You start to wonder why the dialog is so hard to hear during animated cutscenes.
-All characters share the same talking animations and there are only about five of them total. The characters also lack emotion both in face and sometimes in dialog.
-The running and jumping is HORRID. Simple puzzles are made infuriating by needing to jump on a box.
-Fisticufts are slow, tedious, and just boring.
-Since the camera tracks the current character, important items are sometimes well offscreen forcing you to run around hunting for them.
Overall: 3.5/10 Hilarious for how not-good and ALMOST good it is.

Even though I own both Skyrim and Oblivion, I still play Oblivion.
Pros relative to Skyrim:
- Much better writing in quest lines and dialogue.
- No overpowered mechanics - your player character possesses the same abilities your opponents have.
- More varied environments (rather than snow, Draugr dungeons, Dwemer dungeons full stop).
- Better non-combat game mechanics.
- Better spell system for mages and mage-warrior hybrids.
- Your actions have greater consequences.
- Runs at immersive 144 FPS on supported monitors/graphics cards. Skyrim cannot support this as its physics engine is framerate-dependent, while Oblivion's is not.
Cons relative to Skyrim:
- Fewer mods.
- Graphics are obviously inferior (can be improved with mods).
- Horrendous character creation system (can't really be fixed even with mods).
- Inferior melee combat system (can't be fixed with mods).
- Fewer dungeons.
- Annoying character leveling system (fixed with mods).

TL;DR --> This game should be called
. Why? Because even at full price it costs less than a junk food menu.
----------------------------------------------------------------
As a non-casual player of the genre, Run or Die caught my attention very fast, and I was sure I'd grab it when it had any sort of discount.
The game is basically what you see in the trailer: a RNG side-scroller where your main character has multiple skills to help her avoid obstacles and trying to reach the ending (is there really an end, actually? :P).
The main mode of this game is the Endless one. Contrary to many games like this one, you barely gain speed in case you're reaching further zones in the game. Instead patterns become harder to avoid and faster, more complex and more accurate reflexes are needed to keep going through.
GAME FEATURES:
- Endless Mode, Challenge Mode, Training Mode, Tutorial and a Daily Run Challenge.
- Many leaderboards, depending on the mode and the time lapse.
- Five skills to play with (Dive, Leap, Dash, Ion, EMP).
- Complete gamepad compatibility.
- Customizable controls.
Despite having a total of 5 skills, in this game you can only use 2 of them at the same time. As I said, this game is RNG, so skills are chosen randomly and you adapt yourself to them. Patterns will appear according to your skills. In case you get far enough into your run, you'll eventually reach "Safe Zones", where skills can be changed for others and further patterns will become more complex.
So that's it. This game is basically opium for those people who loves de genre and for that price it can give you a very pleasant entertainment.
PROS:
+ Controls are, as usual in these kind of games, very tight and very responsive.
+ Even though there's just 1-2 tracks, music is catchy.
+ Gets the idea of the "Just one more run..." feeling of addiction.
+ Easy to learn, challenging to master.
+ RNG element, making every run dinamically different.
+ Huge amount of patterns; when you think you've seen all of them, a new one simply appears.
+ Pixel art looks pretty cool.
+ Workshop for level editor.
CONS:
- Even though there's a training mode, complex patterns are simply impossible to practise unless you're skilled enough to reach them again in multiple runs. "Try and fail" feeling is never welcomed.
- Even though pixel art is good, the main character looks surprisingly different from the real model.
- The fact that you're always playing with only 2 skills can get extremely confusing. Some skills like "Dash" usually goes to LB (gamepad), but when it combines with "Leap" it changes to RB. Unless you're very, very focused, you can just screw everything basically because your brain just got used to another setting.
- Lack of content. The context shown in the game somehow looks very interesting, as if there was a cool storyline behind it... but then you find nothing.
- Most achievements are farm-based. Ew.
Overall, this was the kind of drug I wanted and as long as devs keep doing games like this one I'll never get tired of the genre.
: 7/10 for the game in global, 8/10 for the game in its genre

This is on the cautious side of positive, as I don't really think the game is great (the endless runner portion by itself would *probably* get a negative review from me) but I do like it in concept and there *is* a lot to like here. 4 of the 5 skills feel pretty good and polish, as do the overall controls. The level design focused around these skills is pretty good too, especially in the challenges, most of which provide a very precision-platformer kind of gameplay, not going on too long and never really asking for too high a level of precision, while also providing the optional challenge of collecting for ranks.
But then there's the negatives.
The goddamn EMP power.
What the hell? Who thought that was a good idea? It doesn't mesh at all with the other powers and the level design based around it is almost always stupid. It takes longer for it to recharge than it does for lasers to respawn; and why do they respawn at all? So often I end up dying because I used my EMP too early and thus couldn't get through the set of lasers following the set I used EMP on. I basically expect death whenever EMP comes up in Endless Mode, even with the newly added continues feature. There are also instances of this kind of cheap level design that pop up in later areas; sections where you're punished a second later for a mistake you made, instead of the expected/fair standard of instant punishment. Sometimes you just get screwed over by the moving obstacles, too; I've had instances involving them that were outright impossible to get through. Very against the nature of the game and the spirit of the genre if you ask me.
There's also one really, really stupid challenge entitled "Danger Zone" that you should never play. Who thought that taking a fast-paced runner game, slowing the pace down, and demanding precision with an inherently imprecise mechanic was a good idea? Sigh.
Overall, I did enjoy this game a decent bit and I'll probably keep playing it when I get bored, but it's not the greatest of runner games and I do wish it were a bit more polished. I've never gotten farther than the fourth zone without continues or the sixth zone with them, and I dunno if I'll ever get to the end, the way later areas seem to be designed.

To me, the endless runner genre was never that appealing.  Keep running, press different directional buttons, maybe collect a few items and weapons, and then die and repeat again.  I admit I haven't played that many in the genre but for the ones I have tried I never found them interesting enough to keep playing after a short session.  It is hard to pinpoint what I do not like about them as they usually have all of the ingredients to be good games, yet somehow Run or Die falls into the same category and manages to achieve what the others did not. It grips me and makes me want to keep playing it.
Is it the tight controls? Is it the well-designed level and how I never felt like I died an unlucky death? Maybe it is the soothing and well-paced background music that alleviates the feeling of being greeted by a Retry screen. Or maybe it is the rotation of two cool abilities during the run keeps the runs fresh all the time.  I do not know.  I am not that good at the game and have died plenty of times, but I want to keep on running.
Overall, Run or Die is a great little gem that people should try. While the Endless Runner mode is fun, the game also offers a Challenge mode (and a Steam workshop to boot for custom maps) for those looking for a static but complex level design where they can grind runs to perfection.  If there are requests I can make, one of them would be for a fleshed out story mode (part of it is introduced in the Intro).  Supposedly the story is spread out through the Endless Run, but I am not sure if I am good enough to reach the end (I know it I keep calling the game an endless runner but there is an achievement for reaching the end). Additionally, having additional Challenge maps and achievements for them would be pretty nice.  Otherwise, Run or Die is a fun and great game and well worth its price.

Tree of life is a survival RPG and multiplayer game. When I say it is a multiplayer game, I am not kidding. In order to get the most out of this game you will need some friends to play with. Tree of life is very fun and deep, but I found myself gathering the same resources over and over again just to craft needed materials to level up my skills. I would also STRONGLY recommend buying the adventure pack because you will find that your item slots fill up very quickly. You can expect to build a lot of excess junk in the game and see a lot of it filling the world. Hope you like gathering materials!
Overall, Tree of Life is a great early access game that, in some ways, feels like a completed game already. So, if you have a few friends, $20, and some times, then Tree of Life is the game for you!

Writing this review just to point out that the Key Features section of the store page for this game is almost entirely false.
"...a thrilling new point-and-click adventure in 4 acts" False. There is no indication that parts three and four will ever be complete.

"Art direction by Lorenzo Ruggiero"  True, but a third tier inker with a bog standard resume seems like stretching the truth a bit too far in order to use the Marvel/DC credit.
"...with high resolution graphics and Full HD support" False.  Low quality models, backgrounds, etc., The HD version will not run on many systems and the developer's (paraphrased) solution is "Oh well, just run standard. The only difference is full HD backgrounds" meaning that "Full HD support" is an outright lie.
"Realistic characters with hours of motion-capture animations" False.  Awkward student-level character model design and laughable "motion capture."
"Well integrated puzzles..." False.
"Animated coloured comics..." False.  Zooming in and out and panning on a still image is hardly animation.
All told, you'll have a better time reading the wonderfully florid text of the store page.  The quality of writing here is far better than the in-game text and dialogues.  It was so well written, it convinced me to buy this below average, overly-ambitious game with all the red flags of a terrible adventure experience.

This is a pretty good point-and-click game, with an interesting story that revolves around mistery and secret plots. The writing is pretty good as well, and it keeps you hooked into the story, not to mention that the environments and the puzzles are well designed. Even as someone who doesn't play a lot of point-and-click games, I found most of the puzzles to be pretty intuitive; although I must admit there were certain instances in which I had to look for a guide, as I had no idea what to do. Still, that's got more to do with me not being used to this genre, than with the puzzles being too confusing; heck, there were a few times in which I had the right idea, but didn't know how to execute it.
Talking a bit more about the writing, the dialogue is pretty good and, despite its mostly serious tone, there's a few funny moments here and there, that actually manage to feel natural. Not to mention a couple of easter eggs hidden across the game.
Well, I don't know what more to say about this. It's a short game, and, as I mentioned, I'm not an expert on this genre, but it's still pretty good in my opinion. Also, I really want to see where the story goes next, as this is part of an episodic series.

Even though I own both Skyrim and Oblivion, I still play Oblivion.
Pros relative to Skyrim:
- Much better writing in quest lines and dialogue.
- No overpowered mechanics - your player character possesses the same abilities your opponents have.
- More varied environments (rather than snow, Draugr dungeons, Dwemer dungeons full stop).
- Better non-combat game mechanics.
- Better spell system for mages and mage-warrior hybrids.
- Your actions have greater consequences.
- Runs at immersive 144 FPS on supported monitors/graphics cards. Skyrim cannot support this as its physics engine is framerate-dependent, while Oblivion's is not.
Cons relative to Skyrim:
- Fewer mods.
- Graphics are obviously inferior (can be improved with mods).
- Horrendous character creation system (can't really be fixed even with mods).
- Inferior melee combat system (can't be fixed with mods).
- Fewer dungeons.
- Annoying character leveling system (fixed with mods).

Even though Jack Keane 2: The Fire Within has some issues with its controls and features a relationship idea that isn’t fleshed out, the time you spend with Jack and his chums is no doubt enjoyable and manages to hit most of the right notes for a point-and-click game. It  moves at a steady pace without interrupting the player much with mystifying puzzles, which is helped by the fact that they can be solved without having to think up inconceivable solutions. Jack Keane 2 might not be the smashing excellence in the genre that The Walking Dead was praised for last year, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t give Jack Keane 2 a try if you like a bit of delightful comedy in your adventure games.

I love Paradox games, but, paradoxically, I hate it's DLC policy.

First off, this game is hard to get into, even with tutorial you'll need to either play around for a few hours or watch a bunch of youtube videos on how to do things properly. For instance, I tried making a duchy... I accidentaly made a guy I just waged war with into a petty king... I didn't know what I was doing.
But this game is fantastic for that, the amount of replay value in this title is insane, just look at other peoples game time. And the community is always willing to help. I'd post about a question and like 3 people would add me and stream to me telling me how to play, they are fantastic.
Now the Elephant in the room. The DLC. Is there a lot? Yes. Is it all necessary? No, by no means is it necessary. A vast majority of it is cosmetic, ruler heads and customization, unit graphics ect. That's just after you've been in tons of hours and want to see new stuff.
Than there is the big DLC, Reaper's due, Mystics and monks, ect. This is all big expansions that add in new systems, new areas ect. It's fun but not all is necessary, again check out the forums and you'll get a good idea as to what you should buy. But here's the thing that I learned, you're not just paying for the DLC, you're paying for the years of support, the major patches that come out before each big expansion.
As well, you don't need all the DLC, you might want to just start with Way of Life and the Old Gods or something, and as you understand more of the game, you buy more. It's a big investment all at once, but if you buy it as you need it/want it, than it's not too bad. This game is fantastic and is super rewarding once you learn the systems and the DLC isn't as bad as people make it out too be.
If you think you may want this game, check out Arumba's channel, he has a "Monks, mystics and mayhem" playthrough of CK2 where he walks through the basics with someone. It's useful. I love this game and look forward to spending hundreds of hours playing it.

In short this game will see you become either a manipulative puppet master or a revenge obsessed madman. Good luck.

Game has one of my favorite late game features: The Armageddon Clock. Nukes are slow to build and expensive, but can be utterly devastating. The problem is each Nuke fired reduces The Armageddon Clock by one. If the clock reaches zero everyone loses, as the world is destroyed in a nuclear firestorm and a thousand year nuclear winter.
The clock ticks ever down, and people quickly become scared to fire their nukes, lest a "defeated" player fires all their nukes and dooms everyone. A stalemate emerges.
The game then becomes centered around the late game techs Missile Shield & World Government.
Missile Shield stops people firing missiles into your territory, and each time it's researched instead of ticking down the Armageddon Clock ticks up, offering a brief chance at peace. The Missile Shield only stops people attacking you with Nukes though. Someone can still fire nukes defensibly if you try and attack into their land, or they can nuke their own land with a dozen missiles to trigger Armageddon.
Cities when attacked normally take a few minutes to be annexed by the invader. World Government makes the countdown timer instant, and also means you instantly conquer any nation if you can take their capital. The Armageddon Clock might be low, but if you can make a surprise attack on your opponents capital and take it fast enough, they won't have the chance to fire them.
However the most important thing is. When you play a massive free for all game always play with open diplomacy. Because at the end, there is a chance that the Armageddon Clock will lead to such a stalemate of MAD, the only solution is for everyone to ally up and have peace.

Do you like programming?

Do you like low-level programming?

I love Paradox games, but, paradoxically, I hate it's DLC policy.

First off, this game is hard to get into, even with tutorial you'll need to either play around for a few hours or watch a bunch of youtube videos on how to do things properly. For instance, I tried making a duchy... I accidentaly made a guy I just waged war with into a petty king... I didn't know what I was doing.
But this game is fantastic for that, the amount of replay value in this title is insane, just look at other peoples game time. And the community is always willing to help. I'd post about a question and like 3 people would add me and stream to me telling me how to play, they are fantastic.
Now the Elephant in the room. The DLC. Is there a lot? Yes. Is it all necessary? No, by no means is it necessary. A vast majority of it is cosmetic, ruler heads and customization, unit graphics ect. That's just after you've been in tons of hours and want to see new stuff.
Than there is the big DLC, Reaper's due, Mystics and monks, ect. This is all big expansions that add in new systems, new areas ect. It's fun but not all is necessary, again check out the forums and you'll get a good idea as to what you should buy. But here's the thing that I learned, you're not just paying for the DLC, you're paying for the years of support, the major patches that come out before each big expansion.
As well, you don't need all the DLC, you might want to just start with Way of Life and the Old Gods or something, and as you understand more of the game, you buy more. It's a big investment all at once, but if you buy it as you need it/want it, than it's not too bad. This game is fantastic and is super rewarding once you learn the systems and the DLC isn't as bad as people make it out too be.
If you think you may want this game, check out Arumba's channel, he has a "Monks, mystics and mayhem" playthrough of CK2 where he walks through the basics with someone. It's useful. I love this game and look forward to spending hundreds of hours playing it.

The tanks and missile units will be capable of amazing range, so much so that they can shoot up to
. This needs to be fixed very quickly to ensure the player has more control over their armored units.

The core idea and gameplay of the game is great and I am excited to see this game grow and improve throughout time. I did not expect myself to be even interested in playing this game, but after around two hours, I started to enjoy it.
PROS:
~The core concept and overall gameplay of the game - Playing with friends I feel is what makes the game, however, your views may differ if you're just playing it by yourself.
~Crafting is interesting and develops very well as your skills level (there are tons of skills in this game that improve over time)
~The game world is huge and dynamic - this allows for you and your friends to find the perfect spot to gather materials and build up your town and trading posts and thrive within your group/guild. Word will spread of those who come around and destroy villages which then emphasises more teamwork to bolster your defenses to prevent destruction to all your hard work.
CONS: (This game is obviously in early access, but I feel I should point out some cons that I have noticed)
~Very unoptimized - I get an average of 22-29 fps in this game (with my 4.0GHz i7 4790, and GTX 970 @ 1504MHz  on core clock)
~Graphics aren't the greatest - this could be an issue to some, but I have faith that the game will improve greatly while still mainting the art style that is trying to be achieved.
If you and your friends are looking for a good group-oriented game to play, I would highly recommend it. I hope to see the developers continue to improve this game as it has a lot of potential.

You build a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ base somewhere. It's nice though, it's home. You might fish for food, you might kill bear, or you might find crab on the beach. From developer ebi-hime and publisher Sekai Project comes Lily of the Valley, a short visual novel with a twist. At £1.99 on the Steam store, this is relatively cheap game; after seeing all the positive reviews for it, and being a fan of ebi-hime’s other works, I had to check it out.
You play as an unknown man who, shortly after his mother’s death and funeral, meets a strange girl in the middle of the Welsh countryside. Who is she?
When I say this game is short, I mean it is short; it takes under an hour to complete with all achievements, but the story itself is phenomenal.
The art work of the game is extremely pretty and I was totally taken aback by it. Simple, but sweet, it really shows that work doesn’t have to be extremely complicated in order for it to be enjoyed. The audio was really sweet, and really helped with the story line. I’m normally not that much of a large fan of visual novels, but this one looked really promising with the reviews.

This is quite the addicting and fun game.
It requires not only good reflexes but also some quick thinking for the right action to perform to keep the run going.
I'm not the best of players, my highest score so far has been in the 1400ish kimos but with every death I seem to learn something. I know exactly why I died, what I could have done to avoid that death, like slowing down, or using the skills in a certain way and this made every death not feel frustrating at all but instead a way to try and become better.
Speaking about the game itself, it's like Speed the movie, only on foot. You have to keep running, you can't stop or you die. If you hit a wall you die. So it's imperative to use the 2 skills the game gives you to avoid every obstacle and keep running.
While I liked the random nature of the skills given in endless run, which get shuffled at every safe zone, I liked more the fixed nature of the challenge mode.
Challenge mode has you try to recover a certain amount of discs while making your way to the end of the level. The skills given in challenge mode are fixed, so learning the level and where and how to use those skills to grab all the discs made it feel a bit like a puzzle game to me. Executing the plan to perfection to get all the discs on the first of the easy levels made me feel quite accomplished, all the while making me think how much better I'll have to become since it was just an easy level.
I think that anyone looking for a challenging but fair game should give this one a chance, because the gameplay feels fun , challenging but not frustrating, where failure helps in learning more about the game and becoming better at it.

I posted a pre-game review to get the 8-slot DLC backpack, which I guess was worth it, but since I had no game experience then, I scrapped it and decided to rewrite it. Anyways...
Tree of Life is kind of fun, in the same way that Rust or other sociopathic sandboxes are. The major problem is the shortage of land between the three servers (America, EU, and Asia). Most if not all good land is taken. If you find a spot, it is probably for good reason: monster spawns that will destroy your stuff; it's near a raiding guild; the invisible grid for structure placement is awkward (such as in tight valleys or tops of mountains).
While the map is huge, I kid you not, you can't go anywhere without seeing a giant walled fortress or someone's abandoned settlement (most likely because they played, logged off, and moved on to another game). With the travel time increasing the frustration of staking out your own claim, you will soon realize that this game is not what it's cracked up to be.
Crafting is not so bad, but the truth is that for each major skill specialization, there's a structure for that, probably a building. Okay, how big? 4x4 square area. When you start to realize that you need multiple buildings to advance, you quickly realize this is not meant to be a solo venture like Minecraft or Rust. Everything takes a LOT of room. I have seen entire fortresses belonging to one person. I would prefer crafting benches instead of buildings (because let's face it, you don't need an entire building to sew something together or cut some wood into lumber).
Other issues like red players (those that have killed other players, stolen, or griefed structures) are not your biggest problem unless they are raiding you. A lot will complain, but honestly I haven't encountered too many and was able to run from all of them. There reportedly is a hacker on the EU server, but only report so far.
PROS:
+ Fun to build your own fortress
+ Crafting recipes themselves aren't too bad
+ Mobs are pretty easy and food is super easy to find (punch trees for apples, cook them in a fire)
+ If you liked punching trees in Minecraft, you're gonna have a blast
CONS:
- There is not a lot of room to build considering the player count vs map size
- Many abandoned and/or raided settlements consume valuable real estate
- The crafting system relies heavily on large stationary structures
- Red players (as it stands as of the write of this review) can become a large problem if you live too close to them
- The graphics are sub-par and character models look like they were whipped up in a matter of minutes
- The day/night cycle is not well balanced (days and nights are about the same, feels like spring/fall equinox)
Rating (as of today): 5/10
TL;DR: If you are looking to get this game, just be forewarned: it is Early Access, so you can only expect so much. It has a lot of potential, but still has a long way to go before it can compete with other sandbox MMOs. As it stands, I can't recommend it.

I've never felt so alone playing an online game.
So why are there so many positive reviews?
Because the developers gave permanent extra inventory slots and a hair style to the people that wrote a positive review.
The game is in Early Acces. With it comes the usual crappy client issues like unexplained fps drops, screen tearing, client crashes, but that's the least of your worries.
I really wanted to like the game, but I'm afraid it's very dull, featureless, boring, repetative, flawed and most importantly - time consuming.
Let's start with the major flaws:
There is no party chat or global chat or guild chat. Wait! There is no party in the game. The sole guild feature in the game is that you can use your guild members' buildings if they put a guild lock on it. So where are your friends in the world? Ask them on Skype or Teamspeak, cuz there is no other way to find out. So for an online game, it's amazing how antisocial this game is, and how hard it is to play with others. And make no mistake. This is NOT a game you can solo, unless you play like 70 hours for the first 4-5 days, and at least 3 hours every day after that.
Night and day follow each other in quick succession. Night time is so dark, that you literally can't see anything. I'm not joking. It's pitch black. Seriously. Black. This means that you either spend LOTS of resources on lightning (which is very dumb) or you limit yourself to tasks that don't require moving or seeing (standing 10 minutes crafting, harvesting lumber or stone). If you try to do anything else then you'll be GREATLY penalized.
Traveling is superslow, superboring, superblehI'lljustaltf4.
But you'll need to travel, because certain resources like "lava sculpture" (red ore) or corn or whatever is not found in your home biome. Let me translate:
You want to get lava? Push WWWWW for 10 minutes. Look at a completely black screen (night) for 10 minutes. Do some mining, then head back and push the same boring WWWWW for 20 minutes, and stare at a completely black screen for 10 minutes. As there is no fast travel.
It took us about 80 manhours to build a base that can put up a small defense. Which means it has 1 of each type of buildings, 6 storage buildings, a wooden wall, and about 14 mark2 towers.
80.
Hours.
Without a base you can't do anything, cuz crafting is dependent on crafting buildings, and storage space, so no fort = no buildings = no anything.
Each night (every 10 minutes) zombies and skeletons will spawn and chip away at your walls. It takes about 5-10 minutes for 1 of these creatures to chip away at your walls. A tower kills them in about 10-15 arrows. Our base has to fend off about 4 mobs each night. So 15arrowpermob * 4mobpernight * 72 nights a day means you'll need about 4300 arrows a day. Those will have to be crafted by a carpenter. Someone will have to collect those mats. 20 arrow = 1 copper 1 lumber 1 feather. So you'll have to craft this recipe about 200 times a day. Just crafting all that♥♥♥♥♥♥requires you to sit at the crafting bench for 20 minutes, and crafting the lumber will take about 10 additional minutes, and that's the easy part! You have to collect these resources first, and that will take at least 2 manhours. You also need to repair the damaged buildings with coins. Certain monsters drop coins, and it will take about 10 minutes of beating up kobolds and skeletons and♥♥♥♥♥♥to have enough to fix your buildings.
So all in all, your completely minimalistic base spends about 3 hours a day just to defend itself from monsters at night with a high success rate.
And that's only if RNGesus didn't spawn the monsters in an uneven way.
And that's only if players didn't grief you. We were griefed every few hours. And you will be too! We went for a 20 minute break on the first day. Base got destroyed. We went to sleep on the first day. Half the base was destroyed. We went to sleep on the 2nd day. All our buildings were lockpicked. The arrows were stolen from our towers, so much of what the players didn't take or destroy was destroyed by monsters entering the disarmed base.
But the best thing is:
If you don't repair the base each day. Don't restock your arrows every 24 hours then your base will be leveled in 1 day, and you'll lose the time put into your lost items and buildings.
Let me rephrase that:
THERE IS NO POINT IN PLAYING THIS GAME, UNLESS YOU ARE WILLING TO SPEND AT LEAST THREE HOURS A DAY ON JUST FORT MAINTENANCE.
And even if you do. Some player might just decide to destroy your whole base for fun. He can do that naked with his fists if he wants to.
But why would you want to play this game? It has virtually nothing to offer besides building a base and crafting.
Combat is really annoying and boring. Targeting is hard. You'll often end up hitting your buddy instead of the monster you are trying to hit. Trying to hit moving enemy players is hard, and not fun. There are no combat skills. So combat is basically clicking left button over and over again.
Fighting monsters is boring. There aren't many of them either. Again: you are just spamming 1 button the whole fight.
The world is dull too. Lack of landmarks or scenery or points of interest or variety.
PvP is pretty much nonexistent except for griefing. You know why? Cuz it's boring, tedius, not rewarding, pointless.
Oh wait. There IS PvP in the game! In the form of griefing. This game is a griefers paradise. Through a long array of game design flaws and exploits people will destroy your base, and get away unpunished.
Your weakass useless defense towers don't attack if they grief in certain ways:
-They can harvest your crops
-They can kill your animals
-They can destroy your farmlands
-They can destroy your workbenches, fire pits, planning tables, cooking tables and a few other things.
When they destroy other buildings or kill you they will become "red" for a few minutes, and your towers will attack them, but it's so supereasy to tank/bandage towers and lockpick them and take out your arrows, or just facetank the arrows until they are depleted and the towers will stop firing.
Long story short, anyone can EASILY break into your base if they want to grief you. We played for 4 days, and we encountered griefers every few hours. I estimate that about 10-15% of our time was spent on gathering resources that the griefers destroyed or took.
The game is FULL of griefers!
I could go on for a long while about how...
The game was probably literally translated by Google translate. I'm not even joking.
Pair this with the fact that item decriptions are pretty bad or miswired (Egg says it's rotten meat, and so on).
Character costumization doesn't exist.
... and so on, but just save yourself from this game.
We scouted the surrounding areas, and about 95% of all bases on the world are abandoned wrecks, so, like us, most players get annoyed by the dull and frustrating game experience and just leave.

This is another instant classic from ebihimes, who has quickly become one of my favorite visual novel authors.  Although it is short (about 1.5- 2 hours depending on reading pace), it is particularly thought provoking and should leave a lasting impression. Aside from the eerily uncanny resemblance between the protagonist’s life and my own (I sent my mother a message warning her to avoid bran muffins), it was rather easy to get immersed in the story.
Lily in the Valley has a much different atmosphere than most visual novels found on Steam. This is one of the features found in several of ebihimes works which make them so refreshing, despite their morbid or morose themes. There is none of the boilerplate anime/VN tropes found in so many of the others. What it does have is a phenomenal non animesque art style, a non Japanese setting, a traditional theme conceived in a nontraditional manner, and refined and elegant language. It relies on powerful storytelling rather than overused cliché. It even has a fantastic soundtrack to boot. If you wanted a sample of a story which could challenge the conventional view of visual novels as being nothing but trashy anime erotic stories, this would be it. While I personally do not think those types of VN are necessarily bad, it is stories like this which give legitimacy to VN being a medium for serious story telling.
Some people seem disturbed that this game has a “kill switch”. This is true; however, trust me, it fits very well within the framework of the story. However, it is easily avoided/reversed with instructions given directly by the author. Do not let that scare you off from a wonderful story. Take a look in the Community Hub for more information.
My only problem with the story is one I have with so many of ebihimes stories. They end, far too quickly, regardless of the wordcount.  You are left wanting more, whether it be the entire world that was created within the story, or just specific characters. (I am holding out hopes for a spin off Meirin and Dee visual novel, there is so much there to work with!) I suppose in the long run that is both a pro and a con.
Overall, I’d rate this an 8.5/10. Honestly, what more can you ask for $3? I think it would be worth it even if it cost twice as much. Seriously, just go ahead and buy it, along with the rest of ebihimes works. You won’t be disappointed.

Ahh Sonic Mania. As the best rating Sonic game since the last 15 years, it has earned the title best Sonic game. But this is my personal opinion. To be fair I wasn't real all that hype for it when I say the trailers and details leading to the release, pretty much when Sonic Forces news came out. I almost stop play attention to this game completely, but I preorder this and still was waiting to play this. I grew up playing 3D Sonic Games, I first played 2D Sonic back when Sonic Generations was out and it had the game with it. I couldn't get passed Marble Zone and pretty much hated my first time, but playing more and more of the classics with a calmer soul and I found it more enjoyable. But with Sonic Mania, it's something any Sonic fan or any gamer to enjoy. Modern Sonic fans can enjoy it as much as the Classic Sonic fans, and there's one of it's highlights. Sonic Mania's Engine is an improvement of the original genesis engine the players controls the same, and added an Drop Dash to Sonic, but however it's something I feel more comfortable using in speed runs rather than regular play. The stages are outstanding, but most of them are original stages.. Out of 15 stages, 11 of them are original, and 4 are new, and pretty much the highlight of the game. I really like how the stages were redone, especially in Act 2. But the new stages are the ones that hold my interest, even Sonic Mania even have a sequel, it needs to have new original stages. Sonic Mania is something I love to play on my free time even tho the PC version has DRM; meaning that you need to be online and have wifi. This isn't a big deal for me, but there're times when my wifi is out, or I just don't want to log in to steam. Overall Sonic Mania is has alot of replay value and is a amazing game. I give it a 9/10. I recommend the PC version. despite the DRM. I still have lots of fun.

I really like Sonic Mania and strongly recommend the game as I think that it is a "must have" if you are a Sonic fan. Especially if your favourite Sonic games are those released in the early 1990s.
Ever since I first played Sonic Mania, I've really enjoyed it. Even during my first try.
Sonic is a brighter blue, and his appearance is probably similar to what he was supposed to look like in Sonic the Hedgehog (1991, 16 bit version). I also noted increased framerate. Compared to the Sonic games released in the 1990s, Sonic Mania runs a lot smoother. The characters have greatly enhanced animations.
Blue Spheres is significantly improved in Sonic Mania - The Purple and Green spheres are cool. Every time I play that mini-game, I almost always use the new version.
The soundtrack is fantastic (except for Lava Reef 2, I don't like the music used in that stage very much) and it gives me a lot of nostalgia, it revives memories when I first played Sonic the Hedgehog (1991, 16-bit version) back in 2009. The music in reused zones (Green Hill, Chemical Plant, Flying Battery, Stardust Speedway, Hydrocity, Oil Ocean and Lava Reef respectively), and the Bonus Stage (Get Blue Spheres) music is modernised in Sonic Mania and much better than what the music is in the games they appear in that were released in the 1990s.
I actually could NOT believe that the Chemical Plant 2 boss is almost the same as Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine when I first reached it. The sound effects in the Mean Bean minigame are good, but they are better in the original versions of Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine.
The Mean Bean minigame is EPIC - expert Sonic fans like me are awesome at it. I rarely lose against the computer, even on Level 5. There really should be a Level 6, because I am an "Extremely Hard" player. There also should be a statistics screen, to show how many Mean Bean games you have played, and how many of those where you have won.
I just don't know why Sonic Mania also had to have Denuvo with it. No-one told ANY Sonic fan about it until the PC edition was released. That is most likely why Sonic Mania was delayed close to the last second. (The PC (except Windows 10) edition of Minecraft also had 1.12 delayed close to the last moment.)
Seriously, is adding Denuvo to the game "optimisation?" That is literally absolute nonsense. If your computer fails the system requirements, and if it takes you 4 attempts in one day, and your computer still doesn't pass the system requirements, you WILL be behind to your first-time experience on Sonic Mania.
And the compensation? Only Sonic 1, even for free? ONLY Sonic 1?! The compensation was NOT good enough. It should have been Sonic 1 AND Sonic 2 AND Sonic 3 & Knuckles, each free of charge. I also don't know why I was also given an extra game. It was SEGA Mega Drive & Genesis Classics. The delay of the PC edition of Sonic Mania also must have made lured some Sonic fans who did NOT have an Xbox One, PlayStation 4 or Nintendo Switch to buy one of those consoles. That means 500-600 AUD down the drain, and all because of a game delayed only 4 DAYS before it was supposed to be released. The PC edition of Sonic Mania should have been released on Wednesday, August 16, 2017 AND THEN recieved a bugfix update a fortnight later.
Due to everything I mentioned in that paragraph, Denuvo better be removed from Sonic Mania IMMEDIATELY, because the method that SEGA and PagodaWest Games used to handle the Denuvo situation was INCREDIBLY DISGUSTING. Both companies need to realise their mistake, and fast, because, Denuvo is actually dangerous and is sometimes treated as malware. Believe it or not, Denuvo can actually SHORTEN the life of a Solid-state drive. (My computer has one of those.) WARNING: Sonic Forces will be protected by Denuvo. It better be banished from all Sonic games that are playable on PC, and removed from Sonic Forces, or Sonic fans could have their computer unbootable.
Sonic Mania therefore really MUST have Denuvo removed from it, before one's computer's SSD damaged or even failed. Currently, Denuvo on Sonic Mania has been cracked, but better be removed altogether, or else, SEGA and PagodaWest Games (and possibly the authors of Denuvo) will face the consequences. If one's SSD fails, they WILL lose HUNDREDS of GIGABYTES (or even a few TERABYTES) of data. If that does happen, SEGA will likely have to pay the victim hundreds or even THOUSANDS of dollars in damages, and the company may have to remove Denuvo from Sonic games altogether! (I REALLY hope they do!)
Either way, I strongly recommend Sonic Mania, and, personally, it is a "must have" if you are a Sonic fan, whether you're new to Sonic, or if you are a veteran Sonic fan like me. (I've known Sonic for at least the past 7 years and 10 months.) The game has over 10 hours of nostalgiac fun.
Two questions I have been trying to find the answer of for several months:
Will the PC edition of Sonic Forces be on the Steam Store? (Answer: Yes) And will it be compatible with Windows 7? (Answer: Yes, SP1 required)

I do like this game. I really do, but please read on for my honest review.
When I first played I accidently killed my friend trying to defend him from a bear and got flagged as a murderer. Then some random yellow name came up and murdered me in return. He doesn't get flagged. He took all the apples I got from punching trees too. I was left with a fear of other players, a few twigs and an empty stomach.
There were buildings everywhere. Buildings with stone walls, buildings with wood walls and some with no walls. Then I saw these little smoking squares on the ground and tried to pick one up. 'Trace of Evil' it said. I didn't really know what it was, but I moved on and found a little flat piece of land to call my own. Starting to build was fun. I found it really exciting. The ideas were all worked out and despite the poor translation of many item names, I managed to figure things out really easily. The controls were pretty intuitive and I liked the idea of not tab targeting enemies.
Those kobolds really hurt when you're punching at them nude.
After I got a nice little tent set up, a campfire and a couple fences my red name turned back to yellow. Feeling a bit more comfortable, I ran off and started to explore, picking up all sorts of resources and coin to help me along the way. The night time was really rough, I didn't realize there would be so many zombies and skeletons attacking my tent. When morning came around I had managed to die a couple of times and could not figure out how to repair my tent.
Another yellow name came along, he had a full set of armor and backpack and adorable cat ears. I asked him how to repair my tent and he explained to me. Of course, you hold your money in your hand to repair a broken tent. Why didn't I think of that?
I thanked the kindness of this stranger, right up until he opened my tent and proceeded to take everything I had gathered, leaving me with two stacks of twigs and the firewood in my campfire. My stomach growled.
After I realized you could make locks, I never stopped. Tinkering became my hobby and I was really enjoying the torches and lanterns it provided. I moved to a new location that had more resources, because the runs to gather copper was draining.
My new place started to get some walls up and I had cabins, it was looking pretty good. A tiny farm, a few chickens, it was great until some neighbor moved in right next door. I had asked her why she kept trying to look at my locked tents and why she kept taking my chickens. She didn't speak any english but it looked like Portuguese when she responded, I'm not sure what she said. However, her town built up faster than mine and even though I invited some friends, I never really managed to get my walls closed before the real raids started.
It only took two of them, but without armor and strong weapons we were defenseless. They moved in, destroyed our walls, our cabins our gates. Flattened our fences and worktables. Stole water from our wells (I know now you -can- lock a well) and used it to run around and murder us repeatedly. After about an hour of this, they left us alone. I repaired, managed to get another crude knife, continued to go about my daily routine, though a little shaken up.
Then they did it again, this time with  more people. We were flattened in thirty seconds, murdered in less that and they proceeded to stick around and wait for us to respawn over and over again, scouring the woods and seeking us out to murder us some more for hours longer. I finally just logged out.
The next day, I went in to realize that there were traces of evil everywhere. The portuguese speaking woman had her base leveled and so did everyone else we could see.
Decided to move again.
After we moved, we had a great time. Skills were going up, we were trading, selling, making new friends. I had no problems with anyone but a few random rednames who tried to steal. Copper was harder to come by, but it was okay, I didn't mind spending over an hour to get an inventory full. I gave to the new players, helped my neighbors by repairing their walls, defending friends against an onslaught of raiders.
Then the griefers came again. A new town, a new place and new walls with a guild hall. At first I didn't believe it. Everything was stolen from once again. My towers had no arrows, my cabins were empty and even the tree I planted to look pretty, was chopped down. What was so shocking though was, all my walls were still intact.
Did they break in and take everything but was kind enough to repair the wall after they left? The gates were all locked as well, I was at a loss.
However, each night, the same happened again. This repeated for three days. (My livestock was stolen by my "friendly" neighbors). Based loosely on the novel "In Nome di Dio" (In God's Name) by Dave Yallop published originally in 1997.  This is a four game series two of which have been released.  (Shadows of the Vatican Act 1: Greed and Shadows of the Vatican Act 2: Wrath)
Storyline: James Murphy left the priesthood in 1996 after the Vatican's investigation into his mentor's death was less then effective and the Vatican proved to be even less interested.  In present day he is a medical doctor in Chicago, IL (USA).  He has returned to Italy at the request of his friend Father Cristoforo who has urgent and vital information for him.  Before Cristoforo can impart this information to James, Cristoforo is nearly killed when he fell (or was pushed) down a flight of stairs.  In Act 1, James is trying to find out what Cristoforo wanted to tell him by following the clues Cristoforo left for him.
Gameplay: Classic type point and game with a strong linear storyline.  The space bar brings up small magnifying glasses for search areas or areas of interest.  Since it is based on a book the storyline follows the plot of the book, and dialogue is essential to follow the story.
Despite the 3D graphics most of the game has, the cutscenes are drawn comic book panels.  This in no way detracts from the gameplay and a simple picture or two progresses the gameplay quickly and concisely.
There is only one actual puzzle, a maze more concisely, in this game.  It is a car chase!
Mystery, intrique, greed, deception and quite possibly murder, what more could anyone want from a thriller?

Looking into TIS-100 for two hours, and it's pretty obvious what kind of game it is and what to expect from it.
Foremost, its obviously trying to inspire that retro-hardship software development was in the past, and this is another one that gets close to hitting the old software terminal nostaglia. An interesting idea is introducing a basic cross-platform assembly syntax, despite being more limited then assembly. Where in assembly you have a few registeries you can interact with and you're responsible for all the memory you mess with, here you get one accessable registry to save and read from, and one inaccessable one you can save and swap to. That's per node (ignoring the stack nodes), which is a limited interface that represents seperated code execution.
For the less tech inclined, this means the puzzles are about using limited resources to design a solution, and the game's mechanics only really get an addition once as far as I see, (I'm unsure but there might be graphical problems too) and it has to be a robust one, a hacked together one designed for the current input you see would fail the testing system. I'm less inclined to call it problem solving game so far because the solutions do appear to have an optimal design, and while technically you're scope of design is close enough to unlimited to qualify for problem solving and there is no strictly garunteed optimal design in that way, the solutions are most times going to only have one optimal design and then strictly less optimal design. But that's ignorable unless you're a 100% obessesive completionist, to most it will be more akin to programming style problem solving. For those who aren't software developers or into lower level code, this game will have a higher learning curve, and having no skills in programming at all, I'd definitely think its a extremely steep cliff, this game does not really guide you and has no tutorial, you're using a reference manual the whole time to deduce the purpose of everything. For those of us used to code documentation, its a quick 5 or less minutes to get started, for everyone else, it will most definitely be longer then 15 to get setup.
And for everything else:
The puzzles are pretty deep for only having three different types of interfaces. (one of which just discards values)
You get stack machines later, where you can push values to the top and take values off the top. Would've been nice to have seen other types of IO interfaces in the game, but the current concept has a nice simplistic idea. And I suppose is easy to wrap your head around
There is the ability to mess with pixels in the executing code, so you can draw small images.
You can create your own puzzles however it only has you designating input values, output values, and the layout of interfaces, nothing specifically new can be added. Though you can pretty easily share the puzzles around.
You can mess with a no objective sandbox where you can input values and get output values, though you have to get through a good few puzzles to get anything interesting.
There is also the ability to copy programs if you did something like say create a basic start framework.
Other then that, the game is very simple and in my opinion is definitely worth the seven bucks, and would be nice to be expanded upon much further in the future somehow. (It likely won't but it definitely is an idea that could be taken much further.

I was really into art as a child, but my interest in it faded as I came up against the limits of my talents. Shapes came naturally to me, while colors very much did not. Langoth feels like a game crafted by someone untalented with colors OR shapes, someone lacking the most basic understanding of palettes or lighting or level design. There’s an alarming lack of artistry in a game that appears to hinge heavily on it, enough to put me off after a scant sixteen minutes of floaty platforming and confusing roaming.
The store page is quick to inform you that Langoth is old English for the feeling you get when you experience paradise and then lose it. I also remember the last time I had Krispy Kreme but this isn’t about donuts, it’s about a digital world that’s been corrupted and set to be rebooted. That’s bad, I guess, because you play one of two tribal TRON rejects out to restore the integrity of the code and save your awkwardly-designed world from maybe becoming a better game. None of this actually comes out in the gameplay, mind you, so feel free to make up your own story to go along with the inexplicable tasks ahead of you.
An opening animation shows your character (Adam or Eve, identical save for massive melting breasts) taking some kind of prism within themselves and making it glow green. Then it points you at a giant locked door. Once given control you’re free to scamper about the grounds, picking up purple gems and scads of bombs, avoiding or killing glowing shapes that serve as monsters, and finding glowy green fountains that somehow unlock the big doors. You’ll need to do some basic platforming across the plain geometric shapes sprouting from the garish desert, sometime dodging swinging instant-kill hammers or hopping across spinning platters. Your jump is extremely floaty, and paired with the swooping camera it can be hard to aim in the right places.
If you’re looking for a point in all this, you’re not going to find it. Langoth’s first mistake is explaining absolutely nothing about the gameplay, either through tutorial messages or clever level design. It seemed to me that I needed to find the green fountains to open the doors, and that worked for the first few areas. But then I climbed across some spinning platforms to reach one and it did nothing. I couldn’t find anything in the area to open that particular door, though I’ll be the first to admit I didn’t look very hard. And that’s the second mistake, giving the player no compelling reason to forge ahead. I don’t know what I’m opening doors for, but the areas I saw were unappealing enough to discourage me from finding any more. The enemies are geometric shapes you kill by touching or pooping bombs on, the purple gems have no discernible purpose, and there are no story hooks at all to inspire exploration.
There are more than enough games on Steam that don’t aspire to much but still manage to create simple, compelling gameplay loops to offer. Langoth can’t even clear that bar, offering only a jumbled, ugly world full of unexplained gewgaws to collect on your way to somewhere else. If I’m reading the achievements right there are only three levels in the entire game, so I doubt I’m missing out on much of a journey to begin with. The achievements also say that 2.7% of owners have even loaded the game, and I can say with certainty that the other 97.3% aren’t missing out on anything at all.

Warframe, my go-to grinding game, is a complex and cooperative free to play third person shooter experience enhanced by an enormous sci-fi world that has been ever expanding since it’s beta in 2013. Digital Extremes have been constantly updating and polishing the game while adding new things every single month since it’s official “release”. Yes, it’s hella time consuming, but the good kind of consuming, it’s actually enjoyable and engaging.

As with all of my reviews, these are my own opinions and experiences; please check out other reviews too!

While Warframe has a tutorial, it is not nearly sufficient enough for the insane complexity. It teaches you basic stuff about combat and movement, and then you are basically thrown out of the nest. Sure, there is the ingame codex that tells you all kinds things but the wiki/wiki threads will always be your best friend while playing Warframe. Many aspects have to be learned and discovered by yourself which can lead to a lot of new players quitting the game early since they can’t figure out what to do or where to go. You often have to keep the wiki open in the background since there is just that much information to the game.

Digital Extremes are in my opinion one of the best developers out there. They communicate with their community and listen to feedback. But even despite that, Warframe suffers from feature creep and old additions to the game that just feel left behind. Great concepts like archwings, raids, PVP or the glorious void fall flat compared to the rest of the game since they get boring pretty fast or just feel unpolished and there haven’t been many updates to them in ages. Additionally, most weapons and mods are just weak compared to other, better versions rendering them either useless or only good if you get a good riven mod for them.

Riven mods help to counter the weapon feature creep if you would be able to get them more frequently but unfortunately you only get them from daily missions, warframes daily quests, or other players. These are weapon enhancement mods for a random weapon with random stats, dropped randomly as a reward from said missions. The chance to get one of these is already very small but then you have to get the right mod for the right weapon with the right stats. While stats can be rerolled, most rivens will end up sitting in your inventory forever unless you turn them into endo, sell them, or find a player who is willing to spend some platinum on it.

Each faction has its own tilesets which are randomly put together at the beginning of each mission making it less repetitive than it would be otherwise. Each area of the solar system is controlled by a different faction and some of them even by two while the whole galaxy seems to be at war which each other. Enemies look original and well fleshed out and there is a big variety of them present in each faction while all of them have uniquely themed bosses.

Warframe offers an overwhelming variety of enemies, locations, weapons and warframes each with their own unique style and charm. It’s easy to get lost in all this and apart from some story quests, it’s really up to the player how he wants to spend his time in this game since Warframe won’t give you any goals, you simply have to set your own, there is no real endgame. Want to be the best looking warframe? Collect all the weapons/warframes/mods? Reach the currently highest Master Rating? Create one of the biggest Clans ever? The possibilities are vast and that is what’s so captivating about this game.

Obviously, warframe is pretty grind-heavy and can feel pretty tiring at some points. Why is warframe so enjoyable though? First and foremost because of the excellent polish and design in general but also because of its fantastic movement system which features wall-running, double jumping, sliding and more that really help in making you feel like a ninja in space. The shooting is just so refined and precise while different damage and enemy types force you to switch weapons and warframes accordingly based on your next mission. Many different mission types like extermination, spy, defense, and many more ensure that no warframe is truly useless. If you should get bored with your current setup, try recommended builds for warframes and weapons or simply create your own. Augments can help a great deal with this since they can basically enhance your abilities or change how they work, resulting in a different playstyle.

Crafting is done similarly to other games where you just get everything and craft it, only in this case you have to wait several hours and for some things even one to three days, but it is fine if you keep building other stuff in the meantime so you get a chain going. Trade missing blueprints from other players or sell your duplicates to them and earn platinum, the premium currency, and use it to upgrade your maximum number of slots, buy weapons/warframes directly of the market or just get some beautiful fashion for your warframe, the business model is just great. But be aware, the number of trades per day is tied to your mastery rating.
Yes, Warframe is free to play but does that mean that this is hurting it? Not at all, since it is using a very fair business model. Almost all of the things you can buy with the premium currency, platinum, can be farmed without spending any money. Earning this premium currency is rather easy since you are able to trade almost anything with other players and platinum is no exception. Of course, buying things directly from the market is much faster but getting them without spending anything is not only cheaper but also a rewarding experience.

While Warframe certainly can’t be called high end in terms of graphics, it’s making excellent use of it’s engine and is very slick and clean looking as a result of that. However, the game wouldn’t even look half as good as it can be if one would turn down everything to the lowest settings. Shaders and reflections as well as many other little things add up to create an experience that is not only pleasing to the eye but one that can also stand up to today’s AAA games.

Because of its nature, story is mostly told through quests which there are 20 of. While a handful of them are interesting and make you want to learn more about this universe, most of them are just a series of regular missions with special voice lines and objectives tagged on to it. Sure, there are bits and pieces everywhere in Warframe’s world, but people who are craving for more lore have to utilize wikis and forums to get the whole picture.

Warframe’s soundtrack can be astonishingly good at times but being as grindy as it is, most of the songs will sadly fall short in the long term or will get boring to listen to if you hear the same ones over and over again. Otherwise the soundtrack just fits perfectly and some songs even make use of voice which fits for every situation and almost all of the different tilesets have their own songs which fit each of the different factions greatly.



Besides it’s fair free to play business model, it offers a huge variety of weapons and warframes and just everything else really but it als offers an insane amount of freedom that is rarely seen in games today. I recommend this gem to anyone who enjoys third person shooters with focus on cooperation or people who are just looking for a grindy experience to pass some time and have fun while doing it.

It's a shame really, this game is amazing but it's so broken. Yes, it's early access but the game is broken to the point that it's virtually unplayable. Single-player mission, crash, multiplayer, crash, co-op, crash, loading a map named "delta", crash. It's constantly crashing and it's extremely frustrating. Sometimes the game will crash halfway through loading. It will crash right when it gets to 100% loading completion. Sometimes it will even crash after the game has started, and that just pisses you off. Support for these crashes has been non-existant while the team continues to add content, content that half of us can't even access because WE CAN'T PLAY. Then if we get into the game itself, it's imbalanced as testicals. The GRM, which are your mock Taliban forces, suck. Plain and simple, they suck to the point that you get stomped out in multiplayer when playing as the GRM, you just get smoked by the US. A lot of times my squad will literally just stare an enemy dead in the face and get shot, THEN after I've already lost people my squad decides to engage. It's not even on "return fire" mode, it's just a broken game mechanic. One guy can wipe out an entire squad of 7, it's ridiculous. The game is amazing when it works, aside from the balancing issues. The graphics are beautiful, the gameplay is fun and competetive, and the modernization of the infantry units and vehicles are spectacular. It's just so many little problems that this game has that make it such a terrible experience. When the game progresses a bit more and becomes playable, then I will change and update my review accordingly. But as of right now, I cannot recommend purchasing this game, at least not now.
Pros: Great graphics, fun gameplay, requires REAL strategical thinking, Friendly players and community
Cons: Runs terribly on my exceptionally powerful gaming rig, constant crashing, imbalanced factions, dead player-base, no technical support.

"Shadows on the Vatican:  Act 1:  Greed" was meant to be the first entry in a series of four games.  Indications are the series was canned after the Italian release of Act 2, meaning that for most of the potential audience this is little more than a taster for a story that will never be completed.  That in itself may be enough reason to consider not buying it.  Speaking for myself -- I'm a massive adventure game fan.  Even with knowing that the series would not be going anywhere, I still bought the game and completed it.  (Honestly, because I feel like I need to play everything in the genre ...)
The controls are fairly standard -- right click to look, left click to interact and/or walk to a point on the screen.
Graphics are mediocre;  the jerky, stiff animations are especially jarring.  There are comic book panels which probably looked good originally, but they were scanned at such a low resolution that they ended up fuzzy and requiring of a fair bit of concentration to make out their contents.
English-language voice acting ranges from good to very poor (everyone is voice acted -- and that will be important for some).  The main character sounds like Charlie Sheen, consider for yourself whether that is a plus or a minus.
Puzzles are varied and inventive.  However, although I would generally consider inventiveness in puzzle design a plus, it does require a slow build-up in order to acclimatise the player -- meaning using a certain gameplay dynamic in puzzles of ever-increasing complexity -- which is something this game doesn't do.  (In other words, some will probably be stumped early on.)
The storytelling feels similarly rushed:  there is next to no world building, meaning that everything you do is an action that serves to drive the plot forward;  adventure games tend to make use of menial tasks (as components of puzzles) in order to facilitate world building and immerse the player.  This game has very little in the way of menial tasks, aside from a short tutorial, which means that you'll be thrown into a series of locations and situations which were probably interesting in the writer/designer's mind but are boring in their presentation.  For example, take me to some ancient buildings, yes, but do something like the Broken Sword games and make me appreciate that I'm visiting an ancient building.  The game is set in Rome, for crying out loud.  Rome is an interesting place.  Show me Rome!
In closing, regardless of whether I recommend this or not hardcore adventure gamers will probably buy it.  (As they should.)  For the rest, I don't see why anyone should be spending money on what is in essence the first quarter of a story that you'll never be able to finish.  The game is rather short too.  (And the poor achievement design means you'll need a guide to get 100% -- I guarantee you.)
Either way, in the name of fairness, I'm willing to alter this review to a recommendation should the missing Acts ever be completed and published on Steam.  For all its faults there's a lot of untapped potential here, and I'd love to see where this small but talented team of developers takes this series next (should they take it anywhere at all).
***
EDIT:
And here it is!  The second episode is out.
I am surprised, but pleasantly so.  For the time being I'll leave this review as is.  Once I've played through Episode II, I plan on coming back and editing it accordingly.

First off: I´ve never been into Old-School-RPGs like Baldurs Gate, but always liked good stories and characters. Additionally turn-based games have grown to me over the years (the likes of Civ5, X-COM: EU/EW, Invisible Inc.), so I thought i´ll give Divinty: Original Sin 2 a try without having played the first one.
If you can´t stand turn-based RPG/Strategy, this game (and this review =P) isn´t for you.
I´m now about 70 hours into it and i haven´t even finished my first playthrough, cause theres so much to do and discover in this world (kinda like in the Elder Scrolls games, but with a main story, that you actually care about).
Sadly it´s a bit seperated by different chapters/maps. A completly connected world would have been awesome and the icing on the cake (like the first Dark Souls in terms of level-design). But storywise the change of places makes sense, so it´s fine i guess.
The class-system is pretty much fantasy-standard (Warrior, Mage, Rogue, Archer and so on), but you can mix it in everyway you like. If you feel like it, you can try and combine everything in even one character. Or build a more traditional party setup like Tank, Mage, Warrior, Healer or something.
The combat-system is pretty solid and has some nice in-depth aspects, like certain elements, resistances, different status effects, height advantages and much more. It favours those who like to experiment and weigh different options against each other, but the the AI in the fights is nothing to sneeze at, they use all those options just like you do.
What suprised me the most was the take on the problem solving the developers added: in most RPG, you just fight and thats it, but in D:OS2 you can for example sneak past fights or talk your way out by convincing your enemy you´re on his side or just. This system is based upon a second layer of character development: not only can you boost your chars combat stats, but also their probability of winning an argument, through certain "social" stats and perks, which allow them different answers.
Which leads to my next point: the dialogs. They are all fully audible (even the best hidden side-quests, which have NOTHING to do with your mainstory), which is pretty magnificient for a game of this size and the voice-actors do a pretty good job. Usually i skip spoken dialogs when its about half finished, cause i´m a pretty quick reader, but this game actually made me listen to them almost all the time.
All in all i would recomment this game to everyone, who do enjoy experimenting with the world with also wanting a nice character/story development (for example: I want to love sandbox-games, I really WANT to, for the idea their are promoting, but without a story/charachter to follow, i just get bored after like an hour).
BUT it´s not like this game is awesomely directed in terms of presentation: the magic and the fascination of the world and its inhabitants happens in your head, like reading a good book.

Are you fond of old school Pen & Paper RPGs?
Have you enjoyed classics such as Baldur's Gate?
If either one of these questions is yes Then Devinity: Original Sin 2 THE game for you!
Nearly unrestricted character creation and development!
Those classicals roles of Warrior, Wizzard, Archer and Rogue not enough for you?

Discover a hidden rear entrance that dog told you about earlier (yes given the right choice of talents you can talk to animals)
Try pribery.
Intimidation.

Just like old fashioned Pen & Paper RPGs Initiative decides who goes first in combat, after that everyone gets their turn.
Mix spells for an even greater effect: douse someone in water and then electrocute them, or freeze them. Ignite poison or oil.

Almost a hundred hours in and nowhere near anything that resembles an end (Single and Multiplayer campaign).
What are you waiting for?

TIS-100 is a game where you get to program a parallel computing system in an assembly language syntax. The instruction set is easy to learn as there are only a handful of instructions. I won't say anything about the story in the game but each puzzle has a specification for what your program should do. You read from n inputs and write to m outputs. The output is tested in four runs to check if you wrote a program that appears to behave correctly. There's also a few sandbox modes where you can play around with stacks, put pixels on the screen and get rudimentary input from a console. Upon solving a puzzle you get score in three categories. The number of instructions you used, the number of nodes you used and the number of clock cycles it took to complete the task. You'll see a histogram of global scores to compare how you've done and friends will have their best scores listed numerically.
Some puzzles have good replayability as they are hard to optimize. Others are quite simple and serve no replayability at all. On reddit there's a listing of records in four categories. Some of them just seem insane to beat. Sure, you might have got the optimal clock cycles down, but can you reduce the number of nodes and instructions while still keeping up with the clock cycles?
Finally, there's also a possibility to write your own puzzles although there is no convenient way to share them with the world.
If there's anything I dislike with the game, well... For sandbox mode, I would really have enjoyed being able to configure so that there could be more nodes, or more instructions per node. I get it, it's about optimization and scarce resources, but it would also be fun to roam around a bit in a creative fashion. But other than that, I don't really have anything to complain about. For a programming puzzle game, it's great!
This is how you overdeliver on expectations. A massive, expansive and seemingly living world, a branching complex plot and a wonderful experience for solo and co-op players alike.

This game has a very intense learning curve, so I imagine most players will be frustrated trying to get the hang of it.  That said, if you want a nice set of optimization challenges relating to information flow, this is a fantastic game to pick up.  It also serves as a good framework for building intuition about parallelized processes in the real world.
The game is played via a very constrained programming language, on a grid of nodes which each can only hold a loop of up to 15 instructions, and two values.  Nodes run in parallel, values are passed from node to node, input is converted to output, and if you match their expected output on all 4 tests you have succeeded in that challenge.
The game has a histogram for every challenge showing the best scores across all players in each category: cycles, nodes, and instructions.  There is typically a tradeoff, to use fewer cycles to generate the output you add more instructions across more nodes, and so on.
My favorite aspect of the game is the skill ceiling.  The subreddit /r/tis100 holds leaderboards that have been updated regularly since the game's inception, and people are still finding ways to make the solutions faster, more compact or more elegant.  With such a limited set of operations, the fact that there are still tricks to find and use can come as a surprise.  But it speaks well to the design of the challenges - there is just enough complexity that obvious solutions, when they even exist, don't even turn out to be the best ones.
