For being early access, this game is amazing. I absolutely love it. Being this is my first review of a game, I'll do the common "pros and cons" list.
Pros;
- Do anything you want. Explore, hunt, fish, cook, be a tailor, build your base, fight mobs, whatever you want.
- So many things going on for being early access
- Community is fairly nice and helpful to new players
- Drives players to work together rather than kill each other
- PvP system is well balanced; Players names will turn red if they randomly kill someone or steal a players items, and if you die in the red, you drop your whole inventory
- Clothing and armor/weapons options to further customize your character
- Symplistic MMO controls.
- Decent art style
CONS;
- I HATE the unbalanced day/night cycle. It feels like daytime is too short, and night time is too long. Night can be absolutely trecherous for a new player, until you can handle the mobs.
- The destruction system; if you are logged out for more than 2 days, your base demolishes itself. You have to collect bronze coins from mobs to repair the buildings. (this is both good and bad, as if a player quits the game, their base doesnt just take up space on the map, but I feel it happens too quickly.)
- It feels impossible to find a place to start a solid base. There are massive bases in EVERY good spot, and by the time you'd catch up, you're out of room to build because 5 more bases pop up around you. This is caused by too many players on 1 map, and everyone building a distance apart. Essentially, the map feels consumed.
Overall, I feel the cons can be tweaked by the devs throughout time, and this game would be perfect. I'd highly recommend it to fans of Ultima Online, Haven and Hearth, Salem, Rust, or any sort of Survival MMOs.
9/10 (positive it will be a 11/10 soon enough)

CK2 is that game that  one game I just keep coming back for more. The concept of the game is extremely novel, being unlike anything I've ever played due to its emphasis on the individual characters of the realm, and not necessarily the realm itself. Maybe your cash flow is in the negative and enemies are ravaging the borders of the empire, but it's all good because your lustful wretch of a character just managed to successfully kill his long-standing enemy of a brother-in-law and seduce his attractive wife. It's the small character stories that really pull CK2 away from every other 4x or empire building/management game. It's one of the few games that you can play a horrible character and that's not only okay, but roleplaying him is very fun!
Generally, I despise constant micro DLCs and sadly Paradox are notorious for it. However, I fully admit CK2 is the one exception where I have been suckered into every single DLC purely because I love this game so much. The bigger DLC are usually quite satisfying and fairly priced (usually around $14) for the content included. There have definily been some swing and misses though, such as "Sunset Invasion" and even the latest "Monks and Mystics" was a bit of a let down. However, on the whole I find the DLCs agreeable. All the unit packs, etc are only worth getting if you really love the game and even then wait for the price to drop to $0.50 for them, which it often does in sales.
Oh, and the final awesome thing about Ck2 -- Like mods? The CK2 modding community is one of the best around with insanely well done total conversion mods like A Game of Thrones
, The Witcher
and Elder Scrolls
. On top of that, Steam Workshop is available for the game as well as an extensive Wiki on how to create your own mods!

the thing is that the major problem i have is with the core element of the game: the simultaneous turns. what the ♥♥♥♥. you just randomly set some orders for your units hoping it will work out against what the enemy is doing. but you dont know. maybe hes just doing something completely different. maybe you just get a lucky shot at someone. you wont know. and in the next turn you wont know again. you will never know. so you just keep on setting random orders while the enemy is doing the same and eventually the one or another will have won after 10-15 rounds.
ok of course you dont set oders completely random. you try to predict what the enemy is doing and then "react" to it at the same time. the problem is that posibillities are endless. its not like chess where you can try to predict by the limited possibilities you and your enemy can take with the different units. in frozen synapse you can just move anywhere. or just keep standing. or (with certain units) shoot anywhere. if you really want to try and predict enemy actions (you can also set orders for enemy units like you think the enemy would move - this is actually even quite a nice feature) you will take 15 or even more minutes for one single turn. There are plenty of other reviews out there including huge threads of people going back and forth on their ideas of what the game should be about. I believe they do much better of a job giving a idea of how the game is in its current state along with how I feel. Like many other people I feel that this game is a tad bit enjoyable for the social aspect along with having a interesting path to make the game really enjoyable as a PVE sandbox. The addition of NPC towns and NPC raids makes me rather hopeful that at one point the creators could even include basic open world dugeons to keep things interesting.
At this point, there really is only the bar bones in the game to waist your time on. You grind and grind the same buildings or objects to gain level while those items have very little useable value when you are making a small place for yourself. The first town I was ever a part of had dozens of stoves, campfires, work benchs, and other such buildings just cluttering up the space we had. This is slightly an okay system as later levels of crafting seems to be designed to work off one another's talents. An example is to have one person a high enough carpenter to create a blacksmith station for someone to take over making weapons and some armor. That same person or another can create the tailor station, walls, and other buildings to let people focus on speciality roles. The whole system just feels so simple while also being unique to bring communities together.
The PVE in the game is so interesting and refreshing that I have to regret that I can't give the game a good rating at this time. At this time, it seems like the majority of the game is plagued by grefers that exploit flaw and bugs to become a pain. This is why I would suggest looking through a few of the discussions that is littered all over the fourms to get an idea of the different groups and how bad they are for one another. It gets to the point that I can't even agree with the people who would rather see the game try and fix the criminal flagging system. There are still a few indiviuals that I believe have the right idea and want to see a more balanced approach, but at this moment I would hold off two months if not more before checking back on the pop/attitude that is in the game at that moment. I'm stuck with the game at the moment because of the grind that caused me to go way over the two hour limit that is on the return policy at the time. I'll just keep this one on the shelf until then and change my review if things change for the better.

I can't realy be considered a "hardcore" MOBA player. I recently started playing League of Legends and am enjoying it. But Awesomenauts is something else. It's a MOBA, yes. There are turrets, and minions and you level up over the course of a game. But the way it blends side-scrolling action shooting into the mix really makes it something more.
If you've been turned off by LoL or DOTA by the large number of items, jargon and steep learning curve, this game sucessfully removes all of that while still retaining a nice level of depth. The lower number of playable characters makes it so that it's easier to learn them all, though they really play very differently from one another. There is a level of strategy that starts as soon as character selection and building your team.
Battles are a lot of fun, and end up being decided more on your skill than your knowledge of the mechanics. While there are interesting combos to perform, and mechanics to master, skill remains the determining factor. There is a leveling system, but you seldom feel at a disadvantage for being a lower level.
That being said, the transition from the traditional MOBA stage to a 2D environment is not perfect. TIS-100 is a good programming game that provides plenty of puzzles that are both challenging and satisfying to complete.
The gameplay is relatively simple.  You're given a list of incomplete programs (puzzles) and you select whichever one you want to work on.  You're then given a set of instructions, a list providing one or more inputs, and a list showing you what the output(s) should be.  So you always know what you're trying to achieve and you know what any given input should be when it reaches the output.  The programs consist of 12 separate nodes which you can enter instructions into.  Every puzzle has 1 or more nodes that have some sort of “communication failure” message in them which simply renders that node unusable and forces you to work around them.  You also must work around the facts that: 1.  You're limited to 15 total commands per node and 2.  Commands you can enter into the nodes are intentionally not very sophisticated.  There are only 13 total commands in the game and they're broken down into 4 categories.  1.  Moving numbers from one node to another  2. Saving/Swapping memory  3. Basic math (Only add, subtract, swapping positive/negative sign) 4. Split path/jump commands (Do this set of instructions if the number is positive, do this set of instructions if the number is negative, do this set of instructions if the number is 0.)  Once you've designed your program how you like, you hit the run button and the game runs the inputs through your program until they reach the output.  If the input numbers that reach the output have been altered to match up to list that you were given at the start then you complete the program.  If there is an error somewhere, you'll have to note where the error occurs and pause your program while it's running at a point before the error.  You can then press the “Step” button which allows you to view your commands running one 'tick' at a time.  You can then use this to follow an input, see which node it enters that causes the problem, and then attempt to fix the problem.
So the game is pretty user friendly.  Pressing escape brings up the option to open up the manual for the “TIS-100” and provides you with some flavor text as though it's an actual manual for an actual machine.  It gives you a description of the nodes as well as a list of all the commands and examples of how to use them.  There's also some other info in there on stuff that will show up later in the game in puzzles such as “Stack nodes” or how to make your outputs display color.  You can also press F1 while in a program to bring up a list of all the commands and references to what they do.  The first row of 5 puzzles are mostly tutorial puzzles meant to slowly introduce you to the basic concepts.  The first puzzle is just moving numbers around, and half of it is already filled in to show you exactly how to enter commands.  The second introduces addition.  The third introduces subtraction and splitting the path of your number.  The fourth and fifth involve needing to use jump commands.  The game gets more difficult from there on out.  You will almost always have access to multiple incomplete programs, so if you ever get stuck on one, you can save your progress, quit out and work on another program.
Pros:  There are 22 puzzles in the “TIS-100 segment map” as well as 25 user created puzzles includes in the “TIS-NET directory”.  At around 20 hours of actual gameplay, I'd only completed 23/47 total puzzles, so you'll get plenty out of this game if you enjoy it.  Once you've completed a couple puzzles, remembered that F1 is your friend, and are familiar with the basic commands, the game is very simple to play.  The hard part isn't in fighting the controls but in figuring out a basic gameplan, where you screwed up, and if/how you can fix it.  It's fairly easy to track down your errors and see what's causing them.  Each program contains a node with an error message that when clicked  provides flavor text for some sort of an attempt at a plot/story.  Puzzles start out simple enough to familiarize you with the basic concepts and grow more difficult and devious from there.  Completing many of the later puzzles is very satisfying, especially when you open up one you've been having trouble with and the solution suddenly comes to you.
The cons.  There's not much here other than programming puzzles.  There's no real plot or story to the game.  The interface is pretty barebones and bland.  There aren't any characters or dialogue.  There's no music.  It would've been nice if they included a reference for the color puzzles when you press F1, but having to open up the manual to reference them isn't a big deal.
Not much more to say.  It's a good game to sit down for 30-60 minutes and rack your brain over a puzzle. If you're looking for a puzzle game with plot/story, characters, and dialogue, then you should avoid this game.  TIS-100 won't be for everyone but for those who enjoy, you'll get plenty of time out of it even if you only complete half the puzzles.  Damn you 'Sequence Sorter'.

Over the past fews months this has been in early access, some have critized this game as being essentially "Men of War: Assault Squad: Modern Assault Mod: The Game." I can see where that comes from, but I don't see it being the case. I just feel I should lend some thoughts on the game so far.
Yes, it certainly does look like the Modern Assault mod for Assault Squad 2. However, it is simply not a mod. Go here if you want to see it for yourself:

There are plenty of vehicle, weapon, and soldier assets made for the mod, but they are just not the quality you will get out of a dedicated studio. The maps and some assets are repurposed, so eastern and western European structures appear in a modern setting more often than not. Not to say that architure doesn't exist in present day. You could say that is just the theater of war for a specific battle, but a mix of original and recycled models, assets, and such can you only get you so far. Digitalmindsoft takes the great concept and presents it in full force. The mod's development is also frozen, so don't expect more content and improvements out of it any time soon.
This is a game, therefore it includes things you would expect of a game. All of the assets are professionally modelled, recorded, and maintained. A full-fledged modern campaign is in the works. It has dedicated servers, courtesy of SteamWorks. It will be featuring a secret-services themed DLC, which will be available to those who purchase the game in its early-access state, free of charge. That, on top of game engine, interface, and mechanics improvements. So on and so forth. In terms of unit count, you can expect that of Men of War games: plenty of diverse units, weapons, vehicles, equipment, and, in this case, weapon accessories. So, flashlights, lasers, silencers, and the like. You also make use of a nightvision view for when the map cycles to night. You can also host local games against AI, which was sorely lacking in previous games. That is a plus from me.
Digitalmindsoft is going out on a little limb here in publishing this game themselves, but I think they have faired well so far. They have been consistent, responsive, and rather frequent with their Dev Updates. Their 14th Dev Update was March 11th, and they have made great strides in asking the community what we want next (what vehicles, modes, etc.), implementing new graphic technologies, improving multiplayer competitivness (in terms of gamemodes, I don't care for the leveling system), releasing the missions of the campaign for testing for those who purchased the Deluxe Edition, and all around keeping us informed as to where our money is going in this critical time for the game. There has been controversy over things like the 3rd person control mode, bullet damage models, and the like, but it all seems to be leading to the betterment of the game.
Truely, with games these days often having a retail cost of $60 (RTS, FPS, etc), its, previously $20 price, now $25 price is still rather generous, if I do say so myself. And, I don't know about you, but I have always wanted a modern version of Men of War, and it grants that wish pretty well. Last time I checked (5 months ago), there wasn't a very high multiplayer population, but maybe that is because it is still in early access. That is not too detrimental for me, because you can now host local lobbies with AI, which is a good time, and I primarily play these games for the campaign. Still, some may not take very kindly to this. Nonetheless, It still maintains that unique Men of War RTS DNA, and I just think this game deserves a bit more love from the community.

Divinity: OS2 is my favorite game I have played in a long time, and there are a few reasons why.
Note: I have not played the first game, and my experience is from Classic (Normal) mode
As far as an RPG/Tactical RPG goes, D:OS2 is an absolute blast to play. Combat is challenging and rewarding, enemies are (somewhat) intelligent, and you can pretty much run any build you want if you experiment a bit. No encounter feels pointless, as there is almost always a reason behind your fight. Even if the reason is cold-blooded murder. Even outside of combat, the gameplay itself can be fun. Finding secrets and hidden treasures, a quest or dialogue line you didn't see before, or letting your thief run wild.
This is where this game really shines. It has been a long time that a game has made me crave more story, more dialogue. D:OS2 does that non-stop. I read in-game books, I talk to every NPC (especially the animals), I explore the whole map. I love this games story, its world, and most of its characters. Larian has done a great job crafting a world that feels like it existed before this game, and an even better job dropping you in it, and letting you poke about a little. You feel like your character inhabits it, and actually affects it as well. Which brings me to my next favorite thing about it.
Everything you do in this game feels like it matters. I mean, you can savescum all day. But even then, it can all go downhill in the span of one conversation, and when did you last quick save? You can screw up quests, you can miss things, you can tackle almost every objective multiple ways, and if all else fails, you can kills most anything in the game. If it doesn't kill you first. Not only that, but it feels like everyone in this game has their own agenda. Multiple quests branch over eachother and will ask you to make choices other parties may or may not like. It asks you to weigh your options, and be thorough, and is all the better for it. And finally...
All of this is just from my single-player experience. I don't have a ton of time in MP, but what I do, I've loved. After a few short sessions in some public games, some friends and I managed to start a game together. The tenuous alliance that was our party was a blast to be in. I've never had a game feel more like a session of D&D than finishing up a combat only to have everyone rush the corpses for loot, dropping Knock Downs on eachother and teleporting others away. The game also allows for
which is a ton of fun, if you aren't on the recieving end.
And we still haven't even touched the GM mode, looking forward to that.

RNG hates you.
RNG absolutely despises you.
And that seagull will wreck your day.
It's always that bird.
You think you're going to win. You're nearly home. And you end up on a red panel. And you see that bird. And it rolls a 7 for its attack.
It's always the bird.
100% Orange Juice might be totally random and it'll really be like that for a long time, before you can build real decks centered around the character you choose.
Then it's still all about randomness and RNG hating you, but a bit less than before.
The trick to building decks is to put cards that will benefit you and not the opponents because the chances of drawing your own cards is 1/4.
Oh, and what is this game about ? It's a board game. You roll a dice, advance on the board and collect stars or fight other players or mobs to get wins. At every step, you need to choose whether you want to collect a certain number of stars or get some wins. Once you do, you get on a home panel to choose the next step, which is the same but with bigger numbers. There is 5 steps (called norma in the game) to accomplish to win the game and to help you, you use cards coming from a common deck comprised of the cards every player selected before beginning a game.
Some characters are fighting oriented and some are stars-collecting oriented and some are mixed but it's up to you how you wanna play it. A fighting win with Marie Poppo is quite hard to achieve but it's quite fun to see.
By the way, don't worry about the DLCs, it's really not mandatory. You can easily do without the card packs, since as I said earlier, your chances of actually using them is 1/4 and the characters are mostly variants of the existing ones gameplay-wise : Fernet for defense, Yuki for attack, Poppo for stealing, Suguri for impressive evasions, ...

I got this on sale because I liked the principles of it and the reviews were promising. I am not dissapointed.
This game has a unique style of play. It is a turn based game where both players(or player and AI) tell their units what to do, when to do it, etc. and then the actions of every unit are done simultaneously for 5 seconds, then you go on to tailor your actions to what just unfolded, until a conclusion is reached. Units readiness for combat, range, weapons, facing, and cover are taken into account. Overall, I enjoy the gameplay mechanics and units but I wished that there was just more content in unit variety and environment. This doesn't really take away from the experience though, its still very solid in this aspect, just leaves a little to be wanted. Don't let that minor thing be the reason you dont buy this amazing game.
In FS, there's (almost)no luck involved. No frustrating percentage to hit or anything like that. The only time that it ever comes into play is when 2 units have exactly the same modifiers on them, which hardly ever happens. This means that the result you get is purely representative of your skill. There's no excuse. The game clearly shows you after a couple missions what factors affect combat and how important each one is. This unforgiving system blends well with the micromanagement of soldiers. In FS, you control a team that you tell exactly how to move. You can make them run, aim while moving, duck, wait, ignore certain enemies, and more. This amount of micromanagement seems to upset some but Its the best method of control for the battle system the game uses, and frankly feels very rewarding, knowing that your victory was becuase of your tactical competence, with no luck involved.
My only real complaint with this game is the bugs. These are by no means game breaking, but can be very annoying. For instance, me and a friend once went through the whole campaign together but were unable to play two missions because of a unficed starting position, and the inability of one level to load. Sometimes the game will crash, but this matters very little except if your life hinges on five seconds, because all actions and games are saved and easily accessed. Ultimately though, these bugs do very little to take away from the experience.
The Red DLC includes some coop options, a new unit, and more gamepla modes and music. I recommend this DLC but as with the main game, its better to get it on sale. The Riot shield is a very cool unit, allowing to enchance the lackluster grenade launcher and offer many more options for tactical flexibility.
I definitely recommend this game for strategy lovers. It is absolutely phenomenal and I am excited for FS 2. Just try to get it on sale if you can. It is a bit expensive but not ridiculously so for the content, Having a 55 mission campaign, multiplayer, and a skirmish generator with lots of different gamemodes. Also, when is TABS coming out? Seriously. halfway through summer break and its still not for sale yet.

Highly addictive puzzle game featuring a limited subset of assembly commands. If you're OCD like me, merely solving the puzzle may not be enough. There are opportunities to optimize your code and limit your cycles, insturctions used and nodes used.

A fun, challenging programming game, with some smart design decisions (e.g., code must literally fit in the boxes). There is enough story to keep things interesting without getting in the way, and enough challenge to make the 100% completion feel earned.
The sort of thinking required reminds me of Manufactoria -- interesting resource constraints give you an excuse to use horrific but strangely elegant algorithms. And, perhaps moreso than Manufactoria, progression involves discovering and refining useful primitives. The way I was using the TIS when I completed the game was decidely more elegant, quirkier, and hackier than during the first few puzzles.
For me, Spacechem felt like work, while this feels like fun.
NOTE: Like most puzzle games, my playtime reflects a lot of having the game running while doing other things.

Call to Arms' core gameplay offers what I feel is an unrivalled tactical experience. It is simultaneously cooperative, unforgiving and incredibly fun.

If you don't feel like reading, yes I recommend Call to Arms. I give it a 7/10. It's a quality game with some distinct flaws, which I reference later in the review. This review will be broken up into multiple parts, the Content List, listing the content, the Game Summary, summarizing the game, and then I'll provide a quick history lesson on Call to Arms' engine which highlights the games biggest faults. If you're a pessimist, stick to the end. Heads up before we begin, I'm no professional critic, just a dude who purchased Call to Arms over a year ago.
CONTENT LIST:
First, here's a the main content of Call to Arms:
-10 Singleplayer/Coop Missions
-23 Total Multiplayer/Battle Maps
-An indepth Map/Mission Editor, a standard of the GEM engine
-2 Factions, USA and GRM, both with many different infantry, vehicle and support units
-2 Additional (Free?) DLC Factions, Germany and Russia, coming in the future
-Complete Workshop Mod support
-A functional, but dated RTS
-A functional, but lackluster FPS capability
GAME SUMMARY
Call to Arms is a unique game, a combination of and RTS with a FPS. Not many games do this, and frankly, that may be for good reason. The game is a solid RTS experience that has been developed by an experienced team. It has AAA quality modelling with some equally impressive textures and audio. The optimization of the game is questionable, but it is no doubt a visually impressive game to play. It is also the first FPS experience designed with the GEM engine, and also the first FPS designed by the developer, digitalmindsoft. This inexperience shows as the FPS addition is no doubt the weakest part of the experience, even though it isn't exactly an integral one. When Call to Arms was first introduced in early 2016, the FPS addition was not present - so it is clear that it was not an initially planned part of the game. However, since it's addition in early 2017, digitalmindsoft has been sticking with the 1st person/3rd person direct control experience, and have made great strides in improving it. As of March 31st, 2017, a few months after the original introduction of FPS, I still have to say it is a weak experience with low quality textures, animations and incredibly choppy gameplay and control. digitalmindsoft has noted these flaws, and are soon introducing high quality textures to the weapons and soldiers - an addition that is almost required to make the FPS experience in any way competent. The FPS gameplay is enjoyable, but it's clearly the weakest part of the game. Otherwise, Call to Arms is a solid RTS. It's fun, intense and enjoyable with a surprisingly strong audio system. Still, Call to Arms is essentially Men of War with a new skin but it has some very interesting new mechanics - functional medics, air vehicles and an enhanced vehicle and infantry direct control experience - that all freshen the gameplay from previous MoW games. If you enjoyed Men of War, you will enjoy Call to Arms. The price point is certainly high, too high in my opinion, so I would suggest purchasing the game while it is on sale.
HISTORY LESSON - CALL TO ARMS BIGGEST WEAKNESS
The GEM engine powers Call to Arms and it is no doubt the greatest hinderence to the game. The GEM engine has been used for over a decade - even before the name Men of War was concieved - with the release Soldiers: Heroes of World War II being the first game to use the engine back in 2004. Sure, Call to Arms technically uses the GEM 2 Engine, but this engine was made in 2009 - and it shows. The animations are clunky and robotic, the RTS controls are archaic and force micromanagment (don't even get me started on the choppy, awkward and buggy FPS controls) and the AI is incompetent and infuriating at times. digitalmindsoft have made the best out of this engine, but I think the cracks are certainly starting to show. The game lacks the ability to toggle a unit's posture when they are not in cover, doesn't allow movement while crouching (this is a big issue for the FPS component) and the lack of autonomy by the AI is another big issue when controlling multiple units in large battles. Call to Arms survives on the GEM engine, but that's just it. It doesn't blow away the player, it doesn't innovate (the FPS ability shows some promise, but doesn't necessarily support the RTS gameplay) and it doesn't do anything drastically new. When it's firing on all cylinders, I do certainly enjoy the game, but it's not mind-blowing. I believe this lack of innovation rests solely on the GEM engine and the limitations that come along with it. It's old, and it unfortunately shows.
It is unfortunate because upon reading early plans for this game, it was intended to use Havoc, similar to Company of Heroes. However, apparently due to economic strain, those plans fell through. It's a shame, because this game IS very enjoyable, but it's clearly dated and that is important to note in the review.
To sum it up in one sentence: Call to Arms is a fun and competent RTS hybrid, but it's core engine's age certainly shows in animation, control and AI ability.

Pros:
-Tactical, turn-based combat: skills can interact with other skills other skills, and the environment is available to be modified and employed to your advantage
-Stunning visuals
-Lots of variability when custimizing your characters and party
-Origin stories add layers to the already riveting narrative
-Choices do matter, and how you build your character WILL influence dialogue, item prices, combat, and even the story
-Honestly, developing your characters and improving them through progress and hard work do feel fulfilling
-Voice lines for every bit of dialogue
-Game master options and co-op (with or without friends) are available; co-op allows for co-operation or competition between players of the party
-Multiple levels of difficulty for people with different amounts of experience
-Devs work hard to come out with updates and patches for the game
-Mod support for the game through the workshop (Any mod will disable achievements, though)
-Multiple endings
-No microtransaction nonsense; the only DLC does not influence gameplay
Cons:
-Major bugs may still exist within the game; however, the devs are working to fix these
-You can easily lose track of time with this, or you may want to keep coming back to play, so watch out
-Scripted events such as characters dying in the beginning of the game but reappearing in another section may break immersion, I guess?
To be frank, I only wrote this review for the Steam awards, so I may have rushed on this review; nevertheless, I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who can afford it. ::Disclaimer::
Unlike the hundreds of other reviews before mine, I want to publically state; I am not being paid or sponsored by anyone to write a review. Apparently, previous reviewers have been given copies of the DLC upgrade in exchange for reviews. Just wanted to put it out there, I am not one of them. I write this, because I purchased the game and I felt it important to write a review to educate and inform others of my experience.
Imagine, 7 days to die(without zombies), mixed with Minecraft(without the blocky graphics), topped off with Harvest Moon. Yep, that is Tree of Life in a nutshell. It has aspects of all three games, making it fun, addictive, and exciting. A Crafting-Survival game, or at least it should be. The game bills itself as a crafting-survival game in a multiplayer world, where you can work with others to create communities; However, Earlier notices from game developers indicated that PVP would play a small part of the overall experience, but that the game was about crafting and survival and would be largely PVE in nature. This unfortunately, does not appear to be the case with this game.
Grief of Life, or Tree of Grief as it is being billed in some online discussion threads, places you on a very large, open world island, with multiple biomes. where you are pitted against the islands inhabitants, and the strange creatures that emerge from the shadows at night. Build structures for safety as fast as you can, but beware creatures as well as other players can and will bust up your fort. The Game currently utilizes a Criminal Flagging system. Criminal flagging is earned by attacking other players and/or their structures. As a Criminal flagged red, you are unable to approach other cities or player watchtowers without automatically being attacked. Also as a criminal, anyone is free to attack you without reprecussions or negative consequences. Once a red player is killed, their backpack can be looted. Since the Criminal flag lasts a number of realtime minutes/hours, this has led to abuses of the flagging system, where neutral players camp and grief them without any reprecussions, going as far as preventing those characters from materializing after death, because they are instantly killed once they resurrect. Yellow players are neutral, and have the option to be a trolling♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or not. They can go near player encampments without being attacked, If a yellow tagged player is killed, they do not lose their belongings, but it is always best to stay cautious when around neutral players. Neutral players can also build in and around your cities, limiting where you can build. They are also capable of stealing your crops, and your livestock, as well as anything not bolted down with locks, without any sort of reprecussions. You have no way of removing them from your area, without flagging yourself as a criminal.
It is still in Alpha testing and there are some bugs, clipping issues etc,  just from the initial experience I've had playing, Tree of Life is definitely a game to look out for as a goto crafting-survival in the future, assuming they are willing to fix some of the major flaws surrounding PVP and Griefing. I saw massive potential with Tree of Life and originally intended on giving it a thumbs up review, because I saw just how much fun the game could be. Unfortunately right now, it appears the game is overrun with a segment of the gaming community who thinks the entire game should be a pvp battleground and wants to change the nature of the game. They are also willing to attack anyone off-game, who disagrees with their interpretation of how the game should be.
The development team, while initially speaking out against griefing and abusive PVP play, have since remained quiet and appear to be hedging their bets on which way they will take the game in the future. So if you are interested in playing with others on a game where cooperation is encouraged and general♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥baggery is frowned upon, this is currently not the game for you. If you are all about wallowing in a PVP Litterbox and want a game where you can free for all against other players without any serious reprecussions, even to the point of being able to play-obstruct others, in a wild west Douchefest, this game is right up your alley. Unfortuantely, If the game isn't changed to prevent player abuse, or at the very least properly labelled for the PVP Litterbox it is, there will be thousands of people very dissatisfied and disapointed with what could have been the go-to game for crafting-survival sandbox multiplayer game

Ultimately Warframe is an example of micro transactions done right. In a world where lootboxes are starting to emerge as a dominant feature in games, Warframe is one of the few prominent games in which while there is an incentive to purchasing Platinum, the game's version of paid currency, there is no requirement to actually purchase them. Platinum can be traded between players, and there is a valid market where players can trade other things for platinum from players, such as mods that are used to make your Warframes and weapons stronger, relics that are used to obtain weapons and Warframes that can't be bought directly from the game with Platinum, and other things. As far as this, the end of 2017 is concerned, this is one of if not the most important feature of Warframe, using the ability to trade Platinum to achieve anything you might need.

My one draw against this is that the AI can seem predictable or downright stupid sometimes.  But you can adjust certain settings to get it to be a little harder.  Great game, would recommend.

I don't like leaving a negative review for this game, I had alot of hope for it when I started. Unfortunately, it simply isn't fun.
First off, I've come to believe that the micro management that seems to be the game's primary selling point is excessive. Initially, I liked the idea of being able to carefully control your units' movements. But in this game, a couple of pixels' difference in where you place your unit is the difference between life and death- this game is THAT unforgiving.
Secondly, in the single player campaign, once the initial few levels are over, the AI massively spikes in difficulty- to the point where it feels like the AI is cheating.
Specifically, after a mission in which you watch a church full of civilians be gunned down (it's at a fairly early point in the game), the enemy AI started to perfectly predict my moves-  despite several attempts at the mission, I could, at most, kill two of the five enemies, with each of my units who got a kill dying shortly afterward. I'm not trying to exaggerate or make excuses for my failures- I know that I'm far from great at this game- but, from their movements, it looked like the enemy units were actually reading my move inputs for the turn and reacting accordingly. I wish I had recorded it so I could show you.
Anyway,
TL;DR While I hoped that this game would be a fun new style of turn based strategy, the tedious and unforgiving micromanagement and the massive difficulty spikes in the single player campaign have greatly disappointed me.

Awesomenauts is by far, the worst purchase I have ever made on Steam. This is not a full review of the game because I have not played nearly enough to give a complete judgement on this game, but my first experiences were very tell-tale of times I have spent with terrible games in the past
It starts out with some of the worst voice acting to ever assault my ears. To follow it up, it throws you into some shotty, slow gameplay that plays like something out of an initial alpha build of a standard game. So if you enjoy low quality and unoriginal clones, then Awesomenauts is for you.
Very fun, great multiplayer, love the charactor types.

DRM aside, this product is something that I really can't explain with words on how good it is.
GRAPHICS: The graphics feel like they belong in a Sega Saturn, which gives it a retro feel that it is pushing with this game. Everything is colourful and vibrant, and I really can't find fault with them. 10/10
AUDIO: The audio is pleasant, with a variety of tracks that classic fans would love to listen to after the 6th, or 23rd, or 1991st heavy metal or rap Modern Sonic tune. Sound effects are generally crisp and clear, too. My only complaint would be the drowning theme ends too late (meaning, the instant the last C note plays, Sonic drowns) and doesn't have a intense climax, but other than that, the audio deserves to be preserved in a time capsule of phenomenal video game OSTs. 10/10
GAMEPLAY: An exceptional reimagining of the 90s Sonic action. Run, jump, and run some more. The bosses are very complex, but by no means bad. They are generally fair in most aspects (except Chemical Plant's boss if you are terrible at puzzle games), and so are the levels. There are some frustrating points, though, like Chemical Plant Act 1's underwater block section taken from Sonic 2's Chemical Plant Act 2, however made even more annoying due to the blocks crushing you (instant life loss, even under invincibility or super state) if you're running at a high speed and no way to stop, or if you're trying to jump to a higher row of four blocks. At least there are automatic saves to help you. Bonus stages are a bit too hard for my taste.
Overall, while it may be unfair at a few points, level design was very well thought out, and bosses even more so, for a model experience on game design. 8/10.
DRM: Wrong move, Sega of Europe. If you want DRM, get a more reputable company, not this controversial one that people claim can mess up things in your game, or maybe even your computer. Though, my computer isn't affected by it for now, so I won't be too harsh on this right now.
Overall: 7.8/10. Just enough water, but too much bad DRM. Then again, there is so many good things in this game that you probably wouldn't care in the end, anyway. That's how good I find it.

When Sonic Mania was first announced, I was surprised to see myself very excited for this game. When I was young, I loved Sonic. I loved playing the Genesis games when over my aunt's house because I never owned a Genesis myself. However, after reaching my teenage years, my love for the sonic games dwindled a bit. For some reason, the old platformers weren't as fun for me. They were actually quite a hassle. So when I found myself excited for this game, it baffled me.
Something about it oozed with respect to the older entries way back in the day. I mean, I've never seen a big publisher ever revive an old style in the same style it was once in. Granted, I know this was not Sega's doing but Christian Whitehead and the gang, but Sega still gave the thumbs up and that means a lot. We had Sonic Generations which was a fanstastic game celebrating both old and new Sonic alike. But when I saw this game and how it was going to look like a slightly advanced Genesis game, I just lost it. After many years, the potential to make a really good Sonic Genesis-Styled game was at hand, giving the chance to improve some issues with the older entries.
And that's exactly what they did. Or at least 90% of it. There are still a couple things that bug me about the game, including the entirety of Lava Reef Zone and the gimmick for Hydrocity slowing the pace of the game too much. However, this is a solid staple in the franchise and it's really hard to argue with that.
I think the most impressive point to make here is while the game gives nods and easter eggs to many older Sonic games, one could enjoy this very easily even if they've never played a Sonic game before in their life. The game is more forgiving than the Genesis games, and it takes the fun part of the Genesis games (Minus the two gripes I mentioned earlier) and makes those the primary focus of the game.
Its moves like these that are risky. The Crash Bandicoot N-Sane Triolgy came out not long before this, recreating the entire three games from the PS1 era with a modern graphics edge. The game sold very well and was a huge joy to play again. Granted, they had all the levels identical to their predecessors. Sonic Mania does not do this, changing up the levels coming from old games up in fun and inventive ways. But it just goes to show that old doesn't always mean dated. I'd love to see Nintendo do something like this that ISN'T from the New Super Mario Bros. series. Going back to the time of sprites and making a challenging, fun Mario game that didn't rely on being easy to make you want to play it.
Anyway, Sonic Mania is a wonderful game for any platformer enthusiast like myself. I can't recommend this game enough. The only downside is Denuvo.. I still worry how this is in the game. If you don't already know, Denuvo is famous for a lot of issues. One of the most notorious being how they don't keep their authentication server up forever. Once they take it down for Sonic Mania, no one will ever be able to play it again. That's extraordinarily worrying. I hope that Sega removes this DRM soon, to avoid that possibility. I have nothing against DRM, but Denuvo was a horrible choice. I have high hopes that Sega will remove it in the future at least.
The game only gets a thumbs down for that. Once that DRM is removed, I can change it to a positive one. People as a crowd can make a difference compared to one on their own. Let us show our concern to make this already amazing game something people don't have to feel like they must pirate to remove Denuvo.

Absolutely fantastic Sonic game. I'd almost be willing to call it Game of the Year.
Pros
*Classic Sonic, the way it was meant to be done.
*Fantastic music; Classic, new, and remixed.
*Rehashed levels feel fresh; The first act is a mashup of all acts from the original zone, the second is totally new with new interesting gimmicks.
*Great level design with a good balance of speed and platforming, as well as multiple paths for replayability.
*Mechanics and physics have been tightened to near perfection.
*Bosses are (for the most part) fresh, entertaining, and occasionally quite challenging.
*The new special stages are a blast and a challenge.
*The completely new zones are easily the best in the game, IMO some of the best in Sonic history.
*Packed to the brim with Easter Eggs and references to all the old classic Sonics and spinoffs, as well as other Genesis greats.
*Nostalgia. Made by fans, for fans, except officially sanctioned.
Cons
*More new zones would have been nice, as I've mentioned, the few there are were easily the best zones. Only 4 new zones and 8 rehashed.
*Blue Sphere to get unlockables, but that's a personal thing lol
*Still has BS crushing deaths. Again, personal gripe.
*Some of the bosses could have been more challenging, and a couple of them are basically a joke unless you're playing as Knuckles with his shorter jump height.
*Could have been longer. It's only about as long as Sonic 3 & Knuckles without any of the hardware limitations that kept games short in the classic era.
Final Note - I find it sad that people still feel the need to bombard a great game with negative reviews just because of Denuvo. It may or may not cause issues, seeming arbitrarily, I get that. However it is now listed as containing Denuvo in the store, and people who would like to avoid the game because of it have that information available to them elsewhere. It has nothing to do with the quality of the game itself and thus has no place in reviews.
Easy 8-9/10 for anyone, 10/10 for classic Sonic fans.

A long way to go, but a lot of potential; aside from the level locking when playing unranked games, this game is definitely a good buy, should you actually get it. It being worth the money is up to the buyer's own experiences. I for one found many things which caught my eye and forced me to dollar vote for this game.
Aside from being a fan of MoWAS2, and the developers of said game, the fact that there are many different ways to put 'micromanagement' in a game is hard to say that this is truly the 'best' micromanagement RTS game there is. Instead of saying this, I will say that the attention to detail required by they player is harrowing, and every mistake could mean a mission's failure or success; however close it might be. So the first thing that drew me towards this game is its potential to be the Modern Men of War game everyone has wanted. It's innovative, detailed, and a rush when you're trying to save a fireteam from being mowed down by a technical or GRM fighter with a PKM. World in Conflict is the only other game that I ever enjoyed that had a modern (still with a fictional storyline) take on RTS combat, without being too futuristic or cartoony.
After these lengthy paragraphs, my ratings in categories that matter:
Realism: 8/10 - Not giving it a 9 or a 10 for the simple fact; even though Seals are badass, being shot ten times can kill any man.
Action: 9/10 - I definitely felt the hair on the back of my neck stand when I almost let my Stryker get blown away by a T-80, and then come back with a TOW to save the day.
Missions: 7/10 - At least the hilarious, but still annoyingly bad voice acting is done and over with (for now?), the missions allow you the ability to play as the US in different circumstances. As of right now there is no GRM campaign.
RTS: 10/10 - Being a Modern take of Men of War, it definitely deserves the highest rating here with a 10, in multiplayer games there's no pausing in the middle of action, you have to be there monitoring all of your important units, and just like past MoW games; if you don't have that infantry support for armored vehicles, you'll find your tanks and Bradley's torched.
All of these stats being laid down, the biggest issue with the game is the playability of other factions aside from the US (and if others are added which are meant to be UN or allies of the US); playing older MoW games and utilizing the Germans or Japanese during WW2 or the Germans in WW1, you still had fun playing the bad guy, but my greatest concern is how it will feel to play as a faction which is tasked with eliminating modern representations of US Soldiers. This concern only coming from a United States citizen that doesn't feel a positive feeling when playing as the GRM. While the game is progressing, I am itching to see if the addition of factions (say UK, Germany, and Russia), how will people from the respective countries feel about playing skirmishes where they turn their unit's guns towards factions representing their own militaries?
All in all, this still is a wonderful game; repeating this: a good buy in all regards.

Digital Extremes absolutely nailed down what it means to be a great Free-to-Play game, and how to handle micro-transactions. They are in no way intrusive or obstructive, and are 100% optional with very few cosmetic items only available for purchase through premium currency (Platinum, which can also be traded between players).
One thing to get out of the way early is, this game is a GRIND. It's all about collecting materials, weapon/Warframe parts, credits, and mods. If you're not a fan of grinding or looter-type games (The Division, Diablo, Destiny), I wouldn't recommend this for you. I only have about 14hrs on Steam, but over 80hrs on XB1, and I was still only scratching the surface of the game. You definitely get more out of this game with more time you invest.
There are tons of customization options, giving you the freedom to mod your Warframe or weapons for near-limitless possibilities. You can mod your gun for critical hits, or mod your Warframe to have abilities going constantly. Furthermore, you can freely change these modifications at any time for free. You will also have cosmetic modifications, applying colors and skins to your Warframes and weapons.
The only shortcomings in this game, in my opinion, is that it is somewhat slow to start and probably turns a lot of new players off of the game, especially if they don't have friends telling them to keep playing. Combine this with the steep learning curve and no real tutorials in game, more players probably give up. Also, the level designs on each planet are randomly generated from a collection of nodes, so while each mission will be different, they all start to feel the same.

A hacking simulation that aims to be more realistic than trope-y games already present. And, on the immersion side, the game does it's job really well. The second you start up the game, onwards to the main menus and tutorial, all is already 'the game'. Uplink does not present itself as a game, but as a 'real' application to hack the world with. Bonus points here for the afromentioned immersion part.
Following that however, is a... creative, and remotely realistic, yet horribly dull gameplay experience. You take missions from a central server, which tell you to delete file X, add 'xyz' to someone's college degree or steal someone's bank details to mail money elsewhere. You then click a button to set up your route that goes across every server you have ever found (because, without exceptions, more servers is always better, as it gives you more time), do the same 5 procedures in different combinations (or lack thereof), usually consisting of picking a program you bought, clicking on a target field, and waiting for the loading bar to finish. Then you do the thing, log out, delete the logs on a single public server to prevent anyone from ever finding out it was you, cash in the money, buy new programs. Repeat.
I appreciate the style of the game, it's creative vision, but in the end it feels more like a mildly complex console-and-gui-based fetch quest simulator.
Overall, I would argue it likely is one of the more realistic, maybe even better hacking sims, but it's simply not a really satisfying, or enjoyable experience.

Disclaimer: There's not necessarily 346 hours of content. I just sometimes forget to shut down the game and/or like to watch some of my solutions more than once. Having said that, this game WILL keep you busy for a while.
So I just finished 100% completion of this game, and figured I'd finally levy my thoughts on it in a review. So first off: I love this game. Sure, the game may tell you flat out what you're SUPPOSED to do (except in the hidden puzzle - RTFM to find it), but it's up to you to take those specifications and figure out how to make them a reality in practice. Trust me when I say this: If you don't even have a basic idea of how to approach your problem you're going to struggle to complete it.
Of course, even if you THINK you have a great idea for how to get a puzzle to complete, you still have to actually write it out and test it. More often than not, there will be a flaw in your thinking or coding that will make your approach not quite work. Your goal of course is to try to correct that flaw, which will more often than not require using breakpoints and stepping. While you may be able to sometimes fix a problem, other times you will make things worse or even run into command space issues. There's only one thing I can say about this: There's no shame whatsoever in deleting a program, and coming back to it later. I've done that more than I care to admit. Once you do eventually solve it it'll feel amazing, and you might even think of new ways to solve it by tackling another problem!
Tl;dr: This game is hard. Even when you think you've got something figured out you might not, and you have to consider whether you want to try to tweak your solution idea or abandon it. In the end though, resolving a problem is one of the most satisfying feelings you can have, especially when it provides inspiration for another problem.

This is an interesting game.  I have been following this game since it was announced by the developer on their website.  The goal of this game is simple: shove your man gentilic in the other gentilic rear ends while trying to be penetrated yourself.  It is a clearly ridiculous premise, but look at the time...you knew what you were getting yourself into.
This game is fun.  Between the squishing noises that your character makes, the announcer screaming PENETRATION every time someone inserts themselves and the fact that the number of points you get each round is represented on the score screen by a number of times your little (or big) member ejaculates gives you a good idea of the overall mood of this game.  It offers some cheap thrills and the ability to play this with up to 5 people on a keyboard and controller (3 on the keyboard and 2 on the controller) make this a great couch game.  Also, there are costumes that are unlocked that are represented by a vat of a (not so) mysterious white fluid...so there's that.
As I mentioned before, there are a lot of cheap thrills.  It does not have much depth (pun intended).  The game types can get somewhat old and from what I can see at the time of writing this review (literally the day it came out), there does not appear to be an offline mode against bots.  I have not tested multiplayer yet, so I cannot attest to that.
If you are looking for a party game to make adults giggle to themselves with the lunacy of inserting yourself into the backside of some man meat, this game is for you.
If you are easily offended, not for you.
However, for $5, it's actually quite a steal and worth the money.
And remember...SLIDE UP TO CONSENT!!!

This is a so called chess game where player roll dices to move and combat, with MOE style CG.
However, the mechanism embeded in rolling dice have undermines the game play, though it is seemly driven by a RNG.
1. CPU 100% rolls the point for strategic move (kill a boss, collect points, etc).
2. Player always fails to K.O a CPU even when it has just 1 hp remained.
3. Combat is definitely dangerous for a player because he will always get killed even his rivalry has the same hp with him. (In which case player roll 1 point as defense, while rivalry rolls 7 more points)
I predicts the dice is definitely not driven by a RNG, but a in-game cost analysis that constantly set obstacles at the front of a player instead.
I think you should argue that it's just I am not so lucky, or I have no evidence of accusing the developer of using a false RNG. I have no right of even debugging the code, but I can confidently tell you by implementing a significance testing
I could simply affirm my assumption. But I need more statistical data of other players playing this game. I would like to know how many times you doomed in a 'critical moment' (Like get K.O. in a combat versus another CPU of 1 point hp).
I think there'll be some player feeling addictive in combat against other CPU over and over again and eventually win. But I think I'm not that kind of player that will enjoy such hopeless dead cycle. A fair game play is also important in chess game, and by using false RNG you will lose more and more player that are willing to play your game at first glance.

Even the horselords conquering the east desired alliances(wives) with Ireland. The only thing next for my dynasty was to become the overlords of all Europe. However this is not your typical strategy game where you just snowball, no, this is Crusader Kings. The muslim peasants from three different sects would continually rebel until Irish priests finally converted Africa. Massive infighting between my vassals constantly changed the sphere of power and left little room for their settlements to grow. I held the strategic and best land under my own domain however one noble or another would always  grow jealous of one of my many crowns and poison their peers into civil war. Then the Caliphates would stop fighting amongst themselves and try and press their advantage against my southern borders. However, these forces were no match for my Gallowglass warriors and all my enemies were forced to bend the knee. With virtually no periods of peace, my coffers were constantly drained and funding for a great European campaign was hopeless. Eventually, with 200 hours gone by, the year reached the end-date of 1453 with my dynasty achieving a score of just above 100k.
Guiding my dynasty from its humble beginnings to rule over the Atlantic coasts was so FUN and exciting. I lost track of so much time playing this game as i was so invested and immersed into the experience. If you thought one more turn syndrome in Civ5 was bad, just wait til you play this! There were so many different phases in my playthrough with each one presenting unique problems and having unique solutions. International diplomacy, internal politicking, marriages, land management, and trait development were all my favorite parts of the game and they were all unique and never dulled.
Its worth noting that the Ironman playthrough i described is the only one I've finished so far as it took over 200 hours to complete. I also started with all the dlc up  to "Sons of Abraham" + also "Way of Life" (i didnt get Charlemagne for some reason). The only experience i have with this game is with multiple paid dlc. Two of my friends got this game on my recomendation and enjoy the game alot too but they only have one or two dlc. When listening to their experiences it seems as though the game is a bit lackluster in comparison with the "full" version with dlcs. With that said though, the base game was enough to hook them in.
I was lucky enough to catch this game during one of Paradoxes bigger steam sales. I got the game for around -80% and the dlcs were all -75%, both historical lows. It is EXTREMELY DISSAPOINTING that the last time these lows were reached was almost 2 YEARS ago in Oct. 2015. Since then the game and dlc has been on sale consistantly for the same 75%/66%. This is a game that is almost SIX YEARS old, SIX. It is not like Paradox is in financial straits or having technical trouble either. They have released many best selling games these past years. While they continue to update CK2, a lot of the big updates mess with solid mechanics and/or have game breaking consequences. These changes are often addressed after player uproar but that is still no excuse for the price model they have for this game.
This game and many of its DLC, while still fun, are very old yet have not had a REAL SALE IN TWO YEARS. Paradox if you want to get a hoard of new players, cut the BS and put this game on sale for, at the very least, its historical low. You are putting Activision, EA, and Ubisoft to shame here with this nonsense. I don't typically buy DLC but i would complete my collection for this game if they were at FAIR prices.
It pains me to say this BUT, until Paradox gives this game a REAL SALE, i CANNOT reccomend purchasing it. It is simply too expensive for an old game and buying now would only strengthen Paradox's  cheapskate policies and potentially ruin future releases.
TL;DR: Extremely fun and unique strategy game with its potential hidden behind unjustly expensive paywall.

Tree of Life is a sandbox surivival game with immense grind and has a HUGE lack of information/translation issues.
But despite of all this it's a pretty darn good game.
Here's a list of pros and cons
Pros:
Community and socializing is encouraged, it helps to have friends play with you or find players in game to play with as the survival solo is pretty boring and having multiple people speeds up how fast you progress.
Different areas host different plants, monsters, animals, ores and trees so no 2 areas are the same. The map is pretty well designed and the transistions between each area is pretty smooth.
Crafting system is very thought out and provides you with multiple choices on how you choose to play the game anywhere from playing as a blacksmith or playing as farmer or just being a vagabond exploring each area. Hell if you want to you can raid other players and start a raiding crew.
The building system is pretty good as well and makes sense as you progress more in the game starting with a small tent to a large scale city surrounded by towers keeping the undead at bay.
To sum up the pros, you have a large variety of areas, buildings, professions, and monsters plus it's encouraged to socialize with others and not be a lone wolf.
Cons, I hate that there are so many but it's early access so it's bound to happen.
Fighting, mainly the targeting is very buggy. You have to stop moving and hope you can target what you what and the cursor isn't what actually targets the monster, it's your head from what I've noticed even then if you can't see what you are fighting it's difficult.
Night time is harsh since you cannot hold a weapon in 1 hand and a torch in the other so you're stuck in the dark and hoping other monsters don't join in. Besides that night time is easily beaten by fire and towers.
Resource gathering is a pain in the butt at times if you don't place yourself in the correct area. So you may have to run half way across the map to get some copper so you can level up in Tinkering or blacksmithing. There's no way from what I can tell to move rocks/logs quickly so if your area runs out of trees you have to make a hell of a trek on a very slow pace. Same with rocks which spawn randomly if you do not live by a quarry.
Criminal system now this is a bit of a problem at times where you get someone who isn't a criminal attack you, so you defend yourself and kill him, this brands you a criminal so now when they come back to kill you, you lose everything and they lose nothing. It's a quite flawed system in that respect but it does work out, though I feel if another player chooses to attack you, you should be able to kill them without penalty. Biggest flaw on the game as non-criminals have huge advantages over criminals, even if they were accidently made criminals.
Lack of tutorial/guide/keymapping or anything relevant, they literally just link to player guides on how to play their game I mean, that's plain lazy in my book I took me awhile to figure out how to eat and play the game in general besides smashing stuff. A tutorial or least key display option would be helpful. Stop being lazy devs.
Translations and this is big, they have bad translations on everything and this really makes it hard to figure out what you are building till after the materials are spent. Granted it's not a lot of materials but it's still labor I put in.
A lumbermill is called a "snow shredder".
Grilled steak is "Small grilled fish"
Among tons of others. I understand they are not native English speakers but having one person to translate this would improve it. Or just be lazy(like you've already been) and have the players do the translations to the items.
Map this is very odd one to say but the map is too big at the same time it's also too small.
What I mean by that is, if you're looking to start your own town/village/loner shack. It's near impossible to find a good unpopulated spot, even then the monsters come at night and destroy your unguarded items(again towers do prevent this but you run out of arrows before you log back on so it's near pointless and easier to repair with goblin coins) still it's hard to find a good spot you like without tons of people. Maybe have a option to have a personalized space in another dimension or an instanced area to build towns only for guilds. I mean magic is already in the game wouldn't be hard to utilize that.
Overall the game is pretty good and is a lot better than many other early access games I have played. At this moment I wouldn't really recommend the game till a proper tutorial is put in and fixing the locking on "feature" along with the translations.

I'm not very good in writing reviews but i'll try to express what i think about this game.
To begin with, sonic is one of my favourite franchises in videogaming industry. I love both 2d and 3d sonic games even though some of them could be way better in my opion.
But classic sonic games take the most important spot of my heart. They were a big part of my childhood (i never had any console besides sega so i can sound a bit biased).
And so, what can i say about this game? Even though i am a little conflicted by the actions sega have done recently which in actuallity do not lower the quality of the game as it's own product but it does undermine overall enjoyment i could get from this game.
The game itself is awesome. It's the same as i remember it in my childhood. Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, old levels (a lot of people hate green hill but i have no doubt anybody would call this stage ''the most iconic sonic level of all times'')
Don't be afraid of older levels being in this game. All of them resemble the old levels, but after some time you won't recognize them at all.
The new levels take special place in my appreciation list. They are very enjoyable, imaginative and i actually would prefer if this game had more of them.
Now let's talk about music. Tee lopes handled it beatifully. Every now and then i found myself dancing to the music and even forgetting to play. He took most of the classic songs and made them even better which is a great accomplishment because in my opinion sonic music is always on a high spot comparing to other things.
Special place in here is reserved for references. Yes, references and a lot of them. The game was advertised under the famous line ''by the mania , for the mania'' which lives up to it's name. If you are a classic sonic fan you will appreciate this game very much. The amount of surprises is astounding. Some of references are so obscure , you have to be a huge sonic fan who dug deeper than you can imagine in order to understand all of them. Which is beatiful and shows the love and passion behind the project.
Overall i think it's a great game anybody can enjoy, and if you a classic sonic fan - you must definetely play.

Sonic Mania is a true return to form for Sonic the Hedgehog. I grew up playing the Genesis (or Mega Drive, depending on your location) games, especially Sonic 3 & Knuckles. And while I played some "modern" Sonic games, and enjoyed them, I always wanted a continuation to the games from my childhood; a game that played (and felt) like a follow-up to S3&K. This game is exactly what I'd always wanted, and more; I'd even go as far as saying that this is my favourite Sonic game (and keep in mind, I like S3&K a lot). Well, I think that's enough of my personal feelings towards the game, so now on to the proper review.
As I said in the opening paragraph, this game feels like a follow-up to Sonic 3 & Knuckles, and so it plays a lot like it, even having mini-bosses for Act 1 in each zone. The gameplay feels just as good as in the old classic games, and perhaps even better. The new drop dash ability that Sonic gets, replacing his insta-shield from S3&K, is pretty good for keeping momentum and speed across the levels. Tails and Knuckles keep their old abilities (flying for Tails, gliding and breaking walls for Knuckles), which allow them to explore the zones a bit more than Sonic, just like in the old games.
The remixed stages are amazing, being a perfect mix of old layouts and new mechanics. Chemical Plant, for example, which was one of my favourite zones from Sonic 2, has a great second act, with a fun boss fight to boot. Another favourite, Flying Battery, also makes it to this game, and again, has some pretty cool new mechanics, as well as being a lot bigger (which is the case for every remixed stage, they feel a lot bigger than their original version, with a lot more paths and such). When it comes to new stages, they feel and play exactly like the old stages; well, not literally, but what I mean is that they'd have fit perfectly in one of the classic games. The boss fights are all really well done, and feel challenging to some degree.
The soundtrack is, simply put, awesome. Even the tracks from the remixed stages have been reworked, and they all sound incredible. Tee Lopes did a great job with it, and he deserves huge props. The game's opening and ending animations are also really well done, and help setting the tone of a return to roots for Sonic.
As for the story, just like in the classic games, it's there, but at the same time it's not. There's some cutscenes, so to speak, that give details to the story, but there's no dialogue or the like. You can get a decent grasp at the story from playing the game, but most of the actual details are found in the manual.
The game also includes a whole bunch of extras: there's a competition mode that's similar to the one from Sonic 2 (personally, I'd have preferred something more similar to the one from Sonic 3, but it's still good), a time attack mode, and secret modes that can either played in a No Save file, or from the Extras menu.
Well, I think that's enough for Sonic Mania. Huge props to Christian Whitehead and the whole team behind it, they did a great job, which is even more impressive when we take into account that this was practically a passion project from the fans, for the fans. I sure hope to see a continuation to this in the future, especially if they put as much love and care as they did with this one. I simply can't recommend it enough.

This is a so called chess game where player roll dices to move and combat, with MOE style CG.
However, the mechanism embeded in rolling dice have undermines the game play, though it is seemly driven by a RNG.
1. CPU 100% rolls the point for strategic move (kill a boss, collect points, etc).
2. Player always fails to K.O a CPU even when it has just 1 hp remained.
3. Combat is definitely dangerous for a player because he will always get killed even his rivalry has the same hp with him. (In which case player roll 1 point as defense, while rivalry rolls 7 more points)
I predicts the dice is definitely not driven by a RNG, but a in-game cost analysis that constantly set obstacles at the front of a player instead.
I think you should argue that it's just I am not so lucky, or I have no evidence of accusing the developer of using a false RNG. I have no right of even debugging the code, but I can confidently tell you by implementing a significance testing
I could simply affirm my assumption. But I need more statistical data of other players playing this game. I would like to know how many times you doomed in a 'critical moment' (Like get K.O. in a combat versus another CPU of 1 point hp).
I think there'll be some player feeling addictive in combat against other CPU over and over again and eventually win. But I think I'm not that kind of player that will enjoy such hopeless dead cycle. A fair game play is also important in chess game, and by using false RNG you will lose more and more player that are willing to play your game at first glance.

I LOVE this game.
I started off as a humble independent count in Ireland whos dream was to unite the duchy. A few generations later and names Scotland and Spain are all but legends, they are Ireland now. North Africa and Jerusalem have never seen a whiter people ruler their lands. All the great houses of the Holy Roman, Byzantine, and French empires had the blood of Eire. Even the horselords conquering the east desired alliances(wives) with Ireland. The only thing next for my dynasty was to become the overlords of all Europe. However this is not your typical strategy game where you just snowball, no, this is Crusader Kings. The muslim peasants from three different sects would continually rebel until Irish priests finally converted Africa. Massive infighting between my vassals constantly changed the sphere of power and left little room for their settlements to grow. I held the strategic and best land under my own domain however one noble or another would always  grow jealous of one of my many crowns and poison their peers into civil war. Then the Caliphates would stop fighting amongst themselves and try and press their advantage against my southern borders. However, these forces were no match for my Gallowglass warriors and all my enemies were forced to bend the knee. With virtually no periods of peace, my coffers were constantly drained and funding for a great European campaign was hopeless. Eventually, with 200 hours gone by, the year reached the end-date of 1453 with my dynasty achieving a score of just above 100k.
Guiding my dynasty from its humble beginnings to rule over the Atlantic coasts was so FUN and exciting. I lost track of so much time playing this game as i was so invested and immersed into the experience. If you thought one more turn syndrome in Civ5 was bad, just wait til you play this! There were so many different phases in my playthrough with each one presenting unique problems and having unique solutions. International diplomacy, internal politicking, marriages, land management, and trait development were all my favorite parts of the game and they were all unique and never dulled.
Its worth noting that the Ironman playthrough i described is the only one I've finished so far as it took over 200 hours to complete. I also started with all the dlc up  to "Sons of Abraham" + also "Way of Life" (i didnt get Charlemagne for some reason). The only experience i have with this game is with multiple paid dlc. Two of my friends got this game on my recomendation and enjoy the game alot too but they only have one or two dlc. When listening to their experiences it seems as though the game is a bit lackluster in comparison with the "full" version with dlcs. With that said though, the base game was enough to hook them in.
I was lucky enough to catch this game during one of Paradoxes bigger steam sales. I got the game for around -80% and the dlcs were all -75%, both historical lows. It is EXTREMELY DISSAPOINTING that the last time these lows were reached was almost 2 YEARS ago in Oct. 2015. Since then the game and dlc has been on sale consistantly for the same 75%/66%. This is a game that is almost SIX YEARS old, SIX. It is not like Paradox is in financial straits or having technical trouble either. They have released many best selling games these past years. While they continue to update CK2, a lot of the big updates mess with solid mechanics and/or have game breaking consequences. These changes are often addressed after player uproar but that is still no excuse for the price model they have for this game.
This game and many of its DLC, while still fun, are very old yet have not had a REAL SALE IN TWO YEARS. Paradox if you want to get a hoard of new players, cut the BS and put this game on sale for, at the very least, its historical low. You are putting Activision, EA, and Ubisoft to shame here with this nonsense. I don't typically buy DLC but i would complete my collection for this game if they were at FAIR prices.
It pains me to say this BUT, until Paradox gives this game a REAL SALE, i CANNOT reccomend purchasing it. It is simply too expensive for an old game and buying now would only strengthen Paradox's  cheapskate policies and potentially ruin future releases.
TL;DR: Extremely fun and unique strategy game with its potential hidden behind unjustly expensive paywall.
