There is not much progression in the game. You grind to grind, and I don't specifically have a problem with that. The problem is with the direction the developers have turned. For the longest time people have been min/maxing their gear and just blowing through content, but now they are trying to slow people down as much as possible. I'm going to use Harrow for an example, fantastic quest by the way. His blueprint is relatively easy to obtain, his chassis is stupid easy to get, and then theres his other two pieces. The neuroptics is an 11% chance drop from a challenging spy mission, which gets boring after doing it twice, and his systems is an 11% drop from a Defection mission.
The point I'm trying to make, is all the min and maxing people have done does not apply to these grindy missions. Oh your 6 forma'd Tigris Prime with a god riven isn't ganna help in a spy mission, and defection missions are annoying having to babysit all those people. I've put my fair share of money into the game and the things I've bought don't help me anymore, the easiest way to do these things is just buying them with platnium. The game just isn't worth it anymore, it's nice to look pretty, but all you do is grind to grind to grind to grind. It's just not my taste anymore, you can give me a thumbs down, but what I've said about the min/max not being as important is very much true.

Well, let's see. I originally pirated Uplink, I got 30+ hours on that one. I see Steam Summer sale, when I finally have money in my account. I got to buy it, and get a few extra Introversion games thrown in. That's beside the point. The main point here? GREAT FREAKING STORY. LOVE IT.
The mechanics required for gameplay? Amazing. People who say they "can't beat the tutorial"? Those are the twelve year olds who don't know how to read yet, or those without common sense. Running programs feels smooth, and the nice thing is that once you have better skills, you can queue up many, many missions, and complete them all with a few presses of a button. You would think that it's easy to do all of this, and it really is.
On to the interface. It's amazing, feels really cyber-punk like, great in a hacking game, such as Uplink is. The ability to have more than one program is perfect, something I can't really find in other games like it (except Onlink, but that's a spinoff.) The ability to have a CPU timer is also amazing, limits the number of things you can have running, and makes them really variable with speed. Something flawed though, you can't move every window.
I personally mod my games a lot, and what annoys me here, is that we don't have Workshop for Uplink. It makes it harder to install mods, though the mods being there in general is nice. The mod UplinkOS? Best mod out there by far, next to Onlink (which, again, is basically Uplink with more features).
Overall: Amazing game, I recommend it to everyone looking for something like this.

The game is extremely well balanced (except for the few weeks after a new character comes out, I'm talking to you Ted) and the unlock system is pretty fair. Others say that long time players of the game (heh, long time, they don't even know) have an advantage by having better characters unlocked. Other than the fact that within the first few games you play, you should unlock everything because the characters are the first things you unlock, I would argue that the most overpowered characters in the game are the ones you get straight off the bat (I'm talking to you Fergy Ger and Leon).
Sometimes a team can get a combination of characters that seem unbeatable, but that's only because they are all good, and working together. You only notice because how they work together is very noticable, i.e. Voltar+ pretty much anyone.
Every character has a counter, every character has a weakness to balance their strength. It's a fun game, play it with friends.

Never in my wildest dreams would I think that I would ever get to play a deserving sequel to Sonic 3 Knuckles in 2017, but here we are.
There really is no point in saying if the game is good or not, you already know it. If you grew up playing those Sega Genesis games, then you owe it to yourself to play this.
It's astounding that a group of Sonic fans managed to recreate something that Sega has been struggling for decades.
The amount of love and care poured into this project seeps out of the screen and leaves you with inevitable dumb smiles and teary eyes, in what is one of the best fan pandering, nostalgia baiting and soul cleansing games ever made.
As you can tell, the amount of bias here is pretty gigantic. The first game I ever played was Sonic 1, and alot of my love for the medium is closely tied to the memories I have of playing that game at the age of 4. I have been dissatisfied with the state of the franchise ever since those glory days of the blue blur, and it is with immense joy that I say that this game brought me back to those times.
The level design is better than it ever was, with an amazing amount of intertwining sections and paths that reward exploration and player creativity, and every single act provides new gimmicks and options for the player to exploit and interact with.
The old "i go too fast therefore i cant see the stuff that hurts me ahead" criticism is the most obsolete it has ever been. The amazing work put into the level design makes it so that there are never instances where you are thrown into a rollercoaster ride only to hit something at the end of it and lose all of your rings.
The recreated levels manage to justify their presence by twisting and subverting your memories and coming up with new ideas that fundamentally change the levels you remember from the past games. The second act of a zone is always the more radically changed, maintaining only the aestethic and theme of the old game's counterpart, but even the first act contain surprises and changes of their own.
Then you have the new levels, which are so good and perfectly match the aestethic of those old sonic games, that you just cant avoid thinking how great would it be if the whole game was new stuff.
Sonic, Tails and Knuckles play just as the old games, providing just enough differentiation  to make you wanna beat the game 3 times with each character. Sonic comes with a new very useful move, the drop spindash, which lets you spin dash immediately as you hit the ground without having to charge it.
For better or for worse, these characters still move exactly like they did in the 90s (which for me is perfect), so if you are someone who always had trouble with these games, its not gonna change here.
The game is actually much more forgiving than the old ones. If you lose all your lives, you get sent to the first act of the level you died at, where as in the old games you would go all the way back to level 1.
However, considering that there are still people complaining online about being sent to act 1 if they lose all their lives like they have never played a game from the 16-bit era before, its up to you if this is bad or not.
Personally, I never lost all my lives and i think if you complain about being set back a few minutes because you died, you shouldnt even be playing games, but to each their own.
What else can I say? Music? Absolutely fantastic. Pixel art? Perfect and Beautiful. Bosses? Creative, challenging and surprising.
As for nitpicks, because i do have them, I would say that the story is very bland and lazy, and surprisingly convoluted and unecessarily redundant.
Also, there are instances in this game where you can feel the limited budget rear its head.
The game uses transitions between levels to create a sense of progression like S3&K, but at some point in the game they just stop using them. Finished levels will fade to black and put you in another level without any explanation of how you got there, when in the first levels in the game you always had transitions. Was it lack of time or resources? I dunno, all I know is that its very noticeable.
Then you have the true ending which SPOILERS ends up as a cliffhanger to set up events in Sonic Forces. Not only i the true final boss disappointing, but to have the game end on an anti climatic note because its in service of another game? Thats just awful, especially when the old games had a sense of finality and closure when you would reach the end. Look up Sonic 2 ending on youtube if you want a better understanding of what im saying.
But whatever, those are all just nitpicks. All in all, this is a project of love from the fans to the fans. Ican only hope Sega realizes whats here and builds upon that. But then again,Sonic Forces is coming out so who knows?...

"It's the assembly language programming game you never asked for!" -Zachtronics
You have no idea how right you are.
The game provides challenging assembly programming language puzzles, and they can certainly be satisfying when you finally figure out how to solve them. Unfortunately, there are multiple problems with it:
-It is difficult to get into without assembly coding experience. It lacks any kind of tutorial, instead giving you a manual that, while introducing you to the commands that you'll be using, doesn't really explain how to use them. Even with my (small amount of) coding experience, I had alot of trouble figuring out what I was actually supposed to be doing with these commands
-The language and architecture used in the game is outdated and doesn't fit with the goal of these puzzles. While this game could teach you to code if you were living in the 80s or 90s, it would barely help you today. The computer that the game simulates doesn't take advantage of modern processing improvements (The game even mentions the USSR as if it still existed in the timeframe of the game-given how the game's computer operates, that's easy to believe.). Additionally, the game asks you to do things which the language was seemingly not made to do (for example: some puzzles ask you to multiply or divide, but the language only has add and subtract commands. Also, you might be asked to compare numbers or change the output based on a condition, which, again, the language doesn't have a command for). It feels like trying to build a house by stacking rocks- you'll get there eventually, but it'll be slow, and the thing's gonna fall over at least a few times before you get there.
tl;dr: While the game tries to turn assembly coding into a challenging and potentially educational puzzle, the outdated architecture and clunky language ruins the fun, assuming you understand the coding enough to actually have fun in the first place.
We're in the 21st century now, game. This isn't what coding is like.

The transputer architecture lets you try totally different approaches to problems architecturally, instead of just obsessing and polishing over a single piece of code.
This game will make you laugh, cry, punch the air, headbutt your desk. You may not see your family or friends for days. Essentially a much condensed form of the programming experience. If you're skeptical, give it a try. What's the worst that could happen?

I am only hobbyist programmer, certainly not even close to professional - I've coded some with Python and Gamemaker language recently, but in college back in the early 90s I did have an assembly language class.  I remember liking that class, but this game wasn't doing much for me 20+ yrs later.  Working around the limitations of code is the game.  Sortof like you're building up a library of simple procedures and functions that over time might allow more complex code to be built on top of.
Anyhow, not much fun for me with no real sense of accomplishment.  I'm about 3.8 hours in and  on about the 6th puzzle, but likely won't play anymore.  But if you like intricate programming puzzles where the solution is the only reward, this might be for you.   I can't recommend it though.  Again, if you like puzzle games like this, I do recommend SpaceChem and especially Infinifactory which I think is excellent.  They're more interesting versions of this basic puzzle idea imho. Well I am truly sad and salty with this title now. As such I am modifying my initial early review and if you are interested in reading why, read on.
I have slept on this for a few nights, to make sure I not just raging but no, this is not right.
The Devs recent "fact check" whilst at the same time defensive, aggressive and patronizing is a thinly veiled attempt to cover the fact that the Devs have taken the decision to release the game  devoid of content; such content only being accessible by making a further purchase of DLC. To placate early backers there is a free "allied" pack containing little in the way of any major new factions which again will not be available at release.
This is managing supporter expectations very poorly and when you consider the effort and feedback supporters have made, to be hit with this put down, it is just wrong if not in breach of UK consumer law.
The devs will no doubt claim that early backers at no point had it represented to them that the game would contain X amount of content or that it would be X type of game. It was implied, with reasonable expectation and samples that the product would contain more content than is being released under the early access, as an updated and improved successor to MOWAS2. In real terms, very little from the changed from early Alpha (tanks and vehicle were added) though the title has mutated into a poor FPS and which in MP is very much a infantry kill fest ala COD on an RTS scale.
I just hope that (prayer to Gaben) Modders fix this game and make it what fans of the series wanted it to be. The current multiplayer is unbalanced and frequently suffers from performance drops. The creates a fustrating experience trying to get a game from an already dwindling player base and when you do, results in poor matches with exploits abused.
Whilst I like the engine, aspects of the game (what of it there is), as it stands I can only recommend the free to play element. The single player is not worth purchasing and the DLC based on what it offer is not either. Frankly this content should have been in the game to begin with. If a game of the year comes out with all the content that the game should have had, on sale, then yes get the game. If you see this studio developing EA in future, steer well clear.

This is a nice little point & click: standard in many ways, but with rather interesting characters, occasionally entertaining dialogs and mostly enjoyable puzzles. The priest-detective concept (fine, ex-priest) is a novel enough idea in games, one I last enjoyed with the Shiva's rabbi. And sure, concpiracies centering around the Vatican are a dime a dozen, but the Italian background of the devs shows in the way they manage to be at the same time respectful and irreverent, making a commonplace story feel refreshing. The story starts slowly but does a nice job of drawing you in, ending (predictably) with a cliffhanger, but one that made me interested in the episodes to come.
The writing mainly benefits from having small moments of actual brilliance in characterization, creating unexpectedly endearing portraits of both the hero and many the people you meet, that very much drive the storytelling. And since this is supposed to be the prologue in a 4 part series, there is alot of lovingly crafted character introduction to be had and enjoyed. In fact I have the feeling that it was the memorable characters (and therefore their story) and some decent pacing that caused me to mostly forget there were puzzles there. That, and the fact that they were mostly easy and logical, and that important information was always pointed out to you, more or less inobtrusively.
Some more general stuff: The backgrounds are nicely made, the animation a bit less so but not jarring. I enjoyed the music very much, though the voice acting can be hit and miss. I also had no bugs or technical problems, which I appreciated (since the first time I tried to play the DRM free version a while back I had serious issues - glad to see them fixed). And yes, the game is rather short, which personally doesn't bother me for the price.
All in all, I was surprised by this one, and will look forward to the next act. It isn't perfect or particularly unique, but it is memorable and endearing, and I very much had fun with it while it lasted.

Shadows on the Vatican Act 1, is an adventure/detective game, set in
a modern-esque world.  You play the part of an ex-priest called in to
solve a mystery that surrounds the church and the Vatican.
The tutorial does a good job of showing you how to play, while
remaining integrated into the story.  The voice acting was mostly
performed in a professional manner, and the art style was good, but the animations
of the characters were robotic and doll-like.
As a detective game, it did a poor job of drawing you to the next clue,
instead forcing you to look for the smallest of objects.  This coupled with being unable to make leaps in logic, instead being forced to complete every task,
in order, made it rather frustrating.
As I said before, the main character is a former priest who takes on
the role of detective.  Sometimes the writing tries to justify
religious arguments logically without taking into account that the
main character is currently in conflict with his religious beliefs,
making it seem somewhat forced, and more difficult to connect with
him due to how he responds to people in the world.
In the adventure part, I know why I am here, what I am doing, where I am going, and who I am talking with. As well as having the information on my back story and small to large info on the back story of supporting characters. It gives you the information you need to progress with out feeling like you do not understand what is going on around you.
Unfortunately the flaws of this game outweighed it's good points,
making me unable to recommend it.

Voice acting is terrible and overdramatic and the conversations are rather uninteresting 90% of the time, which is pretty annoying (they feel just like fillers to make the game longer). The plot is not well set up: after finishing Act I you should AT LEAST have an idea on how good the story's going to be - but barely anything happens, I understand that they cannot unveil too much on the first act but it's just too vague. At this point I have no idea if the story is going to be amazing or a boring, run-of-the-mill, Da Vinci Code-esque type of thing. Pretty bland.
Creativity = 0. If you're a fan of graphic adventure games, all you will do in this game are things you have already done hundreds of times in other mediocre adventures. Things of this sort: find key, use key in the next 2 minutes, get a damp X to clean X, use computer to look up Y information, show item you just found to person Z who is right next to it. There are barely any puzzles too. Nothing to see here.
It's really short even for an episode-based game. 2,5 hours and I took my time. Again, not really anything substantial.
I won't be purchasing the following acts unless they come in a bundle or are ridiculously cheap at some point. Maybe not even then.

I'm playing this multiplayer with my friends and it is really way more fun than it should be. Combat misadventures to follow, but the story interaction that you can have is fantastic. If one player starts talking to an NPC you can listen to the whole exchange as well, complete with the voice acted NPC dialog. You can see where your friend's cursor is as they debate what dialog choice they want to reply with- we always end up talking about which one fits our "attitude" the most, which is fun in and of itself. You are never standing around while someone has an awesome dialog with "their" quest NPC while you do nothing; you can always listen in and hear the story.
Now on to the combat. The combat is really well done, especially the environmental variables and conditions. For instance, the classic Divinity situation of use lightning or cold on someone standing in water or wet and they will be stunned or frozen respectively is great for planning out how you are going to take on a group of enemies. Until someone in your group makes it rain on the battlefield and then uses chain lightning. Now, in addition to your foe being stunned, your allies are as well. I am not saying that I have been stunned or frozen a few times, but I have been stunned or frozen a few times.
Lots of quests and side quests and NPCs to do tasks for, and lots of different ways of completing the tasks as well. We are still in our first play-through but already planning out classes for our second. One of the short comings is related to the quests, specifically the quest log. It can be difficult to discern if a quest is active only because you did a part of it out of order, such as visiting an NPC before you should have, or if you have not done the criteria of the quest. It is not game braking but it is a little bit out of place due to how good the rest of the game is, UI included.

To me it plays like a combination of a faster-paced Age of Empires and Civilization.
This is because city-building and economics play a greater role in the game. In order to develop strong production chains, the player must build multiple cities to expand his influence and create trade routes between them to generate wealth. I also prefer the military aspect of Rise of Nations. The fast-paced nature of the game (compared to a lot of strategy games) could work nicely in an eSports context I suppose. I could adapt to play games like Starcraft 2 for the excessive amount of resources available in every map, annoying strategies such as base block, hardly counterable, or the that every base a narrow corridor to get in which makes attacking highly risky. But Rise of Nations, to me, feels like a good compromise in pace. Cultures play the role of "races" here, all of them are well-balanced overall.
Even if you dislike multiplayer anyway, for the game's campaign you're given a great Risk-style metagame with the goal of conquering as much of the world as you can and moving your armies around the board dictating skirmishes, as well as managing resources and special ability cards.

Rise of Nations was originally released back in 2003, and it still stands as one of the best RTS (Real-Time Strategy) titles out there.  I bought the game back when it launched, put hundreds of hours into it, and still love it today.  The replayability is infinite because every game is unique.  Even with the same game settings, the AI's will build and attack differently each time.  If you are up for a serious challenge, play a few games online.
There are many different nations you can choose from, and each one has its own set of exlusive benifits.  For example, the Americans can build their first wonder instantly (with the exclusion of Space Program and Supercollider), and the Chinese get instant citizen spawning and instant large cities.  Those are just a couple of examples.
As you progress and gather resources, you can research newer technologies.  In the beginning, your nation can learn how to read and write, or learn how to barter.  As you unlock researches, you will be able to progress to a new age, which unlocks a wealth of new buildings and units you can use.  The technologies range all the way from basic reading and writing all the way up to Artificial Intelligence.  Start in the Archaic Age, and end in the Information Age.  As you play this game, it may just teach you a little bit of history (especially if you play the campaigns)!
Many (if not all) of the Wonders in the game are based on real life historical buildings, such as the Eiffel Tower, the Statue of Liberty, the Colliseum, the Pyramids, and Taj Mahal.
The singleplayer campaign is quite good as well.  There are multiple campaigns you can play, such as the Cold War, Alexander the Great, and Conquer the World.
I found hundreds of hours of gameplay here.  I definitely recommend you give this game a try!  If you are a fan of RTS games, you will love this game!

An interesting take on Men of War, there are a lot of great new features, and a couple of controversial ones. It's still pretty early in development and thus fairly rough around the edges, but this is an established company with a proven track record; Not some sketchy indie dev. For better or worse, the game WILL reach a completed state at some point. Gameplay wise, if you're familiar with Men of War, it's more of the same, though not quite a straight reskin. Infantry combat is faster and more micro intensive, troop numbers are considerably lower, and the Special Unit category is entirely missing(Which has it's own pros and cons, most notably it's impact on the pacing of multiplayer, especially in 1v1). Overall, despite some of it's more glaring downsides(Namely unlock progression, a gimmick forced in to the series at Assault Squad 2 and carried over despite loads of outcry, as you've probably read from a sea of negative reviews by now.), I can't help but recommend it. It's Men of War in a new setting, a refreshing break from the constant shilling of WW2 that most war-themed games seem comfortable to graze in endlessly.
Pros:
-UI improvements
-Better take on direct control for vehicles.
-New setting allows for more creativity and diversity.
-Fairly tight and balanced. Could easily become competitive if nurtured properly by the developer.
-Various 'quality of life' improvements over Assault Squad.
-Combat is more than just a reskin. Has an entirely different feel to unit behaviour.
-Vehicles are extremely satisfying to use, and come with new quirks and weapons unique to the time frame.
-More interesting campaign missions(That are playable in coop)
-Reshuffling of unit hierarchy. No more cheap autocannon spam.
-No more Brandenburgers(This is a selling point all of it's own. Seriously DMS, those things are beyond broken in AS2)
-No more Brandenburgers 2: Electric Boogaloo. No seriously, ♥♥♥♥ these things.
Cons:
-Unlock Progression. Terrible, utterly terrible post-2007 gimmick shoe-horned into every multiplayer game in existence. Has absolutely no place in an RTS and will 100% kill the matchmaking if it's mandatory for ranked play like in AS2. Forces everyone to play lobby matches to turn it off in Assault Squad.
-Currently no option to turn off Unlock Progression even in lobby matches. Forces everyone to grind like some Korean MMO or Call of Duty. Seriously, no one wants this, DMS.
-As with all RTS games, Barrier to entry is high if you don't have the patience and humility to learn and tank a few losses early on. Lack of a tutorial of any sort exacerbates the issue, with Unlock Progression being a cheesy means to slap a bandaid on the issue by restricting what units you can buy.
-Units have no descriptions, but have their specification stats filled out. How hard is it to take an hour to type in 2-3 sentences per unit briefly explaining what they are/what they do? Especially after taking the trouble to fill out their stats. Buying units is guesswork when you're first learning, unlocks or no, just to find out what equipment they carry. I recommend starting a solo match in test mode.
-Still a heavy work in progress. Don't come in expecting a finished product needing a few tweaks here and there. It's got a long way to go before it catches up to it's precessors in content, and with only two factions, it's going to need a MUCH larger unit roster.
Even with all it's problems, I've had a positive experience. As it exists now, however, I'd only recommend it for RTS or Men of War enthusiasts. It's got a long way to go before it properly competes with others of the franchise, let alone the genre.

Never in my wildest dreams would I think that I would ever get to play a deserving sequel to Sonic 3 Knuckles in 2017, but here we are.
There really is no point in saying if the game is good or not, you already know it. If you grew up playing those Sega Genesis games, then you owe it to yourself to play this.
It's astounding that a group of Sonic fans managed to recreate something that Sega has been struggling for decades.
The amount of love and care poured into this project seeps out of the screen and leaves you with inevitable dumb smiles and teary eyes, in what is one of the best fan pandering, nostalgia baiting and soul cleansing games ever made.
As you can tell, the amount of bias here is pretty gigantic. The first game I ever played was Sonic 1, and alot of my love for the medium is closely tied to the memories I have of playing that game at the age of 4. I have been dissatisfied with the state of the franchise ever since those glory days of the blue blur, and it is with immense joy that I say that this game brought me back to those times.
The level design is better than it ever was, with an amazing amount of intertwining sections and paths that reward exploration and player creativity, and every single act provides new gimmicks and options for the player to exploit and interact with.
The old "i go too fast therefore i cant see the stuff that hurts me ahead" criticism is the most obsolete it has ever been. The amazing work put into the level design makes it so that there are never instances where you are thrown into a rollercoaster ride only to hit something at the end of it and lose all of your rings.
The recreated levels manage to justify their presence by twisting and subverting your memories and coming up with new ideas that fundamentally change the levels you remember from the past games. The second act of a zone is always the more radically changed, maintaining only the aestethic and theme of the old game's counterpart, but even the first act contain surprises and changes of their own.
Then you have the new levels, which are so good and perfectly match the aestethic of those old sonic games, that you just cant avoid thinking how great would it be if the whole game was new stuff.
Sonic, Tails and Knuckles play just as the old games, providing just enough differentiation  to make you wanna beat the game 3 times with each character. Sonic comes with a new very useful move, the drop spindash, which lets you spin dash immediately as you hit the ground without having to charge it.
For better or for worse, these characters still move exactly like they did in the 90s (which for me is perfect), so if you are someone who always had trouble with these games, its not gonna change here.
The game is actually much more forgiving than the old ones. If you lose all your lives, you get sent to the first act of the level you died at, where as in the old games you would go all the way back to level 1.
However, considering that there are still people complaining online about being sent to act 1 if they lose all their lives like they have never played a game from the 16-bit era before, its up to you if this is bad or not.
Personally, I never lost all my lives and i think if you complain about being set back a few minutes because you died, you shouldnt even be playing games, but to each their own.
What else can I say? Music? Absolutely fantastic. Pixel art? Perfect and Beautiful. Bosses? Creative, challenging and surprising.
As for nitpicks, because i do have them, I would say that the story is very bland and lazy, and surprisingly convoluted and unecessarily redundant.
Also, there are instances in this game where you can feel the limited budget rear its head.
The game uses transitions between levels to create a sense of progression like S3&K, but at some point in the game they just stop using them. Finished levels will fade to black and put you in another level without any explanation of how you got there, when in the first levels in the game you always had transitions. Was it lack of time or resources? I dunno, all I know is that its very noticeable.
Then you have the true ending which SPOILERS ends up as a cliffhanger to set up events in Sonic Forces. Not only i the true final boss disappointing, but to have the game end on an anti climatic note because its in service of another game? Thats just awful, especially when the old games had a sense of finality and closure when you would reach the end. Look up Sonic 2 ending on youtube if you want a better understanding of what im saying.
But whatever, those are all just nitpicks. All in all, this is a project of love from the fans to the fans. Ican only hope Sega realizes whats here and builds upon that. But then again,Sonic Forces is coming out so who knows?...

There are two parts to this review. One for people with no coding experience at all, and those who have coded, even at a basic level, in Assembly.
To the people who have never coded:
This game will be a little challenging at first. You may sit and be stuck at the first one for a while, but if you keep at it youll start to get the hang of it and get into the swing of this language. The benefit is this is a simple language once you understand it, so it's a good intro to assembly level coding and how it functions on a fundamental level.
If youre not tech savy at all, I might not reccomend the game to you, however I am a firm believer that anyone can code given enough time and practice.
All in all, from a standpoint of a person with no background in programming, I think this is a good buy, especially on sale.
To the people with coding background:
If you're like me, and are either studying Computer Science in college, or are self taught, or have decent experience in real world applications, this game might be a little on the easy side. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoyed it completely and would buy it again. However by about the 3rd puzzle I had the general system down and was able to have pretty decently optimized programs without much effort. Now I dont know how the rest of the game will be, but I got pretty far in one 2 hour session (I left my PC on overnight so thats why I have 24 hrs).
If you are somoene who codes assembly daily, you may find this too easy. I havent coded Assembly in months, so it was refreshing and relaxing to me to pick it up and practice a little. That may not be the case for you.
Still, I think its worth a go. At $7 thats not too bad, and if its on sale its a no brainer.

Yep, nope. It's another MMO promising that you can build whole cities and and find yourself in epic conflict or collaboration with your neighbors. But in execution, it really just lets griefers run wild and steal or slaughter everything that isn't tied down, and then break everything that is tied down, all the while hurtling insults and cheering about how "gangsta" they are.
It's a shame because after spending half a day with this game, I rather want to like it, in the way that I want to like most any game that seems to be about gathering, crafting and building. The tech tree is deep and wide, and survival is non-trivial and seems to have been designed to encourage players grouping up into bands of at least 3. And this is what the game markets in its media messaging, so I would imagine this is the ideal that the developers are shooting for.
Unfortunately, if that is the vision for the game, then the developers seem to have forgetten John Gabriel's Greater Internet ♥♥♥♥wad Theory, and accidentally given a great deal of advantage to griefers. This game is a griefer's haven, to be frank. You can expect griefers to begin harassing you within about 30 minutes of building anywhere near the starting area - stealing anything you set down for any purpose, even preventing you from crafting things. You can avoid the griefers, somewhat, by heading out into the larger island, but you can still expect them to hit whatever you've built roughly every 24 hours, usually when you're logged off and incapable of defending your things. Even the structures that are supposed to offer more "aggressive" defense just aren't a threat that will remotely dissuade any but the most casual raiders.
So, I do not recommend this game as its been marketed. I like building things with others, which is what this game claims to be about, but in reality this game is basically Rust with more traditional MMO trappings.

Trust me in about a year this game will be something to look at.
CONS
-
- That's right, after you've invested many hours gathering resources and building walls miracle zombies will spawn directly inside your camp and sit there destroying it (even while you are offline). This leads to mostly the first 2-3 hours upon logging in, rebuilding the destruction, further decreasing your ability to progress.
-
- Currently in game you can hop a wall (or easily enter through a broken destroyed by a zombie) of a great empire and proceed to plunder their farms, kill their cattle, steel their vegetables, carts, mounts. All without any affect from the criminal system. I'm sure this will be addressed at a later date, but for now, it's unbearable.
-

Walking 45 minutes in hopes to find a vein of iron so you can build a beginner building is currently not acceptable. This will be great when (imagining) trade routes are setup between major cities with players carrying goods between one point or another for profit. +
+ Leveling system I really enjoyed as well, what you do levels that skill. So if I'm farming I will level farming ect.
There are a ton more items I could touch on both negative and good, but I will digress.

Of course, with so much of the game's design rooted in the Civilization model, it's no wonder that Rise of Nations' research system also stands head and shoulders above the systems featured in other real-time strategy games. Although it isn't as comprehensive as the technology tree of Civilization III, Rise of Nations' research fields are still broader than those of just about any other real-time strategy game yet. There are four main areas of research: military, civil, commerce, and science. Each area has eight levels, as well as a top-level technology for each area once you reach the eighth stage. However, each of these technologies is balanced fairly well against the others, so you're free to choose the technological path you most prefer without worrying that your unbalanced research might leave you vulnerable in some way. Additionally, you'll conduct most of your research in a single building: the library. The consolidation of most of the game's technology under one roof is a breakthrough in logistics--you no longer have to go hunting for different buildings to conduct research.
Like Age of Empires, Rise of Nations features eight different ages: classical, medieval, gunpowder, enlightenment, industrial, modern, and information. Even though game's timeline begins in the Dark Ages and ends in a futuristic era, it manages to strike a perfect balance between the different ages and the breadth of technologies available in each. And despite all that depth, Rise of Nations is paced well and isn't overly complex--the game's interface makes it easy to understand what you need to do to advance to the next age, and the resource costs of advancement are challenging to meet without being ridiculously expensive.
The only really serious complaint that hard-core strategy fans could level at Rise of Nations is that the game doesn't have a story-based campaign like so many other recent real-time strategy games. Instead, Rise of Nations features a single-player "conquer the world" campaign in which the world is divided into sections, like in the classic board game Risk. You start out as one nation on this map and attempt to literally conquer every other country in the world. Controlling your nation on the world map is turn-based, but when you enter into territory you don't control, the game changes to real-time mode. Interestingly, the campaign offers different scenarios for different territories. In one territory, your mission might be to withstand a barbarian raid for 30 minutes. In another, it might be to race across a map to destroy a barbarian encampment. In a contested territory, you might have a normal conquest game in which you must eliminate the enemy. Capturing and holding additional territories gives you benefits, such as an extra army or resource bonuses you can take with you into every tactical battle. However, this campaign, which is really just a glorified version of Risk, isn't as developed as the actual real-time game. Still, it's enjoyable, if a bit simple, and it adds a substantial single-player component to the game.

Well, where should I start? There's probably two completely different perspectives to look at this game from, one being long-time Sonic fan and being thrown back into the depths of nostalgia with this game, and the other being a completely neutral person. I'm one of the former.
Just as a quick note: Unlike everybody else, I will NOT acknowledge this game having DRM (I even forgot the name of the company again), I don't care AT ALL about it. It does not have anything to do with the game itself, so it should not even be mentioned here.
I've heard someone give this game a (-) just because it's Special Stages are in a "ugly looking 3d effect mode". I think it's hilarious.
Please don't continue reading if you don't want Spoilers about the game.
-------------- SPOILER ALERT ---------------
So, I will put some + and - and I'm totally not biased by my childhood here. Not at all. (I'm totally not)
---- UPs: ----
+ The Soundtrack is godlike. The new tracks are great and the old ones are very good remixes of their old versions.
+ The Design is classic Sonic. 16-bit graphics, Stupid traps, way too many rings, challenging bosses, just like back in the day.
+ TItanic Monarch Zone reminded me of a freaking cathedral, it's awesome
+ Oil Ocean is one of the least popular zones of Sonic 2, and in this game it's become a very solid and fun stage. I loved how the fire shield can set the oil on fire.
+ They've brought in interesting new ideas on new and old zones alike. Like the different fluids in Chemical Plant or the smokey fog in Oil Ocean (which I know was used in Sandopolis' pyramid, but it's a very cool idea for Oil Ocean too)
+ TONS and even more TONS of references to older Sonic games, other Sega franchises, and even their commercials and slogans (just play Studiopolis and see how many of the references you catch)
+ PUYO PUYO BOSS
---- DOWNS: ----
- Green Hill and Chemical Plant are pretty overused. They were in Generations already. How about Emerald Hill or Labyrinth?
- The Special Stages are pretty bad and not fun to play.
- 32 special coins to collect meaning 32 Blue Sphere levels is a bit too many. Especially considering you can unlock it as a minigame anyway
---- OTHER NOTES: ----
o I felt like the game is a bit short. But what can I say, it's pretty much average of classic Sonic game length.
o I don't know what to think of the & Knuckles feature. I highly dislike that meme, but I guess I can consider it funny.
o The game offers Sonics skills from CD and 3&K, however, only for a No Save Game, which sucks, but it's not too bad
o Time Attack on PC is prone to hackers, making serious competetion absolutely impossible.
---- FINAL NOTE: ----
The task the developers were given was to "make a Sonic game how it would've looked like on the Sega Saturn." (That's why it looks like 16-bit by the way, nothing new, Mega Man has been doing that for years)
That's what they did, and I personally I think they almost hit the bullseye with Sonic Mania. It's not perfect but very close. I think it would've been very successful on the Saturn.
Sonic Mania is an absolute must-play for any Sonic Fan and Jump'n Run/Platformer Fan. It is also great for people new to the Sonic Franchise. Here's a challenge for those new to Sonic: Play this game, then play Sonic 1, 2, 3&K and CD, and then try to recognize the enemies and stage parts you've seen in this game.

Honestly, I haven't had this much fun with a Sonic game in a long time.
Now, I'm not gonna jump on the "There hasn't been a good sonic game in 20+ years hurr hurr" train because, honestly, that's dishonest, and really would be a letdown to how much fun I had with later Sonic games. I enjoyed Unleashed (mostly) and I enjoyed Lost World, Both the Adventure Games And Sonic Rush/Rush Adventure.
But I will agree that this is the best Sonic has been *Since* Sonic 3&K. Other games were good, they were fun, I had a smile on my face for (almost) all of Generations. (Sonic 06 Level though? really?)
But none of them gave me the Pure "Sanic Fan" joy I felt 13+ years ago every time I'd boot up my old (Now defunct, RIP) Genesis.
This game Recaptures what made those games so damn *good*, right down to a Selection of levels from all 4 (I'll count 3&K as 1 game instead of 2) Main Classic Sonic games, With some new Levels Sprinkled in to *kind of* keep it from basically being Sonic Generations 2: Electric Boogaloo. Each level has Some old setpieces as well as entirely new Segments, and they're put together REALLY well. I've played Taxman and Stealth Romhacks, so I was well-aware of their Level Design expertise, which only helped me feel hyped before release.
The game isn't 100% *Perfect*. No game is, after all. I agree with a lot of people that there should have been more New Levels. A couple of old Level choices are ones I would have made differently. (I really just... Don't like Oil ocean)
But Overall, this is the game that takes Sonic back to a time before being dragged through a mixed bag of Decent Experiments in 3D that were overall fun if a bit Flawed, as well as Steaming Disasters that in retrospect make you ask "Wtf were you even thinking Sega, Human girls should not do that to sonic"
Fun notes about PC version compared to Console Versions:
A dedicated Super Form Button when using the Controller (Possibly with Keyboard too, but I don't use the keyboard for Platformers.) The PSwitchOne Versions do it Sonic 3 Style, where you double jump to transform, while this Version Has you Jump and then press Y. (this may have been added as an Update to console releases but I haven't really seen it yet.)
The game has a LOT of unused assets buried inside, which can be Modded back into the game (Including assets from the Mobile ports of Sonic 1, 2, CD, and the Cancelled port of Sonic 3, the original title for the game as it was pitched to Sega "Sonic Discovery", etc) While the data exists on the Console versions, naturally you can't access it nearly as easily as you can on PC.
DISCLAIMER:
I am 100% aware of the Denuvo BS DRM. I really do Recommend finding a crack for the game after buying it, *if you feel it's necessary*
I've had none of the strange performance issues many complain about, but I might just be lucky. Still, make your voice heard, spam the ♥♥♥♥ out of Sega to remove Denuvo, because that's honestly 100% stupid. But I still recommend buying the game because that tells Sega you want More Games like this. Maybe we'll get a Sonic Mania 2, with more new levels and Maybe Ice Cap Zone (I fkin love that level)

EXCELLENT in it's simplicity. This 'game' seems a lot more complicated than it is. While you are basically learning Assembly programming (which is the best part of this. it's practical learning), Assembly's concepts are -extremely- simple. I'm talking concepts like basic addition and subtraction. If you can do those two things, you CAN underatand this game. It comes with a very elegantly written fourteen page manual that tells you everything you need to know plus a little bit of flavor text to get you into the narrative. The main difference between actual Assembly and this 'game' is that the fictional computer you're using basically has several different CPUs or "nodes" that can each be programmed seperately and are usually capable of talking to each other. There are always multiple ways of solving a problem. You can make it as hard or as easy on yourself as you want. There are achievements for figuring out how to optimize your code in clever ways. You can, however, beat this game ignoring all of that. To top it off, the game comes with a 'sandbox' mode that allows you to create any program you want without the limitations of the main puzzles. There is even a mode that allows you to create your own puzzles to challenge other people. A very complete package that includes everything you could want but never gets in your way.
If you have any interest in computers or programming what-so-ever and also enjoy 'puzzle games', I HIGHLY reccomend that you give this a try. It's very novel, well priced, very fun, and will teach you valuable real-life programming concepts.

Aside from that, the game is fun, but can be difficult. It is easy to tick people off or get ticked off, so war is essentially inevitable. It is a primitive yet complex (i know its contradictory) battle set up, with the movement of the armies going from county to county (NOT country to country) in a real time situation. Once 2 armies start to battle, the complexity shows itself with things like army morale and different angles of attack as well as different situations in the battle (like the pursuit of fleeing armies once the battle has been won). Usually, even on the slowest setting, a battle takes about a minute, but there could be a number of battles one after another in a heavy conflict, which becomes tedious but is realistic and can be either rewarding or detrimental to progress in the game.
I am recommeding this game only because of the gameplay from the vanilla game, and not at all because of the overpriced DLCs that aren't even necessary. There are also plenty of FREE mods to make the game more fun in the steam workshop (and a few on nexus mods as well), and it can consume a lot of time, but expect to be disappointed from time to time from situations like if your king dies, and your heir is still underaged and a regent takes over which prevents you from doing anything substantial when your regent ends up destroying the country or leading to a civil war. Huh I didn't write a review of this? Well Frozen Synapse 2 is coming and looks awesome, might as well plug this real quick!
So here's the rundown of Frozen Synapse, it's a Cyberpunk themed Turn-based Tactical game made back in 2011, It was my favorite game to come out that year and I'm happy to say it still holds up very well
So in order to describe what makes Frozen Synapse awesome I gotta break some things down on how it works. Gameplay turns are taken in two phases. Planning phase and Outcome phase.
I'm actually going to start with outcome phase first, because it sets some ground rules as to how the game works. Outcome phase is what happens when both sides send orders from the planning phase. The important takeaway here is that Combat is deterministic, the first guy to get a shot off in most cases wins, and THERE IS NO RNG IN COMBAT. There's actual algorithms running underneath that checks the state of the attacking vatform (soldier) to determine if he hit or not, and when he will shoot. This is important but i must move on. Don't worry this will make sense soon.
Planning Phase is where you give orders to your troops, I.E move, Aim, duck, ect.
First off you'll notice a timeline which shows the history of what happened and if you hit "play" it will simulate the next turn depending on the orders you gave your vatforms. Remember how I said combat is deterministic? Well it applies here too. What you see is what happens in the "Outcome" phase (assuming the other guy does the same thing). But here's the cool part. You can simulate Enemy moves and actually TEST your strategy! So you can go "What if he rounds that corner? Will my machine gunner kill him in time?" or "can my shotgunner duck this incoming rocket?" And actually find out without committing them to that move.
That is what Makes Frozen Synapse awesome. Actually giving you the tools to think out tactics and strategy. It allows you to play mind games, test manuvers, see how well it works before hitting "Primed" button and having a go at it!
To top it all off nervous_testpilot's music completes the package.
Like a vast majority of games it's not perfect, and there are a few noticable flaws.
-The single player campaign doesn't have a difficulty curve, more like a series of spikes. Some scenarios are downright infuriating.
-While the world is interesting I found it to be a somewhat confusing and  got a little lost to be perfectly honest YMMV.
-The UI isn't the most polished thing on the planet, though it's not terrible and working around it isn't frustrating IMHO, some have reported problems however again YMMV.
-While I dig the Cyber-punky artstyle, it does look rather plain in-game, and the models are low poly, even for 2011 standards, not to mention the relativley flat textures.
Your mileage may vary with the level procedural generator (every match of Frozen Synapse uses it), it's not super important but it has screwed me over a few times. Still it is nice that it allows you to redo missions from a different angle, I found it cuts on some of the frustration as you can freely "restart' any time in Single player (You obviously cannot do this in multiplayer).
That all said despite the aforementioned issues, Frozen Synapse is a classic in my book. And the DLC is worth it since it's less "DLC mission pack" and more "Expansion pack" (New Unit, New Campaign, Co-op Play, new scenarios).

Rise of Nations is a unique RTS game where not every match will end with violence. Indeed the game also puts a focus on economy in addtion to military strength.
Gameplay is pretty much standard across all factions with the only differences being in regards as to how the structures look and a handful of unique units for each faction. There are a few economic differences but that's about it in terms of differences.
You take command of one of several different nations, guiding your nation from its humble beginnings in the stone age all the way to the modern age. Along the way, you research and develop new means of improving your nation such as by  developing currency based economics and acquirig wealth over a simple barter system. Over time your nation's boarders will expand and you'll control more territory which means more resources become availible to you. You start by needing simple food and lumber, later you develop the need for ore by mining at the base of a mountain. Later you discover a need for knowledge and so you construct universities to generate this knowledge through the schollars there. You also develop a need for wealth and set up caravans to travel between your various cities to generate this wealth.
As you progress through each age, buildings and units will aesthetically change to match the period so your small initial starting village in the stone age will become a large metropolis in the modern age. Most military units have to be upgraded to the next stage of development and some units will disappear completely. Your sword and spearmen will eventually be replaced by gun toting minutemen and your horsemen will be replaced by an armored tank. Your old Triemes will be replaced by modern warships capable of inflicting incredible damage by comparison.
Once in the modern age, you CAN develop nuclear weaponry but be advised that you should use it sparingly as there is a "doomsday counter" that begins the minute the first nuke impacts its target. Every time a nuke goes off, that counter goes down by one. If it reaches zero, everyone loses as the world burns.
Another gameplay aspect takes the form of Wonder Points. Each faction can construct a number of wonders, each of which offering different advantages to the faction that builds them. Be warned however, if another faction builds a wonder before you, you cannot build that same wonder to gain the same benefit. The only way to get it is to capture the city that the wonder was built in, which will in turn, turn the wonder over to you. Each wonder is also worth a specific number of points with the Pyramids of Giza being the lowest and the Supercollider being worth the most.
Victory conditions can be modified so that you can win in a variety of ways including but not limited to a military victory (i.e. conquering your enemies), a Wonder victory (accrueing the most Wonder Points), territory based (controling the most territory), or generic score based which includes military and economic scores.
The game is a little dated as its 2D graphics for everything but they're good graphics even for their time and the gameplay holds up well against the tests of time.

Well, where should I start? There's probably two completely different perspectives to look at this game from, one being long-time Sonic fan and being thrown back into the depths of nostalgia with this game, and the other being a completely neutral person. I'm one of the former.
Just as a quick note: Unlike everybody else, I will NOT acknowledge this game having DRM (I even forgot the name of the company again), I don't care AT ALL about it. It does not have anything to do with the game itself, so it should not even be mentioned here.
I've heard someone give this game a (-) just because it's Special Stages are in a "ugly looking 3d effect mode". I think it's hilarious.
Please don't continue reading if you don't want Spoilers about the game.
-------------- SPOILER ALERT ---------------
So, I will put some + and - and I'm totally not biased by my childhood here. Not at all. (I'm totally not)
---- UPs: ----
+ The Soundtrack is godlike. The new tracks are great and the old ones are very good remixes of their old versions.
+ The Design is classic Sonic. 16-bit graphics, Stupid traps, way too many rings, challenging bosses, just like back in the day.
+ TItanic Monarch Zone reminded me of a freaking cathedral, it's awesome
+ Oil Ocean is one of the least popular zones of Sonic 2, and in this game it's become a very solid and fun stage. I loved how the fire shield can set the oil on fire.
+ They've brought in interesting new ideas on new and old zones alike. Like the different fluids in Chemical Plant or the smokey fog in Oil Ocean (which I know was used in Sandopolis' pyramid, but it's a very cool idea for Oil Ocean too)
+ TONS and even more TONS of references to older Sonic games, other Sega franchises, and even their commercials and slogans (just play Studiopolis and see how many of the references you catch)
+ PUYO PUYO BOSS
---- DOWNS: ----
- Green Hill and Chemical Plant are pretty overused. They were in Generations already. How about Emerald Hill or Labyrinth?
- The Special Stages are pretty bad and not fun to play.
- 32 special coins to collect meaning 32 Blue Sphere levels is a bit too many. Especially considering you can unlock it as a minigame anyway
---- OTHER NOTES: ----
o I felt like the game is a bit short. But what can I say, it's pretty much average of classic Sonic game length.
o I don't know what to think of the & Knuckles feature. I highly dislike that meme, but I guess I can consider it funny.
o The game offers Sonics skills from CD and 3&K, however, only for a No Save Game, which sucks, but it's not too bad
o Time Attack on PC is prone to hackers, making serious competetion absolutely impossible.
---- FINAL NOTE: ----
The task the developers were given was to "make a Sonic game how it would've looked like on the Sega Saturn." (That's why it looks like 16-bit by the way, nothing new, Mega Man has been doing that for years)
That's what they did, and I personally I think they almost hit the bullseye with Sonic Mania. It's not perfect but very close. I think it would've been very successful on the Saturn.
Sonic Mania is an absolute must-play for any Sonic Fan and Jump'n Run/Platformer Fan. It is also great for people new to the Sonic Franchise. Here's a challenge for those new to Sonic: Play this game, then play Sonic 1, 2, 3&K and CD, and then try to recognize the enemies and stage parts you've seen in this game.

Honestly, I haven't had this much fun with a Sonic game in a long time.
Now, I'm not gonna jump on the "There hasn't been a good sonic game in 20+ years hurr hurr" train because, honestly, that's dishonest, and really would be a letdown to how much fun I had with later Sonic games. I enjoyed Unleashed (mostly) and I enjoyed Lost World, Both the Adventure Games And Sonic Rush/Rush Adventure.
But I will agree that this is the best Sonic has been *Since* Sonic 3&K. Other games were good, they were fun, I had a smile on my face for (almost) all of Generations. (Sonic 06 Level though? really?)
But none of them gave me the Pure "Sanic Fan" joy I felt 13+ years ago every time I'd boot up my old (Now defunct, RIP) Genesis.
This game Recaptures what made those games so damn *good*, right down to a Selection of levels from all 4 (I'll count 3&K as 1 game instead of 2) Main Classic Sonic games, With some new Levels Sprinkled in to *kind of* keep it from basically being Sonic Generations 2: Electric Boogaloo. Each level has Some old setpieces as well as entirely new Segments, and they're put together REALLY well. I've played Taxman and Stealth Romhacks, so I was well-aware of their Level Design expertise, which only helped me feel hyped before release.
The game isn't 100% *Perfect*. No game is, after all. I agree with a lot of people that there should have been more New Levels. A couple of old Level choices are ones I would have made differently. (I really just... Don't like Oil ocean)
But Overall, this is the game that takes Sonic back to a time before being dragged through a mixed bag of Decent Experiments in 3D that were overall fun if a bit Flawed, as well as Steaming Disasters that in retrospect make you ask "Wtf were you even thinking Sega, Human girls should not do that to sonic"
Fun notes about PC version compared to Console Versions:
A dedicated Super Form Button when using the Controller (Possibly with Keyboard too, but I don't use the keyboard for Platformers.) The PSwitchOne Versions do it Sonic 3 Style, where you double jump to transform, while this Version Has you Jump and then press Y. (this may have been added as an Update to console releases but I haven't really seen it yet.)
The game has a LOT of unused assets buried inside, which can be Modded back into the game (Including assets from the Mobile ports of Sonic 1, 2, CD, and the Cancelled port of Sonic 3, the original title for the game as it was pitched to Sega "Sonic Discovery", etc) While the data exists on the Console versions, naturally you can't access it nearly as easily as you can on PC.
DISCLAIMER:
I am 100% aware of the Denuvo BS DRM. I really do Recommend finding a crack for the game after buying it, *if you feel it's necessary*
I've had none of the strange performance issues many complain about, but I might just be lucky. Still, make your voice heard, spam the ♥♥♥♥ out of Sega to remove Denuvo, because that's honestly 100% stupid. But I still recommend buying the game because that tells Sega you want More Games like this. Maybe we'll get a Sonic Mania 2, with more new levels and Maybe Ice Cap Zone (I fkin love that level)

After seeing the store page, I thought
was one of those simple and perhaps lame platformers but I was happy to note I was wrong. Despite (or perhaps because of) its simple presentation it packs with quite a lot of high-quality content.
Game has 30 levels placed in groups of six through five worlds with their own distinct graphics styles and soundtrack (that fits the game very well), with enemies and traps going with that. In that it strikes a similarity with Super Mario Bros 3 and its diverse worlds. Of course
totally lacks a story and
Mos' suits are merely visual.
Game play mechanics are almost as simple as they can be: Mos (I take it's the name of the protagonist) may run, jump and wall-jump and occasionally swing from a rope. Controls are simple and very slick and hit boxes are good, so every once in a while when you die, you know its your own fault.
By the way, I used Xbox 360 controller but controls were simple and fine enough to play with a keyboard. My only regret is that up key is both "up" in menu and "jump" in-game, despite there being a separate jump key. I had to remap "up" to another button on the controller to make it playable but I'm glad this was possible.
Level design is top-notch. While levels are usually rather linear with minor sidetracking, there is also a secret area or two in each and every level. In the course of the game Mos goes from avoiding giant bees, rats and spike traps to dodging ghosts and fireballs while avoiding saw blades and lava. Disappearing and reappearing blocks are probably the only platformer trap trope missing from the game.
The difficulty curve is good, starting from rather easy first levels but going to pretty challenging levels close to the end. However, as a gamer who plays a lot of platformers, I would not call any of the levels very difficult, even if they are not a cakewalk either. There are respawn points every now and then to alleviate unnecessary restarts, although they work only once per game.
Game supports "ghosts", i.e. the runs of other players (and earlier runs of yourself) are shown, so you can use them to perfect your run or even try to beat them to the top of the leaderboards if you like that sort of thing.
There are a lot of collectables in all levels. In addition to completing and speed running, to fully complete a level one has to grab all the coins (they are never hidden in unfair fashion), grab the hidden golden skull of the level and find the hidden daily collectable, day charm.
The day charm is in a different level in each day of the month. There's an achievement for grabbing all of them, so ideally one would find them over the course of a single 30-day month. I liked this challenge a lot, though some people might disagree with time-limited achievements like this.
Finally there's even a super secret that encompasses several levels throughout the game. It felt very rewarding to find this ultimate secret after a couple days of confusion and mad exploration.
Getting achievements grants you suits, hats and skins for Mos. It's useless but fun feature to bring some personality to your character. You can be a dinosaur wearing a suit, a pipe and a top hat, which is just priceless.
After about 17 hours and little over a month I was done. After all this time I can say
is a great platformer that is not too easy but not too difficult either and that has a lot of stuff to do and find out. If you love platformers, get it!

So I got this game in a humble bundle.  I didn't think much of it, but thought the name sounded cool.   I mean it was a staff pick, so who knows what I'm going to get.
Then I played it.  OH WOW!  This game reminds me of another game called spacechem, and now that I'm writing this review, I can see on the page that it was written by the same guy, and it really feels like that.
The entire game is about coding.  You work on a microprocessor and have a number of tasks to complete, and to be honest, this isn't a game where you pretend to code, or you use a very fake coding language.  No, if you play this game and you beat it, you HAVE programmed and you have used assembly, it's as simple as that.   This is a game, but at the same time, this is essentially the same thing as real coding (only it's a bit harder on this game for artificial constraints).
To play the game you get a manual (which you really should look at) and an assignment.  It can be as simple as take in two variables and add them together.  Or as complex as multiply them together.... and yes multiplying the values is significantly harder than adding them.   You also get up to 12 processors that are connected through ports.  They can read in information, operate on it and push that information to another port (or the same one).
The complexity comes in that each processor has a limited number of operations you can record on it.  There's some beautiful control codes (jumps, labels and the rest) but rather than give you unlimited space ( which could make the multiplication simple) you have about 10 operations (maybe a little more) and that's it. Then the code loops.  You can use any number of available processors (sometimes there's small limitations, but you always have more than enough) but trying to make the computer do exactly as the tasks says is challenging.
There's a few other wrinkles.  Each processor is given ONE register.. (and that my dear friends is why multiplication is a nightmare. )
So overall how is it?  Well I'm a programmer, I love programming, and I am absolutely in love with this game.  It's not for everyone but it's a BOTH a great introduction to REAL assembly, and a fantastic game.  It's definitely not for everyone, but I can't praise this game highly enough.   I don't know if everyone will fall in love with this game, but if you have played spacechem before and want something a little harder, give this a shot.  If you haven't played spacechem and don't know if you'll enjoy programming, I'd recommend Spacechem only because it's a little more accessible, however both games are excellent and I highly recommend them.

If that sounds like it won't deter you then this game is great. Warframe is a very fun game that is free. I was broke, and wanted a new game, so I go this. I reccomend the game, just remember that you shouldn't spend money on the game! I spent $50 on the game, and within 3 days I quit. It is really fun especially at the start. Love the movement mechanics, and always use a bow!

When you first boot up the game you will likely be confused on what charachter to pick, the game mechanics, and what on earth is going on, but that will pass soon after you cleave the first grineer in half.
But this game truly excels at a few major points that make it worth a try for any player, but it also come with a few diminishing returns as well.
PACING--- One thing that is for sure is that this game will not hold your hand explaining and slowly taking you into it. It moves at quite a quick pace, and for those of you who catch on quick thats amazing, but for others, like me, youtube is you closest ally -- that or your friend that got you interested in the game.
VARIETY -- This game offers a variety of playstyles choosing your warframes, there are warframes anywhere from a gunslinging cowgirl to a dragonlike tank- each with unique playstyles and roles, and with the addition of the open world map Eidolon has hundreds of hours of gameplay stored within itself, I myself have played about 580 hours and have only gained 14 out of 24 mastery ranks (I have not been trying to get the ranks, just a casual player).
STORYLINE -- The game has a storyline, but it is nothing impressive, and at times something may happen that will make you say either heck yeah, or what the heck depending on how you feel about the characters. But the storyline is nothing impressive although i have not seen this story played out before, so if you are going for a story heavy or story oriented game this may not be for you, otherwise it should not make a major impact.
REPETITION -- The game has a variety of tilesets, and missions, but it becomes somewhat boring afet a long time if you do not have friends to play with or a podcast/ book to listen to. Another problem that the limited tilesets, and missions encounter is the situation where you need to grind for an item and you play the same tileset over and over until you gain that item, which for those of you who are not a major fan of grinding for items this may be a turn off because to build any weapon you need to farm materials, the build the weapon which can take anywhere from 1 to 2 days, or you can do what a majoriy of people do, andpay to win which brings me to the next topic.
MICROTRANSACTIONS -- This game uses microtransactions in almost everything. It is by no means required to play the game, but it is extremely tempting, and there is even a way for you to get this in game money through the game by trading with other players, but for those of you who have a loose wallet, I would be wary. In total the in game transactions are no big deal, but if you want to pay to win you can, and for tose of you who hate those games where one can pay to win, I would not reccomend this game.
By all means this is not by all means all the items the game has to offer but it is all that I will cover. Other items it has are Daily events, Weekly events, anniversary events, and hourly events to keep the gamers playing the game invested and excited.

100% OJ ought to be my all-time favourite board game!
The goal is to be the first person to turn-in 5 missions.
By default, the first mission is to collect 10 stars. Head 'home' to collect the next mission; where you can choose between more stars or kills! Kills do not include only monsters encountered on the board, but other players as well Muwhhahah!
The more stars/wins you get in a game, the more "star points" you'll get afterwards.
You can spend those in the shop to buy new cards, characters, dice, character colour packs, unlock discounts, new maps and much more!
You can play the game by yourself through the campaign. Completing it gives you "star points" and helps you unlock certain items in the shop (i.e: Tomomo character)
But you can also play with your friends and strangers! If you go to "free play" you can create/join lobbies and play with others :) Also win "star points" and "oranges"!
During free play, the lobby leader can choose which map to play on and select good/bad boosts for the match -- Some boosts includes star tiles x2, movement dice x2, add random trap to the board, walk backwards, insert bomb...
Like most games, 100% OJ has DLC.
In the steam shop, you can purchase extra characters (they come in bundles of 2 characters!)
There are also "boosters."
Here's the thing, while you might think you're buying a pack of booster cards, on the contrary, purchasing this actually unlocks a booster slot in the in-game shop!
For example, when you begin to play, you will notice 2 booster slots in the shop (first two items). Purchasing one from the steam-shop will add a 3rd and 4th one! With brand new cards for you to collect! :D
I bought this game as a "friendly bundle" and all 3 of my friends loved it!
Currently grinding candies for the Halloween costumes and I can't wait to collect them all!! :D (Woohoo! I officially collected them all :D)
Like any other game, it's more fun with friends, but 100% OJ is very playable by yourself too~

"Easy to learn but hard to master" was the first phrase to come into my mind when I played "Ūplink".
And that's pretty much the phrase to think of when discribing "Ūplink". But what does diverge "Ūplink" from other games? And for first: What kind of game is "Ūplink"?
"Ūplink" is a linear hacking game. Among the others, "Ūplink" is their "old brother". What I mean is that "Ūplink" has been the first remarkable game based on hacking to come out. At my point of view "Ūplink" has therefore some advange. It's not that all others stole ideas, but who knows wheather without "Ūplink" hacking games would be the same. I now want to talk a little about the gameplay.
You're playing as an "Ūplink Agent", so someone working for the company named "Ūplink" and your exercise is to successfully complete missions. Some missions require you to steel data, some others need you to delete files and sometimes you need to replace stuff... On others' systems. Sounds easy? It's not! First of all, you'll need to connect to your aim using a long chain through multiple ports, which slows down the time they need to trace you. Then you probably won't have the right gear; you need to ūpgrade or purchase different software and better hardware with hardly gained credits, to ensure your hack will run like it should. Eventually you will need to delete you log and then quickly disconnect, not beeing traced. If your victims get to know your position, you can get in serious trouble and that happens faster than you think. The graphics are, as usual for Introversioner, as simplyfied as possible, but therefore the game requires less than 100 megabytes of memory, so you will always be able to store it.
Although "Ūplink", which has the dot within the "U" accidentaly, is not my type of game I'd recommend to all fans of strategy games, especially those who like hacking-puzzles. Ūplink is innovative and a lot of fun, coming in the Introversioner bundle it's also pretty cheap. I cannot assure this will appeal to you, but I think "Ūplink" is worth a try.
