Praise the Gods of gaming, they have looked down upon my retched digital soul and have lifted me and redeemed me of my platforming inadequacies. Lo! As the CRT lights of their brilliance shone upon me, they placed in my palms the grail of Platform Puzzle gaming “Marblize”! PRAISE YE THE GODS!!!!
Marblize is a 3D platform puzzler that really brings nothing new to the genre but it’s done it so well it really dose feel like a fresh coat of paint.
You, as a marble (Man, have I got one big ball), roll, skid, jump and slide your way through beautifully rendered platforms, some in woods, metals and even some as old fashion wooden colour blocks. On each level you will need to think and explore you way, finding triggers to push or set, or find powers to unlock alternative paths. In amongst this you have the choice to find coins and/or paints & patterns to unlock so as to customise you marble and deadly traps with no escape.
To move around Marblize, requires you to use your mouse for looking (you are just above and behind your marble) and your WASD keys for movement but where ever you are looking with your mouse, it is the forward direction you will travel, so a bit of hand-eye co-ordination is needed (and some real cool Drifting will your ball(s) hanging off the edge). LMB to jump over obstacles or chasms and Q to steady and slow your movement on narrow ledges or paths. If you do get stumped upon a section of the level, you can zoom out, albeit a limited distance, with the Z key to find a route and X to zoom back to your marble.
If you fall, you die and re-spawn to the last checkpoint you touched, and the death will get recorded on your stats for that run of the level. Get caught in a dead end trap or simply get too confused with an area, you can press R to re-spawn to a checkpoint but that also will be counted as a death.
Yes, racing through the levels to set the fastest time is a good thing but Marblize encourages exploration, which is fun, rewarding and dangerous at the same time. Every block or path you see is  solid game area, there are no fake background blocks or invisible walls, so the temptation to jump to them is so overwhelming you just have to try. Cheer if you succeed or laugh as you miss and die. Or, as you fall to your death, you can get very lucky and happen to land on a very narrow ledge and then fight you way back up to the play area (do-able but frustratingly fun). But if you want those coins or want that paint or pattern for your Marble, the game taunts you to try, nay, it double dares you to.
That is another thing, there is no quit rage on this, when you die or fail, you are having too much fun, you just laugh at yourself, dust yourself off and go again.
Traps and triggers are not a simple ‘hit that button and go’ affair. You need to actually stop and think through each piece of the puzzle presented. You will have Timer, Toggle, Hold and Permanent triggers to play with. Also some of the powers will be Freeze (to cross over water), Magnet, to climb and/or roll along walls, Radio Powers that you can flip through to turn on/off certain coloured walls and floors and finally Jump/No-Jump that will mess with you ability to jump over obstacles or chasms. You will even have to backtrack over certain areas of a level to unlock new areas to advance, so you will need all of you Vulcan logic in this game.
The Menu Options are chock full with graphic, lighting, rendering options that even a low end computer can enjoy very beautiful graphics, still rendered shiny and pleasing to the eye, even at the lowest of settings. Sound can be turned off or scaled down to your pleasure and the music is pleasing and suits the mood of the game but over time may become monotonous (to counter this, I recommend anything from Nine Inch Nails). It is all very neat and tidy, gorgeous.
Customisation of your Marble is a welcome sight, and there are so many combinations of colours (64 in total) and Patterns (168 to choose) that you unlock as you find them throughout the game. The tutorial (comes in three sections, Basic, Logic and Power Ups) is wonderful and explains the mechanics of the game very well.
There are four sections in game containing a total of Sixty levels (there was eighteen levels in the first sector alone) so this game is no quick walk in the park, and replay value will give you hours more, trying to better your time or finding all the hidden/missed items.
There was only one niggle glitch through the whole time I played. That being your marble would sink into the floor once in a while, a small clipping error, but it is one that you can live with and dose not detract from the game.
Plexagon Studios has put together a game that will stay on your drive and be played for the next ten years. If you love 3D platform puzzlers, buy Marblize. If you don’t love 3D platform puzzlers (Like me) buy Marblize. If your a complete, heartless, penny-pinching, green blooded ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, go and mind meld with a Targ!

It is hard to fit this game into a Genre. Obviously it is a strategy game, and it has turns, but it is not a turn-based strategy game per se.
You see, Turn based Strategy like XCOM or Civilization often rely on the simple scheme of Player A, then Player B, then Player A etc. Frozen Synapse however takes a unique approach on it: Both Players at the same time. Each turn takes 5 seconds where each player has to plan the movements of their units - at the same time. Once both players are happy with what their units are going to do they hit the "Prime" button, and the scenario is played out. At this stage there is nothing the player can do to inflcuence the outcome. You can't command your units and have to watch as they win or loose, based on what you told them to do.
This concept might sound weird at first but it allows for very balanced gameplay as no player has an advantage. You as the player are just a camera from above commanding the units, waiting for them to fulfull their orders. It allows for a higher strategial depth, a 5 second turn can take 5+ minutes to figure out. The game provides a "simluation" button, where youc an preview what your units will do. You can, at the same time, give the enemy units commands for the purpose of simulating to test your scenario. It is easy to get lost in the amount of tinkering you need to do, and you never know what is going to happen.
Overall this game is game is great, it offers a great breath of fresh air into the genre of strategy games. I would suggest waiting for Frozen Synpase 2, as it will release in "Late 2016". It looks like this game and probably playes like it as well.
If you can't wait or just want a great game in your library buy this.

I was going to make a positive and negative list of this game but frankly I cannot think of many bad things to say about it so I'll just make a list of points why I recomend it:
- You can run it in almost any device, including laptos and tablets.
- regular matches (minus waiting time) are very quick plus you can stop and resume playing at any time.
- you can just play one game at a time or you can open many multiplayer games at the same time and just play your turn in the ones that are ready.
- because of the 2 previously mentioned points it is perfect either for a dedicated session or just for a quick play during a break, while commuting or when the boss is not looking.
- because the turns are executed simultaneously and calculated in the server there is no randomness or unfair advantages like in some games where players take alternate turns.
- Variety and options for custom matches look sufficient to me.
- the music is excellent.
- probably the best tactical only game out there. some have tried to copy it but this one is still the best.
- Frozen Synapse may scare new players with it's unattractive main menus and apparent complexity, however in my opinion it is a very simple game to play. You don't have to check stats, keep track of resources, memorise maps or abilities. Just give orders, press a key to simulate the results of those orders and once you're happy commit your turn.
- Regarding the price after all this time it still looks high however it is not very uncommon to find this game discounted somewhere or as part of a bundle. Still for the hours I've spent on in I'd gladly pay full price, especially considering I've paid > £40 for many AAA games so boring and generic that I couldn't spend more than 15 minutes in them.

For a game made by a one person development "team", I found this game to be pretty well made. This game still has it flaws, but they are understandable as this game was more of a barebones version of high end RPGs. Exploring the different maps was enjoyable, the puzzles were good, and the boss rooms were pretty fun to fight in.
The beginning of the game might be a little off putting, as you have no idea how the game works and pretty much everything is level locked, but once you get into it, the game is pretty good.
Some things that could be worked on:
The aiming in the game is really really bad. The hitboxes don't match the skills animations and there is a soft auto aim feature that attempts to aim (poorly) at the monsters your mouse is hovered over. You have to position your mouse not on the monsters to get any spells to go the way you want.
Mana is depleted pretty easily especially when you're fighting mobs of monsters. You have to carefully snipe/lure monsters one by one or else risk being mobbed and brutally killed. Then after a kill, you have to stand still for 10 seconds to replenish your health/mana.
I totally understand why certain hurdles are in the game though. If the game had a constant health regeneration, the monsters would have to be rebalanced. There are aspects that are made very simple and feels clunky, but it was so the game wouldn't be too comlpicated to balance.

100% OJ ought to be my all-time favourite board game!
The goal is to be the first person to turn-in 5 missions.
By default, the first mission is to collect 10 stars. Head 'home' to collect the next mission; where you can choose between more stars or kills! Kills do not include only monsters encountered on the board, but other players as well Muwhhahah!
The more stars/wins you get in a game, the more "star points" you'll get afterwards.
You can spend those in the shop to buy new cards, characters, dice, character colour packs, unlock discounts, new maps and much more!
You can play the game by yourself through the campaign. Completing it gives you "star points" and helps you unlock certain items in the shop (i.e: Tomomo character)
But you can also play with your friends and strangers! If you go to "free play" you can create/join lobbies and play with others :) Also win "star points" and "oranges"!
During free play, the lobby leader can choose which map to play on and select good/bad boosts for the match -- Some boosts includes star tiles x2, movement dice x2, add random trap to the board, walk backwards, insert bomb...
Like most games, 100% OJ has DLC.
In the steam shop, you can purchase extra characters (they come in bundles of 2 characters!)
There are also "boosters."
Here's the thing, while you might think you're buying a pack of booster cards, on the contrary, purchasing this actually unlocks a booster slot in the in-game shop!
For example, when you begin to play, you will notice 2 booster slots in the shop (first two items). Purchasing one from the steam-shop will add a 3rd and 4th one! With brand new cards for you to collect! :D
I bought this game as a "friendly bundle" and all 3 of my friends loved it!
Currently grinding candies for the Halloween costumes and I can't wait to collect them all!! :D (Woohoo! I officially collected them all :D)
Like any other game, it's more fun with friends, but 100% OJ is very playable by yourself too~
There is also frequent updates and new content. Every now and then there will be EXP bonuses for multiplayer games. The little things that shows they still care and polish the game :)

Що на сьогоднішній день стоїть на вершині гори ігробудування? Графон. Багатокористувацький режим. Мікротранзакції. Лутбокси. І обов’язково з деталізованим туторіалом, де гравця за ручку проведуть по всім (ВСІМ, Я СКАЗАВ!) аспектам гри і покажуть що і як.
Але розробники Desync поклали жирний болт на всі правила і тенденції. Графон? В топку! Даєш кубізм і неонові кольори а-ля «Трон». Дружелюбність до гравців? Ні, не чули. Вступна місія? Ага, вже. Толкові підказки при найменшому зсуванні гравця по лінії азимуту? Чотири монітори з поясненнями і пара-трійка повідомлень під час відкриття нового аспекту гри підійде? Легкий, релакс геймплей? Перепрошую, але слабакам тут не місце. І знайте що? Гра таки міцно тримає в своїх обіймах.
Що, на перший погляд, тут може приваблювати?! Відповідь проста: той самий хардкорний, рафінований і недружній до гравців геймплей у жанрі «стрілялка». Схема проста: нас телепортують на рівень, додають ворогів, а далі «нехай переможе найкращий». Ціль: розфасувати «неонове м’ясо» на цеглинки і пройти в портал-вихід. І все? А от і ні. Боти дають неслабі затріщини, плюс перероджуються в найбільш незручний час. Це якщо вже не брати до уваги їх різновиди. Хтось врізає дуба від одного замаху капцем, а хтось спокійно переживає постріл повністю покращеної «рельси». Поведінка теж не одноманітна. Є такі, що пруть в лоб, хтось підскакує і лупить згори тощо. Але особливо мене бісив місцевий аналог хайтек монстрятини, яка відкидає ласти моментально, варто лише помітити. Але якщо вельмишановний гравець буде ловити гав, то отримає гарпуном поміж очі, який потягне жертву до мисливця. Напряму. Через шипи, кислоту і прірви. Результат трохи передбачуваний.
Саме час сказати пару слів щодо дизайну рівнів. Виконана кожна локація по принципу «яке прикре самогубство». В розпалі стрілянини потрапити на пастку, шипи, сокиру-маятник чи просто гулькнути в якусь прірву можна як два пальці об асфальт. Гіпотетично, даний ландшафт мав би не тільки провокувати гравця розтрощити клавіатуру і мишу після чергового фейлу, а й допомагати в подоланні супротивників, які не обсипаються з однієї подачі. Але це в теорії. На практиці практичніше буде всіх перестріляти до бісової матері не особливо думаючи про додаткові бали стилю (привіт Bulletstorm!). Так-так, ви все правильно зрозуміли. Прояви вашого злого генія у вигляді особливо винахідливих способів анігіляції ворогів будуть щедро винагороджуватись бонусними балами. Ті, кому абсолютно фіолетово на «священу корову всєя відеоігор», принцип «в кого більше/довше/швидше/крутіше» можуть задати логічне питання: «навіщо підливати гас в і без того гарячий геймплей і, як наслідок, палаючий ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥?!». Відповідь: покращення зброї. Точніше не самі покращення, а фрагменти – місцевий аналог валюти. Так, в цій грі є пара штук, які роблять життя простішим і складнішим одночасно. Чому простішим? Бо наявна мінімальна кастомізація. Чому складнішим? Бо для отримання місцевого аналогу Бенджамінів Франклінів на зеленому папері доведеться чудити ті самі фінти. Працює система просто і елегантно. Є чотири властивості ворогів (помічених відповідними кольорами), які вносять свою «родзинку» в цей вінегрет: сила, швидкість, сповільнення часу і стабільність. Є спеціальний термінал, де занесені абсолютно всі фінти з короткою інструкцією. В тому ж «кампутєрі» можна задати трюк під кожного крутого супротивника. В результаті, коли ми вбиваємо відповідного гада потрібним методом, врубається режим «desync» під час якого за кожну розмазану по підлозі гадину наш гаманець будуть поповнювати фрагменти, за які можна буде покращувати зброю.
Якщо вже зайшла мова про зброю, то арсенал тут стандартний: пістолет, дробаш, ракетниця, рельса тощо. Кожна зброя має свою специфіку і альтернативний режим вогню, який допоможе у виконанні хитровкрученних комбо. В кожен ствол можна запхати до 3х покращень. Також наявна додаткова зброя в якості окремого бонусу, який активується на короткий час. Набої можна підібрати з розгачених ворогів.
Кампанія коротка (особливий шик – боси, які сприймаються як місцевий аналог заспокійливого. Боси. Заспокійливого), але тіпати від неї буде дні три. Кому буде мало – є бонус рівні з мутаторами. Правила даної забави: вам дають в руки два стволи і випускають на рівень. З кожною кімнатою будуть додаватись веселі особливості, а-ля «можна вбити лише в голову» або «не працює підкат».
Музика – РЕСПЕКТ. Всі, хто любить електроніку або зависає під synthwave, залишаться задоволені. Решті пропоную послухати на ютьюбі Daniel Deluxe. Якщо зайде – ласкаво просимо.
Вердикт. Гра, яка не лялькається з гравцем, як з діснеєвською тендітною принцесою. Високооктановий хардкор only. Є непогані задатки для міряння скілом. Купа досягнень, які видаються за кожний чих. Графоній стильний, але на втомлені очі ліпше не бавитись. Однозначно рекомендую фанатам рафінованої, дистильованої і жорсткої класики.

Not gonna talk about the gameplay itself other to say I played both vanilla and then later Thrones and Patriots before the Extended Edition and that I really enjoy(ed) both.
The Extended Edition has a number or improvements that I appreciated as a >100 hours player:
+ Much smoother animations (I highly recommend you watch gameplay - it's noticeable within seconds of playing and was especially noticeable during projectile-heavy combat with arrows and siege weapons).
+ Anti-aliasing, which helps a lot since there are a lot of small visual details which were previously quite badly aliased.
+ Improved multiplayer / online matchmaking etc.
+ Improved support for modern systems (although I recall having minimal issues on Windows 8.1 with my old version).
A few neutral points:
~ New backgrounds in menus. I miss the old ones, but do understand that they were pretty low res and generally don't look that nice on newer systems.
~ There are Steam achievements in the Extended Edition, but they're very generic and I don't feel like they add to the game in a meaningful way. I guess some people might appreciate them though.
~ Textures are supposed to be better but I can't really tell tbh. Counterpoint is that at least nothing looks different from what I'm used to, which is good.
~ Water is supposedly improved but I personally don't like the updated water that much. It's not /bad/ per se, I'm just not convinced it's an improvement over the original water in any way but technical. To me it feels like the updated water makes it harder to distinguish the boundary of Fog of War, but it's not a big deal.
~ There don't seem to be many good Workshop mods for the game as of Jan 2016. There's a few decent ones but nothing that I saw that made me think "damn that sounds really good, I'll definitely download that". Most of the 4-star mods are just pop-cap increases, which can make things messy balance-wise so aren't necessarily desirable (unlike something like TA where the original amount was quite constrictive).
~ Despite there being a DVD release of the RoN soundtrack, the Extended Edition still uses the original ADPCM 178kbps 22,050 KHz tracks. While the music itself is great, it's a real shame that the higher quality tracks were not put to use in this version of the game. (Thrones and Patriots tracks were released in higher quality to begin with)
~ There are some bugs not related to hardware or OS that I experienced occasionally in the original that may or may not be present in the Extended Edition. I haven't seen it said that they were explicitly fixed, but I've yet to experience them. (e.g. silos sometimes bug out and "fail" their missile launches, causing missiles to simply fly up and then disappear against non-missile-shielded targets)
And unfortunately there's a few negatives:
- Widely-experienced issues with music playback (music volume always resets to max and tracks often do not play, including regular ambient tracks (sometimes) as well as every victory and defeat (always)). Developer Skybox has yet to fix the issue and I did not experience it in the non-Extended Edition.
- My friend and I had trouble using the direct connect option for multiplayer, despite both configuring our firewalls to allow RoN through just like other games from this era. Fortunately the regular multiplayer lobbies work well enough anyway and we were able to get private games working via the Evolve VPN.
- A few other mildly annoying misc bugs etc. that I did -not- notice in my non-Extended Edition copy of the game. (see the RoN: EE Discussion forum on Steam for some examples)
- A few misc bugs which -were- present in the original haven't been fixed, but these are mostly minor. (e.g. in Entire World CtW you can accidentally "give away" your army the next turn if you sell a territory that you're moving into and don't cancel the move order)
Worth buying again if you already own Thrones and Patriots? Maybe. I got it at 75% off so the smoother animations and anti-alising alone were pretty worthwhile for me. If getting the game running properly on your PC was a pain before then the relatively hassle-free Extended Edition might be worth your investment.
If you've never played the game but think you'd enjoy it then I'd say the Extended Edition certainly seems like a much better option than grabbing the original. If you have vanilla, then maybe grab it on sale so that you can get Thrones and Patriots.

This is one of my all-time favorite games, and this game also means a lot to me since it's one of the earliest game I played with my best friend that's 9000 miles away from me now. Even though I played a LOT of different games during my time playing Rise of Nations, I always spent some time playing this game. I am no expert even though I spent hundreds of hours playing this game, since I only play games for fun, not to be a master at it. I did use the cheats for fun (cheat nuke on Classical age LOL) and it results to my lack of the skill to play the game. So pardon my incapability to speak about the technical details of the game.
The reason I spent so much time fooling around back then rather than seriously trying to master the game was because the fact that Rise of Nations is very fun to mess around with. You have a sandbox mode where you can pretty much create any scenario you want or make any kind of battles. The built-in cheats are also very fun to play with. I play games for fun, not to win.
Now about the game type, Rise of Nations is a classic old RTS game. You gather resources, build buildings & upgrades, build an army, attack your enemy and destroy their cities. It's just like Warcraft III's multiplayer (not dota, dota is a mod), Age of Empire, Stronghold Crusader, StarCraft, etc. These kind of games had its golden age back in early 2000s. Now, it's mostly dominated by Total War series, which are way more complicated and detailed since it's more focused on realism and strategy rather than the old RTS games, which are focused on the balance between building and combat. Old RTS games tend to be much more simpler due to limited technology at that time + they must have doubt people will like complex realistic strategy game, until Total War showed its success with Total War Medieval. Rise of Nations started to implement some complexity in-game by giving the effects of the terrain on the unit's performance, attritions, upgrades, more resources types, etc rather than a simple build-and-attack RTS game, but its gameplay is still kept simple and easy to learn.
Rise of Nations offers a lot of choices in the game by giving you a lot of nations, ages, game mode and maps to choose. You can fight on air, sea, and land with a lot of unit types. Each nation has their own unique units, which are usually the iconic units of the country (e.g British's Scottish Highlander, US's Continental Marines, Russia's T-80 tank, German's Tiger Tank, etc). The ages is a really good system that rarely got implemented in other RTS games. I only know Age of Empire also implemented this but it was very limited, and Empire Earth, just like RIse of Nations also implemented a large amount of choices for ages. Each ages has their own unique strategy and play style, offering way more variety to the gameplay.
The game itself is without question, heavily unbalanced. For example, Chinese's ability to instantly generate citizens itself is already very OP, allowing rapid constructions all over the territory and rapid resource gathering. I doubt the devs will do anything about this in the future since there are A LOT of elements in the game that are tied to one another but it's still definitely fun to play. If you're looking for a simple, fun, and easy to learn RTS games, Rise of Nations is definitely a good choice. You can also check out Empire Earth if you don't mind ugly graphics and small unit count for the same amount of fun. Rise of Nations is like the upgraded version of Empire Earth, it looks much better and the gameplay is much better too.
TL;DR It's simple, has a very large variety of gameplay, very easy to learn but hard to master, mediocre but acceptable graphics and animations (it's a 2003 game give it a break), and super fun gameplay.
Enuff said.

After playing it for six hours (and my daughter playing for 15) I have to say that the game is pretty good.  It's reminiscent of another indie game, "Haven and Hearth," where you group together with other people and build a community but feels more polished and with more support.  The community of people seems really friendly as in one night we made friends with two groups nearby.  I've only been killed by one player thus far, and more people just seem happy enough to be left alone and leave you alone in exchange.
That being said, I'd have to say that there's a few things that should be worked on.  One thing that would benifit this game would be some sort of system of "permanent lighting" to discourage night-time mobs from spawning in certain areas as you're developing a town.  Bonfires are great at the start for keeping players huddled from the darkness, but there needs to be a more permanent lighting source I feel.  That, or it needs some way to discourage mobs from attacking your gates and walls all the time.
The reason I say this, is because if it's not implemented, you'll spend a good amount of time building arrows rather than upgrading your town, battleing, or exploring.  While the game is certainly "early access," it was fun until I spent roughly 10-15 hours maintaining what I've built.  Another issue with this game for interested refunders, is it'll take about 5-10 hours to get to a point where you can make an accurate assessment on whether you like the game on the offset, then an additional 10 hours to see if it's something you want to continue investing in.
I'd recommend this game for mid-heavy sandboxers with community-friendly ideals.  I definately wouldn't suggest this for "lone wolves" as you'll most likely be out-numbered, or not be able to have such an excellent set of skills to survive by one-self at end game (definately seems more fun with friends anyhow).  I would say hold off and see where the game goes (especially in the protecting your stuff against monsters while you're at work/sleep).  If I could I'd get a refund and then watch the game, but alas I'm outside the window.
It'll be an amazing community/society building game at some point, but it isn't there yet.

This game will consume a whole afternoon and night, because there's just so much you can do to improve your character's skills and your base, along with exploration and the discovery of the game's core mechanics. Now, combine that with friends and the fun is multiplied.
It is really fun and has a quite interesting concept, but there is one undeniable truth that must not be overlooked: it is an early access game. However, by this I don't mean it's buggy (we actually had a bug-free long session of play), what I do mean is that it's still terribly unbalanced in the whole PVP/Crime system. In brief, if you pretend to play as a responsable, moral player, it's gonna be great while you're actually in-game (since people are pretty nice and conversative), but the second you stop playing, there is a 90% chance the next time you log in, you will find your nice, little settlement burned, destroyed and viciously raided. And there is nothing you can do to prevent this; you can protect your base against monsters (which is kind of weak, since the "auto-turrets" do so little damage and cost so much), but not against players. Players can destroy everything you built and nothing happens to them.
The system punishes your "crimes", which are killing players who are not red and lockpicking other player's stashes. The punishment is making you a red player (red players drop everything when killed). But what happens to destroying another players property or trespassing? Stealing crops and killing my livestock animals is not considered a crime, so everyone can do it the second my crops and animals enter their vision. If you try to defend your stuff against a non-red player, and eventually kill him, you will turn red. They know this and use them to their advantage; you can't kill them, all you can do is watch as they raid your little village and type stuff, unless you really want to kill them and turn red. If you decide to kill them and turn red, they will spawn back and kill you, taking all the stuff you are carrying, and they won't turn red because they are killing a "criminal".
This is the only thing that truly prevents me from reviewing this game as positive, since I find this is a joy-killing broken feature. I do not mind a PVP world, as long as I can actually do something to protect what's mine.
I do hope developers come out with some way to balance this broken system so I can go back and enjoy this evolving world. Only then I will change this review.

This is my first review of a game even though I have 76 games in my library, most of them ARPGs.  One of the reasons I'm reviewing it is that unlike a lot of games in my library, I bothered to play it through to the end.  For someone like me who bores easily, that's saying something good.
On some levels In Exilium doesn't begin to compete with ARPGs like Diablo 2, Titan Quest, etc.  But that's okay with me because it doesn't really try to.  It takes a different approach.  It focuses more on exploration and puzzle solving than smooth, fast paced combat and tons of awesome loot.  And even though I love those latter things, I found In Exilium to be a refreshing change.
The puzzles were just the right difficulty for me to not get too hung up on but still have to think about a little.  You have just enough freedom in regards to what areas to take on first to make your first playthrough more interesting.  The combat, while perhaps clunky compared to bigger budget titles, was still adequate.  You have a variety of skills to choose from whatever type of character you choose to play.  The atmosphere is cool enough.  There's some replay value if you want to build a character for each of the 3 main playstyles.  The drops, while plentiful enough at least in the latest version, weren't all that interesting to me and are an area that could maybe be improved on a bit.
All in all I just found this game enjoyable.  It was refreshing, fun, and relaxing to play through.  And if you're looking for a  game to have fun and relax with then I recommend you give it a try!

Chivalry is one of my favorite games, and will always be one of my favorite games. I've spent countless nights playing it, and don't regret any of it. From the hilarious voice acting, to the numerous weapon choices, it's a fun game to hop on and not take too seriously while still having fun. All the maps are pretty good, and there are a lot of different gamemodes to choose from that are all fun.
Now lets get to the cons of this game, and why I personally can't reccomend it in it's current state; Torn banner has pretty much completely stopped supporting this game, sadly. The only "updates" they do now are for cosmetic items which cost real money to buy (I have no problem with the cosmetics, ive bought a couple skins myself) and other than that, they do the occasional bugfix. Aside from Torn Banner's neglect, the game isn't that friendly to new players. There are servers that you can only play when your rank is below level 15, but once you hit 16 you might as well just stop playing unless you want to completely re-learn the game and how it works. What I mean by this, is that all the high-levels use things called "drags". This basically slows down/speeds up attacks which can be frustrating and confusing to deal with if you don't know how it works. There are also exploits that let you hit people behind you nearly instantly which can really destroy a new player.
With that said, the lack of community for this game nowadays + the crazy mechanics make me not reccomend it at $25. However, if you find it on sale and want to buy it, go for it! If you REALLY want to buy it, you should just wait until 2018 for Mordhau to come out. It's basically a spiritual succesor to Chivalry, except without the exploits (and it's also a
more realistic) and a better combat system.

I think I should be honest : This game ain't for everybody.
Now, being a frustrated roleplaying fanatic, we're in 2017 and this game is one of the best thing I've played in years. Take Civilization and mix it with The Guild, which are two of my favorite gestion games, and you get this beauty.
Crusader Kings II is, hands down, a masterpiece. It's the kind of game you can just replay a hundred times and never get the same result. The possibilities are endless. Starting as a simple tribal chieftain or as a feudal king ( up to you, with many in-betweens ), you'll be facing different odds EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. Not one game will be the same as another.
I could go on for hours about how amazing this game is without giving it half the credits it deserves. I've played Civilization V and VI and I've been a big fan of The Guild 2. This game allowed me to play all of these at once.
Many will complain about the prices of the DLCs or how little action there is in the game, and it's why I'm saying it's not for everybody. To me, it's worth every penny, and it's worth it twice. The game was beautifully written, it's funny, interesting, and can be played online with 32 people on the same map.
Seriously. Imagine a table-top roleplay game with 32 people and you got this. I mean, what the ♥♥♥♥ else do you want ? This thing is GREAT. IT'S ♥♥♥♥ING GREAT.
If you're a stinking geek with a taste for STRs, gestion games and roleplay like myself, this is for you. You wont honestly find anything even close to be this good these days. So get it,♥♥♥♥♥♥
Did I also mention that you could port your game from this to Europa Universalis IV, then that to Victoria 2, then that to Hearts of Iron 3 ? Yeah. That's right. You get the whole ♥♥♥♥ing history covered.
This game is a 10/10 to me. And this review fails to bring up half the reasons why, so I'm just gonna leave it out there. I thank anyone reading this♥♥♥♥♥♥and hope that we'll get to do some massive world cluster♥♥♥♥ one day together.

*Original Post*
Pros:
The AI doesn't seem to magically know where your unspotted troops are, so It's possible to setup actual ambushes and flank enemy positions without them already having troops aimed in on you (unlike WarGame: Red Dragon, where the AI sends troops straight towards your Command Vehicles hidden way off in the coner of the largest maps in extremely dense forests).
The combat is very close to realistic without being too realistic (ex: higher caliber weapons will take out enemies with one or two good hits.
Distance and hit location affect the effectiveness of projectiles (ex: a bullet from 100m will do less damage than one from 10m, and one bullet in the leg will not kill an enemy).
Uses RNG, so the weapons don't have pin point accuracy every time (ex: squads can sprint or crawl from cover to cover under enemy fire and possibly survive.
Most units carry medkits and can heal themselves as long as they're not incapacitated.
Each unit can be controlled individually for better placement.
Being able to manually control a unit from 3rd person is great (vehicles can be controlled in 1st person too).
Cons (most of which maybe resolved in the final release):
Balancing.  GRM is definitely superior to the USA.
Riflemen don't shoot at vehicles that should easily be penetrated by bullets like technicals.
Riflemen don't shoot at manned turrets even though you can manually aim and kill the gunners.
You can literally spawn 1 technical at the beginning of the round and take out 4 AI players with just that vehicle.  Spawn a small squad after that, and you can cap their base.
In Annialation, spawn points and bases are too close to the main battlefield.  Most matches can be won very quickly by capping the enemy base after whiping out their first few squads.
Battlefields should be larger to accomodate the use of the modern weapons, especially for the vehicles.
Some of the current maps have too much crammed together in small areas (ex: the middle area of the airfield and military base have way too many objects placed closely together...no room to strategically place troops).
Use of artillery seems pointless at this point as the maps are too small to use it effectively.
Don't know if much can be changed about the AI, but it just send troops straight towards objectives rather than going from cover to cover; so you can easily mow them down as they charge accross the open towards the objectives (They do however utilize cover once they get to the objective).
It can be tricky trying to place troops on upper levels of buildings.
My thoughts:
Even in Alpha, this game is amazing.  I can't imagine how much fun it'll be once it's finished.  I didn't have Men of War...just saw Call to Arms by chance on steam and started reading up on it.  I was an avid fan of COH and was hoping this would fill the void...and it has.  At only $30 for deluxe...CtA is definitely worth it.  Hell, I'd pay $60 for it!  Great game!
I've fiddled around with the editor a little as I'd like to eventually create my own maps and missions, but it will take time to be able to do that.  I can see the replayability of this game being virtually endless.
I'm assuming the Multiplayer lobby doesn't have many players at the time since it's still alpha but hopefully that'll change.
Even while still under development, it's one of the best strategy games I've ever played.  It took me about 2 days to understand how to play.
In all honestly, both CtA and MoW: AS2 are a must have as they both cover completely different times very well.  However, if you can only get one of them now, I think MoW: Assault Squad 2 would be the better buy.
After watching Pixel playing MoW: AS2 with his buds, I'll definitely be getting it...hope CtA progresses to be just as good.
The decision to restrict units in by level is a game breaking disappointment.

This game absolutely is not for everyone. You have to be familiar with at least basic logic and programming concepts, or be willing to look up some introductory assembly. Absolutely do not look up solutions to any of the problems, as that completely defeats the purpose and will leave you unsatisfied, although if you can find or solicit hints and tips that don't give away solutions then that is ideal.
A common cut-off point where players seem to give up thinking it's too difficult for them is the second problem on the second row. If you make it past there, then you have the logical understanding needed to solve the rest of the puzzles.
Good luck.

I finally won my first war - and what a war it was!
First off, let me say - "Just do it."  Buy the game, play the tutorial, have fun, then just do it.  The game can seem overwhelming at first, but when things start to click, it sucks you in.
I played the base game before buying any DLC, then quickly gobbled most of the DLC up (and will likely gobble the rest up).
Now let me tell you my story.
1066 A.D.
Just like with the tutorial, I started as King Alfonso VI of Leon.  I have long been fascinated by the reconquista, and so it was a natural choice.  Also (spoiler... kinda), playing as the Jimena brothers puts you in a good starting position, as regardless of what happens between the three of you, you (as the player) are likely to wind up in control of Northern Spain.  But I digress...
After the tutorial and a few trial playthroughs (in which I was handily defeated), I sit down to play in earnest.  I fire up Alfonso and decide to go slow.  Focus on development for the first couple of years, assess my vassals, see how things develop around me.  I rapidly marry the princess of Aragon to get my direct bloodline going, and set out to murder my older brother, Sancho, the king of Castille to the east.  It would seem luck is not on my side, I've got a fairly weak plot going against him, so I continue to focus on internal matters and bide my time.  After a bit of bribing and cajoling, I finally pull someone in who can get close to him.  My plot is now very strong.  So meanwhile, new courtiers are showing up at court.  I'm shuffling council members and watching my vassals while my brother, Garcia, king of Galicia to the west fights off a muslim invasion.
All the while, I'm cartefully monitoring a my sister, Urraca, the Countess of Zamora, and one of my vassals.  We have little love for each other, and she has formed a faction in opposition to my reign.  Still, her cause is weak and since it's discovered, I will soon have a good case for imprisoning her.
The time comes to imprison her not long after.  She hates me, her husband barely likes me, but I figure as long as she is in jail, she's no threat to  me.  All the while, my strong plot to murder Sancho is stalling.  There has been more than enough time, with no results.
In any case, I figure with the strength of my plot it should be soon, and Garcia is weak from fightin the muslims, so I borrow money from the jews, exercise my claim to Galicia, and declare war!
Now, shortly after this (and much to my surprise), my Sister gives birth to a son in prison.  Now I have them both imprisoned.  But her husband still marginally supports me, and the boy is of the line, so I chance it and let him go.  It works in my favor, as the boy now favors me.  I'll let his mother go, eventually, but it will be a while.
No sooner do I raise my levies, but another spanish muslim, Sheikh Muhammad of Mertola decides that Spain would be better off without me.  As I march west to face Garcia, Muhammad marches north to invade Leon.  And, to top it off, Sancho has soldiers marching through my lands because, as it turns out, he's fighting Garcia, as well.  Though not technically "at war" with Sancho, this puts me at odds with all three rulers, including Scottish allies that Garcia has brought in due to his marriage!  This is going to be interesting.
But luck is on my side.  Garcia and Sancho have both been weakend prior to my joining the fray, and while I can muster strong, fresh levies, they are scrambling to rebuild theirs.  The Scots are too far away from home to reinforce effectively, and no one else in the Aftasid Emirate seems interested in joining Muhammad's war.  To top it off, my wife's brother, King Sancho of Aragon offers to join me in my fight against the muslim invaders.
Northern Spain erupts into war.  With Garcia fighting me, and Sancho fighting Garcia, and me and Sancho undermining each other's gains, and the Scottish tropps joinging in to aid Garcia, and the Aragonese troops joining with my vassal's levies to defend against the saracen invasion.
My beloved wife dies in childbirth in 1076, after having given me two sons and two daughters.  I promptly marry myself to Chamoa, the sister of the Count Ergas of Castelo Branco, so as to strengthen my claim on Galician lands.  Meanwhile Urraca, my imprisoned sister, has been busy herself.  She seduces one of her guards and escapes from prison.  Now I have vassal smack dab in the middle of my kingdom who dislikes me intensely.
But the war(s) are going in my favor, and so I focus my attention on them.  The money is dwindling, but I'm managing the loss by carefully releasing vassal levies when they aren't needed, and leveraging my own levies and that of my ally as much as possible.  Then, something strange happens... well, two thing, actually.
The first thing that happens is Galicia suddenly belongs to my Brother Sancho!  What the devil?  I had this down to a science!  Did Garcia die in battle or something?  Nope.  Turns out that Sancho forced him into an unconditional surrender.  Garcia is now the Duke of Galicia, and Sancho is the king of both Galicia and Castille.  This is bad... where is that murder plot!?
The second is that Urraca, my sister who hates me and wants my throne and who imprisoned?  She and I end up settling family matters one night... in the most intimate way possible.  Now she is firmly on my side.  Of course, me finding her getting shtupped by Bishop Pelayo one night doesn't do much for our new found affection.  But a little blackmail and mum's the word, with no great loss of love on either end.
When the last saracen army is beaten back I can press them into surrender, and my very small deficit becomes a healthy treasury overnight.  Only now I'm sandwiched between Sancho's kingdoms.  I swear to God, the day after I settle with Muhammad, my long awaited murder plot comes to fruition, and Sancho is now dead.  Praise to Heaven!  Only the map doesn't change... ♥♥♥♥... it turns out that Sancho got busy and had a couple sons of his own.  Now everything I've worked for is at the mercy of a 10 year-old child.
So I do the wise thing - I offer peace.
Soon after the peace accord was agreed upon, that 10 year-old fell victim to an unfortunate fall while playing in a very high tower.  God rest his noble soul.
Though no lands were reclaimed for Chrsitendom, at long last there is peace in Christian Spain, a large portion of which is owned by my nephew, the 8 year-old King Diego of Castille.  I pray that God watch over him, and that the same misfortunes that befell his father and brother don't befall him as well.
10/10 - Would fight a bloody, incestuous, murderous war with my family and the heathen Muslims again.

When you come out of the gate as a heavy with a medic in tow, you're a formidable offensive force, but if a spy loops around to backstab the medic and you round the corner on a pyro, it can all come undone in a matter of seconds. Snipers can cover expected enemy paths, but rocket-jumping soldiers have a knack for finding alternative routes and raining explosive death from above. You may think you have a comparatively weak scout dead to rights, only to be stunned by a baseball and beaten to death. As you watch your giblets splatter on the ground and see a freeze-frame of your gleeful killer, it's hard not to chuckle at the sheer variety of ways you can meet an untimely demise. And the humorous quips, ridiculous outfits, and histrionic announcer help cultivate this lighthearted tone.
Of course, this core dynamic has persisted for most of TF2's life span, so if you stopped playing it a few years ago and come back for a few matches, you'll find things are very familiar. Learning the ropes and getting the hang of your chosen role is still a gratifying experience, and mastering advanced techniques doesn't just make you deadlier; it gives you more options for how to approach combat. Keeping your options open is still valuable too, because being flexible with your choice of character can help you avoid ending up on a catastrophically imbalanced squad. It is Team Fortress, after all.
But though there is much that has remained constant about the core game, there have been some notable changes over the years, as well as regular infusions of new weapons and items. Of the hundreds of things available in the online store, some can be unlocked through play, while others must be purchased with actual money. From small doodads that cost less than a dollar to massive bundles that cost hundreds, there's a wide range of ways to customize your experience.
Many of the items offer nothing more than a playful twist on the game's already cheeky cartoon aesthetic. You can buy hats, shirts, shoes, and other cosmetic gear to dress up like a character from Adult Swim or don spooky seasonal garb that you can wear only during Halloween or a full moon. Even if you don't fancy shelling out for any of this stuff, it's fun to see some visual variety as you try to light your opponents on fire.
Other weapons have more of an impact, like the ones that give your character a new chargeable and expendable power. The scout can build hype, which turns his usual double jump into a triple, quadruple, or quintuple jump, and the soldier can build rage, which allows him to rally his nearby teammates to do extra damage. Skills like these have more of a meaningful impact on the action, bringing something new to the table that your enemies must contend with. And then there are the totally out-there loadouts, like the one that turns the grenade-launching demoman into an extra from the movie Braveheart.In addition to the cosmetic options, there are a lot of weapons and items that offer small buffs or subtle tweaks to your attributes. Depending on which healing gun the medic equips, for example, he can imbue himself and his targeted ally with extra damage resistance or enable himself to match the speed of his target. Differences like these don't do much to change the core action, but they do give experienced players substantial room for strategic variation.
These options broaden the field of viable strategies, which helps keep combat lively and varied. And fortunately, none of the purchasable weapons or items tip the scales unfairly towards those willing to pay. Buffs and bonuses usually come with caveats, and the weapons that bestow new abilities are usually unlocked for free. For this review, I spent some money on goofy hats and some of the stranger weaponry on offer, like the pyro's flamethrower that actually shoots bubbles and rainbows. It was fun to play with the new gear, but I still found myself switching my loadout between free and paid weapons regularly to adapt to the match situation.
All of this is... fine. I had enough fun playing Gotham City Impostors, but I was never hooked. The flat trees and blocky visuals aren't impressive, and, outside of deathmatch, the modes bore. While perfectly functional and crammed with unlockables (there's at least a level 500), it really amounts to just five maps, a sense of humor and the Batman license. I don't know if that's enough to warrant $15 and another first-person shooter multiplayer suite.
What's really interesting -- at least from a console perspective -- is Gotham City Impostor's love of the microtransaction. You earn costume coins you can use to buy new gloves and emblems for your character throughout the game, but if you don't feel like waiting, you can use real money to buy the superficial looks. I'm fine with the ability to buy cooler calling cards and mascots that float next to your character, but the ability to buy an hour of Double XP over and over again is a bit weird.

First impressions...
In Exilium is a nice little RPG dungeon crawling game!  I'm impressed!  I didn't hear anything about this game, so I wasn't expecting much at all.  I like it a lot!  It is very reminiscent of Diablo 1 and a little of Diablo 2, but much better graphics and animations, but short on story.
You start off by creating a character.  You get to choose from 3 classes.  Warrior, Mage & Archer.  Starting stat points are static and cannot be changed.  You also don't get any points to distribute in the beginning, but you get 3 points each level gained.  You also get to name your character, but you cannot change their appearance, although, your character does show the weapons and armor they are wearing.
You have 5 main stats to pump your points into.  They are Strength (melee), Dexterity (ranged), Focus (mana), Intelligence (magic) & Vitality (health).  There are many skills as well.  It is a basic buy the book RPG dungeon crawling game, with some forgiving features.  This is a great game for newcomers to the genre!  It's becoming one of my favorite dungeon crawling games!
You start the game at your base camp with a shared storage chest for all your characters, an anvil for crafting, a fast travel campfire, a training area with infinitely spawning target dummies, plus a forest and dungeon entrance.  There are other places to go once inside these areas as well.  The game looks huge.  Not sure just yet, but looking at the trailer, it seems to be a large game.  You also start off with a camp teleport skill.
The sound, music, graphics, lighting and textures are very well done.  There is a great selection of enemies to annihilate! lol  Character and creature models are animated well.  Nice level layouts.  Mini-map, camp teleport, shrines and gems for enchanting weapons.  It pretty much has it all.  I'm very impressed and very happy with my purchase!
The one thing I love about this game, is you level up so fast!  I'm already level 30+ after a couple of hours!  You can level up sooner if you want in your camp by killing target dummies in your training area!   I am not sure there is a level cap, but I doubt it seeing how fast I'm leveling up and haven't gotten very far into the game yet.
This game is for people that like to level up fast, but still have to fight for your goodies.  Beware though, the monsters are pretty tough!  This game requires some grinding as there are not a ton of weapons and armor like the Diablo series.  Yes, there are some good items, but you have to fight for them and they come very slow, until you find a store.
Your health and mana regenerate automatically, but you can still die easily so beware!  I don't think there is a penalty for dying.  I died and was just sent back to camp with all my belongings and currency.   Currency is weird.  Not sure what it is, but the monsters give it to you when they die.  Kind of like souls floating to you.  It's a cool effect.  It is the only means of purchasing items that I have found, so you must kill monsters to get currency.  Luckily monsters respawn and pretty fast too, so don't get cornered!
You move your character and melee attack with the left mouse button and use the right mouse for ranged attacks, including magic and skills.  You can set traps also.  I haven't checked out skills too much as my Archer it pretty strong and I am on a leveling up spree. lol I have laid traps though and they sure help out!  I also use a dagger with my Archer and an axe.  He's pretty powerful considering my stats point placement.  You can also buy a scroll to reset your stat points.  Cool game so far!
I fully recommend this game to anyone looking for a light RPG game done very well!  Not a huge story, but lot's of dungeon crawling! :-)

In Exilium was an amusing indie action RPG in the style of Diablo, but I felt it was very questionably balanced and that its minimalistic design unfortunately worked against it. It was still fairly impressive work for a very tiny team - according to the credits, only one programmer, three artists, and one musician worked on the game - but it didn't really come together into a solid game in my experience.
The questionable balance made the game rather not fun for me at first, as I started playing a warrior (there are no classes, but there are three primary statistics and three skill trees, so there are still "classes" that naturally develop) and found the game rather difficult and not terribly fun, as I'd miss many enemies six times in a row due to needing huge amounts of Dexterity to hit anything, but also Strength to have abilities and equip weapons and armor, Focus to have energy to use those abilities, and Vitality to not die when hit. That's four out of the five stats... and you only get 3 points to put into stats at each level. Then I decided to restart the game as a wizard, who only needs Intelligence to unlock abilities and Focus for accuracy and energy to use those abilities, and blew through most of the campaign like it was nothing. At the same time, wizards don't really benefit from much of the loot, making item drops not very exciting.
Unfortunately, item drops not being common or exciting was a general problem with In Exilium, part of its minimalistic design. The stats were all very tiny improvements for each point, and likewise many of the items were just incremental improvements to damage or defense or whatnot, rather than being very noticable. This wouldn't have been that bad in a fully Diablo-style game where items dropped freely and upgrades were constant, but even major bosses in this game only dropped items under 10% of the time when I played.
I liked the fact the game provided enough information that I could figure out where to go next without it leading me by my nose, and had fun with my wizard playthrough, but it wasn't really something I'd recommend, nonetheless.
(Note: I did not try the multiplayer mode at all, nor did I do the randomized bonus dungeon more than once. The latter is supposed to add a bit of replay value, but in my experience it was just fighting rather incoherent mobs of stuff from the campaign that I'd beaten when I was 20 to 50 levels lower, and so only posed a challenge in the rooms where you faced multiple bosses at the same time.)

DESYNC is like a TRON infused Dark Souls-Bulletstorm-LITE FPS.

In DESYNC you're a dude ... programm ... Whatever you're something that can jump, shoot and dash. That's pretty much all you need to know.

Recently I listened to some people discussing Super Mario World romhacks, and they mentioned a test for level quality. If you could strip out every single piece of visual design, just replace it with gray cement blocks, and it was still interesting to play? Then it was a good level, and not just cool visuals.
If you stripped out every piece of Desync's visual design, then it'd be a good game. But the more of it you leave in, the worse it is.
The screen-glitching is pointless and occasionally makes menus almost unreadable. Weapons take up almost half your viewable area when you've got a sidearm active or an akimbo weapon up. Enemies' glow, your projectiles' glow and enemy projectiles' glow all merge together into the same mush of random glowy crap, and traps are poor at indicating when they're a danger to you as well as to enemies.
This isn't getting over all of the other design issues which largely involve not being very explicit about effects and stuff. For instance, my Terrablaster is a shotgun that has a secondary fire. The secondary fire leaves a glowy, spinny star somewhere for a second. As far as I can tell all this does is waste ammo. Nothing in-game elaborates on this secondary fire. I pick up 500 different shades of glowy blinky stuff from dead enemies, some of it seems to replenish my ammo, this is all I can tell. My Aegis sidearm is occasionally charged and pops in, but I genuinely can't tell if it does anything, pressing either sidearm fire button does nothing, and after a bit, it winks out of existence again. Supposedly my "Diameteor" fires explosive shells, (normal and large for primary and secondary fire respectively), but they appear to have no explosive range and only affect enemies on direct hits.
I can get all sorts of "sequences" by killing enemies the right way, and I can upgrade them to provide "desyncs" to enemies and genuinely I have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what this does. I think it might weaken enemies of a specific class? Maybe?
Sometimes enemies spawn glowing yellow, red or blue. The game tells me this means they're buffed. But it never tells me what the buffs do. I can't tell if they hit any harder or move faster, though they seem to take a bit more punishment. Is there a difference in the glow types? The game never tells me.
The game also loves to slow down for tutorials in the middle of fights(usually when you discover a new sequence) which is INCREDIBLY jarring since it takes a bit before your fire buttons respond again and it usually means you take a hammer or sword to the face in the meantime.
The really sad thing is that a game like Necropolis had basically the same visual design, but was really clear and obvious about everything, mostly due to having more clear geometric planes and less pointless glowy♥♥♥♥♥♥everywhere. Though it also had the same purposeful obtuseness about stats and effects a lot of the time.
Ultimately this could've been a much better game if the devs weren't busy listening to retro music and jerking themselves off all the time. There's still a decent game hidden underneath but... for fifteen bucks you should be expecting better by now. Get it on sale, or don't get it at all.

At what point does a game stop being challenging and start being annoying? One of the age-old questions, and DESYNC, despite plenty of clever marketing and flashy colors, unfortunately falls into the latter half.
Plainly speaking, the skill ceiling is too high. I never had time to "git gude" as the game was too busy trolling me. I didn't approach every new level with excitement, I approached every new level with dread. THAT is what separates a challenging game from an annoying one. I never felt empowered, I felt like I was a victim. I should not have to be thinking, "WOW I'm stupid for not changing one aspect of my loadout ten minutes ago", I should be thinking, "Wow, I just got used to these new mechanics, hopefully I'll be given some space to try them out before I get a curveball." NOPE you're dead, enjoy restarting fifty times. That kind of crap died out with the NES.
The desync / sidearm / whatever systems are extremely obtuse and non-intuitive, their tutorials amounting to nothing more than fortune cookies, because these days it's cool to make casual players feel stupid for daring to actively engage in a hobby that is the equivalent of playing with digital toys. I obviously upgraded the pistol ASAP since it's the only gun that doesn't run out of ammo after three shots. Much skill, such wow. Perhaps I need to go back and replay previous levels to acquire experience? Yeah no I paid for an FPS not a grind-fest.
Many people enjoy this kind of "challenge", but I am not one of them. So I guess this is for everyone else. You know who you are. Despite its flashy presentation, this "game" is a discrace to first-person shooters. The boss fights are more annoying than intriguing. Having to change your tactics for each single enemy over and over and over again on the fly is not action, it's chess. And if I wanted to play chess, I'd go to the park and play chess with Cletus.
7/10 for smooth responsive shooting and TRON-themed art design. -1 for each unfair death. Final score: -22/10.

An actual review. The Denuvo fiasco will be put aside for this.
Sonic Mania is the latest gaming media darling, scoring impressive 9s when, in reality, it deserves nothing more than a 7.
Once the nostalgia wear off, you start seing the HUGE design flaws in each stages, especially during boss battles.
It is not overall a bad game, but can really only be recommended to purist Sonic fans and people that grew up with the original game trilogy in the 90s.
Anybody else, steer clear.

Ever since I tasted the pure joy of the amazing Sonic 3 & Knuckles I've dreamt of something that can come at least close to the emotions, which that game had granted me. With Mania, I remembered what it's like to be a kid, to simply enjoy. This game is a gift - from the brilliant soundtrack to the awesome visuals, through the thought-through design and the absolute love, with which it has been crafted - which shows in almost every second, I can be only thankful to anyone involved with this project.
The game is far from perfect. Absurd difficulty jumps are abound, the classic bugs from the past are present, and even some new have found their way around. Also, I can't help but notice that Knuckles plays significantly different than he should. He has extra frames of animation, which really stutter his fluidity, in other words - he is simply not the same, and sadly, here he is much worse than in 3&K. But besides the last remark, which has to be the only let down of Sonic Mania, everything else simply isn't a bother. For one - we're used to it, it's part of the nostalgia, and then... you simply look at everything else this package has to offer. Nothing can tramp that, nothing can obliterate this utter joy of Sonic being himself, because he can.
Sincerely, I thank anyone involved with this product. I hope Sega continue this venture and remember that the Blue Blur is best in his design in 2D, and that 2D doesn't mean you can't have more characters or a deeper plot (even without dialogue, mind you). I am hesitant to be excited for the future, but with this being something that has finally happened - the first truly good Sonic game since Sonic Advance, which wasn't even that great - just servisable, how can I resist?
A full recommendation of this game comes to anyone. I promise that if you keep a leveled head, even the gripes become an adventure. Then again, I was born and raised on this stuff. I'm as biast as it gets. And I love it.

Denuvo relies on a third party server to verify ownership on the first launch, then at regular intervals, and again if the game is reinstalled. So, a long while back, I wrote a joke review about my experience screwing up a bank job.
Instead, I'm going to write an actual review.
Uplink.
Where to begin?
The hollywood hacking simulator is one of my favorite games, and all the people writing negative reviews on it yelling "buggy" or "go buy hacknet its better"
Well to that I say, Yes, it is buggy. But it was made in ~2003, and it shows. Yes, it crashes. But the game has a certain charm to it that leaves me with a better impression of it than Hacknet.
Granted the newly-in-beta graphical overhaul
helps alot to make the game more user friendly (and I highly recommend it)
-----Gameplay------
I can say the gameplay is top notch and semi-realistic
You have to get a "bounce" (long linked trail of connections) to get extra time for when the network you're hacking decides to trace you.
The thrill of trying to get in, do your job, and get out before the trace kicks you out is exilarating.
Then you gotta go to one of the links in your trail, and clean up the logs to get that passive trail off you.
-----Music-----
Kind of a minor thing, but the 5 song track list is a nice mix of cyberpunk-ish techno, and fits well with the hacking theme. (its also great to listen to when trying to concentrate on a paper or something)
-----Story-----
The story is pretty good, though you don't really have follow it, as you can just continue doing freelance work, as the storyline doesn't require you to follow along.
10/10

This is a really interesting take on the MOBA genre. Instead of the moment to moment minion/item based power scaling of other games, Atlas Reactor is Turn-Based and focuses on player skill and cleverness. It's free to play, however the in game currency is easy to earn, and anything that can only be paid for with real money is either purely cosmetic (skins), easily attainable (GG boosts) or the "All Freelancers Bundle" which doesn't mean too much because you'll find the ones you like with the free weekly rotations and can buy those with in game currency. Trion is doing pretty well with this game, it's not the most popular at the moment, but it still receives patches/hotfixes every ~2 weeks and a new freelancer about every ~3 months.
The community (in all the games I've played) is not toxic. Whether a person is doing great or horrible, no one harasses others, and any "trash talk" is done with a GG boost used mid-match, which only helps everyone in the room by giving more experience/currency. If you've ever been a fan of MOBAs and like turn based games, give this a try, it's worth it.

"a slightly childish, but simplistic version to a MOBA.I'm very happy to say, they succeeded."
I've never been the biggest of fans when it comes to MOBAs. I've played small slices of games like Dota 2 and League of Legends, but enevietibly fail. I just can't scratch the surface of those games enough for me to want to bother. The learning curve(Remember, Personal Opinion!) is just too steep. However, this title, is just made to suit those complaints. It's a simplistic MOBA. Something basic in the MOBA form we all know and love. Instead of getting lost in the shop for the fifty six hundred item that will massively boost your team, you have a loadout of a SMALL group of upgrades within the shop. twelve, which can stack, but twelve different upgrades for one game. But that's just setting up the character. The combat is very well done aswell, where skill is involved, not just mashing buttons on some super powerful gimmick, however, that is impossible to remove in a competitive game with choice.
But before we get into the juicy parts, I always elaborate the problems of the game in the second paragraph. First glance, the game is wacky and weird. I personally love games like that, but others may find it offputting, and as a competitive multiplayer game, this may enrage you while playing it, It isn't a calm serene game. The graphics themselves are abit basic when you zoom in unfortunately, but blame that on the consoles. Another point is the cosmetic DLC is fairly pricey, so watch out for that. Finally, the characters are abit slim. They all have some nice detail, and no characters look the same, but theres only around 20. Hopefully, this will improve, with more DLC packs coming in, as the last one, kickstartered and made almost three times there goal, reaching $345 835.
Now, the good part. The combat can be slow and can be fast paced, but everything is sudden. You can find yourself suddenly on a sliver of health only to be rushed by someone with a dash ability, or a grapple. All the characters do have the same abilities under normal circumstances, so memory can be important as well as finding a tactic to handle every character. I found myself within closely matched games, figuring out the specific player's tactics on a certain character, and finding a way to counter it half way through the game, which was a blast. All the characters are fairly different too. You have your generalisation of course, but they all feel different to play. Playing ayla, I find myself taking massive risks, since she does more damage on low health, which is completely different, when I play Penny Fox, which I retreat back to heal much more. They, however are both the same category. Also, if you don't like people, Like me, theres also bots for you to absolutely demolish within the game. No internet required.
Really, I think the developers wanted a slightly childish, but simplistic version to a MOBA. I'm very happy to say, they succeeded. Awesomenauts, brings about the same level of skill involved with a moba, just with less thought. You may think its a bad thing, but I've always considered COD to be a very dumb competitive series. The kind of series, where you don't put much thought into it, just jump in and go nuts. But how many people play that series. Case Closed.

In the case of opposite directions you learn quickly to not press any direction and simply sit there as it plays out. This can lead to just watching the screen for 8-10 seconds at a time.
In-between the speed sections are "Platforming" sections. You would expect platforming from a platforming section but they are simply stop gaps to the next speed section. Navigate the overly simplfied path to the next speed booster that leads to the next speed section, no depth in these.
The bonus stages for the Chaos Emeralds are hidden around the level, you would think "Great a bit of exploration". Not the case. Because of the way the platforming sections are set up to be simple stop gaps between speed sections you will often times find yourself hurled out of them at speed and stopped from going back. Very very rarely will you see a bonus stage on the actual path through the level. The bonus stages themselves are fun to play but finding them is a chore.
Boss fights are a total let down, either childishly easy or they use some gimmick mechanic that is more frustrating than fun.

First, a disclosure: I am the furthest thing from a Sonic fanboy you will find. The only Sonic game I enjoyed after Sonic 3 was Sonic Adventure (and I only enjoyed that because it looked great at the time. I recognize now that it's not a very good game). But I did love the originals for the Genesis system. Oh, and I had a great time with Sonic Spinball. I think everything Sonic has been crap since then....UNTIL NOW (cue dramatic music):
This is best Sonic game ever released, made with loving care by people you can tell are truly fans of the original games. The levels, while taking inspiration from our old favorites from the Genesis games, are updated with all sorts of new contraptions. Each level is wonderfully expansive and complex, providing hundreds of different paths and rewarding exploration with items, bonus games, and the like (though seeing all the new bells and whistles would be reward enough!). You will be left wondering how it was possible for someone to put such complex levels together, with all the insane crisscrosses, and yet, somehow, everything fits together beautifull.
The gameplay is the best of any Sonic game to date. Unlike the old Sonic games, hitting a bounce pad and then running through several crazy loops and ramps never results in you suddenly landing on spikes or something dangerous at the end (that was always an extremely annoying problem), so you don't feel the need to slow down at the points where the level designer wants you to go fast and enjoy all the cool visual tricks your character is doing. Still, the platforming is both difficult and creative, and the enemies become increasingly deadly. The boss fights at the ends of levels are also great fun.
Huge kudos to the art department for their absolutely gorgeous pixel art, and the music department for their foot-tappingly joyous tunes.

This is a somewhat tentative thumbs down, a problem with a rating system like this.
All of Desync's systems are well thought out and funnel the player into a way of thinking that score is more valuable than anything, by making score a practical goal and not an arbitrary one. Do damage or kill enemies in difficult/obtuse/lucky/flashy ways and you'll immediately feel rewarded for it with power. It is challenging, allowing you to repeatedly retry a room (and not restart a level) when you die, but killing you quickly and punishing you for dying. The systems and balance are good, or fine.
But, based on the game feel, which is a very subjective thing, I don't see myself playing Desync farther. Even at 60 fps, for me, the game feels a touch sluggish and attacks feel flimsy. The movement is also totally boring, which may not be a problem for anyone that has the niche itch that Desync scratches, as it's possible that more movement options and balancing around them would distract from the focus on opportunistic punishment of enemies. I go into any shooter expecting movement to be fun, and it's totally generic in Desync, boasting a dodge which does nothing for me.
Non-tactical shooters should provide nonstop blazing fast action, and Desync likes to stop you repeatedly. Each time you discover a new attack or kill sequence, the game slows down. Time between rooms errs on the side of too long of a walk for a linear room-by-room action shooter, and could easily just be a Smash TV side-by-side rooms transition. The game's menu takes place in the game world and is annoying to navigate. Weapon switch speed is slow for a game of this nature. Enemies also have multiple attacks and behaviors which can instantly change how your weapons interact with them, by way of lessened knockback or the ingame stagger system; fine in the vacuum of the game itself, but just one more gripe that can pile up when you aren't enthralled.
These seeming nitpicks may be irrelevant for the average player who lives for Desync's niche, but it's worth highlighting the game's flaws as these many minor, sometimes subconscious turn-offs often are ignored by reviewers who don't play for long almost exclusively because a game is too hard for them.
Desync is not a game I would recommend avoiding entirely. That's not what this rating is for, and I've told several friends about it in case it may appeal to them. It's just an attempt to voice what about the game immediately pushed me away, as I like the game's premise, but I have a backlog of viscerally satisfying, challenging games that I can't put Desync on a pedestal next to.

Uplink (2001) is a hacking game in the fictional "future" of 2010. The game was created by Introversion Software, a merry little indie company with active developers. While development for this game has ceased, fans, such as Miah and Tycho from Ferrous Moon (Onlink) and Cpt. McBacon of Uplink OS, continue to make the game stand on its own as not only an "oldie but goodie" but the continuing benchmark of its genre in 2016.
The game itself appears complex, minimal, and dated on first glance. The entire game is basically text and buttons. While not as aesthetically appealing as even some games from the NES, the gameplay is still action-packed. The game features several races against the often invisible clock as the player tries to seize millions of credits in funds, destroy mainframes, and evade the one-world-government's ever-motivated police force. One wrong move often spells curtains for the player if unprepared.
Uplink was a game without creative comparison during its time. Instead of the endless derivations from popular console titles, Uplink was a rare success for a game inspired by movies. As we learned from the Angry Video Game Nerd, games based on movies are often on a poor foundation (and LJN certainly didn't help)! Uplink answered the demand for Hollywood-style hacking that no other popular game could offer at the time.
One common complaint about the game is that it is complex and very difficult to play without additional walkthroughs and documentation beyond what is provided by the game. The in-game tutorial only covers one type of mission and offers a very inefficient method for removing logs - a chore that can end the game if neglected merely an hour into the game.
The game, however, seeks to emulate a hostile environment where you learn as you go and by trial-and-error. The game, unlike other games of this time period, does not wish to hold your hand through it. And through this dearth of information, it has great replay value as you learn from past mistakes, learn even more about how the game works in more complex situations, and find new challenges and secrets.
I highly recommend this game, and proclaim this game should be the rightful owner of the "Test of Time" Award.
