As you can tell from the amount of hours that I've played this game, I find it very enjoyable.  It is not only a good strategy game, but it is also a good way for you to familiarize yourself with the Medieval world.  There are certainly historical inaccuracies as is inevitable with any attempt to model the past.  Beyond that though, there is a richness in the game that can only be achieved through a great deal of research on the part of the devolopers (dynasties, county/duchy borders, succession laws, some facets of religious practice, claimant system, etc.).
In order to access all this game has to offer, it is necessary to invest more learning time than you normally would with other games of the genre.  You will either need to have a friend teach you or watch Let's Play videos on youtube.  At the beginning you will find the interface bewildering and not know how to navigate very well.  Even upon explanation of where various functions are located, you will still not always know right away what you should be checking on a regular basis.
If you press on past this stage of initial confusion, you will find yourself sitting around watching the dates flicker by in the upper-right portion of the screen.  It will seem that this game primarily consists of inactivity occasionally interrupted by notifications of relatives dying or your heir gaining the traits of a bully.  This is where you would be wrong.  You have to be proactive in the preservation and flourishing of your dynasty.  You have to take advantage of lulls between crises by looking up the claimants of various territories you desire, beneficial traits of spouses for yourself, heirs, and family members, conditions that need to met to execute important events in the decision list, or even potential avenues whereby you can inherit titles through clever marriage proposals, thus avoiding the need to even raise a sword.  So on and so forth.  It's up to you to make this game achieve its full potential.  If you sit around, you will most likely be allowed to rot on your throne until your realm gets slowly gobbled up by other dynasties or by pretenders to your titles.
Unlike many other strategy games, success in this game revolves around the medieval system of titular advancement.  It is titles that you want, not necessarily land or money.  You cannot and should not attempt to expand via brute military force.  The titular system is the Medieval attempt to keep geo-politics within a legal purview.  You only ever fight to take things because you have legitimate reason to (you have a causus belli: case for war).  You can't just outright bully your neighbors into submission.  You need at least a plausible reason that you deserve what they have.  This titular system will leave you constantly hamstringed in pursuit for conquest.  This system is supposed to be an obstacle and an attempt to model the reason why borders often changed so slowly in the Middle Ages.  The titular system is a particularly large obstacle for the expansion of Western European Catholic nobles.  You need claims on titles in order to fight a war for that title.  You get claims through marriage, inviting people who already have claims to your court, having your chancellor fabricate a claim, etc.
I like that most additions to this game are meant to either provide more options for the player or prevent the player from snowballing mid-late game.  The developers have added things like a council conclave, potential for mass-pacts to be formed against powerful character, invasion of the mongols (Mid game), invasion of Aztecs (Late game), etc.  These additions may aggravate some people, but I see them as balancing the game and sifting out those players without the fortitude to power through these challenges.
There are minor things about this game that are neither reasonable in light of the attempted historical setting nor good balancing mechanisms for the game.  A small example of this is how the game prevents you from usurping titles of other characters who are currently involved in their own wars.  Why should I cater to my rivals, especially when they (according to the reasoning associating with usurping) illegitimately hold a title that I should actually own?  Another is the general prohibition to inter-faith marriages which, in the Medieval context in light of the political aspect of noble marriages, were actually commonplace.  Another problem is that occasionally characters will receive event troops and these troops will in peace-time just sit around as a standing army without penalizing the holder of the troops either financially or maybe through local instability (riots, requisitioning, dissident deserters, etc.)
Overall, this game gives your innumerable hours of play especially if you get the dlc's which enable you to play other characters of other religions and cultures besides just Western European Catholics and the Byzantines.  I highly recommend this game to those who are willing to put in the time and who already are interested in strategy games.

I received this game as a gift from a friend off my wishlist, and it is a tremendously fun game for computer programmers to challenge their logic skills on a very minimalistic computer simulation.  I've done machine code and assembler programming since the mid 1980s on real hardware and quite frankly it is a dying art with all of the modern high level languages floating about.  I haven't done much low level code for a few years now and it was something I always enjoyed.  While TIS-100 is nowhere remotely near what you can do on a real processor, it is immensely fun to solve its puzzles - specifically because of the severe limitations of the processor.  It also challenges the mind to think in terms of parallelization to reduce the cycle count for a better score on many puzzles.
Non-programmers probably wont get much further than solving 3-4 of the most basic puzzles, however if you're a computer programmer who loves solving coding and/or logic puzzles, then this is the game for you.
I've literally never stared harder at my screen for hours on end.
It's like doing homework for a programming class.

What's there to say about this gem of a game that hasn't been said already? To me, the Sonic Mania experience was one that really hit home. It's no secret that the game plays heavily on nostalgia and fan service, but oh boy does it do so wonderfully.
It's really the subtlety of the references that get you; Like the mashup of zone elements and enermies from the original trilogy & Knuckles as well as Sonic CD. The music is absolutely to die for (God bless you Tee Lopes) with swingin' original tracks in Studiopolis, Mirage Saloon, Press Garden, and Titanic Monarch zone, along with timeless pieces from the well rebooted zones we all love like Green Hill and Chemical Plant. I was really hoping they would include an alternative soundtrack (perhaps a 16-bit Genesis styled one) like they did in CD, but I guess they decided not to.
While the zone choices originally left me a bit dissapointed (I didn't really want to see Oil Ocean since both Lost World and Sonic 4 ep 2 had elements from it, or green hill for the bajillionth time), Mania has been able to 'remix' the zones in a way that really breathes new life into them. With fun new elements like the syringes in Chemical Plant and the smog and submarines in Oil Ocean, it's like playing the zones for the very first time.
Despite all my high praise for the game, I do have some gripes with the save system. It just doesn't seem fair to me to make the player repeat Act 1 stages if they 'game over' in Act 2 or the boss stage, especially when they will have to face the mini-boss again. Mania is an easier title than the classic ones, but that is no excuse to make 'game overs' a living hell for players, especially those who are starting their Sonic journey with Mania.
And for those whining about the DRM issues, it's really not that bad. I can understand people fussing over it if it were an issue on the Switch where portability is key, but this is PC we're talking about! An internet connection can't be that hard to find. It's not fair to give the game a bad review just because you need to be logged in the play it. They're getting it fixed soon anyway. What did leave me confused were the controller support issues as the game is obviously meant to be played with them. A fix for this is to disable all theck check boxes under Steam > Settings > Controller >  General Controller Settings. A restart of steam is needed for the changes to take effect.
For anyone considering buying the game, just buy it! It's unlikely we'll see another masterpiece like this in the franchise for a good number of years. Also, play it with a controller! The special and bonus stages are significantly harder without one.
With such a great game as the Sonic Franchise's 'Summer' release (I'd say the delay was worth it), here's hoping that the Holiday season's Sonic Forces is able to maintain the standard.

The first game from Australian-based developer The Foregone Syndicate, Desync is a distillation of everything I love about synthwave, difficult shooters, and score attack modes. Drenched in a CRT scanline-heavy visual style that isn't out of place in a Tron film, Desync is a completely radical experience, while being pretty fun to boot, too.
The lovechild of Bulletstorm and a Tron movie is about as awesome as it sounds. Despite a few hiccups in gameplay, plus some systems that aren't wholly explained, Desync finishes strong, and provides a great score-attack shooter experience. There isn't much story to speak of, though Desync doesn't seem to mind much, as the core feedback loop of killing enemies to get higher scores is already so enthralling.
Desync is a game of combinations, of finding new and exciting ways to kill whatever it is that's attacking you. These “attack sequences” range from the simple, such as landing a headshot on a staggered enemy, to the complex, such as launching an enemy into the air with the rocket launcher, then switching to the shotgun to finish them off. Attack sequences award points based on their relative difficulty, with more points awarded if you add variety in the sequences you use. You can also perform “desyncs” on enemies, where you execute a particular attack sequence based on the color of the enemy. These desyncs impart “bullet-time” and award a whole pile of points, and become essential in the later levels.
Your arsenal consists of basic shooter fare: a pistol, shotgun, rocket launcher, plasma rifle, and more. Each gun has a secondary fire which can be used to string together attacks; for example, the shotgun's secondary fire sends out a spinning shuriken, which is a requirement to trigger certain sequences. There's also sidearms and passive abilities, awarded after filling meters by killing enemies, which is usually how you'll get ammunition back, too.
Levels are broken up into combat arenas, which feature claustrophobic hallways and low ceilings, pits of lava and massive geometric obelisks. They're varied enough to keep the game fresh, yet the overarching theme of the levels offers consistency in enemy design and strategy. You move faster for every string of kills you manage to link together, and with a dodge key, you whirl around in a violent dance of neon colors and pumping bass waves. If this wasn't obvious, Desync is a game that needs to be seen, rather than read about.
The tight, rewarding gameplay culminates in a boss battle, set at the end of each three-level section. Whereas the individual levels were a test of how well you could manage ammo and stringing together kills, the boss battles are tests of combat prowess. Tense, extended one-on-one duels, learning patterns until you're able to sneak in a win are a hallmark of any challenging game, Desync  Desync smacks of Super Meat Boy in that regard, where death is common, quick, and relatively inconsequential.
Between levels, you wander a small hub area, where you can set abilities, modify weapons, review leaderboards, and otherwise marvel at the architecture of your surroundings. Loadouts and information is conveyed through CRT-styled screens that hang from the walls, with strange wires protruding from every direction. There was, strangely, one screen that remained unused, even after I beat the game, so whether this is indicative of a future update, or something I've yet to unlock, it's hard to say.
A game so stylish is not without its faults, however. The middle levels suffer from an overabundance of shield-bearing enemies in close quarters, making it difficult to progress if you can't stagger the beasts. Too little of the game's systems are explained, particularly weapon upgrades and sidearm requirements,  and the music tracks, strangely, don't loop within levels, leading to periods of awkward silences, save for sound effects. There were also a few freezes and crashes that I experienced, though such hiccups were thankfully only encountered in Desync's hub world.
These complaints are few and far between, however. The thudding bass and synths of the soundtrack by Daniel Deluxe and Volkor X make Desync the complete synthwave experience. The grinding, distorted guitars send adrenaline shooting through your veins as you're frantically blasting away at all manner of creatures closing in; the warped melodies combine with the lo-fi sound effects to create a wonderfully cacophonous symphony.
Desync is relentless, stylish, and a must-play for any fan of score-attack shooters. Even if you're not a traditional fan of “harder” electronic music, experiencing Desync in motion, with creatures and projectiles flying while the bass thumps in your headphones makes it well worth the trip. With a host of post-release support and quality-of-life changes, The Foregone Syndicate has a lot to be proud of in Desync.

Desync is a classic example of "at first you don't succeed.."
I will admit, I was drawn to this game because I found it aesthetically pleasing, and with a good soundtrack is always a bonus (just like Hotline Miami). FPS is not a genre I generally play on a regular basis, so I found Desync to be rather challenging with its face-paced, high level difficulty.
But certainly not impossible.
Unlike most games, Desync will throw you in with little to no tutorial and you will fail over and over again. You will be forced the hard way in learning the mechanics of each enemy, the layout of each level and what each unlockable weapon does. Desync will not dumb it down for you. There are times where it becomes so unforgiving that you'll want to punch your screen, pour water over your keyboard and set fire to your house. But keep at it. With practice and patience, getting over that hurdle or boss battle is the most rewarding feeling!
Desync achieves what its set out to do, and that is to improve your skills. Revisit previous levels and you'll see exactly that. Again Im not a pro in this genre but if I can get through this intense, tron-like world, anyone can.

A very fun game that plays with the idea of "Hollywood hacking" and takes it to it's logical conclusion. Break into computers and change records, cover your tracks, upgrade your hardware and try not to get caught.
Nice relaxing soundtrack combined with very tense moments as you rush to delete server logs before the trace catches up with you
However, I do have a couple of complaints which make the game a lot less fun than it should be.
Firstly, it's possible to miss the story, entirely. It's not just a sequence of random assignments, there is an ongoing story as well. But if you're not in the right situation at the right point in the game, you don't get the email which sets the plot in motion. Or, you could not read it, or you could get it but not be in a position (lack of money or equipment) to do it...in which case the game carries on regardless but with no objective.
Secondly, once you reach the stage where you can break into banks and alter your account information, money effectively becomes meaningless in the game, so the challenge of raising funds to buy better hardware and software is entirely removed from the game...which takes away a large part of the game.
Thirdly, you do seem very dependent on the RNG. You can be in a situation where the only jobs you're offered...you can't do because you don't have the equipment needed to complete them. And so...you just end up stuck with no way to raise money as you're no longer being offered jobs within your remit. The only way around this is to have the RNG be favourable, or be psychic and know in advance what equipment you're going to need.
Fourthly, I really, really hate how if you have the pointer over a text entry field you're filling in....and you move the mouse outside the box..it automatically loses focus. Wouldn't be a huge issue if you weren't always racing against the clock, but it can be very frustrating.
Fifthly, once you discover that InterNIC never, ever change their passwords and never run a trace, it becomes utterly trivial to avoid getting caught - all you have to do is make sure your connections run through them and delete the logs after each mission.
Still, I do recommend it. It's fun to dip into and play for an hour or so at a time...but the aforementioned points do make it rather frustrating at times. Oh, and when you run at higher resolutions the text becomes absolutely tiny, rather than scaling to compensate.

This is a great game of tactics. Simultaneous order execution is the perfect implementation for this type of game. It also supports a play-by-email format, of sorts. Simply start a game and issue orders. Once your opponent has issued orders, the orders are resolved and the next turn becomes available for both players to log in, view the previous turn outcome and then issue orders anew. Really great game. Prime looks like a waste of time and money. FS2 looks like it could be a worthy successor.

The entire game and DLC is worth about $10 max IMO. I was disappointed that the RED DLC was only ~10 stages. Also for several people (myself included) it takes a LONG time to calculate the results of a turn. For me it was 30+ seconds sometimes. I think it is a bug. If I had not had a second monitor to watch videos in, I would have quit. Overall the gameplay is pretty basic and it takes a long time not to feel like it is just plain unfair--because it often is. But once your skill level exceeds the friction of the clunky difficulty it can be a somewhat challenging and rewarding game. I'll be keeping an eye out for the sequel.

I finally won my first war - and what a war it was!
First off, let me say - "Just do it."  Buy the game, play the tutorial, have fun, then just do it.  The game can seem overwhelming at first, but when things start to click, it sucks you in.
I played the base game before buying any DLC, then quickly gobbled most of the DLC up (and will likely gobble the rest up).
Now let me tell you my story.
1066 A.D.
Just like with the tutorial, I started as King Alfonso VI of Leon.  I have long been fascinated by the reconquista, and so it was a natural choice.  Also (spoiler... kinda), playing as the Jimena brothers puts you in a good starting position, as regardless of what happens between the three of you, you (as the player) are likely to wind up in control of Northern Spain.  But I digress...
After the tutorial and a few trial playthroughs (in which I was handily defeated), I sit down to play in earnest.  I fire up Alfonso and decide to go slow.  Focus on development for the first couple of years, assess my vassals, see how things develop around me.  I rapidly marry the princess of Aragon to get my direct bloodline going, and set out to murder my older brother, Sancho, the king of Castille to the east.  It would seem luck is not on my side, I've got a fairly weak plot going against him, so I continue to focus on internal matters and bide my time.  After a bit of bribing and cajoling, I finally pull someone in who can get close to him.  My plot is now very strong.  So meanwhile, new courtiers are showing up at court.  I'm shuffling council members and watching my vassals while my brother, Garcia, king of Galicia to the west fights off a muslim invasion.
All the while, I'm cartefully monitoring a my sister, Urraca, the Countess of Zamora, and one of my vassals.  We have little love for each other, and she has formed a faction in opposition to my reign.  Still, her cause is weak and since it's discovered, I will soon have a good case for imprisoning her.
The time comes to imprison her not long after.  She hates me, her husband barely likes me, but I figure as long as she is in jail, she's no threat to  me.  All the while, my strong plot to murder Sancho is stalling.  There has been more than enough time, with no results.
In any case, I figure with the strength of my plot it should be soon, and Garcia is weak from fightin the muslims, so I borrow money from the jews, exercise my claim to Galicia, and declare war!
Now, shortly after this (and much to my surprise), my Sister gives birth to a son in prison.  Now I have them both imprisoned.  But her husband still marginally supports me, and the boy is of the line, so I chance it and let him go.  It works in my favor, as the boy now favors me.  I'll let his mother go, eventually, but it will be a while.
No sooner do I raise my levies, but another spanish muslim, Sheikh Muhammad of Mertola decides that Spain would be better off without me.  As I march west to face Garcia, Muhammad marches north to invade Leon.  And, to top it off, Sancho has soldiers marching through my lands because, as it turns out, he's fighting Garcia, as well.  Though not technically "at war" with Sancho, this puts me at odds with all three rulers, including Scottish allies that Garcia has brought in due to his marriage!  This is going to be interesting.
But luck is on my side.  Garcia and Sancho have both been weakend prior to my joining the fray, and while I can muster strong, fresh levies, they are scrambling to rebuild theirs.  The Scots are too far away from home to reinforce effectively, and no one else in the Aftasid Emirate seems interested in joining Muhammad's war.  To top it off, my wife's brother, King Sancho of Aragon offers to join me in my fight against the muslim invaders.
Northern Spain erupts into war.  With Garcia fighting me, and Sancho fighting Garcia, and me and Sancho undermining each other's gains, and the Scottish tropps joinging in to aid Garcia, and the Aragonese troops joining with my vassal's levies to defend against the saracen invasion.
My beloved wife dies in childbirth in 1076, after having given me two sons and two daughters.  I promptly marry myself to Chamoa, the sister of the Count Ergas of Castelo Branco, so as to strengthen my claim on Galician lands.  Meanwhile Urraca, my imprisoned sister, has been busy herself.  She seduces one of her guards and escapes from prison.  Now I have vassal smack dab in the middle of my kingdom who dislikes me intensely.
But the war(s) are going in my favor, and so I focus my attention on them.  The money is dwindling, but I'm managing the loss by carefully releasing vassal levies when they aren't needed, and leveraging my own levies and that of my ally as much as possible.  Then, something strange happens... well, two thing, actually.
The first thing that happens is Galicia suddenly belongs to my Brother Sancho!  What the devil?  I had this down to a science!  Did Garcia die in battle or something?  Nope.  Turns out that Sancho forced him into an unconditional surrender.  Garcia is now the Duke of Galicia, and Sancho is the king of both Galicia and Castille.  This is bad... where is that murder plot!?
The second is that Urraca, my sister who hates me and wants my throne and who imprisoned?  She and I end up settling family matters one night... in the most intimate way possible.  Now she is firmly on my side.  Of course, me finding her getting shtupped by Bishop Pelayo one night doesn't do much for our new found affection.  But a little blackmail and mum's the word, with no great loss of love on either end.
When the last saracen army is beaten back I can press them into surrender, and my very small deficit becomes a healthy treasury overnight.  Only now I'm sandwiched between Sancho's kingdoms.  I swear to God, the day after I settle with Muhammad, my long awaited murder plot comes to fruition, and Sancho is now dead.  Praise to Heaven!  Only the map doesn't change... ♥♥♥♥... it turns out that Sancho got busy and had a couple sons of his own.  Now everything I've worked for is at the mercy of a 10 year-old child.
So I do the wise thing - I offer peace.
Soon after the peace accord was agreed upon, that 10 year-old fell victim to an unfortunate fall while playing in a very high tower.  God rest his noble soul.
Though no lands were reclaimed for Chrsitendom, at long last there is peace in Christian Spain, a large portion of which is owned by my nephew, the 8 year-old King Diego of Castille.  I pray that God watch over him, and that the same misfortunes that befell his father and brother don't befall him as well.
10/10 - Would fight a bloody, incestuous, murderous war with my family and the heathen Muslims again.

Back in the day, circa 2002, I played vanilla Morrowind and enjoyed it thoroughly, and actually completed it, largely because (I think) the mod scene wasn't anything like it is now.
Oblivion and Skyrim are my white whale. My sisyphean tasks doomed to never be completed. I've never actually finished Oblivion (or Skyrim, for the same reasons). Each time I've tried to start I've instead found myself modding it for hours on end over the course of several days before eventually getting distracted by something else and I "forget" about it. I once spent two weeks modding the non-Steam version of Oblivion back in 2008. I still remember buying all the original DLCs from the official Bethesda site, including the infamous horse armor DLC, and then spending hours upon hours combing through the mod collections on Nexusmods to find all the best mods, from unofficial patches, to UI improvements, to graphics mods, to whole new content packs with their own dungeons or questlines. I still have all of those original files saved on my NAS, totalling 16GB, neatly organized by category, all these years later.
If you enjoy tinkering with mods, play-testing each one after install, troubleshooting mod compatibility issues, using/learning archaic and obscure third-party mod managers (BOSS, OBSE, OBMM, Wrye BASH, TES4Edit, etc.), optimizing the load order of each mod, learning new scripting languages, and generally not getting anything done because you waste all your time on modding a game instead of actually playing it, then Oblivion (or Skyrim) is the game for you.

Snowman is a 2D sidescrolling game where you have to collect presents and jump over the hazards coming towards you on the ground. It is also one of the worst games on Steam.
To even start playing it you have to click on a trophy icon from the main menu and then reset the game. If you don't do this first, the level select screen just won't respond. Once you actually get in to the level you'll likely find that the music track has decided to duplicate and play itself two, three, or even four times over creating a cacophony of sound so offputting that you have to mute the game (something you have to do from your OS, because this game offers absolutely no options menu).
Once you start playing, you'll immediately regret that decision, as this game is something straight out of 2001-era flash gaming, except somehow with less content and worse graphics. Comically awful hitboxes make the game range from frustrating to downright impossible, with there being several patterns in the final level that are guaranteed damage, and about half of the appearances of birds in all levels impossible to avoid, meaning you have a coinflip chance of losing progress whenever one shows up.
There's two "power-ups", both of which seem to make the game more annoying - one is a guitar that gives you +5 presents but causes a giant popup to appear covering half of the screen and making it impossible to see what's coming, and the other is a rocket boost which makes you go significantly faster, but significantly extends the length of your jump, meaning that every time you press the up arrow you're committing to having to land 2-3 screens further than you can actually see, and if something spawns there your abysmal lateral speed means you take damage.
Forget paying a dollar for this, I wouldn't play more of it if the developer was the one paying me.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is Larian's magnum opus.
Equal parts labor of love and affectionately kickstarted community project, D:OS2 takes the RPG conventions in games like Neverwinter Nights, Baldur's Gate, and Planescape Torment and brings them to the forefront of an epic story that combines modern design sensibilities with old school gameplay methods.
The game is a marvel to look at, with gorgeously detailed environments and eye-popping spells that each have unique, detailed animations. Everything from the multiple animations for each of the game's four unique races, to the way they spin their weapons in their hands whilst idle in combat, down to the way the shadows in the forests hide all but the eyes of a looming wolf give this game a sense of awe and impressive scope without compromising on its graphical fidelity.
Original Sin 2 plays much like the first, utilizing a turn-based combat system that allows you to execute a certain number of actions per turn thanks to the AP system. How much AP you start with per turn is deterrmined by your stats, which can be raised and changed throughout the game's campaign, and cap at a max of 6 points per turn. Everything from movement, to consuming items, to attacking consumes AP, and the key to mastering Original Sin 2's combat is to understand the limitations of  both your AP, and the enemy's.
Perhaps the best thing that can be said about D:OS2's combat is that it feels fair in a way that many RPG's struggle to balance. Yes, you will often times be outnumbered and outgunned in impossibly difficult combat scenarios, but the game understands this and doesn't pile on impossibly high AP on top of it. The enemies follow the same rules you do, they just tend to have the advantage at the start of combat.
Manipulating the combat scenarios in your favor is key to overcoming many of the challenges in Divinity, and the game knows you'll die. You should know you'll die as well, and take every defeat as an opportunity to glean information on the battlefield. Perhaps throwing that fire grenade you had sitting in your inventory at the conveniently placed oil barrel would have blocked a pathway that would have allowed you to funnel enemies into a chokepoint where you could easily pick them off one by one, instead of being flanked and trying to fight on two fronts. Maybe you should have blinded that far away archer instead of wasting AP knocking down that low health warrrior. Each of your choices in combat carry a sense of weight and importance that many games struggle to match, and it's this outstanding combat system that really helps Larian stand a cut above the competition.
However, no RPG is complete without an engrossing story, and Larian delivers in spades. Perhaps the best thing that can be said about Larian's storytelling is that they don't take themselves too seriously. Make no mistake: the game is full of dark twists and turns with macabre scenes and sullen sights, but it also knows how to work in a good joke or two in between the very serious plot, and this tongue-in-cheek approach to storytelling is refreshing in a time where gritty reboots and grimdark storytelling seems to be part and parcel for the games industry. It's not to say you won't see some emotionally draining, miserable scenes. Quite the contrary: D:OS2 has a darker, more mature storyline than the first. Yet, Larian also knows that every now and again, you just want to laugh at a good fart joke. Both these things mesh together to create a world that feels alive, lived in, and pregnant with lore and details.
If there's any flaw to Original Sin 2, it's that the game can oftentimes be a bit obtuse, and its pacing could certainly use some work. Oftentimes, you'll spend hours in towns and cities squeezing every last drop of information from NPC's, only to feel exhausted by the end of it all as you've heard them do nothing but talk, talk, talk, talk, talk. Then, the game sends you off to combat, but these combat sections suffer from the same pacing issues as the towns do: you'll enter a slogging gauntlet of endless combat, and while the combat in this game stands up better than some of the conversational RPG elements, it can be exhausting to clear a cave of half a dozen or so encounters, only for you to have to suddenly mentally prepare yourself for a massive bossfight.
Another issue is balance. While an RPG this complex and interactable is almost impossible to balance, it can't be helped but to feel that certain classes just outshine others in ways that make them borderline overpowered. A mage in a party will oftentimes outshine a sword and board warrior in more ways than one: more CC, healing abilities, and damage. Meanwhile, the tanky warrior is relegated to being a CC soaking machine for enemy NPC's, and it's not unusual for melee characters to find themselves dead for long stretches of combat in the starting sections of the game. While experience will eventually mitigate these early deaths, players who are wet behind the ears might find themselves aggravated at a difficulty curve that seems to almost always favor attacking from a distance, and all too often punishes players who push in for aggressive melee strategies. Now, as I said, experience and familiarity will eventually make these encounters much more favorable towards melee characters, but first time players be warned: melee can be punishing for the unsuspecting.
Still, despite those flaws, Larian has delivered an unprecedented masterpiece: a rich world rivaling the scale of games like The Witcher 3 and The Elder Scrolls franchise if not in size then in scope. It is a 50+ hour game with so many choices in dialogue, combat approaches, and solutions to questlines that it almost feels unfair to try and review the game because there's simply too much one could miss. One man's difficult quest is another man's cakewalk, easily solved by some maguffin the first player didn't see on their first playthrough, but that's the beauty of Original Sin 2: no 2 playthroughs will ever play out identically. No 2 strategies will ever be quite the same, and outside of cheesing boss encounters and difficult combat sections, Original Sin 2 is a punishing but rewarding RPG experience that doesn't babysit its players. Larian clearly respects the people who play their game, and it shows in this outstanding labor of love.
Lastly, as an aside, Larian Studios also included a DM mode that allows players to create custom campaigns in the same vein as a D&D or tabletop RPG experience. While the tools could use some polishing, and the system could certainly use some quality of life adjustments, the DM mode is ultimately an incredible addition to an already massive game, allowing players from across the world to create and tell new stories at their leisure. In fact, the DM tools could stand to have their own review with how robust they are, so I'll leave it at this: if you haven't, get some friends and give the campaign editor a try. You won't be disappointed.
So, to reiterate: Original Sin 2 is a masterpiece. It is not perfect, but games never are, and this is the best TRUE RPG experience we've had in almost a decade of games. Beautiful, deep, and richly complex, Original Sin 2 is less a game and more an endless sandbox of possibilities that, to Larian's credit, invites players to indulge in its whackiness, its silliness, its darkness and its sadness. Unrivaled by any other RPG in the last ten years, Original Sin 2 is easily 2017's RPG of the year, and a strong contender for Game of the Year.

A great turn-based strategy game that is completely free-to-play, with ZERO pay-to-win aspects.
Following the trend set by the MOBA front-runners like League of Legends and Heroes of the Storm, Atlas Reactor's cast of heroes are immediately available for purchase with in-game currency after a little bit of grinding. The grind is not long, and might actually be beneficial for new players as they are able to learn the abilities of each hero as they progress and earn more.
The heroes in this game are also near perfectly balanced. I have never been in a situation where I feel I was bested by a character's overpoweredness. Losing is always a product of a misplay of my own, which seems to be rare nowadays—especially with strategy games.
The game also has constant events and new ranked seasons so that you are able to earn a multitude of rewards, like skins and in-game currency, all FOR FREE. You do not have to spend a dollar to earn skins in this game.

As disclosure, I've programmed since I was very young.
This game is quite a fun programming puzzle and also a very kind introduction to assembly programming. You don't need any experience to enjoy the puzzles because the system is very simple and intuitive! The game runs smooth, no crashes, and the graphics are just right to evoke the experience of using early GUI systems.
There's a small story to accompany the system, which you unlock as you progress through the game, as well as a few collectables. For those new to programming, you will spend a few hours thinking about each puzzle and debugging your solutions, but you will find it very rewarding as you acquire mastery.
For those who've programmed before, you'll find many of the puzzles simple, though you may sometimes struggle to fit logic into each cell; it's very difficult to have one cell do all the work, so don't be afraid to have cells communicate with eachother!
For $8, this game is well-priced and well-made, along with accompanying sandboxes and a challenge creator. The TIS-100 is a great programming toy and puzzle, although experienced programmers will need only ~10 hours of playtime to beat the game.
That said, programming is not for everybody. You'll spend a lot of time on each puzzle and the only reward you will get is seeing things working as intended. In fact, far more often you'll be frustrated that things *aren't* working. Nonetheless, this game captures the fun and challenge of programming with a much lower barrier to entry than normal!
I highly recommend this game as a diversion that may eventually consume your time at school and work while you feverishly try to design a solution for segments you've been stumped on. If you know somebody with a clever mind and a bit of patience, this game is a great gift.
For the developer:
Well done, and although the story was a bit cliche, the game itself is solid design. Keep it up!

A nice little problem-solving game. Features a fictional computer with a very simplistic architecture and minimal instruction set, so it should be easy for novices and perhaps even non-programmers to catch on.
No prior knowledge of any assembly language is necessary, though some understanding of how computers work may be beneficial. Though I already had experience writing assembly as a hobby, I can definitely see this game being a nice and gentle introduction for people interested in learning but unsure where to begin (and perhaps intimidated by the specification of commonly used architectures like x86). That said, it does seem like more of a puzzle game than an actual programming game. I definitely recommend moving on to learn a real entry-level instruction set like MIPS/ARM if you enjoyed learning the primitive TIS-100 language.
I recommend this game to anyone who is passionate about programming and computers, though I think the average person may find it a bit dull.
I will definitely be keeping an eye on this developer in future.

Well I suppose it was expected that I would write a review for this considering I have been pretty much a die-hard Sonic fan since 1991.
Our poor little Blue Hedgehog has been through a lot of rough times over these past 15 or so years. Sega have just had a really hard time finding the original formula that made their games work. In the 3D Sonic world, I think Generations was a really strong step in the right direction. However when I was playing that, I always felt the 2D stages felt really lacklustre as the graphics were in a sense, too flashy for the product it was trying to promote.
With abominations like Sonic '06, Sonic 4 and Sonic and the Secret Rings etc that have sullied his reputation almost to the point of no return, I was honestly a bit skeptical like a lot of fans were when it was announced that there would be an "all new 2D adventure". I held off picking it up until it's release date was approaching and I'd heard a few fan remixes of some of the music and thought "why not, it can't be worse than Sonic 4."
The first impressions I got as the opening 'cutscene' rolled made me think I was gonna start a remaster of Sonic 3, however getting teleported to the Green Hill Zone was a bit of a nostalgia kick. I do feel that the zone has been overdone a bit, Emerald Hill or Angel Island wouldn't have been bad as a starting zone if they were insistent on returning to a first stage. I can understand why they did it though as GHZ is synonymous with Sonic and would be a good way to pull once loyal fans back. The thing I quite enjoyed about the rehashes of the original zones was that the first act would almost be a remake of the original zone but the second act in each zone would introduce new mechanics to the game. (I absolutely loved the bouncy chemicals on Chemical Plant Zone 2)
The new zones are solid, the final zone being particularly memorable, it's easily my favourite of the entire game and I've went back to replay it a good few times. Studiopolis isn't bad either, the bosses of both acts both being particularly fun encounters.
The graphics are very reminiscent of Sonic CD, it has a crispness that the original Mega Drive games had without being overbearing. There is a decent amount of background clutter without it detracting from the stage, a problem I had with Generations.
The real high point of the game for me though is the music, every stage has had a lot of love given to it whether it's a remix of an older stage or one of the brand new ones. A lot of the songs are ridiculously catchy, the boss themes in particular are notable. Trying not to tap your foot along to Hi Spec Robo Go in Studiopolis' first boss fight is a near impossibility. The Robotnik boss one is really good as well. The final boss theme (Not the extra hidden one) is probably my favourite boss theme of all time from the Sonic franchise which is high praise as there have been so many good ones even from some of the not so highly regarded Sonic titles.
Bosses are pretty challenging with some taking particular spikes in difficulty, that Oil Ocean boss....man. I haven't had a challenge from Sonic bosses for a while as generally control issues or camera related niggles have caused unnecessary frustrations. The Hard Boiled Heavies are an interesting addition to the game and a lot of the Robotnik battles are pretty entertaining.
I'll list of Pro's and Con's for the people who have the tl;dr mindset to sum up my thoughts.
Pros:
+ Graphics are crisp for a 2D Sonic
+ Real impression of speed
+ Music is incredibly good
+ Decent length. (S3&K amount of zones)
+ A lot of variation between zones
+ Bosses are generally challenging without being frustrating
+ Special Stages to get the Emeralds are quite exciting and offer a decent challenge.
Cons:
- Blue Sphere Special Stages are a real drag. Star Posts offer nothing more
- No Achievement for getting the true ending.
- The game can feel on rails sometimes
- Special Stages to obtain Emeralds can be quite tricky to find.
All in all, this has been the best 2D Sonic I've played since the original Sonic Rush on the DS. Do I recommend it, yes, of course. Anyone who is even remotely interested in picking a new Sonic title up should give this a serious chance.

Sonic Mania is a sequel to the games Sonic 1, 2, 3 & Knuckles that I played when I was younger on the Sega Mega Drive/Genesis. The music and environments are a wonder to play through, a mixture of old remixed levels and some new. I'm having a fantastic time playing through the game and uncovering all the secrets.
I'm not a fan of most of the new boss fights. They seem too gimmicky and are too much of a departure from the normal gameplay. Some of the boss music is also strange, where rather than it sounding like you're fighting for your life, it sounds like you're at a bizarre carnival or something. Overall the negatives are very minor.

Okay, first of all; let's address the elephant in the room: The thing that causes everyone to instantly claim this port is garbage. The DRM. Sega used Denuvo as an attempt to deter pirates from breaking into Sonic Mania; a move that instantly made a lot of people angry. Not only is it known for slowing down hardware on some machines; but it comes with the added problem of forcing someone to be online. If your steam gets disconnected for any reason; the whole game will crash and become unplayable. This becomes unforgiveable when you realize that Sonic Mania is a ONE PLAYER GAME. There is a multiplayer mode, and they have confirmed online multiplayer will be a thing; but if this is needed to make that work, it's likely going to be hard to swallow. Especially since if and when Denuvo stops offering support; Sonic Mania will become 100% unplayable. Hopefully Sega will take Bethesda's example and remove this as soon as possible. Especially since it was cracked days after release.
Now that this is out of the way, let's talk about the actual GAME, shall we? Sonic Mania is a 2D style platformer, made in the wake of the classic Sonic 2D games. It honors the classic traditions with a familiar; yet fresh new approach to the old Sonic formula; using nostalgia to not only remind us of the things we love; but improve upon them. There are several zones ported over from older games (1 Stage from Sonic 1, 2 from Sonic 2 and CD, 3 from Sonic 3&Knuckles) and 4 brand new stages based on stages of a similar type from older games. This allows players new and old to find some enjoyment out of the designs. But these aren't just the stages you remember as they've become mismashed with other zones of a similar type to create a super zone hodgepodge. For example: Flying Battery Zone is a Sonic 3 & Knuckles rep; but this Flying Battery also contains Wing Fortress and Sky Base Zone elements from Sonic 2 and Sonic 1 for Gamegear. This creates brand new setpieces and designs for stages allowing one to completely reimagine and even improve upon the design.
Adding to this; Replay value is all over the place: Time Attack mode returns from Sonic CD; 2-Player Competition from Sonic 2 is brought back; you have the option to play as Sonic/Tails, Sonic, Tails and Knuckles; there's just so much effort and creativity put into the game, that it's hard not to enjoy it. 3D Sonic fans maybe disappointed that there are absolutely 0 references to any games in the 3D era (This sticks strictly to the 2D Sonics before Sonic Adventure, with traces of Sonic 4 as well); but overall; it's still a great experience).
Does it come recommended? On Nintendo Switch, Playstation 4 and X-Box One? Yes, 100%, buy it. But on Steam? With the Denuvo DRM in the way; I'd recommend it if you're a hardcore Sonic fan, and can get over the fact that one day; if Sega doesn't remove this, it may become unplayable. But if you just want to experience the game on your PC; at 25$, I'd say it's at least worth it; The game is not bad; don't let the negative reviews fool you. It's a good game, people just hate the stupid DRM this version got hit with for no reason. It's understandable why there is so much backlash towards that.

This is one of those times where I wish Steam had a more graduated rating system than the binary "recommend / don't recommend."  I feel like I'm either outright praising a game or completely condemning it--and in my opinion, DESYNC doesn't deserve either treatment.
At its core, DESYNC is a stylish arena-shooter with an arcade-style scoring system that rewards skill, finesse, and creativity.  As you progress through the game--particularly in the beginning--you'll probably feel like you're constantly being updated with new combo types and unlockables.  The camera zooms in on a corpse as it pirouettes in slow-motion; a prompt alerts you to the fact that you've found a new way to kill enemies as a score is quickly tallied.  It's a great mechanic that constantly pushes you forward in search of new weapons, items, and obstacles to kill things with (and on).
In a lot of ways, DESYNC feels like a breath of fresh air in the genre.  It eschews the hyperrealism of "kitchen sink" FPS games for a blunt and highly stylized aesthetic; it trades mission markers and NPC dialogue for the pursuit of the almighty high score and wordless combat.  For these reasons, the game feels paradoxically simple in presentation yet complex in nature.  Have other FPS games accomplished the same things?  Sure.  But more haven't, and for that, this game is worthy of commendation.
Yet there are many aspects of DESYNC--among them, subjective items that others will surely disagree with--that often spoil the things it does
, and left me with a sort of frustration that, unlike a Super Meat Boy or Dark Souls game, discouraged me from coming back:
PROS:
+ Great Soundtrack
+ TONS of combos attached to a fairly exhaustive scoring system that will keep perfectionists striving for higher scores
+ Weapons feel mechnically distinct and nuanced, with multiple firemodes, strengths, and weaknesses
+ While the AI of most enemies devolves into mobbing you at melee range, there's still a decent degree of personality and strategy in handling each opponent, whether it's the lumbering, shielded knight-like enemies, the diminutive "headcrab" monsters, or the acrobatic, shuriken-throwing ninjas.
CONS:
- Underwhelming weapon "feedback" and sound effects, which is particularly disappointing in a game built around shooting things
- Murky techno aesthetic makes it an all-too common occurence to bumble between arenas--everything looks too similar and dull.  There was so much potential for varied and colorful areas, but it feels squandered with "samey" blue and purple locations.
- Some ambiguity isn't a bad thing, but Desync does an all-around poor job at communicating concepts and mechanics to the player.  Am I trying to learn the language of a new puzzle-system in "The Witness" or am I playing an arcade-arena FPS?  Worse, the mechanics aren't particularly complex once you figure them out--either through trial & error or message boards--so there's no reason why the game can't do a better job teaching you about them, and I'd argue that their vagueness adds nothing to the game.
- I'm not sure why the initial hub was designed the way it was:  Access to mechanics like weapon customization, stats, sidearms, and modules are provided by interacting with in-game terminals that are spread around, yet look virtually identical and result in you frequently walking up to the wrong one until you've memorized all of their locations.  Additionally, player customization and level selection "menus" are separated by an elevator that takes far too long to ferry you from one area to the other, and will inadvertantly whisk you back to the starting point if you don't disembark quickly enough.  Why do we need to have an elevator in the first place?
- Difficulty can be frustrating at times, particularly since enemies will happily spawn on top of you.  The result is that much of the "challenge" (certainly not all, but a considerable portion) is mitigated by trial-and-error memorization of spawn locations and composition...at least until you develop a sizable set of weapons, power-ups, and modules to choose from.  There's nothing wrong with a game being built on difficulty, whether it's Dark Souls, Super Meat Boy, or FTL--in fact, it's vastly preferable to games you can sleepwalk through.  And when DESYNC does difficulty well, it does it
well.  However, all too often the game presents situations that are challenging in ways that are tedious and unfun, where the satisfaction of finishing isn't so much a sense of accomplishment as it is a sensation of "glad I don't have to do
again."
- I felt like the "Aberration" Levels took novel concepts (such as akimbo weapons or unusual rules) and turned them into something that is frequently unfun.  In one instance, you are given dual railguns (cool) and pitted against enemies that can only be damaged while stunned AND at long range.  Unfortunately, most enemies tend to move nearly as fast as you and want nothing more than to get up in your face; the result is an incredibly tedious act of kiting a group of enemies around as you attempt to increase the distance between the two of you so you can stun and kill them.   Ammo (or lack thereof) frequently becomes an issue in these levels, as well, which brings the action to a screeching halt in the form of a prompt that literally tells you to restart from the last checkpoint--when you still had ammo.  And because Aberration levels comprise nearly half of all available levels, it's not simply an argument of avoiding those levels.  They're an integral part of the game.

DESYNC's theme is "absolute ♥♥♥♥ing assault on the senses". Pulsing electronic music blasts out as you dodge and weave between viciously fast monsters and environmental hazards, desperately trying to avoid dying.
Nothing I've ever played has had quite the same kind of atmosphere. There's no hand holding. You have to figure out what all the weapons, enemies, upgrades do almost entirely by yourself. In fact, the devs have stated that initially they wanted to have no language at all; instead relying on cryptic symbols to explain everything.
The whole "kill enemies in a specific way for bonus points" gets this a lot of comparisons to Painkiller and Bulletstorm, but I'd actually say it's more like a 3D Hotline Miami: fast, unrelenting and wants nothing more for you to give up, but when you hit that end level screen there's nothing more satisfying.
It's with no irony or elitism that I say this game is not for casuals. If you're looking for a fun light-hearted game, look elsewhere. But if you can handle the glitched-out aesthetics and very challenging gameplay, after a few hours DESYNC will make you feel like an FPS god.

First, let's address a central question that may or may not be in your mind as you're reading this review.
CTA = MOWAS2 reskin?
Effectively, yes.  The sounds of guns, tooltips of weapons, hints and tips in loading screens, UI, font choices for events (vehicle hull damaged/destroyed, penetrating hit, exp tickers when achieving kills etc), direct control of infantry and vehicles and the overall functionality of game mechanics are identical.
So what gives?  To preface my actual review of the game and its content in terms of pros and cons (I mostly play RTS games and have racked up a few ten thousand hours across varying franchises), I'd like to open up a bit further about the whole Call to Arms / Men of War Assault Squad 2 mess.
As you may or may not be aware, MOWAS2's development issues, while layered in part to incompetence from staff, can also be explained by the Ukraine Crisis, as a part of the development team were Ukrainians and, one of the main publishers of Men of War in the past has historically been a Russian company.  MOWAS2 is virtually unsupported today, and even during active development it was very apparent that the game did not build upon MOWAS1 in any way.  To me, a humble consumer, MOWAS2 seemed like a blatant cash-grab.  Mind you, I'm not a veteran of the MOWAS franchise, so I can largely forgive the nature of its development as I assumed the game would be developed past a certain point.  It was not.
CTA blumbered out of no where and was in part funded by crowdsourcing.  The daily playercount as far as the consumer is concerned is from 40 to 50 people, with a spike of perhaps 15 people online at once (oh boy.)
That was the preface, now on to the review of the product itself:
Call to Arms is topical, it features a fictional arab fighting force (GRM) which you'd be forgiven for mistaking for ISIS, and a Gulf War era US military, though without Javelins.
When considering multiplayer versus play (1v1, 2v2, 3v3, 4v4) the game's pacing takes place in 3 stages:
Infantry,
Mechanized,
Heavy mechanized.
Each of these stages lasts roughly 5-7 minutes, so your average game should not take past 20 minutes no matter the size, as the amount of resources given per player is a fixed amount (boring, in my opinion) and after incurring X losses you just stop getting income, period.
There are no heavier tanks past the Bradley, BMP-3 and Stryker MGS, though the fact they want to implement the Abrams is almost painfully obvious.  AT Weapons are limited to the RPG-7, LAW and AT-4 rocket launchers.
This is where any original ideas end.  The rest of the game and its mechanics are familiar to anyone who has played more than 5 hours of the MOWAS franchise, which is a let-down.  There are 2 arguments that are popular to excuse this fact, first:  "It's only 20 dollars!" and second "It's in Alpha!"
To the first point, 20 dollars is a nice price.  It's genuinely what this game is worth if you intend on purchasing it.  To say that it's "only" 20 dollars is like saying that a cheeseburger is "only" 1 dollar - is it a bargain?  Or is it just the maximum amount of money the producer can ask without being scoffed at, at this point?
To the second, and this is funny, CTA is actually more stable and better streamlined than AS2, which is just bizarre to me.  This 20 dollar title is better polished during Alpha, than MOWAS2 ever was after years of development.  I'd love to give CTA the benefit of the doubt in terms of developmental stage but I highly doubt it will ever become more stable than it already is.
Pros
- It's a cheeseburger, good value
- More stable than the platform used to develop it (Assault Squad 2)
- Better balanced overall in terms of infantry small arms, penetration values of AT Weapons and vehicles
Cons
- Its a cheeseburger, not a filet mignon
- Already has achieved its full potential minus 1 or 2 units prefaction, and it's in "Alpha"
- A few desynch-inducing bugs
- Tiny community
- No new creative thought, it's same old mechanics with a new narrative
- Elite infantry are far too good, infantry AI is detrimentally bad
CTA relies on its multiplayer component for replay value, without a community this replay value does not exist.  While I would like to recommend the game based purely on the fact that it's stable, relatively balanced and rewards skill and tactics (but only to a certain point, sadly, especially the BTR-80 can wipe out infantry armies in seconds at long distances), I cannot recommend it based on the fact it does not have enough players to give you, the customer, any reasonable replay value.
This game needs around 10,000 active, daily players to be able to deliver what it promises.  However, due to being a MOWAS game and therefore having a learning curve that requires patience, it does not seem to have a very good retention rate for players.  People tend to buy the game, try it for 10 hours, and then never looking at it again so sales figures are deceptive.
Should you buy it?  If you're a MOWAS fan and want to support the developer, yes.
If you're an RTS fan who's looking for a new game to dedicate to, create content (YouTube, Twitch) or be part of a community, this is not the game for you.

Full disclosure: I got the full version of this game in a bundle and I'm normally not into card games.
HP Lovecraft stuff has never really been a thing for me, though Chtulhu Saves the World was fun, and the first couple of Penny Arcade games held my attention. Granted, these are comical parody/homage materials in reference to an otherwise creepy setting. Cthulhu Realms is much like these other games in that it is a silly version of HP Lovecraft settings and entities. I smiled at the narration and enjoyed the story.
This is not one of those loot box, card pack, gambling BS freemium tripe games, either. All the cards come in the game, and they're available to you immediately. You cannot spend real world money to get cards, and you work to earn them within each match, and you go back to your basic cards at the start of every match, just as your opponent does. I had figured all of the digital card games were making those sleazy freemium games now, but apparently I was wrong, which relieved me about Cthulhu Realms.
The card game itself baffled me when watching/listening to the explanation of how to play. I think that the word "abjure" gets tossed around a lot, and until you really do it yourself, it might be unclear. Essentially, aburing cards means you're tossing them out for the rest of the match. This is great to do to your crappiest cards, because the next time you draw a hand of cards, you're less likely to get a copy of that card. By the end of a match, you'll be likely to draw great cards almost constantly, though your opponent can do the same.
Abjuring probably had me confused at first because there's also a discard pile...but while abjuring is permant, the "discarded" cards that you aren't abjuring actually get shuffled back into your deck. I'd recommend doing the "how to play" tutorials with the really-enthusiastically-voiced woman talking over the game, followed by playing the first match. When I played my first match, things started to click almost instantly despite feeling overwhelmed a bit with how everything works when it was explained initially in the tutorial.
I enjoyed not only the art on the cards (comical HP Lovecraft stuff), but also the cards themselves in regard to their mechanics. All the cards after the rubbish starting cards are either yellow, purple, or green. Yellow cards typically either cause you to get extra cards to pick from each turn or for the enemy to have to discard one each turn, while purple cards heal you each turn, and green cards allow you to abjure (perfect your deck by having only the best cards in it) and destroy enemy buildings (protective cards each side can get).
Although getting healed from purple cards is very helpful, I also had fantastic luck with the other colors of cards, too. With the green ones, my deck was constant great cards, enemy buildings were basically free to be destroyed every round or two. Then, with the yellow ones, I was able to swap out cards for better cards and cut down on what my opponent could do each round, thus minimizing damage I took and the A.I.'s acquisition of more cards, allowing me to get ahead. I thought it was a pretty great system.
Now that said, it's probably not very complex, because I was able to follow it and complete it on the normal difficulty, and I'm not ordinarily into these card games. If you're a huge fan of the genre, perhaps this is too simple a game for you to get the sort of challenge you want. I had a great time, though, both with the gameplay mechanics and the story. There is a higher difficulty as well, though. I did not try it out of fear and being a super wuss. Perhaps it could provide some challenge for more skilled players than I.
One neat thing I liked about most matches, which was actually what I disliked most about Final Fantasy VIII's card game, Triple Triad, is that most of the matches have some kind of special gameplay change/modifier. One might forbid you from buying purple cards. One might make cards cost less for you to conjure from the middle (purchase stack). I loved these modifiers. They made each match interesting, making me play a bit differently each time, while still giving enough of a berth of freedom.
From the menu, it looks like there is a generic vs AI you can play, with no modifiers, as well as online competitive (the game has mixed reviews which means there might not be a lot of folks online, but I didn't check as I'm generally a single player and sometimes cooperative gamer.
Apparently the first half of the game is free, and the second half costs $4.99 not on sale. I would definitely recommend checking out the first half, and if you like it, buy the full version to play the second half. I think the story was much, much, much more interesting, well-written, and fun (at least in my opinion) in the first half. The second half was just decent, though my biggest complaint would be that upon finishing the second half, the story has no ending or even a cliffhanger. If you win the final match, you just go back to the match selecton screen. I'm not asking for anything animated or even drawn...just the super-enthusiastic-lady to do a nice delivery of a well-written, silly conclusion to the game, the same length as each narration introducing each match.
In conclusion, really liked this game, and other than the second half's story feeling weaker than the first half, and the game not having an ending, I have no other complaints, and $4.99 would have been a steal for me if I hadn't gotten this in a bundle. Maybe I won't give up on video card games after all...

A great machine instruction programming game. It has a steep learning curve if you never programmed a microcontroller before. However with previous assembly experience you can mostly just quickly skim through the manual and start coding, TIS-100 just has a very restricted instruction set and very few registers.
The game allows you to enjoy coding without the less fun parts of software development and then compare your cycle counts with others and optimize your code.
The only thing I didn't like is that comments and labels count as instructions (in the sense that they decrease the number of available lines of code, which is restricted to only a few lines per processor).

Brilliant puzzle game for anyone who likes to code, or design information flow and calculation with fun constraints =)
If you liked spacechem, this will not be difficult to pick up (spacechem is essentially visual coding), but keep in mind this game has a far more spartan design, with more emphasis on the puzzles and a minimal (but satisfying) story. The puzzles are really challenging and fun when you get in deep!

I suppose you don't necessarily need to have programming experience to learn how to play and enjoy TIS-100. But you do need programming experience to know in advance whether you're going to like it or not. Do you like difficult coding challenges? Did you get a rush out of solving tough BareBones problems in Intro to Computer Science? If so, you'll love TIS-100 (and probably get a little addicted to it).
If that's not you, though, then you're probably going to regret getting this game. These challenges get genuinely hard, even for someone familiar with assembly.

Well I suppose it was expected that I would write a review for this considering I have been pretty much a die-hard Sonic fan since 1991.
Our poor little Blue Hedgehog has been through a lot of rough times over these past 15 or so years. Sega have just had a really hard time finding the original formula that made their games work. In the 3D Sonic world, I think Generations was a really strong step in the right direction. However when I was playing that, I always felt the 2D stages felt really lacklustre as the graphics were in a sense, too flashy for the product it was trying to promote.
With abominations like Sonic '06, Sonic 4 and Sonic and the Secret Rings etc that have sullied his reputation almost to the point of no return, I was honestly a bit skeptical like a lot of fans were when it was announced that there would be an "all new 2D adventure". I held off picking it up until it's release date was approaching and I'd heard a few fan remixes of some of the music and thought "why not, it can't be worse than Sonic 4."
The first impressions I got as the opening 'cutscene' rolled made me think I was gonna start a remaster of Sonic 3, however getting teleported to the Green Hill Zone was a bit of a nostalgia kick. I do feel that the zone has been overdone a bit, Emerald Hill or Angel Island wouldn't have been bad as a starting zone if they were insistent on returning to a first stage. I can understand why they did it though as GHZ is synonymous with Sonic and would be a good way to pull once loyal fans back. The thing I quite enjoyed about the rehashes of the original zones was that the first act would almost be a remake of the original zone but the second act in each zone would introduce new mechanics to the game. (I absolutely loved the bouncy chemicals on Chemical Plant Zone 2)
The new zones are solid, the final zone being particularly memorable, it's easily my favourite of the entire game and I've went back to replay it a good few times. Studiopolis isn't bad either, the bosses of both acts both being particularly fun encounters.
The graphics are very reminiscent of Sonic CD, it has a crispness that the original Mega Drive games had without being overbearing. There is a decent amount of background clutter without it detracting from the stage, a problem I had with Generations.
The real high point of the game for me though is the music, every stage has had a lot of love given to it whether it's a remix of an older stage or one of the brand new ones. A lot of the songs are ridiculously catchy, the boss themes in particular are notable. Trying not to tap your foot along to Hi Spec Robo Go in Studiopolis' first boss fight is a near impossibility. The Robotnik boss one is really good as well. The final boss theme (Not the extra hidden one) is probably my favourite boss theme of all time from the Sonic franchise which is high praise as there have been so many good ones even from some of the not so highly regarded Sonic titles.
Bosses are pretty challenging with some taking particular spikes in difficulty, that Oil Ocean boss....man. I haven't had a challenge from Sonic bosses for a while as generally control issues or camera related niggles have caused unnecessary frustrations. The Hard Boiled Heavies are an interesting addition to the game and a lot of the Robotnik battles are pretty entertaining.
I'll list of Pro's and Con's for the people who have the tl;dr mindset to sum up my thoughts.
Pros:
+ Graphics are crisp for a 2D Sonic
+ Real impression of speed
+ Music is incredibly good
+ Decent length. (S3&K amount of zones)
+ A lot of variation between zones
+ Bosses are generally challenging without being frustrating
+ Special Stages to get the Emeralds are quite exciting and offer a decent challenge.
Cons:
- Blue Sphere Special Stages are a real drag. Star Posts offer nothing more
- No Achievement for getting the true ending.
- The game can feel on rails sometimes
- Special Stages to obtain Emeralds can be quite tricky to find.
All in all, this has been the best 2D Sonic I've played since the original Sonic Rush on the DS. Do I recommend it, yes, of course. Anyone who is even remotely interested in picking a new Sonic title up should give this a serious chance.

Sonic Mania is a sequel to the games Sonic 1, 2, 3 & Knuckles that I played when I was younger on the Sega Mega Drive/Genesis. The graphics and gameplay are a perfect recreation of the old games, where a combination of momentum and exploration were the main gameplay themes. The music and environments are a wonder to play through, a mixture of old remixed levels and some new. I'm having a fantastic time playing through the game and uncovering all the secrets.
I'm not a fan of most of the new boss fights. They seem too gimmicky and are too much of a departure from the normal gameplay. Some of the boss music is also strange, where rather than it sounding like you're fighting for your life, it sounds like you're at a bizarre carnival or something. Overall the negatives are very minor.

Okay, first of all; let's address the elephant in the room: The thing that causes everyone to instantly claim this port is garbage. The DRM. Sega used Denuvo as an attempt to deter pirates from breaking into Sonic Mania; a move that instantly made a lot of people angry. Not only is it known for slowing down hardware on some machines; but it comes with the added problem of forcing someone to be online. If your steam gets disconnected for any reason; the whole game will crash and become unplayable. This becomes unforgiveable when you realize that Sonic Mania is a ONE PLAYER GAME. There is a multiplayer mode, and they have confirmed online multiplayer will be a thing; but if this is needed to make that work, it's likely going to be hard to swallow. Especially since if and when Denuvo stops offering support; Sonic Mania will become 100% unplayable. Hopefully Sega will take Bethesda's example and remove this as soon as possible. Especially since it was cracked days after release.
Now that this is out of the way, let's talk about the actual GAME, shall we? Sonic Mania is a 2D style platformer, made in the wake of the classic Sonic 2D games. It honors the classic traditions with a familiar; yet fresh new approach to the old Sonic formula; using nostalgia to not only remind us of the things we love; but improve upon them. There are several zones ported over from older games (1 Stage from Sonic 1, 2 from Sonic 2 and CD, 3 from Sonic 3&Knuckles) and 4 brand new stages based on stages of a similar type from older games. This allows players new and old to find some enjoyment out of the designs. But these aren't just the stages you remember as they've become mismashed with other zones of a similar type to create a super zone hodgepodge. For example: Flying Battery Zone is a Sonic 3 & Knuckles rep; but this Flying Battery also contains Wing Fortress and Sky Base Zone elements from Sonic 2 and Sonic 1 for Gamegear. This creates brand new setpieces and designs for stages allowing one to completely reimagine and even improve upon the design.
Adding to this; Replay value is all over the place: Time Attack mode returns from Sonic CD; 2-Player Competition from Sonic 2 is brought back; you have the option to play as Sonic/Tails, Sonic, Tails and Knuckles; there's just so much effort and creativity put into the game, that it's hard not to enjoy it. 3D Sonic fans maybe disappointed that there are absolutely 0 references to any games in the 3D era (This sticks strictly to the 2D Sonics before Sonic Adventure, with traces of Sonic 4 as well); but overall; it's still a great experience).
Does it come recommended? On Nintendo Switch, Playstation 4 and X-Box One? Yes, 100%, buy it. But on Steam? With the Denuvo DRM in the way; I'd recommend it if you're a hardcore Sonic fan, and can get over the fact that one day; if Sega doesn't remove this, it may become unplayable. But if you just want to experience the game on your PC; at 25$, I'd say it's at least worth it; The game is not bad; don't let the negative reviews fool you. It's a good game, people just hate the stupid DRM this version got hit with for no reason. It's understandable why there is so much backlash towards that.

In its very minimalistic and clean way, Uplink delivers one of the best (if not the best) hacking simulation ever in a game. You start in your gateway: a believable desktop-like screen where you run your apps, manage your missions and connect to the internet through a worldmap. With limited processing power, bandwidht and low grade softwares at first, you must finish missions from dozens of companies to earn money and improve your Uplink ranking, unlocking more challenging and dangerous missions as well as an improving all hardware, software and security at your Gateway.
From destroying and stealing sensitive data, recording voice patterns, decyphering algorithms, decrypting files, compromising LAN networks, completely crippling complex and high-top secure systems, Uplink creates a level of immersion and atmosphere that is rarely seen in any other of the genre, much due to its soundtrack that nails at setting the right mood.
Whatever you choose to be: a white hat hacktivist or a blackhat sworn to end all data , there's no do overs: once caught, good riddance. No Load Game in Uplink, which is the cherry on the top of a well crafted cake.
Must have for the genre fans.

You lead a crew of Deadnauts as they scavenge the wreckage of derelict ships.
PROS
+ Interesting idea
+ Decently built atmosphere
CONS
- Confusing gameplay all around
- Boring
- No tactics
- No music?
- What's the story again?
I loved the idea behind the game. It reminded me of Lt. Gorman from Aliens when the Colonial Marines went into LV-426 to investigate and he was on the dropship watching and directing their movements. Then I was dropped into the game with no tutorial. I took a minute to work my way across the console. Very interesting idea. I like it. There could be a lot of things streamlined, but it adds to the almost steampunk nature of it, in my mind. I think I understand the console well enough. I find out how to breach my first ship.
I work my way across the ship realizing there are no tactics. You just select all your people and move them together... they shoot together... You could take the time to individually move each person, but by the time they all got into position the alien they faced would be dead or gone. There are no tactics. So I continue investigating the ship and collecting data. I figure out how to read ship logs and get some idea of a story. I keep searching. I have no hacker so I can't hack. Don't know what hacking does anyway. I have some defensive player. Don't know what she really does even though I read her gun stats. Battles happen way too fast for me to make use of her anyway. I keep searching. Where's the music? This is getting boring. The graphics are basic, obviously, so there's nothing to really look at. Even reports on the aliens lack any identifying features. No photos. You're fighting orbs. I finish and evacuate the ship.
I find another ship. Repeat everything from ship 1. Hey, one enemy orb shoots rockets or something at you. A new enemy! It looks like the other enemy orb. Oh, somebody died. I can't really read this health gauge properly. I try to move my people to cover or something but it's just a wild west shootout. A couple more die. I decide I don't care. It's either death or the lonely blackness of space with no music. I don't know which is worse. I keep playing for a while. I'm bored with it all. I quit.
That's esentially the game. The negatives could have EASILY been corrected. Add ambient music or radio chatter (chatter comes through in text). It should be a turn based system with cover to add some excitement during battle and allow us time to use our weapons and gadgets, not just a shooter. There needs to be a better explanation of what everything is and why. The messy interface is interesting, but make it logical so people know where to go to find things they are picking up.
These turn based SWAT team simulations never really rang with me.
