Slap Village: Reality Slap is developed by MonkeyToons and published by Tizona Interactive. The first game to be released for both parties involved, I’d say they hit the ground running with this title. Belonging close to the space western subgenre, it features both satire and adventure in healthy doses.

As most other point & click games, you will have plenty of time at your disposal to think through, all of the puzzles and mysteries within Slap Village. Item combination and the in-game hint system are also indispensable in your quest. You play as a female protagonist, Lurditas, looking for her grandmother. As you progress, you shall meet all sorts of goofy characters and equally intriguing locations. Most of them feature anachronistic details which wouldn’t have anything in common with a traditional Old West theme. The game’s entire appeal stems from this strange and hilarious mix-up. You interact with native tribes, talking animals (as well as your pet mouse/sidekick, Rasta), surfers and fast-food workers among others. Slap Village is a far cry from today’s many (and boring, if I may add) hidden object type of games and I admire that wholeheartedly. The puzzles have just the right level of difficulty and there are even a few minigames that spice things up. One related to rhymes proved to be challenging, but ultimately it was a good memory jogger.
Your inventory expands and loses unnecessary items over time, so it never clogs with useless stuff that would hinder your puzzle solving efforts. Attention to detail can also be observed within the dialogue trees and general interaction with other characters. Collectors of in-game bonuses will surely be pleased to find several lists filled with your achievements, items both collected and made from combinations as well as glossary of sorts for the ensemble of wacky characters you meet along the way. Despite having no 3D acceleration, Slap Village truly feels modern and with a revitalized game formula paying homage to LucasArts classic adventures and countless others. Even if you never played them, since very few were ever remastered, such games will always fill a niche for funny and creative storytelling.

Its 2D graphics and hand drawn assets really fitted like a glove this gaming genre and the precursor style it evokes. From the static scenery to the animations, it all ran smoothly and with next to no loading screens. Can’t really complain about its artistic style since it has no visual hiccups. Sadly, the sound department isn’t as flawless. Playing the game with English dubs and subs (though I am quite fluent in it, I will always turn the subtitles on given the option, mostly for grammar purposes) I noticed some discrepancies, especially in the way some of the words were pronounced by some characters. I know that Slap Village features a wide selection of subtitled languages and a Spanish dub, which definitely gives players the liberty to play in the game’s original language. I couldn’t really judge the accuracy of other subtitles or even if the Spanish pronunciation is perfect. But the voice actors seemed more pleasant in it than in English. Speaking of which, I still had to use those subtitles and noticed a few typos.

+ Nice hand drawn graphics and setting
+ Funny and interesting storyline
+ Steam Achievements
- Some English translation issues
- Slightly overpriced
- No Steam Trading Cards
While Slap Village: Reality Slap is just the start of an intended trilogy (or simply put, three episodes related to one another), its story stands out on its own. It managed to fuse together humor, absurd scenery and pop culture references in a manner that dearly reminded me of the Monkey Island series and all the wonderful memories I have with those games. Apart from a few typos and mispronounced words in English, the game had few flaws. And I’m certain that its price will drop as the next episodes get released. Give it a try if you like old school adventure games and you won’t be disappointed.

What is Slap Village: Reality Slap? Well it's a point and click adventure game with a fantastic story. The story takes you on a wild adventure that goes to interesting environments which range from bustling towns to quiet beach sides. The main draw when it comes to Slap Village are the charcaters. There is a HUGE variety in people you will meet, some mysterious and strange, others are halarious drunks and townsfolk who couldn't be more rude if they tried. The characters in this game are truly unique and produce quite a few laughs as you see them take shots at the main protagonist's feet and her killer mouse companion. I will now go into more detail about everything mentioned above, if you dont have the time to read all of this tom foolery I will say this: The game takes elements from classics like Deponia and Monkey Island and implements them into a western theme. The game doesnt take itself seriously which is a GREAT thing when you have charcaters like the ones found in the game. If you like point and click adventure games this one will fit you nicely. The game also produces a few challenging moments when you have to re-think your ideas.
Story
The story in Slap Village winds down like this: The main protagonist is on her way to see her grandma for the summer in a town known as Slap Village. However when she arrives her grandma is nowhere to be found, you as the player have to locate your grandma through any means necessary.....and when I say any means I am being serious, foot wrestling is included;) After I finished the story I was satisfied with the ending the game gave me, I know a few people might not be content on ending with a comical scene however in my mind it fit the entire game nicely.
Graphics/Animation
The game utilises a cartoonish style, which much like the ending of the story molds with the game extremely well. It's also very nice to see the characters movements and facial expressions stay consistent through the game. It would have been frustrating if the developers didnt bother with facial expressions and emotions, luckily they did bother and boy do they match up very well. The main protagonist loves animals so when she sees a very rich lady wearing a fox around her neck.....she gets mad and her face changes to represent how she feels. It's really nice to see these developers in particular, learning from Deponia's mistakes.
Gameplay
This game is a point and click adventure game, much like other point and click adventure games Slap Village uses items found in the game to interact with charcaters, depending on what does work and doesnt, you can combine items accordingly to make them work. For example at the start of the game you need to wake up an animal from sleep so you combine chilli sauce with a power drink. The system works well overall, I didnt come into any problems or issues with the system during my time with the game.
Performance
Not much to say on performance, obivously the game is not CPU or GPU intensive as the game doesn't go through any REAL action scenes or crowded environments with programmed AI. The game doesn't really have many options in general, there were the language inclusion options and you can change what setting the graphics are set to, but I don't really see any real noticeable differences that come from this, except some slight changes to how vibrant the colours look. Other than that, not much really to comment on. The game is a point and click adventure game so it relies on the mouse heavily as it should.
Characters and World Building
As I said before, the charcaters in this game are on point! They fit the comical, funny vibe the game intends for you to expirience. Most characters will be your commedy relief to make sure the player doesnt get too bord during times where they might be stuck with a certain objective. As for the world building it is pretty solid overall, when you go near a saloon in the game, you can hear the sound of glasses clanging and feet stomping. These small sounds add an extensive layer to the world the developers are trying to build around you.
Negatives
I found very few negatives in this game, if i'm being honest half of these things that i'm about to mention are extremely tiny things, that I only picked up on because I went looking around for them. My first negative with the game is that the backgrounds are frozen in to place which wouldnt have been a big deal until you finally get to Slap Village where there are a lot of people around, the only problem with these people (who are hiding in the background) is they dont move, so for the entire game you will see these random shadowy people hanging around, in the same spot standing still. The charcaters you can interact with move every so often, wether it be to drink some coffee or not, the same should have been done with the pedestrians in the background. My second negative is a VERY minor negative but I still need to mention it, when you choose your resolution in the start up menu, it lists the resolution but it doesnt list the screens refresh rate, so if I was using a 1920 x 1080 display which was running at 122hz apposed to 60hz how would I know if it was going to automatically match up with my refresh rate? To fix this I would add a note at the bottom of the screen just to notify the player.
Conclusion
Should you buy it? YES Why? Because not only does Slap Village deliver an excellent narrative but it lets you meet with halarious charcaters that are guarrenteed to make you laugh atleast once. And is overall a VERY solid point and click adventure game.

Slap Village is a cute Point & Click adventure game set during the historical Wild West period blended with aspects of modern times. Filled with familiar puzzles and objectives found in many games of the genre, Lurditas and her trusty rodent sidekick Rasta will face many challenges on their trek to Slap Village and beyond. Oh, if that seems a little too ordinary, a visit from an extra-terrestrial alien might shake things up a bit.
The first thing many players will notice upon launching the game will be the menu screen. More specifically, the game's subtitle "Chap. 1 Reality Slap!" It isn't too clear on the Store page, but it seems that Slap Village will be a trilogy of sorts, with each game acting as a "complete" gaming experience (as stated by the developer
). This particular game is the first installment. Whether or not that may be a deal breaker is up to you.
Various "puzzles" are presented throughout Slap Village which comprises the bulk of the gameplay. Although some of the solutions can be very frustrating or obscure to solve without a guide, there wasn't too much backtracking required. These puzzles are very common in many other P&C/HOGs, such as:
To supplement the puzzles, unique mini-games are also interspersed within Slap Village to help breakup any monotony. The first mini-game is incorporated as a part of the story, a method to transition from one place to the other in the form of a traffic runner game. These mini-games will reward you with achievements based on your performance, and can also be replayed from the title menu.
The cartoon-like artwork of Slap Village is very colorful and extremely well-polished, providing a large sense of immersion into a TV-like sitcom. Although there are copious amounts of various Western-themed color palettes used, strong opposing blues, purples, and greens help break up any feeling of monotony and enhance the cartoon aesthetic. Many different locales are also utilized to help create Slap Villages world, in case you have any fears that the game is only set in barren shanty towns. Some of the more interesting ones include: a Native American town of film-makers, a steam locomotive with WIFI, and a karaoke Saloon.
When observing the subtitled dialogue, it seems that the developers are primarily Spanish speaking, or the English localization could use some work, due to the prevalent use of inverted punctuation marks and minor grammatical errors. There are also moments of disjointed dialogue peppered throughout. During the cut-scenes, I have also noticed some dropped frames every now and then. Although these observations are nothing too terrible, it can be immersion breaking at times.
Regarding the audio perspective, the voice acting is nothing spectacular, but it does manage to fulfill expectations of what animated personalities should sound like, which is a difficult feat to achieve. The entire spectrum of cartoon voices are explored, including: mysterious strangers, Native Americans, eccentric elders, and omniscient extra-terrestrials.
Slap Village succeeds in creating an interesting adventure worthy of embarking upon, filled with well voiced personalities in a cartoon-like Modern-Western era. This game is definitely recommended to fans of the Point & Click or Western adventure genres, or those wanting to experience a well voiced cartoon game.

Frozen Synapse is a game where player input is taken in turns but the actual outcome is played out simultaneously.  In game matches, each player is given several soldiers and has to complete a certain objective, like getting to a certain location or killling the enemy's units.  Players then give orders to their units to try to outmaneuver their opponent.  Every plan can be tested ahead of time and will always play out the same way; there is no luck or randomness in the combat.  After both players confirm their moves, soldiers on both sides will execute their commands.  The entire game is about predicting the moves of your opponents and trying to counter them.  It also has great music and a pretty good single player campaign (although the multiplayer is much more enjoyable IMO).  I would definetely recommend it to anyone who is a fan of tactical gameplay.

I'll be honest. I got this game solely on the strength of the dev's previous game, Zafehouse Diaries.
I was disappointed at first. I was expecting Zafehouse Diaries In Space. Instead I got what appeared to be some sort of bad Alien/Rogue/Hacker hybrid.
After playing for a while, it began to grow on me. Its damnably hard and unforgiving.... I've never cleared more than 2 missions without losing my crew.
The game itself is a real-time, tactical top-down/isometric game with strong elements of team management. You play a controller, safe on board your own ship, while your crew of Deadnauts goes out to explore derelicts. You have absolute control over your crew, but they have their own personalities and agendas which can influence others on the team and mission outcomes. The crew can operate autonomously (and may have too, but I'm not going to spoil that), but they don't seem to do much without your direct input.
Graphics are extremely mediocre. You're controlling your team via a radar screen.... enemies are shown as dots, the team is shown as dots, and areas of interest are shown as dots. It makes for an intense, immersive feel, but those who like a bit of eye-candy are going to be disappointed.
Both sound and music are OK... muted and muffled, they add to the claustrophobic intensity and are well utilised, but again aren't anything special.
Its hard to say who I'd actually recommend this game for. Its really a niche game... which makes comparison difficult. Think sort of early X-Com meets The Sims meets Dark Souls meets SystemShock... if that sounds appealing, its worth the gamble.

Deadnaut features an abstract but immersive atmosphere of exploring and surviving just like Screwfly's previous work Zafehouse Diaries. But to be honest if you buy Deadnaut out of appreciation of ZD, it's very likely you will find this game kind of disappointing.
The biggest difference between a real time RPG and a turn-based one is the involvement of reflex and speed. Although Deadnaut doesn't lay much stress on them, this still makes Deadnaut more like a Point&Click game instead of an intriguing board game, which unavoidably weaken the depth of strategy and jeopardize the easiness of scheming. However I'm not against real-time RPG; Deadnaut just did it the wrong way. Squad die out almost instantly in most encounters if outpowered, but the lack of pause feature leaves player little time to arrange plan and issue orders, not to mention carefully analyzing battlefield and monitoring team conditions, especially when your squad members are seperated in different rooms. The simplification in interaction doesn't help either: you just click every clickable button to hack, investigate and unlock and then move to the next room, which makes up the majority of exploration and is in no way fun at all.
In the end, it is still a strategy game, not a squad tactic FPS. Once again Screwfly shows how to implement a great idea poorly and ultimately deliver a decent but boring roguelike game just like their no longer supported Zafehouse Diaries.

I recommend this game! . . . hmm i think the blue thumbs up might be easier to read than that statment . . . I might as well explain why I recommend this game.
First up is the premise of the game. You play as the commander of a team of Deadnauts who's job is to explore stange and alien ships in varying degrees of decay/destruction, your team are "deadnauts" because they aren't expected to survive. The game is set during a time in which knowledge has become the standard monies of the day and so that is why your errant band of suicidal explorers are doing this . . . for the knowledge . . . which is money . . . anyway, over the course of the game you will seek out new life, and destroy it cause it's trying to eat you, and dead civilisations or at least the friendly aliens are dead . . . cause all the hostile ones are trying to kill you.
Next up we gots us some gameplay. Well the game plays very much like you are sitting at a console and are keeping tabs on your guys through use of the ship's scanners and com systems . . . actually i think that is exactly what you are doing. At times this can be an issue when you lose connection to one or more of your crew members while at other times you may even see something your guys don't and so you can have them investigate. In terms of combat, you will undoutably encounter lots of this as many of the derelict ships are derelict for a good reason and that good reason is hungry after a few thousand years of having already eaten everyone onboard. There are also automated systems like the ever unhelpful 'watcher' and the delightfully ill-placed sentinals . . . I hate sentinals with a passion and every time i encounter one it wipes out my entire team in a matter of seconds because they are always in killzones so i waltz into a room and three people are dead before I even know what killed them.
Customization is a thing in the fact that you can create custom team members, even import custom faces for them if you so chose but there are a couple ones there already and you can just stick to random team members for extra challenge but I like the story you can create with a custom crew. Crew members will also react to each other's flaws and traits through dialouge which is the only way you will know if that flaw is currently active because someone will mention it. Team mates will also banter a little, especially after they just saved the life of a team mate ("I better be getting a christmas card for this . . . ") and this makes things all the more interesting.
overall I think this game is actually pretty good but I think the small size of it is a little bit of a flaw because it's campaign will only go for about 4 missions can theoretically only lasts an hour at most but fortunately there is permadeath to up the hours it takes you to win. In my own personal opinion, I am waiting for the "real deal" with this being an experiment and the sequal being a much larger game with far more content and story but even if that isn't the case, this game is more than deserving of it's price tag and has enough content to make the hundreds of replays you will do worth it.
Final score is 8/10 and an expectation that more will appear eventually

Most modern Roguelikes have permanent unlocks to keep players going through failures. Lost a match? No problem, at least your guys now have +5hp and you unlocked a new class. Nothing like that here. You get a 4 mission campaign, and the unlocks are only for that. Win or (far more likely) lose, your next game starts you with nothing.
At it's core this is a preparation game, you get a very limited write-up of what your crew will be up against and you equip accordingly. In theory. there isn't any equipment to customize during the first mission, and you'll be playing that first mission alot. No guarantees you'll be playing long enough to actually make the decision of whether the pistol or the fireaxe is a better equip.

I'm sad to say that I don't really want to recommend this game. I appreciate the aesthetic, and I knew it was meant to be challenging going in. But the game fundamentals didn't work for me. Ultimately, it boils down to the incessant pausing that occurs throughout combat. It makes the combat frustrating and clunky.
Combat works fairly simply: a basic weapon attack, a strong weapon attack, and an attack with your torch. A lot of the combat is built around the timing and maneuvering of your attacks versus the enemy's. Reading their attack signals is important as it lets you know to move out of the way or try to time your block. Okay, it's all fine so far. That's not a bad system. The game also seems to try to add a claustrophobic tension by having you fight often in cramped quarters versus large opponents. Again, a fairly neat idea.
Where it falls apart for me, however, is the way that all strikes and blocks cause the action to freeze for what feels like nearly a half a second. There's no obvious beneficial reason for this pause--my best conjecture is that it's an "action-enhancing" effect--but it results in some serious complications regarding the combat. As the combat revolves around the timing of attacks and blocks, these pauses inhibit my ability to "feel" the timing. Take a common scenario: I attack, but my opponent has also begun its attack animation. I feel that I can still block it once my attack animation finishes. However, successfully landing the strike has caused the pause effect to happen. I now have miliseconds to successfully trigger a block, but now, instead of timing it from the beginning of the attack animation, I have to time it from the end of the pause, which creates an even shorter window and that's if I manage to guess when the pause ends. The typical result of all of this is me missing my window and taking yet another hit.
I suppose if my attacks broke the enemy attack animation, there wouldn't be a problem, but they don't. Also, I'm sure that there are those of you out there who are able to compensate for the pause and still pull of the block. I'm not saying no one can do it. I'm saying I can't. I tried to get better at it, but it ended up just making me mad.
There's some very cool ideas in here, and I really wanted to expore more, but I don't like to spend my free time doing things that make me mad. I know I've got less than 2 hours of play time on the game, but that's split over three play sessions, each of which had to end when I found myself actually yelling at the screen. (And no, that's not a common occurrence for me.) This left me with an upleasant experience and as a result I can't, in good faith, recommend the title.

Honestly not a great game. I can't say much in terms of play time, or how interesting it is throughout, or if the story/ending is enjoyable... Because I never made it past the first level. I never got to a point where I even had a weapon, outside of the tutorial.
While I'm talking about the tutorial, I should say, it's quite terrible. It has you fighting an enemy with button promts telling you what to do, but sometimes the prompts are on screen for literally half a second, not even close to enough time to read the. Trying to figure out the controls on your own/reading the promt one word at a time gets annoying, but once you figure out what to do, the game gets no less annoying.
The controls are very clunky and the timing of combat feels rather slilted. Maybe this is something one could get used to, but I wouldn't know as once I completed the short but frustrating turorial and started the main game, I got nowhere. It appears to start you off without a weapon, and I wandered around the assumed castle several times, each time dying because I couldn't figure out where to find a weapon. I even wondered into a boss room by mistake, and it turns out boss rooms lock you in when you enter, so I just had to stand there and let myself die so I could reset. I'm a fan of games not hand-holding more than they have to, bit this was a bit much. Being told what to do constantly isn't fun, but wandering around not nowing where to go and not being able to do anything isn't fun either. The most I could do is walk around rooms and hallways, light candles with my torch (I never did figure out if this was benifical in any way or not...) and maybe unlock a door with a key every once in a while (which resets when you die, by the way). I'd like to tell you if the game gets better, but based on the tutorial fight, I wasn't really eager to wander the dark castle halls for another half an hour to aqquire a sword or something so I could find out if the clunky combat is worth getting used to.
Visually, this game is actually quite nice. It may not be for everyone, but I find the simple, minimalist art design to be a rather interesting one, and everything that I did see looked pretty good. For what I assume is a low-budget indie game, the visuals and art took a smart direction and did what it could with less, and did it well. But bear in mind I did not see much of the game. The animations for your character aren't the best, but they're not game-breakingly bad or anything. I could have easily looked past it if controlling your character at least felt good. The enemy animation that I saw was honestly not too bad, although I imagine I only saw a fraction of the enemies in the game.
I will also note that there is no option to turn down the music volume, only the master volume. While the music wasn't bad, it was a little louder than I would have liked it, and I would have liked to be able to turn it down without also turning down the sound effects of enimies and such.
Overall, I can't recomend this game. It's simply not fun to play. If you really want to give it a shot, I won't tell you to avoid it at all costs. It looks nice and could be fun if it controlled well. But approch with caution.

You have to learn a few strategies to adapt to what the market has to offer. You can decide to get yellow cards, which accelerate your combo and allow you to get all your cards in one turn. Or you can go with the green cards, which allow your hands to consistently deal 15 to 25 damage. Or mix both. I used about 6 different strategies in the campaign.
The universe is fun, the campaign is about 3h long in easy, where the real challenge is to collect the trophies. Hard mode is really hard. There are people available all the time for playing in multi.
All in all it is a bit poor on the content, a good gameplay, and fun moment to play.

I'm a lover of stories, and that is why I have always enjoyed history, but this game gave me an entire new appreciation of it. There is no objective in this game, save for the ones you give yourself. It's safe to stay that generally speaking though, your goal is to ensure the survival of your starting character's dynasty. Yet from that rather generic starting point comes a thousand decisions and an always fascinating story that never has a narrator.
In the world of kings and nobles, your family is all that exists to protect you, but is also key to obtaining greatness, and is also the greatest threat to both your rule and your life. You'd be amazed at how quickly you'll invade the lands of your cousin or uncle, and don't be surprised when you hire assassin's to plot the death of your wife or unworthy son. Without a black heart and an iron grip on your courts, you'll find yourself against the ropes by people you thought could be trusted.
Of course, this is the iconic Paradox Game, and with the exception of Stellaris, the easiest to learn. Don't let me mislead you though, this game pretty much requires spending some time watching Let's Plays and tutorials, but the pay off is well worth it. There is no other game that does what this game does with such a scope.

I'll cut to the chase - Tree of Life is an entertaining and intriguing MMORPG. It mashes together features from some of my favorite video games into a melting pot of sandbox fun. I haven't played the game for a long time, but I feel I have played long enough to leave an early access review.
Pros:
+Several skills (24 total as of this writing) and skill-based gameplay. The more you use a skill, the better you get at it. There is a cap on skills, forcing the player to specialize.
+Great sandbox gameplay - many different items to craft, lots of materials to gather, huge map to explore, several mobs to encounter and subsequently kill.
+Open world gameplay - you really can build anywhere that is accessible.
+Above average community. I have yet to encounter any trolls...most people are either friendly or aloof.
+Great soundtrack, although it gets a bit repetitive. Hopefully they release more music soon.
+Day/night cycle that affects gameplay. Dangerous creatures come out at night and it gets really dark - daytime is the time to explore and collect materials.
+Interesting PVP/faction system. Aggressors and thieves become red, which means they can be fully looted. The reward for killing a 'good' player? One item drop. It creates an interesting risk/reward balance...we'll see how it plays out.
+Somewhat unique art style.
Cons:
-Somewhat of a grind. It isn't intolerable and it adds value to skills, but it can be tedious.
-Numerous translation issues...I wonder if OddOneGames realizes that the word 'sh!t' is not exactly the professional word to use to describe dung/manure/droppings?
-Several missing features. This is to be expected in early access, but it could still be a negative for a prospective buyer.
-Graphics are a bit outdated.
-Server lag can be a bit much.
Bottom line: If you're in the mood for a fresh sandbox experience and can get past dated graphics, you should give this one a try. I think it's worth the money if you are willing to purchase an early access game.

This is the third SONIC game I've ever played. The other two were Sonic Advance 3 and Sonic Colors. Based on these two games, I never really got a good impression of Sonic.. But before picking up Mania, I tried a bit of Sonic 3 and it was a lot of fun. It gave me a taste of the "good sonic" games that everyone always talked about. And now that I've finished Mania and I completely understand what the hype is about. Going to try the original 3 games now.
The music is amazing and perfectly fits the fast-paced action of the game. The sprites are incredibly detailed and impressed me on many occasions. Gameplay uses momentum perfectly and doesn't get you caught up on cheap deaths (which I had to deal with in colors and advance 3). Bonus stages are fun and there are plenty to unlock. Environments are all pretty and creative.
Honestly I hope this game represents more than "a good Sonic game", and that other devs take notes from it on how to impress fans in modern day. There was no way I couldn't pick it up: I wanted to support SEGA taking steps in the right direction. But also if you are a fan of tight and challenging platforming, this is a lot of fun and worth the money.

From the moment I booted this up I knew it was something special. What an amazing experience. If someone had told me this was a lost Sonic Genesis, I would completely believe it (with the exception of some nice little graphical touches). Imagine taking the gameplay of Sonic 2/3/K, the soundtrack quality of Sonic CD, a set of brand new, spectacular zones that match anything the series has to offer, and wrap it all up into a beautiful modern package- that's Sonic Mania.
I don't want to spoil anything as the game is best experienced for oneself, but suffice it to say there are endless touches showing the immense love and care that the developers have for Sonic and the glory days of the Genesis. One of the early boss fights is absolutely brilliant and you'll see immediately what I mean.
I dislike intrusive DRM as much as the next person, but I'm reviewing the game here, not the DRM. More than enough people have done that here. As far as the game itself goes, this is as good as any Sonic game ever, if not better, and I know; I've played them all (OK, I'm sure there's some obscure title that only came out for refurbished Wonderswans or something, but I've certainly played the vast majority of them).
There were some moments that nearly brought me to tears for how perfectly they evoked the nostalgia of Sonic's heyday, and this is mixed in with some truly excellent gameplay and level design that rival anything to be found in the entirety of the Sonic franchise.
Turns out, you CAN go home again. It just takes Sonic Mania.
For some reason, it runs pretty slow on my laptop, so I have to use windowed mode. But I can recommend this game anyway, leaves a good nostalgic feeling.

After finishing the Mania Mode with Sonic and Tails I was fairly impressed with the variety of features Sega put into this game to make it actually feel like "Sonic 4 & Knuckles" or a fresh new Sonic Game.
Get ready for some nostalgia smoothies. The way Sega blended together old levels with new features kept the gameplay interesting.
I highly reccomend playing through all levels to the end. The Final Zone is worth the wait.
The music is great. Though some Zones sound a bit "Jazzy", not exactly a Sonic rythym I thought.
Difficulty is not too hard. Only the boss battles will take a few tries. If you're new to Sonic in 2d then I would say this is a difficult game.
Overall, Sonic Mania might not give you Mania but it will certainly remind you of why the Sonic Series are a worthy Retro Masterpiece.

Slap Village is a Wild West point-and-click adventure game where you play a young girl named Luriditas. Even though it uses a cartoon art style, it is very distinct with very detailed areas. The various characters you come across are unique, to the point where you can recognize them by the outline (and most likely their voice and how they speak). Slap Village has a very fluid and consistent animation. This game may be colourful, but it balances it well enough to where it doesn't strain your eyes after long periods of time.
Slap Village's story can easily hook you in during the first few minutes, and easily draws you in the more you unravel what is going on in the country Luriditas resides in. The various problems you need to solve requires you to think outside the box, and most of the time you will find the solution is right in front of you! It features good humor and minigames that will unlock as the story calls upon them, while making room for references to pop culture.
The dialogue (English) dub is well made, with some awkward moments (and pronunciations) but it doesn't take away from the experience. I'm guessing this was originally a Spanish game translated to English, based on some leftover punctuation marks, but that shouldn't turn you away as it is still made well.
The only problems I have came across is a misplaced dialogue, and some before me has come across bugs that halt their progress, but it has been fixed pretty quickly.
Slap Village is very enjoyable and the mechanics are well rounded. If you like the art style, this game genre, and/or have been on the fence on getting Slap Village this game will be a great addition. I highly recommend playing Slap Village.

Its not a perfect game, and from the various minor issues with physics and the annoyance of trying to read the text on screen that is apparent... but that does not detract from the fast paced and excellent gameplay it offer. Unique combinations of weapons, powerups and combos provide excellent flow to the game.
Talking about combo's - that is what most of the combat revolves around: you killing enemies in various ways - from using two weapons, hitting them in the back, 180 no scope (or whatever its called) all provide bonuses in terms of raw points and powerups.
And you need these powerups because they are the way to get ammo, health, and so on. which brings me to my two main problems with the game.
If you cant keep up combos for any reason, the game slows to a crawl and the difficulty curve become more of a difficulty cliff and the game loses a lot of flair in its mechanics, where in stead of being active and flowing into intense combat it turns more into a 'oh... run backwards and shoot'.
My second gripe is the UI and artstyle. While on one end its very unique and clean and cool and keeps everything flowing more or less effectively, it is also extremely taxing on the eyes. This is the first game in ages i've had to stop playing after about an hour to take a rest because of the strain it was causing on my eyes. Which while playing a timing and skill based game... isn't great.
So overall the game is intense, unique and fast paced with great score attack mechanics. But it is also a little unpolished and heavy on the eyes.

I am not typically a fan of games which are as unforgiving as Desync, but this one's an exception.  The art really drew me in, and the music played a huge part in keeping me pumped when I would have otherwise rage-quitted on an encounter a dozen tries ago.
The game still makes me want to flip my table over plenty of times of course, but it's also very satisfying to finally beat a level where you were struggling on the last encounter.  And there's something to be said about the way you settle into a rythm the 20th time you re-play a failed encounter.
There's a shard system which is neat and lets you personalise your playstyle, so you can make whatever combos you enjoy performing easier to do.  In a game which encourages self-expression, I immensely enjoy getting up close and personal with the game's shotgun-equivalent, one-shotting weaker enemies, or sending them flying through the air, as I dash right into their faces.
I have a few critiques, but only two main ones (off the top of my  head): first, I wish enemies that are killed have their corpses vaporised immediately.  Sometimes they ragdoll a bit before vaporising, and it's hard to tell if they're gonna get back up again, or die.  In a game which is otherwise extremely fluid and responsive with good immediate feedback, this makes the flow of an encounter feel a little off sometimes.  Second, I wish that there was just a little more hand-holding early on, especially in the explanation of how the shard upgrade system worked.
While I think those two points are pretty salient, they ultimately do not ruin what is ultimately a game with very clear vision and purpose behind it.
I've hit a wall where I'm not quite good enough to progress, and I need to take a break before trying again.  But even when I die, I can see how I *could* have survived, if I was just that half-a-second faster on a dodge, or didn't miss that one shot. It says a lot that I'm going further with Desync than I have compared to any other game in a similar vein.
For fans of extremely challenging shooters, radically different-looking art styles, and some truly sweet music; Desync is an easy recommend.

Desync is Painkiller meets Tron aesthetic with a hotline miami style "hard with instant reload and synthwave soundtrack" and a multiple playthroughs score-attack/flying numbers twist that supports creative kills with chained attacks, similar to bulletstorm but different in implementation.
It plays like a synthwave fever dream with hotline miami difficulty and lots, i mean LOTS of distortion and scanlines.
The FOV is very very high by default, i don't think I changed it, to accomodate for the large amount of scanlines and movement.
There is no multiplayer and on my amd fx 8350/rx480 combo with 32gb of 1866 mhz ram I usually run anywhere from 68 min 74-98 avg and 132 max fps in the hub and in combat, and 182-235 fps ingame while not in combat.
Enemies are highly lethal, with all attacks being near-instakill melee and projectile based, with some enemies needing to be killed by attack chains (desyncs) and a static enemy placement. your movement speed is painkiller like, your weapons are painkiller like, with the exception of an infinite dash button.
I reccommend for fans of tron, hotline miami, bulletstorm, daniel deluxe/synthwave, minimalist "like its made in unity" art design done to good effect, and competitive score attack made from the ground up for multiple level playthroughs and skilled movement.
I would not reccommend to anybody who needs to "git gud" or to anybody wanting any semblance of story whatsoever. If you hate hard games and replaying things, or hate distortion/scanlines, or dont need games to run at 300 fps at all times (60 hz), this isn't for you.

key series features like individual soldier inventories have been "nerfed", you can't pick up helmets anymore for example. the body armor item has been removed as well, despite this being a game set in the modern era. direct control, a major selling point of the previous games, has been effectively removed because the developers felt it was "unfair". if you played the previous men of war games and appreciated the depth these two changes should be enough to scare you away.
the developers have force-enabled unit lock, there is no way to disable it. if you're new to the series, unit lock is a "feature" the developers have put in meaning that the game plays like a F2P mmo, think war thunder. you can expect a 100+ hour grind before you unlock everything and yes, the higher tier units are better and yes, you will be forced to play against them despite not having them unlocked yourself. you may find yourself trying to kill an M1 abrams with a BMP-1, unable to call in your own tanks because you have not unlocked them yet.
the developers have fallen short in virtually every area relevant to long-term series fans. the major problems the game had in 2009 are still there. the best way to describe this game is as a flawed but ambitious full-conversion mod - but mods don't usually cost money. the final insult from DMS isn't the game, though. it's their behavior outside of it, where they've gone so far as to make a VAC banned cheater their community manager.

I can see Deadnaut becoming one of my favourite games. According to the creepy gameplay watcher, I've played 4 1/2 hours so far, and that sounds about right. A full campaign lasts around an hour to an hour and a half, maybe two if you like to take it slow. I just finished my first successful campaign; all others failed on the first ship... within about 5 minutes of breaching the airlock.
So what is Deadnaut? Basically, it's Space Crusade, except, instead of 7 foot killing machines in power armour, your squad bears a greater resemblance to the crew of the Serenity, or maybe Red Dwarf, depending on the characters you end up with; they're pretty good at what they do, even impressive at times, but they're hardly intimidating. You sit back on the mothership and command your squad through the interfaces that you can see in the screenshots up at the top of this page, pointing out which terminals you want hacked, which doors you want opened, and which -OH HELL WHAT IS THA-JUST SHOOT! KILL IT!!!!- and which centuries-old corpses you want rummaged as you go about completing your objectives. Meanwhile, your crew are chattering away amongst themselves about their stim habits, love of blood-soaked gore rooms, and what kind of card the techie wants for their birthday.
Do a good job, and next time you'll have the opportunity to die a meaningless death a million light years from home with some slightly swankier gear. Pretty cool, huh?
I only have one complaint about the game, apart from my wails of dismay when my entire team is, yet again, suffocated or torn to shreds by indescribable horrors – within the campaign, you unlock new equipment for your crew... none of that carries over between campaigns. Personally, I'd prefer a persistent meta campaign between the campaigns; develop the crew over a series of missions, replace the losses, say goodbye to the retirees and wish luck to those get attention from the powers back on Earth. I think that would add even greater depth to an already brilliant game, but it is what it is, and what it is is brilliant.
In my opinion, it's easily a 9/10. (Add that meta campaign in, devs, and I'll give it a 10! :D)

"Cthulhu Realms" is a card game where the goal is to make your opponent go insane!
CR is a deck-building game (where you acquire cards to your deck during play) with lovecraftian theme and not-so-serious, cartoony artwork. Game mechanics in its foundation are similar to excellent "Star Realms", and while veterans will feel at home, this is not just a re-theme. This time mechanisms are more advanced, and there is a whole lot more of possibilities for strategies and combos.
Presentation is absolutely gorgeous - a lovely cartoony style, a greatly improved UI (comparing to crude one in "Star Realms"), music that fits the theme - all of it combined makes this game a great digital card game experience.
The only negative thing about the game I can think about is that "Cthulhu Realms" lost part of the simplicity and casual appeal which was so great about "Star Realms". Despite its cheerful looks, this is not a casual game anymore, but something deeper. While the game system is simple enough, the iconography may be a little bit confusing at first and requires time to get use to. To sum it up, "Cthulu Realms" is great, but it's not a game that I can teach somebody in 5 minutes, and a specific theme may not appeal to everyone. I don't think it's a husband-wife game, unless your better part is into tentacles and stuff.
If you enjoy card games, I wholeheartedly reccommend "Cthulhu Realms" to you. It's free to try and upgrading to full version is cheap.
Pros:
+ a simple, but surprisingly deep game system
+ charming, cartoony graphics
+ Cthulhu theme!
Cons:
- iconography may be a little confusing at first
- theme may not appeal to everyone

As a long-time tabletop gamer I've enjoyed my share of interesting card games, from Munchkin to Magic and everything in between. Digital conversions of these games tend to be a mixxed bag, though, with everything from interface issues to a lack of customization meaning the experience is never as smooth as it could be.
I'd like to say Cthulhu Realms does better, but in truth while the core concept -- that decks are generated as you play rather than before the game starts -- eliminates balance issues for the most part, the interface and opaqueness of the gameplay to a newcomer are enough to leave me wishing the game had seen a little more care at the design stage.
First of all, the good. The game itself is fun, with a cartoony presentation and fun artwork that help  to alleviate some of the creep factor often associated with the Cthulhu mythos. The way the game is constructed leads to almost every card being unique in some way beyond just the artwork, and helps to guarantee players have to stay on their toes, adapting their strategies to match what comes up rather than what they've brought in themselves. This gives the game a very interesting strategy aspect: do you try and aim for a single style of play, looking for cards with certain abilities and hope they come up, or work with what arrives and embrace the chaos that can cause? It's all very fun, and keeps every game fairly fresh.
Unfortunately, that freshness is lost relatively quickly, as card variety is somewhat low. Likewise, the cards tend to have very specific uses, meaning that many cards are entirely dependent on you gaining access to other cards in order to operate effectively. This is obviously an artifact of the game's CCG inspirations, but one that a few weeks more tweaking is likely to help fix.
The biggest issue is in the game's accessibility to new players. The tutorials are quick, blasting you with every piece of information they can without giving you time to absorb how that information can inform your gameplay choices or much in the way of examples thereof, and no mention is made of how to perform actions like zooming in on your hand to review card information or ways to effectively combo cards. For anyone familiar with card battle style games these are concepts you will be able to work out relatively easily on your own, but the jump from the tutorials to the core game is an exercise in confusion at first as you're given no real chance to piece together the information you've received to make informed choices.
With the game still being quite new, most of these issues will almost assuredly be ironed out as time goes on. What's most important is the core gameplay, and while it lacks variety for the long haul the core mechanics are solid and offer a lot of room for expansion in the future.
If you're a fan of CCGs or other battle-style card games, like Munchkin or Zombies!!!, then give the game a shot: the core version is free, after all, and at five bucks the full version is cheaper than a couple of booster packs. If card games fail to enthuse you, or you're not willing to give a game time to mature before you make a final judgement on it, then perhaps wait until the game's had a bit more time to gestate before delving in.

In a nutshell:
Imagine you are the leader of a group of derelict ships scavengers sitting in your command capsule somewhere, and the latest in scanning technology only allows you to see the internal structure of the ship and detect any life forms as blips on the screen. Other than their natural response to shoot at any hostiles they encounter, provided they can detect said hostiles, your crew depends on your radio-transmitted orders to navigate them through the interior of these long-dead ships. You might not be able to see what your crew sees, but you will definitely be able to hear ghost echoes and phantom screams through the radio transmitter.
Deadnaut is a real-time, squad-based tactical (and almost simulation) game which should be played in the dark so as to immerse in, and appreciate the ambience presented by the game setting. Random generation and various dynamic factors  provides replayability, but a relatively short campaign only gives a sense of accomplishment upon completion but would not quite give you the euphoric fist-into-the-air kind of feeling.
Gameplay:
A campaign consists of only 4 missions, and each mission might take between 20 minutes to 30 mins to complete depending on how thorough you want to explore the ships. However, players are likely to spend more time on planning and suiting up for the missions. Primary interaction are the usual right-click to move, left-click to interact with doors and computers, and middle-mouse (or Ctrl-left click) to activate personal item like sensors, and to project shields. A large portion of the game is randomly generated, from different hostiles with strengths and weaknesses, to the blueprints of equipment you might come across. If you prefer so, you can start playing with a randomly generated crew of 5, each with their own character traits and flaws, which might or might not sit well with the rest of the team. The class of a character is largely dependent on the equipment, and although character traits predispose them to a certain role, flaws might raise conflict against that very same role (e.g. a combat-centric grunt that does not like combat nor be around dead bodies). Alternatively you can customize your own crew, so as to improve your odds very slightly. Investigating the dead bodies scattered around the ship yields ‘knowledge’ about what had befallen upon the ship’s crew, and ‘knowledge’ acts as a form of currency to acquire new weapons and equipments. The dynamics of all these random factors provides an open field that tests players on their ability to make do with what’s available and adapt the appropriate tactics.
Aesthetics:
The somber color scheme is only fitting for a game of such tense nature but for a game with minimal graphical stimulus, the audio warrants special mention as being very much up to the task of putting you on edge of your chair. Crank up the audio and the random shrieks during radio-silence of space will sends goose bumps up crawling on your skin. The UI is reminiscent of a submarine (or in this case subspace) command chair and is very much simulator-like, with many buttons to click on, switches to flip and several monitors to look at, including heart rate and brain wave monitors of individual squad members. All these features add to the immersion factor by providing background and flavor reading material.
Final word:
Deadnaut is a very interesting game with a slightly niche market, likely appealing to those who values immersion over graphics. That said, the game contain the essences of game longevity; dynamic randomness and replay value. The short campaign encourages strategic planning with available resources, but does leave one with a desire for more missions. On the other hand, having a long campaign runs into eventual content exhaustion whereby players will have everything available towards the end, and thus causing players to gradually lose interest and shelving the game until their next craving for a game with similar nature. It’s almost like a choice to have your favorite food as a snack everyday versus stuffing yourself to your heart’s content.

A lot of people from the Humble Monthly are not familiar with Star Realms, but to break it down simply, this game is basically a variation on Star Realms, it is not meant to be like Hearthstone or Magic--in fact, I think it's deliberately trying to avoid that format for something that you can pick up and play without worrying about "long-term investment." Once you know the rules of the game and the basic mechanics, you're set. It's NOT a collectible card game. That's kind of the point.

It is a deckbuilding game, predicated on factional synnergy. It's highly similar to Star Realms, so let me explain the differences from that:
1) Cthulhu Realms has three factions rather than four. Yellow - Draw and discard, Purple - Activate on sacrifice, Green - Initiate sacrifice. It may seem like green/purple is the natural combo, and it kind of is, but you can go pure purple if you also splash in some initiates who can self-sacrifice, or if you get "high house in the mist."
2) Cthulhu Realms has some mechanics that involve returning sacrificed cards. In Star Realms, when you sacrifice, that card is gone for good. In Cthlhu Realms, you can sacrifice, Wilbur Whately to deal 5 damage, then "Acquire" him (putting him on top of your deck) with Dean Halsey.

3) Cthulhu Realms has no "one-drop" cards. This simplifies things a bit, especially in the early turns, and I think is good since the 1-drop yellow "draw another card" was always too good in my mind in Star Realms.
On top of that, this game frankly has a lot more personality and flavor than Star Realms, especially in the campaign which I found quite humorous.

Tldr; simplified dark souls style game, narrative is pretty good, atmospheric and striking visuals, good music.
I am really impressed that an indie game company has been able to develop a game with mechanics similar to Dark Souls. I enjoyed this game for the most part.
The visuals are beautiful and very clever.  I really enjoyed the striking contrast of the colours with the simplistic polygon style.  Malebolgia comes off as clean and never overpowering or crowded. I loved the use of light and the torchlight really lent itself to the atmosphere.  I particularly enjoyed as the game progressed through the acts, the atmosphere became darker without being too obvious.  If there's any critique to be made, I feel that Leopold's model could play with light and shadow a little better, as he was a bit awkward looking at times.  I also understand that it's much more difficult to have light interact with dynamic objects though, so I am not too bothered. I also thought that important NPC's could have more defined models, as some of them share models with regular monsters.
I enjoyed the OST for this game.  Very atmospheric and well done. I also enjoy a game that can appreciate  silence as  important in setting tone for a scene or area.
Narrative is great.  I enjoy games that don't necessarily hand you the entire plot. The game trusts the player to remember small details and connect the dots themselves. The pacing is good, apart from the one of the last portions of the game, where it requires you to set specific things on fire.  I thought this was so out of place, especially right after a big boss battle. It was easily the poorest part of the game in terms of pacing and mechanic.
Gameplay is good. It differs from Dark Souls in that there is no customization or weapon/armour collection. The fighting system is particularly simple, probably because it takes a great deal of work to code this type of game. This game can be quite difficult if the player isn't acquainted  with Dark Souls style gameplay.  I found it to be a bit too easy at times, as some mobs could be defeated by backstepping > attack > backstep > etc. I didn't utilize the block function very often. I found it frustrating that I couldn't unsheathe my weapon unless there was a mob around, and that when fighting multiple enemies, I couldn't choose which one I wanted to target with ease.
Overall, I enjoyed Malebolgia and I look forward to seeing future projects from this game dev.

Someone remade Bulletstorm, making a more hardcore experience in the process. Ammunition is gained from doing sequences (move / skill based kills on stunned enemies, or environmental kills). If you run out of ammunition with one weapon due to not styling on enemies you'll need to fall back to less powerful weapons. You have a pretty small health pool and that really changes how you move. You'll often be attacked from a direction you weren't looking, some enemies can cut you down instantly. Keeping on the move is absolutely key. Enemies have fixed spawns so repeated areas can be learned when you're getting bodybagged.
Pros:
+Environmental kills. I really forgot how much I miss this in games. It encourages players to space themselves in ways that can be designed around so the combat engagments are air tight.
+Weapons are varied and have multiple firing modes.
+Gameplay focused around moving fast and stylin' on bad digidudes.
+Rock solid framerate.
+Really great soundtrack. Great usage of music in menus. A lot of attention to detail went into the audio.
Cons:
-The minimalist aesthetic works in some places, but another polish pass wouldn't hurt. Animations, effects, and enemy visual design suffer the most.
-Animations had corners cut for sure. There's not a lot there. The larger enemies have big wind ups for their attacks but feel really stiff.

The short:
This is a sluggish frustrating shooter.  Literally it feels like someone decided to attempt to mix Dark Souls into Quake.  In doing so, this game loses all aspects of a fast skill based shooter.  If you want something like Painkiller, Shadow Warrior, Quake, UT, etc; look elsewhere.
The long:
Before I get started, I'd like to say that I am an avid arena shooter fan.  Tribes 2, UT2k4; these are the games I know and love with thousands of hours split between the two.  Recently I have gotten into Paladins and have managed to consistently stay in the top 500, according to paladins.guru.  This isn't meant to come across as bragging, just to show that I know my way around a FPS.
Second, I only have 1.5hrs on reocrd.  I want the refund so I didn't play any longer.  I have never played an fps with such an oppressive set of mechanics.  The core of the game feels terrible enough that I didn't want to play any further.  So maybe it gets better, I just couldn't find a way to enjoy it.
The movement in this game feels like you are stuck in molasses.  It's more sluggish than the U3 iteration of UT, which was made to be played on consoles.  Jumping and dashing feel like awkward burdensome efforts, not mechanics that are meant to be the bread and butter of how you navigate the world.
Enemies feel like abstract blobs.  Given how dangerous they can be, many can 2-3 shot you quickly, there is relatively little to indicate where they are around you aurally.  So it is a routine experience to die from an enemy who you didn't see simply because there was no indication that they existed behind you until they hit you.  This problem extends to hazards where you'll backtrack into them routinely because there is no non-visual indication of their presence.  It literally feels like encounters wth enemies have to memorized simply to navigate them and do well.  That's not a skill based interaction.
The cherry on top is that there is a progression system.  I wish I was joking.  Do your hard core platformers have progression systems that effect how you move and jump?  No.  Why is it acceptable to have one in a skill based fps?
Finally, there's the presentation.  To load a map to play, you are loaded into 3d hub world devoid of life.  There are terminals that you can go up to that allow you to manage the various progrsession systems and to view your player stats.  You then proceed to an elevator to go to a different floor, to then manipulate a 3d level selector where each level cooresponds to a different triangle.  Why aren't these menus?  Why are you wasting my time?  This is billed as skilled based game with a score system and leaderboards, not a single player story experience.  It would be like if Super Meat Boy had a navigatable cadavor instead of a level select menu.

This is a 3D puzzle game in a similar style to games like The Bridge, Evo Explores and Monument Valley but there are two major differences:
The game involves walking along the catwalks of a 3D maze structure suspended in space to activate coloured waypoints and finally reach the exit gate to the next level. Curved corners change the direction of gravity so you can step over the edge to "fall" onto other catwalks. New mechanics are introduced as you progress such as nodes to rotate sections of catwalks, buttons to toggle the 'lights' on and off which make catwalk sections appear and disappear, and portals that allow you to "fall" to other sections of the puzzle. I don't think it has controller support but WASD/mouse works well. You find yourself constantly looking around to try and work out where you are and where you're going since the puzzle is constantly moving around you as you change your direction of gravity. Disoriented is the perfect name for it because that's how you feel most of the time.
The graphics are stark and functional with a no-frills monochrome environment apart from the coloured waypoint markers. Note: the chequered design in the Steam videos for the game has since been changed to plain white. Nothing wrong with that, it removes any distractions from the puzzle at hand. Likewise, the background tunes are the usual ambient sounds that accompany most games like this.
It's a minimal environment and runs well, no lag or glitches. There's fullscreen and windowed options but no in-game resolution options for windowed, and the default is quite small. I discovered the reason for this is because you can resize the window by simply dragging it like any other window, which is nice.
Windows only - I would have liked to play it in Linux.
The game mechanics are simple to grasp and no explanation or tutorial is necessary. The first half of the game I found easy but then there's a sudden spike and it becomes very difficult. Part of the difficulty, as I mentioned before, is due to the fact that you can't get an overview of the whole puzzle. You activate a button or node and you have to look around you to see what's happening and maybe move away a bit to get a better angle. It makes you feel immersed in the puzzle as if you're part of it. I like that.
Another aspect to the difficulty of this game is that it's new and unpopular so right now there are no guides or walkthroughs whatsoever. If you get stuck, you're on your own! This can be a good or bad thing depending on your view :)

Look. I'm not one to write in-depth reviews or anything. However, Uplink has been one of the moost interesting, if not fun, experiences of a game I've had in quite some time. I've not played JUST 1.1 hours, as my Steam would suggest, as this is not the account I primarily used to play the game back in 2013. A couple of things to note right off the bat: this gae looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm sorry, but it does. If that doesn't bother you, go right on ahead. Graphics aren't everything, and this has a very 80's vibe about it that can be quite pleasent if you like that sorrt of thing. IF it does bother you, consider downloading this mod:
. (This mod is not finished at the time of review, but if and when it is finished I would like it to be on the front page of the game if possible.)
The second thing I would like to mention is the investment, time-wise, that this game is. I would not play this until you have about 6 hours free, as the experience is very cumulative and your knowledge and short-term memeory are slowly cultivated by the game for the true 'hacker brain' experience, which I found quite enjoyable. Ultimately, you really want to be able to remember strings of numbers. If you can't... get out the old pencil and paper. You'll have a better experience, trust me.
Now onto what I loved, and still love, about Uplink: it goes through a (rather long) tutorial, and teaches you everything you need to know. Then it goes "Well, hesre's all these networks. We'll give you an objective. Have fun!" It's very restrictive, but the open world is there, and finding that out felt really good. Be warned though: this game is hard as diamond nipples in an icebox. Stuff's easy, at first, but it gets hard very quickly. SAVE. BE CAREFUL. DO NOT TAKE ANY RISKS THAT COULD AFFECT YOUR GAME STATE. If you must, make another character and try it out there. The end of the game isn't exactly worth the wait, but it's cool nonetheless.
I could be more in depth, but it's late and Dark Souls is calling my name like a siren in the night. If you want a fun, but very... different... experience, give Uplink a whirl. Happy hacking!

Uplink is one of the best hacking "simulators" out there, obviously it's not as easy to break into a system for real as it shown here, but it does a good job. The story kicks in after a few weeks of freelance hacking, accepting missions from other corporations to steal, delete or otherwise screw with other corporations info.
You work for the Uplink corporation, well known for being a place where hackers can pickup missions to gain credits and improve their Uplink rating, unlocking more difficult missions. After a brief tutorial which you can skip, you're dropped into the world with a few thousand credits and a low Uplink rating. Your first missions will consist of: Break into X's system and delete/steal Y file. It picks up later with missions like: Here's this person's account number for X bank, break into it and send us their bank balance or loan. Sometime's they'll want you to transfer Y Credits to Z account.
Security gradually increases over time, your basic internal servcies machine will only be running a monitor, which basically just says: Hey this IP is running software that's trying hundreds of passwords very quickly, start tracing this IP and mark those logs as suspicous. Then it introduces thing like Firewalls and Proxy severs, Proxy servers allowing you to read, but not modify files or logs and firewalls performing a similar role, you'll have to bypass them or disable them.
Bypassing is the "stealthy" route if done right they'll never know anyone broke into the system, but as a trade off you require a certain HUD upgrade and the bypassers themselves, which are quite costly.
Disabling on the otherhand is the "noisy" route, as once something has been disabled it will be noticed immediately. But these disablers are cheaper and don't reqiure the HUD upgrade but they take time to work.
Various missions pose troublesome though, most notably the "Trace a hacker who recently broke into our system" missions.
You accept it and go to their system, they say the attack occured at X time and you login with the details provided, but you cannot access the logs, you need admin access, so you have to go back, load up your bounch path, break in, look at the logs and match them to the time given, and then gradually follow the chain back until you reach someone's PC. However if you accept the mission when It's going gray on the BBS, these missions are almost impossible to complete, as the attacker has cleared their tracks and you don't know who did it. So you have to abandon the mission, which causes your Uplink rating to drop, heavily.
Unfortunately there is no offical sequel, but there is a spirtitual successor called Hacknet, comparing the two I call this the "Hollywood" hacking sim. It's not as realistic but it's more fun, you're given free reign to do whatever you wish.
Still an amazing game after all these years and definately worth picking up, I'd reccommend watching some tutorials if you're new.

This is the third SONIC game I've ever played. The other two were Sonic Advance 3 and Sonic Colors. Based on these two games, I never really got a good impression of Sonic.. But before picking up Mania, I tried a bit of Sonic 3 and it was a lot of fun. It gave me a taste of the "good sonic" games that everyone always talked about. And now that I've finished Mania and I completely understand what the hype is about. Going to try the original 3 games now.
The music is amazing and perfectly fits the fast-paced action of the game. The sprites are incredibly detailed and impressed me on many occasions. Gameplay uses momentum perfectly and doesn't get you caught up on cheap deaths (which I had to deal with in colors and advance 3). Bonus stages are fun and there are plenty to unlock. Environments are all pretty and creative.
Honestly I hope this game represents more than "a good Sonic game", and that other devs take notes from it on how to impress fans in modern day. There was no way I couldn't pick it up: I wanted to support SEGA taking steps in the right direction. But also if you are a fan of tight and challenging platforming, this is a lot of fun and worth the money.

From the moment I booted this up I knew it was something special. What an amazing experience. If someone had told me this was a lost Sonic Genesis, I would completely believe it (with the exception of some nice little graphical touches). Imagine taking the gameplay of Sonic 2/3/K, the soundtrack quality of Sonic CD, a set of brand new, spectacular zones that match anything the series has to offer, and wrap it all up into a beautiful modern package- that's Sonic Mania.
I don't want to spoil anything as the game is best experienced for oneself, but suffice it to say there are endless touches showing the immense love and care that the developers have for Sonic and the glory days of the Genesis. One of the early boss fights is absolutely brilliant and you'll see immediately what I mean.
I dislike intrusive DRM as much as the next person, but I'm reviewing the game here, not the DRM. More than enough people have done that here. As far as the game itself goes, this is as good as any Sonic game ever, if not better, and I know; I've played them all (OK, I'm sure there's some obscure title that only came out for refurbished Wonderswans or something, but I've certainly played the vast majority of them).
There were some moments that nearly brought me to tears for how perfectly they evoked the nostalgia of Sonic's heyday, and this is mixed in with some truly excellent gameplay and level design that rival anything to be found in the entirety of the Sonic franchise.
Turns out, you CAN go home again. It just takes Sonic Mania.

I'm a lover of stories, and that is why I have always enjoyed history, but this game gave me an entire new appreciation of it. There is no objective in this game, save for the ones you give yourself. It's safe to stay that generally speaking though, your goal is to ensure the survival of your starting character's dynasty. Yet from that rather generic starting point comes a thousand decisions and an always fascinating story that never has a narrator.
In the world of kings and nobles, your family is all that exists to protect you, but is also key to obtaining greatness, and is also the greatest threat to both your rule and your life. You'd be amazed at how quickly you'll invade the lands of your cousin or uncle, and don't be surprised when you hire assassin's to plot the death of your wife or unworthy son. Without a black heart and an iron grip on your courts, you'll find yourself against the ropes by people you thought could be trusted.
Of course, this is the iconic Paradox Game, and with the exception of Stellaris, the easiest to learn. Don't let me mislead you though, this game pretty much requires spending some time watching Let's Plays and tutorials, but the pay off is well worth it. There is no other game that does what this game does with such a scope.

Fun sandbox game as a solo player but as of 6/01/15 It's pretty far away from completion. Weapon masteries don't seem to do anything but give stats but if you want stats crafting gives the same faster with actual content unlocked. Aggressive field monsters currently can spawn inside your walled off  base and attack your stuff when in range either way while you are offline, though killing monsters will give you coins to repair it easily enough but some small buildings like basic fences and basic crafting stations aren't repairable. Arrows take forever to make and 20 minutes of grinding will probably give your tower enough to kill one enemy while you are logged off but the range is too far and hits enemies not even attacking your stuff.
Stats don't seem to be balanced at the moment, STR seems to be the best stat by far giving 1~1 damage per 5 STR with any weapon letting you do nice unarmed damage and not have to deal with the low durability weapons. DEX seems completely useless at the moment giving 1 critical per point which isn't 1% and 1 stamina that doesn't affect regen speed. CON only gives 1 health per point, might scale with stacking inventory space with high quality bandages and having an amazing weapon and armor and INT/magic isn't implemented. Weapons have no differences currently with the same speed and range while giving you an x~x damage boost for 1 durability per hit even on rocks and trees, pretty useless without a high level blacksmith/tinker crafting them for more damage and durability.
Currently there is no way to tie livestock to you so people can make a building outside of your walls if you don't use stone walls and jump over them to kill them with no penalty. As with above mounts are randomly spawning rarely apparently but they don't log off with you and suffer the same problem as above.
When these problems are fixed I would recommend the game but this is just the beginning of Early Access and will be fixed.
EDIT as of 6/4/15:People being able to jump over walls has been fixed by increasing their sizes fixing a lot of issues. They also turned arrows from 10 per craft to 40 and reduced the dumb extra  requirements of above copper fixing monsters at night mostly while making aggressive day monsters not attack buildings. They announced plans of a leash item to tie livestock to you but it isn't implemented yet. I will recommend the game now but be warned if you care about PvP or fighting monsters weapon masteries still don't do anything and magic is still not implemented, rollbacks from server crashes have been frequent.

It's set up like a cooperative game, but you mainly play cards to buy cards from the middle, I guess in the hopes that you can get a few cards that damage psyche. You have to click on each card to use the bonus you want. That's very messy for the kind of card games available right now. The board just doesn't seem very interactive and there's nothing pulling me in.
The theme feels more Goosebumps than anything particularly Lovecraftian (Edit: if you want a real Lovecraftian experience, play Sunless Sea). I just don't see myself getting into it like Hearthstone, Runescape Legends, or the lesser known titles. Seems like a big waste to have been included in the Humble Monthly Bundle, to add an unknown and seemingly untested title.

Overall, the game seems to be okay. The mechanics are enough to keep me interested and I can see myself linking this to my phone an play on the go.
