So to mimic what just about everyone else has said. This game is great I put 101 hours into the game and loved every single moment of it. So much so I will probably go back and do it again sometime. A game so good it may find it's way into my top ten off all time when all is said and done.
You play as a GodWoken a being chosen to ascend to divinity. You awake on a ship heading toward the ironically named Fort Joy a prison for sorcerers like yourself to stop a scourge being plagued upon the land. How you interact with the world around you is entirely up to you. Want to just kill people you don't like? Go for it. What to be the hero and try to resolve almost everything through non-violence? Sure why not. Maybe you want to go the whole thing alone being a one man army yea you can do that too.
A couple of quick stories of things the game let me do that most games wouldn't. I found myself in a torture chamber surrounded by enemies but because I had not yet activated the combat I was able to sneak around and fill the room with oil slowing them before they even were able to come to me. Another time I had one of my characters start talking to an NPC while I used my sneaky ranger to stealth behind him and rob a room that had an item I needed for a quest which both allowed me to progress and avoided a fight I'd rather not be in. The games room for experimentation is endless and it's almost as much fun to just play around to see what it will allow you to do.
It puts the RP back in RPG especially coming from the D&D style games. Between the great voice acting (Special shout out to the narrator) and the sheer volume of things you can do and ways you can handle any given situation you feel as if you're in a world that is alive. The affect you have on the world around you is palpable and when you make it to the end of the game seeing how everything played out is rewarding.
The combat is turn based and very strategic. A playground of each encounter as to how you combo your abilities with the world around you. You can teleport your enemies into a barrel of oil and set them all on fire. You can fly next to their mages and silence them and jump next to them with your tank and try to smash them. The difficulty is a major positive as on the normal difficulty it can be brutal but with if you have your wits about you and have created a team the works well together you can push through. If you find it too difficulty you can always turn it down which isn't as challenging but it never feels like your getting babied. If you're kind of a masochist crank it up and feel like you're playing a chess match where you start out without your knights and rooks at the start. It's adaptable for whatever you want and gives you a dark souls esq feeling of accomplishment when you take down one of the very tough fights.
If you're a fan of the Baldur's Gate games than this is by far the closest game to giving you the sense of awe and character development since that game. Better than Mass Effect or Dragon Age this characters are some of the most memorable and years later when you're putting together a top ten list of NPC's you'll find yourself being hard pressed not included at least a couple of these characters.  What this game does so well in terms of it's characters is giving them a sense of purpose in the world to accomplish the main goal of the story as much as you do. Which unlike many RPG's where your partners are just kind of tag alongs almost every character that you come across is has purpose and is driven in a way that is both realistic and endearing.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is a masterpiece in every way. If you're a fan of RPG's you have to play it. It would be a disservice to yourself not to.
Final Grad A+
If you liked the first you need to play the second. It's not perfect in everything it changes but overall it's a massive improvement.

Uplink casts you as a blackhat hacker, out to make money in any way possible by sabotaging companies, falsifying documents, and stealing money from banks.  Cover your tracks well, or the FBI (or even other hackers!) will find you and shut you down.
This game evokes paranoia like nothing I’ve ever played before.  The simple UI and relatively simple mission structure leaves you with a false sense of security.  Fail to delete logs of your hacks, leave a trail of breadcrumbs, and the government or a rival corporation will find you.  When they do, its game over.  All your hard work destroyed instantly.  If you want to keep playing, you’ll have to restart from the very beginning.  Yet this failure is not instantaneous.  You’ll have time to run other missions and you’ll think that you are safe, when in reality, the noose is tightening ever so slowly.  And there’s nothing you can do about it.  There are no take-backs in the world of hacking.
You should always route your connection to your target system through as many other servers as you can.  This will give you time to perform your hack, as well as shield you from investigation.  You can delete logs from any system along the chain and you’ll effectively be untraceable.  But you have to be fast.
Slowly you’ll gain expertise in how to infiltrate different systems.  Banks are more secure than academic databases, and corporate mainframes have different security measures from public servers.  You’ll need lots of different software tools to manage each of these challenges, which Uplink Corp. will happily provide you.  The downside here is that you’ll never know exactly what you’re going to need before you run into it.  In a game that requires perfection, forcing you to learn by trial-and-error is a little annoying.
The main storyline about an impossibly-strong  computer virus is engaging, but rather short.  Most missions fall into about 10 different types, which get a little repetitive once you are know how to tackle each one.
Uplink is really interesting, though slightly flawed.  This is THE game that anyone aspiring to be a movie hacker should play.  Fight against the clock to steal valuable secrets and leave no trace of your presence.  Paranoia will be your constant companion in this one.  If (or rather, when) you do get caught, it will be no one’s fault but your own.

A solid, enjoyable, and accessible RTS with equal playability for combat and econ/tech.
RON is a multifaceted real-time game with well-implemented resource gathering and tech dimensions, in addition to the industry-standard combat elements. It's customizable enough so that a newcomer or veteran who would rather not worry about tech, econ, or combat can disable those elements in the starting menus.
There are six economic resources in the game (three of which appear after appropriate research). Most combat units, buildings, tech, and upgrades cost one or two types of resources. They also tend to increase in cost the more of the same unit/building you have already built, which encourages players to diversify their buildings and units rather than just rebuild one type over and over.
Combat units usually adhere to a rock/paper/scissors balance mechanic, although at later ages there are a decent range of specialized units that accomplish unique functions in warfare. Controlling a battle group is relatively intuitive - command buttons on the console also show shortcuts for the more-familiar player, and extra modifiers such as facing, General craft powers, and terrain also allow modest benefits for the detail-oriented player.
Each nation has its own special powers, which lead to interesting matchups (although at higher levels of play, certain nation powers mandate a narrower choice of strategy than others).
Those already experienced with RTSes can expect to jump right in and get playing against the AI competitively, and then jump online to test their skills against humans. This game may be a steeper learning curve for newcomers to the RTS genre because of its breadth of econ, tech, and military.
Players who like modding their games will also find this game rewarding and versatile, including the ability to mod entire campaigns and to create new units in the game's .xml files.
An excellent balance of accessibility and complexity. My favorite RTS game.

Easy for anyone to start playing, but takes time to master. Really, you need to understand not only your selected freelancer, but also understand how other play. The best part of this game is that it's a turn-based strategy game where all actions happen simultaneously happen after everyone has locked in their actions. The only thing holding the game back at this point is the fact that there are a few freelancers that just suck. Not that they can't do anything at all, but rather to fully maximize their abilities, you need other freelancers, i.e. teamwork, to make the most of them. And being a strategy game, you do need a level of teamwork to actually take your enemies down.
The freelancer unlock system by buying them through credits you earn as you play is actually well placed, assuming you play with other people. The game is very slow and repetitive if you play with bots. The game really incentivizes you for playing with real people. The way to purchase things with real money is available, but not forced on you, and nearly all of them are cosmetic anyway. Do I recommend playing this game? Yes I do! Do I recommend buying it? That's all on you and how much time you think you'll spend on it. Play it for free and find out! At this point for me, with basically 200+ hours sunk in over 6+ months and have played all the freelancers.... I actually feel a bit obligated to buy the game to actually play the freelancers I like without waiting for them to come up on free rotation. But, I've also unlocked a few of them just by playing and have started to master playing them.

If you miss the days of playing Gunbound but are looking for a game with different/more strategic gameplay, this is perfect for you.
This is an online turn based multiplayer game where everyone decides what move they will make at the same time and the results play out after everyone has finished choosing their move (within the 20 second timer)
The gameplay is very unique and can be described as XCOM meets hero shooter. During the decision phase you can attack anyone within range and get a good idea of how much damage you'll be doing, unless that opponent has chosen to dash out of the way on this turn! As you become more accustomed to the game, predicting when and where people will dash to is a skill that will feel extremely satisfying the few times you are able to do it correctly. Movement takes place after all attacks and dashes have completed so you will not know where your opponents will move before you get to make your move. Predicting movement and positioning yourself well are things I am still enjoying to learn every match I play in this game.
If this sounds intimidating, you are free to play bot matches at any difficulty with friends, strangers, or AI teammates to help learn characters and the flow of the game. All character abilities are visible from the character select screen (with videos of each move popping up as you select them) so you are never forced to start any match without having a good idea of what you character can do. In public matches, players have been extremely friendly (or completely silent) despite having some pretty devastating losses.
I begrudgingly started playing this game on a friend's recommendation but it has quickly become my favorite multiplayer game. Good strategy will always put you ahead in a match, but games will often finish before 20 minutes.

The best sword, melee or dueling game out there. It does duels extremely well in that players are separated by skill, knowledge of mechanics, knowledge of other class's weakness and strentgh, quick reactions and how much they have practiced. The gameplay is literally amazingly smooth and you really feel in control and in a very good duel. There are a lot of bad reviews because this game is hard. You need a lot of hours to get good at it and it's true once you are above level 15 you are not allowed to play in beginner servers anymore and it's brutal. Think of a US Marine being put into a fighting ring with any average joe, it will be a massacre. The average joe has no chance. And that's part of the beauty of the game. The outcome of a duel is dictated completely by skill and there is no way that someone who has practiced 200 hours will ever lose to someone who only practiced 10.
I will admit the are about 2 attacking mechanics that can be abused and are basically impossible to counter but they are few and far between as even they take skill to execute well. And  a player who is otherwise bad will not be able to suddenly beat pros by abusing a single mechanic. Duels depend on mastery of dozens of aspects of play. If you want to experience the best skill-based melee game out there, this is for you. If you just want to go in and hack and slash and expect not to be absolutely shreded by pros if you choose to face them, this game is not for you. Take note you can avoid pros by sticking with a group in team vs team game modes. Or just play archer.

Between countless Fire Emblem games, some tabletop roleplaying, and a recent campaign of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, I've come to enjoy turn-based strategy. There's something very satisfying about using your brain to look at the situation, and by taking careful risks, use each and every single one of your units to make a satisfying move which puts you further towards winning the game.
That was what I was hoping for when I bought Frozen Synapse - a nice, fun, turn-based strategy which lets me plan carefully in order to win. Personally, I was almost crossing my fingers for an XCOM/Fire Emblem rip-off, since to me, they represent the core ideas and mechanics of turn-based strategy and more of that sort of gameplay couldn't be a bad thing.
Unfortunately, what I found instead was a boring, drab game where the "strategy" comes down to "have you guessed what your opponents were going to do?" Sure, that's an essential part of most strategy games, but usually you get help, like showing where your opponents can move, or knowing how much damage they'll do so you'll know which units can survive a fight with them. Instead, in Frozen Synapse, you choose which actions you want your units to take, press the button to end your turn, and then your opponents make all of their moves at the same time.
Whilst this doesn't sound like a bad thing, it means that you can spend time setting up your units, planning for your opponents to do something, only for them to bypass that method completely and catch you by surprise, all because you didn't have the precognition to see into the future and realise that they could do that. Sure, you could try and plan for all outcomes, but that means using more units and therefore cutting off your options elsewhere. Essentially, gameplay boils down to you crossing your fingers that the enemy walks in front of your units and dies before they notice your units.
On top of all that, the controls are confusing as all hell and very unintuitive. There's a tutorial, but it rushes by pretty quickly and being given step-by-step instructions is much different to having to think ahead and choose and work out what to do in a real level. I should say something about the graphics and story too, but really, what is there to say? The graphics are ugly, uninspired, and boring, and the story is a bunch of cyberpunk technobabble which made my eyes immediately glaze over because it was so boring.
Normally, I try and finish games to the end because I want to get my money's worth, but this is the first time in a very long while that I've simply quit and said "No." I tried to get into the game and give it a good go, but as I struggled to predict the enemies' paths for the umpteenth time, I recalled that in video games, players should be interested within five to fifteen minutes. Well, I gave the game nearly an hour of my time, and as far as I'm concerned, I shouldn't have gone further than fifteen minutes.
Overall, I would not recommend Frozen Synapse. This is not the type of turn-based strategy I enjoy, and whilst it's certainly a nice try and something different, there's a reason that turn-by-turn strategy has remained dominant in many games - for example, chess - for so long: because it works and it's fun, unlike Frozen Synapse.

TLDR: It's good, but not great.
This is how I'm going to rate this:
If something is good: 1 point
If something is okay: 1/2 point
If something sucks: 0 points
Servers: I've never had trouble finding a game and I've always gotten into a lobby pretty fast once one has been found.
(1 point)
Community: This game has a crazy toxic community. I haven't been in one game where people haven't been cussing eachother out or calling hacks or smurfs. Everyone is always angry.
(0 points)
Gameplay: It's pretty much all combat and there are 4 main different moves, a heavy but slow attack, medium moderately paced attack, a weak but fast attack, and a stun. All work pretty decently. There's also a ranged attack, and depending on which class you choose, the amounts and the types of ammunition will differ. The different classes all control a little bit differently, with the archer moving the fastest, the knight moving the slowest, etc. The classes seem fairly balanced, but it seems to me that the second class option, being the Man-at-Arms character is the one that's used the least. For the most part though, everything works here.  There's also a sprint button. Groundbreaking, I know.
(1 point)
Game Modes and Maps: To start with, the game modes for the most part are pretty decent. They revolve mostly around attacking and defending an objective. Depending on what team you're on, you'll either attack or defend the objective. It's simple but fun. the objectives change from either a payload that needs to be escorted from one side of the map to another, or defending a village from being burnt down. These modes have different stages to them depending on what objective a team can complete in the given time, which keeps things fairly fresh. The other game mode is Survival of the Fittest, which is pretty much self explanitory. As for the maps, they're all pretty decent and fun to play on, although some maps aren't as well optimized as others, which I will get into in my next point.
(1 point)
Optimization: Okay, so this one is a bit trickier. On some maps, the game runs completely fine, particularly the snow map (I don't remember the names of the maps) seems to run pretty decently. On most maps though, preformance is a mixed bag. Just to be clear, it has nothing to do with my PC specs, I have an i5 7600k, 16gb of ram, and a GTX 1060 6gb OC. So well above the recommended PC specs. On most maps, maxed out graphics, I can only get around 45-50 fps consistently, and even lowering the settings down to medium or low just as a test, the fps is always in that ballpark range. The colliseum map is the worst though. I get 25 fps there on average, with 35 fps tops. I'm assuming it's all of the geometry being rendered at the same time, and the complete debacle that all of the players create in that map, but it's still not great.
(1/2 points)
Overall points out of 5:
3.5/5
Although there are some things holding it back, it's a pretty solid game to pour some hours into. It's a great game to play while listening to stream, or watching YouTube or something like that. I wouldn't buy it at full price ($28.99 CDN) but if it ever goes on sale, pick it up!

Crusader Kings II, this game has got to be my all time favourite game that I have ever played.
Crusader Kings is fun and unique to most other strategy games because you do not play as a country, but instead play as a midieval dynasty. You can play as almost anyone like Emperors of the Byzantine & Holy Roman Empires, to the islamic Sejulk, Abbasids, & Ummayads; the germanic norsemen in the north & the great khans of the nomad steppes, to the italian Doges of the medditerranean. Any level on the feudal scale from the smallest of vassal counts to dukes, kings, and great emperors of Europe.
Despite wars and conquests and empire expansions playing a big role in this game it is not what makes this game great. What makes the game great is the internal conflicts and realm management. For as you grow stronger so do your vassals who have their own ambitions. It is this struggle, between feudal lord and vassal and between fellow vassals that makes this game great; intrigue, murders, plots, political marriages, factions, seduction, if you like Game of Thrones you will for sure love this game
There is only 1 objective: your family line must live on... or its game over. So make sure you have an heir of your dynasty at all costs. Do whatever it takes seduction, polygamy(religion specific), Xwedodah, it does not matter
. Other than that, you are free to do whatever you want, you can set your own goals: reclaim the holy land, unite the steppes under one khan, build the most serene merchant republic the world has ever seen, mend the catholic/orthodox schism, restore the imperial borders of rome. Europe is your playground.
Definetely reccommend to anyone who seriously loves strategy games or has any interest in the midieval era.
One more thing I should touch on: DLC
There has been 12 major expansions released for Crusader Kings II over the last 5 years. While the game is perfectly playable without any of them, each one brings unique flavour to the game. Also, some government types like Merchant Republics & Nomads require dlc to play, as well as all non Christian religions. As someone who is just getting into the game I would reccommend starting out with none and play the base game and then when you are ready to pick up the dlc that interest you. One more thing: if you do not have a dlc but are playing multiplayer with someone who does have the dlc all features in the dlc are available to you, so if you have a friend who owns this game this is a great way to try out the dlc to see if you like what it offers.

Call to Arms is the spiritual (if not physical) successor of the Men of War franchise.
Set in a modern setting, at this stage with the United States operating in the middle east against a generic Middle Eastern Force, CtA provides the same realistic and frantic setting we have come to expect of Men of War.
The combat is quick, desisive and violent.
You can feel the tension from the supression from larger weapons, and when your soldiers start dropping around you because you made the decision to move them from cover, you realise how badly your tactical decision has been.
Limited singleplayer at this point.
Multiplayer remains as good as ever with what I can only describe as 'condensed' battlefields, leading to more close quaters battle. Multiplayer responds well with the 2x2 Games I have tested. Very fluid run.
Lacking some content such as further vehicles and units, but it is to be expected for this EA.
If you have enjoyed any of the Men of War series...I strongly urge you to pick up this gem and support the EA, you will not be dissapointed.

Rise of Nations is what I would call a nice introduction to RTS games.
+It's fairly easy to get a hang of and you don't need to invest countless hours to understand the basic concepts.
+It has all your basic RTS features such as setting a way point for new units to arrive at when they are created, continuous unit creation, and scouting.
+This game offers a nice "Age" progression system where you can go through the stone age, the bronze age, ect, and build new units and unlock "Wonders" to build that will give you neat little bonuses such as reduced costs of resources on certain research, give you bonus resources, or straight up give you soldiers to use.
+Each nation has a special passives that can cater to your style of play and adds diversity.
+The game modes are very customizable with a ton of options.
+You can choose to play the game either in a "Quick Play" session or you can choose a "Take over the world" campaigns.
+/-It has twitch streaming options, I have yet to fool around with these and I don't hold any interest in them.
-The graphics are still a little dated.
-The simplicity can be limiting at times with the lack of things to be able to do.
-The game can get lack lustre quite fast if you ever stick to one style.
-Quick Sessions are just as they sound, barely ever lasting an hour of gameplay against bots.
I still enjoy it to this day. It's a solid game that I think new comers to the genre can enjoy.
Even more than 10 years after release it's the best Real Time strategy ever.

I'm not normally the kind of person to write a review for any kind of game but Sonic Mania with all this negative backlash definitely deserves some kind of casual Joe to step forward and say some things.
Is it bad? No, not at all.
Does it have some kind of DRM? Yes.
Does it deserve the hate just for the DRM, and does it deserve no purchase? No, again.
Sonic Mania is everything you could love in a game for what it is, an amazingly detailed and robust platformer, with plenty of difficulty. $20 dollars and you're setting sail on the nostalgic trip to the 90's,  Sonic Mania has a wonderful quark about combining the old levels you knew as kids where you and your friends are taking turns beating levels and getting stuck on certain bosses for a few tries, and adds new and refreshing content to boot.
If you think a simple DRM on this game is worth ignoring this wonderful game, you are sadly denying yourself a truly entertaining experience.
You have the option of playing as either Sonic and Tails (Duo), Knuckles, or simply Tails alone, which gives you a total of (3) multiple play styles, each catered to fit certain players and playstyles. This means everyone should explore there options with characters, I played through with Sonic and Tails my first try, but found Knuckles with his Glide and Wall Climb to be much more fun!
In addition, the levels themselves offer multiple routes for players to take, promoting exploration and replayability for the longevity of the game. (It's only $20 bucks, c'mon!)
As for bosses, they are extremely versatile and different in regards that you never know what to expect, so certain players may find some bosses really easy, and others oddly challenging due to their unique nature.
I would shamelessly give this game a 10, delete it, then give it a 10 again just because it's that damn good. Sonic Mania so good it makes you want it again. So what are you waiting for, stop reading this stupid, long-winded and over exaggerated review? Buy the damn game already and play it!

A Sonic game for the fans by the fans. Sonic Mania was created by Christian Whitehead, known for his Sonic fangames in the past, and contribution towards remastering Sonic 1, CD, and 2. If you're a classic Sonic fan you'll be extremely satisfied, the gameplay perfectly emulates the feeling of the originals, with incredibly fun momentum and speed based platforming. One playthrough simply isn't sufficient, like every classic Sonic game you're encouraged to visit multiple times, discover new paths, etc. Mania brings this back in full scale, as these are some of the biggest levels in any Sonic game comparable to Sonic 3 & Knuckles. The game takes the best elements from the classic era to bring something completely new yet also familiar. The music done by Tee Lopes is an absolute godsend, you'll see familiar classics remixed and new original tunes. There are a whopping 12 zones with 2 acts so you have a game on par with Sonic 3 & Knuckles in terms of length, very suiting for the $20 pricetag. The only downsides I could really list are the lack of new original zones as majority of the zones are just classic stages remixed, and also the denuvo drm which is incredibly anti-consumer. Because of denuvo I'd want to leave this review neutral, but otherwise this is the best Sonic game we've had in years, go out and get it, you would definitely find enjoyment out of this even if you don't have any prior experience with the older Sonic games.

Sonic Mania is a 2D platformer made in the spirit of the old Sega Genesis (and one Sega CD) games. Kinda a celebration of what Sonic was and what people liked him for.
Before I start, I should state that I played all of the 2D Sonic games to death as a kid, including Sonic CD. I loved the games, although playing through them again recently I can say they have a number of flaws (especially Sonic CD, which has really bizarre level and boss design and the time travel mechanics were finicky at best). Still, really great games that stand the test of time, some more than others.
Now for Sonic Mania. First thing about it is that it looks gorgeous. All of the spites are amazingly detailed, with a wide variety of fluid animations. The levels are colorful and full with personality and life, and are a blast to explore and look through. This is all to an amazing soundtrack composed of remixed themes of old Sonic levels, and brand new tracks that fit perfectly. Absolutely top notch soundtrack.
The level design is for the most part top notch. Each of the levels (even the ones you grew up playing!) have interesting gimmicks and plenty of paths to explore. You can play the same level multiple times and find multiple ways to get to the end, and maybe find a few new secrets! Many times my first time through, I came relatively close to hitting the time limit just because there's so much to explore and look at. 'Course, there's also plenty of ways to speed through the levels if that's more your fancy.
There's one or two instances where the level design was chaotic and confusing, though, mostly near the end. The last level in particular neared Sonic CD levels of confusing.
Most of the enemies are variants of old foes you've seen in the original games, although there's some new, interesting foes to fight. The bosses in particular will surprise even veterans of the Sonic series, playing on old mechanics with brand new twists, or flat out being brand new. A number of bosses require you to think a bit more than just jumping into them 6/8 times.
However, there are a number of bosses that feel they take too long to beat, and a number that are flat out no fun and frustrating. I can name two bosses I absolutely hated fighting throughout the game...But that's a vast minority. I enjoyed most of the boss battles, and loved a good handful of them. Overall, a blast to fight!
The brand new Special Stage (which is found via the Sonic 3 method of exploring and finding hidden giant rings) took some time to grow on me, but I ended up loving it after I got the hang of it. And you will need to get the hang of it: It's difficult to control until you understand how it works and you'll find yourself running into spikes or into pits a lot until you get it. It took me around 6-7 attempts to get the second Special Stage (out of seven) down, but then I cleared the one after like nothing.
If there is a real complaint, it's that finding the Giant Rings is really hard. In Sonic 3 & Knuckles, you were given a few gimmes and some were just in plain sight, but in Sonic Mania, they are hidden in far areas of the map and you really gotta search for them in these huge levels. That's good in a way, but I would strongly suggest not to think you can get all the Chaos Emeralds your first run without a guide.
One other complaint is the prevalence of Blue Sphere, which makes a triumphant return from Sonic 3. Blue Sphere replaces the mini games from the checkpoint lampposts, and only requires 25 rings to activate. This means you will likely activate the Blue Sphere portal every single checkpoint you reach. This means a
of Blue Sphere.
It takes levels from Sonic 3, Sonic & Knuckles, and even the Sonic 1 + Sonic & Knuckles combination, and there are 32 levels in total. You can clear these to earn coins that unlock extras and secrets, but if you take the time to clear every single one of these stages, you really ruin the pacing of the game. I ended up ignoring Blue Sphere entirely after getting around 10 coins because I wanted to actually play the game.
I would have prefered Blue Sphere just being a separate game mode, and put back the mini games that give you powerups like in Sonic 3. There's just...Too much Blue Sphere.
Overall, I really enjoyed Sonic Mania, and I'm looking forward to repeat playthroughs with all the extras and other things included. I also will eventually take the time to get everything in Blue Sphere. Eventually.
I would recommend this beyond people with nostalgia. If you like 2D platformers, you're sure to love Sonic Mania even if you're not a Sonic fan. I give it a hearty recommendation despite it's slight flaws.

You know what, I'm gonna balance out some of the hate and negativity seen in the gaming community. It's now a free game  (literally free to play, not "f2P' where you get dinged with pay to win BS) and with that, there is no reason to leave a negative review. Once upon a time I started using FPSC and tried to create my own game. Needless to say it was about the level of this project and I never released it. About a decade later I've just shipped my first game made with Unreal Engine 4. Every (nerdy) kid dreams of having their game on Steam, and it's kind of cool that this developer could get his work featured here, however rough around the edges it may be. Like any FPS Creator project, expect a ton of bugs, that's just the engine at work. I see they've added hands to the weapon models, sprint animations (however terrible they are), and aiming down the sights (amusingly with no actual sights to look down).
The levels seem a little too big, just for the sake of being big. The enemy AI is still terrible and they still have that hilarious bug where they have to reload their guns upon first sighting you. The cohesion and overal storyline is well.. non-existent. You go from one level to the next without any idea of why you're doing what you're doing. Oh well, it's FPS Creator. Find keys, shoot baddies, use remote pads to unlock doors.
The assets are all stock pretty much, maybe one or two model packs worth of stuff, but overall almost everything gave me a rush of nostalgia for the good ol' FPSC days. The SFX are all stock and even worse than I remember.
Overall, you get what you paid for. If someone paid for this and didn't refund it, I pity you, but since it's free, I'd say give it a shot, what do you have to lose? It's fun for a couple minutes and you'll get a giggle or two out of it, so why not try?

SECTOR is something of a breath of fresh air for a genre of games which incresingly seems to lack anything in the way of innovation, stripping everything back to the very core of what makes an FPS game. The uniqueness of SECTOR lies in how it brilliantly strips away distractions like good graphics, flashy weapons, a well written story, an options menu, gameplay, and so on, allowing you to get on with what you came here for - shooting things. Thats where SECTOR truly excels. There's no messing around here - just point your gun at an enemy and shoot them until they die. All the while you get to experience the finest sound design that no money could buy -  from the noise that plays when you look down what you expect to be the sights of your weapon (though of course, actual sights are just another unecessary frippery which SECTOR brilliantly does away with), to the sound of the weapons firing, your ears will be treated to a selection of the finest sounds that came free with FPS Creator. Whats more, you get to experience the brilliance of these exchanges time and time again.
Thats before we come to the game's real genius. Other FPS games set their community against each other, with game mechanics which incentivise players to boast of how their sexual prowess vis-a-vis each other's mothers. SECTOR on the other hand brings people together with its brilliantly designed puzzles. Whether you need to find the key to unlock the first door, or find the hidden button to open the second door, or even simply figure out what the hell the control scheme is, SECTOR makes you co-operate with others so that the community can come together to find the solutions to the puzzles the game throws at us. Some people who are spoilt by CoD, Battlefield, and a plethora of other FPS games which are actually good may say that is a consequence of poor design choices. "Why wouldnt you highlight where items are, or hide a vital key without which you can make absolutely zero progress behind a f*****g pipe you'd never think to check behind in a million years?!" they may say. However, they simply dont understand UD's unique creative vision of a game that could become the focus of bigger things. Perhaps one day there will be children who would never have been born had their parents not first met and bonded over such questions as "where is the button for this door?" or "why is this game so s***?".
It is no understatement to suggest that SECTOR is perhaps the greatest FPS game which has ever been created. It does everything an FPS has to do to be worthy of the name - it uses a first person view and allows you to shoot things - and does not waste time going beyond these core principles. UD has created the kind of game nobody who also spends their free time watching paint dry could ever get bored of, and one which truly brings people together in a unique way. Truly, SECTOR is a masterpiece which can provide literally minutes of entertainment for even the most hardened veteran of modern video games.

Uplink is a game that simulates being a hacker. It is novel and superficially well-done, but after I played for an hour or so, the novelty wore off and I was left with a lot of flawed and confusing game mechanics.
Pros:
+ Very immersive. The game does a nice job of making you feel like the main character. In fact, it almost feels like you are a real hacker at times.
+ Good sense of gradually building yourself up from scratch. There is a certain satisfaction in upgrading your programs and computers step by step.
Cons:
- A lot of aspects of the game are very poorly explained. Once you get through the basics, you have to look everything up on the internet because what the different hacking programs do and how/when to use them is very unclear. Several times I literally didn't know what I was supposed to be attempting in a mission.
- Poor mission variety makes the game very repetitive. Add to this the fact that a given mission can be completed exactly the same way every time you get it. Mission are fun the first one or two times you get each one, but then just become a chore.
- The game mechanics are very susceptible to tricks, loopholes, and exploits. This is the type of game that seems very hard until you figure out a couple of little tricks that make it painfully easy. Then it just becomes a repetitive grind of using the same tricks over and over. I'm honestly not sure if several of the techniques I used were the intended mechanics of the game or were game-breaking oversights.

At the time of writing, I've just finished the first major area (Fort Joy) in about 25 hours, and very much looking forward to the rest. I never could get into Divinity: Original Sin 1; I'm not really sure why. It just didn't feel very compelling to me, even though I knew there was lots of heart in it. On the other hand, Original Sin 2 seems to be much more like what the previous game wanted to be.
Pros
====
- There's lots of little intricacies that give the game so much depth. No stats are hidden from the player (except maybe the actual "dice rolls"), so you can strategize effectively before heading into battle, if you want to. The idea of physical armor, magical armor, and vitality was a little weird at first, but I've found that it makes a lot of sense, and it really adds to the depth of the combat overall. All the dialogues have many different choices and outcomes depending on all sorts of different things (class, race, items you have, skills, and even which of your allies you're speaking with).
- Freedom. You can pretty much do anything you want, and in nearly any order. Just about everything behaves as it should. There's many different ways to accomplish quests/tasks/battles, and yet the game seems to be able to handle even when you do something think you aren't "supposed" to do. This combined with the aforementioned intricacies create a truly unique experience. I can see myself playing through this game more than once; there's just so many things you can do, but without the feeling of being overwhelmed.
- Sound/Music. The sound design and music in this game is phenomenal. All characters and narration is fully voiced with very good voice acting across the board. All the sound effects really add to the game immersion, and nothing sounds stock. The music is so good, and I thought the ability to choose your "lead" instrument is a really cool idea. The music in this game is definitely in my top 5 favorite video game scores.
- Loading. Load times are surprisingly fast, and even when I have some of my allies in completely different parts of the world, jumping between them is seamless.
- Full controller support. I don't particularly recommend playing this game with a controller, but the fact that the option is there is really nice. And it isn't one of those poorly done mouse-emulation-style control schemes when you use a controller, either. It changes the interfaces and icons and gives you direct control of your character, so if you are playing with a controller, it acutally feels like it was designed for it. This sadly can't be said about many games that try to support multiple control schemes (especially for this game's genre), so to see it done well is really refreshing.
Cons
====
- Inventory management leaves much to be desired. Perhaps I've been spoiled by other game inventories. I think this game would hugely benefit from an inventory redesign like what was done with The Witcher 3. There's just too many items across 4 different characters with little-to-no organizational tools.
- Click hit-detection. There's many cases where my mouse is directly positioned over something, but the interact highlight doesn't appear. Sometimes I have to twist the camera around and hunt around with my mouse for that tiny clickable area. It's never really caused me any serious issues, but it's VERY annoying.
- I was disappointed that I couldn't use my Resurrection scrolls on characters other than my player-controlled allies. When I talked to the baby bear cub whose mom died, I was very disappointed that I couldn't resurrect her :(
- I've had a few instances where my quest journal UI gets all jumbled up and/or certain entries disappear, and I have to close and re-open the journal window. Mainly just a minor annoyance, but it scares me when it happens.
TL;DR
====
If you like DnD-style, turn-based RPG's, this is a true modern gem of the genre. If you don't like those style games, but have always wanted to like them, give this one a shot.

I give this game a recommendation
First, I was very skeptical of this purchase. Digitalmindsoft has been known for releasing strategy games that had no to  little changes from its predecessors. One example is MoWAS 2 which was basically a upgraded graphically version of MoWAS 1 and a few new vehicles. They could have released it as a expansion but...anyways.
After seeing good reviews of the game and a few bad, I decided to purchase the game.
And I really liked it.
CONTENTS AND MECHANICS
Although it has the same basic mechanics of every Men of War game, the game feels complete to me mechanically wise.
Any veteran MoW player can jump right in the game and can already learn the controls without having to go over a tutorial or manual again. The controls are really responsive. One thing I did not like are damage mechanics though. Infantry and machine guns kill too fast, soldiers barely recieve 5 hits from a SA when they die.
Content is a strong suit of this game. Each model is accurately rendered and displayed. You literally can see the grooves of the M4A1 barrel. The content is still lacking though. There are only a few weapons and vehicles both air and land as of now although that is understandable since the game is still in Early Access.
SINGLEPLAYER AND MULTIPLAYER
I can't speak for the SP right now because I don't have access to it yet as I am not a deluxe user.
MP in this game is balanced. Basically you have two factions, one consists of highly trained soldiers(US) while the other is a terrorist group that has a few elite units but really are just people who were given a gun and sent to war without going to the firing range(GRM). The US,although has really good units, comes at an expense of costs and fewer soldiers per unit. This is compensated by their skill in medium to long range combat and has good close combat units too.
GRM on the other hand, although their soldiers are poorly equipped, has an advantage in costs and number of men per unit. They also excel in close combat where the few US soldiers could be decimated quickly. Their advance unit also has more advanced weapons and are more versatile.
GRAPHICS
Graphics are almost the same as MoWAS2 except maybe for that gritty look. Textures are of course in high definition and very well implemented.Mortar and grenade craters look very realistic. Weapon textures are also something worth looking at. Environmental props are also improved and really provide that sense of modernity. The number of objects on screen is also much more many than previous titles.
Well, that's it for my review. I'll keep it updated as the game also updates.
EDIT:Vehicles have been released in MP
Although vehicle in MP is still limited(only a few light vehicles for now), they are really a game change. They have really good anti-infrantry statistics and can actually be a replacement for a squad or two. They might seem overpowered however they have an exposed gunner so a single sniper can take out a vehicle. They also perform poorly in close range as they have little time to react and move their turrets slowly.

I just started playing CK2 and cannot believe how much I've been missing over the years.  I love history. I love strategy games.  And I love roleplaying.  This game scratches every itch that I have as a result of those fascinations.  And it's the only game that I have ever played that can do that.
This game tells a story unlike any other game that I've ever played - while also providing a good dose of strategy and challenge. Admittedly, due to the extensive amount of information provided, it requires a good bit of imagination to keep up with the story - but the game comes in at just the right level of abstraction so that new things can happen every game.  Paradox clearly understands emergent gameplay - which so many modern developers fail to understand.
I own the vast majority of DLC and do not mind purchasing it.  If this keeps the game relevant and growing, then keep it coming.  I do not expect developers to work for me for free after I buy their initial product.  (Plus, many of the free patches added so much to the game by themselves.  Negative reviews seem to ignore this fact.)
Anyways, I've been gaming for over 30 years and have not encountered a phenomenon like CK2 before.
Count me in for as long as the developers keep pushing this wonderful game forward.

So far the frame rate seems a little better than ESS but this is only on the first ship, the port boat; it's not much of a difference in terms of performance. The real litmus test will be the speed boat; on ESS it was practically unplayable, very low frame rates, laggy and stuttering. Will update this review when i get to purchase that boat.
A little strange use of ambient lights. There seems to be an eerie glow to the port and sea environment but maybe 'coz it's dusk. Will update later when i encounter midday condition. There is weird graphic glitch when i looked at land while a bit far out from port; the reflections of buildings are not right. By that i mean there are reflections of clusters of buildings where i see only 1 cluster of tall buildings and that cluster is repeatedly reflected multiple times at fixed interval distance as if there are multiple clusters of the exact same configuration of buildings on shore when there is only one. It looks  embarassingly bad. In short, building reflections on the shoreline just look wrong in some places.
Port lights at night are poorly rendered making it extremely difficult to see the entry gateway; walls and sea are pitch black. Boat lights are just as useless until you're very near to the designated mooring point, possibly helped only by the bright yellow luminous area marked by the mooring marker.
Boat driving physics - while there are improvements over ESS by expanding and subdividing it into 3 modes; locked, semi-locked and unlocked, there is a glitch, a very bad game breaking bug. In unlocked mode pressing W (forwards) only moves it forwards to max speed for a while then it slows down to a complete stop even when the throttle remains at max forwards. Releasing W will immediately put the boat into max reverse and it will also stop completely. So the net effect is the boat will return back to its original spot. Definitely a bug and probably repeatable.
At first the throttle worked as expected; releasing W cause the forward momentum to slowly cease but after accepting a mission at the port, the above mentioned game breaking bug occured making the rest of the waypoints unreachable. I had to exit the game at this point as there is no way to abort the mission.
At port, where you go to get jobs, buy and repair ships, the frame rate is horribly slow, less than 30 fps. No matter what the graphics settings or resolution is the frame rate stays the same. Totally unoptimized piece of crap and looks ugly too but i can look past all that if the rest of the game is playable.
The developers were trying to make this a little like Sea Dogs where you accept jobs at ports and make it an open persistent world unlike ESS where you select missions from a list (too simplistic) making exploration impractical. Here the idea is good but the execution looks like a broken mess right now and frankly quite underwhelming. The whole map when zoomed out, only contains 3 ports at the edges of the map. Presumably this is to make the distances epic? The ports are; Service, Tourism and Cargo. I can guess already what sort of missions are offered in these places.
At least ESS is playable although half the time at crappy frame rates. This one seems to be littered with game breaking bugs. One redeeming factor though, you can now exit the cabin and walk around the boat.
Don't buy it; seems to be abandoned like ESS but in a worse state. Another game that seems to be optimized only for Nvidia as seen from the store trailers. Only try it if you're curious. Shouldn't be priced at SG$20, SGD$10 is more reasonable, before discount that is. I had way more fun out of Sea Dogs and PIrates of The Caribean.
So far only 4/10 - failed to impress.
I'm changing the score to 5/10 since the bug is not repeatable (maybe not a bug). So overall - a maybe just to be kind and changing to recommended but only cautiously to users with GPU mentioned in the System Requirements.
Maybe i was too harsh in my initial critique. Even though ESS looks better in daylight and the reflections are more realistic with better resolution and colours. WSS does have some redeeming qualities; namely more graphics options and an open world persistent free-roam sandbox mode. Therefore the missing career mode in ESS is now implemented here rather nicely with monetary rewards, captain's ranking/reputation and option to purchase (which is actually unlocking) more ships / boats. I don't think the career mode is expansive or comprehensive enough to include fleet management as was done way back with Sea Dogs though but i haven't reach midgame so i could be wrong.
Another plus point is that key-mapping can be reconfigured to your liking. Oh there was/is one glitchy behaviour i noticed on an AI ship; it moves back and forth on a short straight distance near the gateway and i thought i was gonna crash into it. Luckily the problem resolved itself when i changed the graphics details or resolution, not sure which action did the trick. Unsure also if this is a scripting issue, pathfinding, AI or 3D mesh problem but it's rectifiable on the fly.
When all things are considered and compared, maybe WSS has one up over ESS? or do they balance out? You be the judge.
Sample gameplay (fishing) where i returned to port in near total darkness in part 2. Even though the frame rate was reasonable when starting out, on returning it dropped to below 30 fps.
Before i forget, a few more plus points; piloting is a lot easier with the new throttle and steering unlocked positions and time acceleration is usable throughout your time on the water unlike in ESS where it's not always available.
One minor con is the mini-map and big-map; it doesn't show other ships so you have to rely on visual sighting in the 3D world.

I recently tried "Act of Aggression", and yet again we have another RTS trying to get in on the MLG bandwagon that Starcraft started.  Even Grey Goo, which is a great game, is limited to 2v2 or smaller on strict maps to get into the MLG scene; it's just the way the industry is going. So I went through lists of every RTS, most of which I've played, and stumbled across this gem.  I can't believe I've never played Rise of Nations before!!
RoN is like an awesome blend of Age of Empires, Civilization V, and Supreme Commander 2 (all my favorite RTSs [ok, Civ V is a TBS]).

Frozen Synapse is a turn based strategy game where you utilize several different types of units to execute a variety of commands. Combat mechanics are based on: Direction, movement, cover, and weapon speed.
I have yet to figure out what type of creature I am… in the campaign mode, I’m under the impression that I’m an artificial intelligence named “Tactics”, whoever had the bright idea of making me an AI apparently need to be shot in the foot, because I proceeded to fail the next ten attempts at the campaign.
The campaign has a total of 55 missions, this game’s appeal is in its competitive aspect, think of this game as a “modern” chess game, although the objectives can be changed from simply “capture the king” to, capture the flag, team elimination, etc.
There are five basic units in the game: Machine Gun, Shotgun, Sniper, Grenade Launcher, and Rocket Launcher. Each have different abilities, for example the shot gunner can run fast and does is the fastest at weapon draw, while the Sniper is slow to shoot, but can shoot from almost across the whole map and moves very slowly.
As you get into the game the different units make more sense and you start to learn how to implement them accordingly. I practiced against the computer on campaign… which admittedly felt like bashing my face against a brick wall, but eventually strategies started to stick.

There are 16 achievements for this game, one of those achievements requires beating a player named “bin” who is apparently no longer playing… Ergo, this achievement is broken in my book. The rest of the achievements are very straight forward and require either winning a game mode, or doing something specific in the game.
The two hardest achievements are probably “get to level 100” and “Beat the campaign”. Hardest might be the wrong term though, maybe “the most time consuming”? Regardless, there is a fair amount of activity in this game if you’re going after achievements.
Frozen Synapse commonly goes on steam sales, so that is when I would suggest purchasing the game, at the time that I’m writing this review the game is actually 88% off for the next 43 hours. At the standard price of $24.99 that’s probably too high of a price for a strategy game like Frozen Synapse for most people, you can easily pump 20-40 hours into the game… again; if you already know you like strategy games and enjoy learning new ones.

Again to recap: the story/campaign wasn’t particularly intersecting for me, the game play is very precise (a requirement for strategy games), achievements are “meh”, the price is high unless on sale.
I’ve enjoyed playing this game, I would suggest it to people who *already know* they like strategy games. When you first jump into this game it’s definitely daunting to comprehend what’s going on. The game itself tries to help with a lack luster tutorial, but in the end it doesn’t prepare you for the cruel reality of “campaign”.
Amazingly addictive unique strategy game. Recommend for anyone curious in it!

I love it when a plan comes together, and Frozen Synapse is my favourite turn-based game.
It’s similar to ground operations of X-COM, for example, but in a purer, simpler form. There’s no base management, inventory, RPG elements. All units of the same type have identical stats. And, unlike X-COM, RNG does not make much of an impact on outcomes of firefights, if any. The typical ‘chance to hit’ mechanic is replaced with ‘time to hit’. If enemy unit is in cover, your unit will need more time to hit him; if enemy units runs into your stationary unit, your unit will shoot first because he had a bonus to this timer, and the enemy had a penalty for running. Thus, if you can predict what your opponent is about to do, you can be 100% sure what will happen when they encounter one of your units.
.
The best thing about this game is the ability to plot your opponent’s expected moves and run a simulation that will show what will happen if you do this, and they do that. You can run as many iterations of this as you like before submitting a turn.
In multiplayer FS becomes a game of psychology, misdirection, bluffs and double bluffs. You have to be able to make accurate predictions, but also behave unpredictably, be stealthy, feed misleading information to your foe. And make plans that account for every eventuality.
The maps are random and asymmetrical, but scoring takes this into account. Plus, you can use premade symmetrical maps or make your own. You can even play a flat version of cs_office if you’re so inclined.
There’s a long single player campaign with interesting missions and a cyberpunk-themed story. You can play it in coop, too. And it’s fairly hard. Only 0.6% of players have completed the campaign according to Steam achievement stats. But  two of the missions at the end are somewhat glitchy and many people may have quit just because of these.
I’m not too fond of the graphics. 3D perspective makes it hard to see whether you have line of sight sometimes, I would prefer to have a flat 2D mode. Thankfully, there’s a line of sight tool that works like a ruler. There’s no offline chat in multiplayer, which is disappointing for a game you can play via e-mail.
Red DLC adds shield units (really cool) and the ability to host co-op games and play single-player campaign with a friend, among other things. You can use the new features in multiplayer even if your opponent/partner doesn’t have the DLC. So I’d get the Complete Pack while it’s on −88% sale.
Edit: Co-op turned out to be pretty buggy. The share plan function tends to glitch out a lot.

Don't get fooled by the bad (almost non-existant) graphics. If you like turn-based tactical games, this game is definitely one of the best I've tried. It differs from other turn-based games in that this one has simultaneous turns, which means each side chooses its moves and then both are resolved at the same time. It's like pausing the game, selecting what your men should do, then unpausing, with the difference that you cannot pause again until the turn is finished, so if you screwed up, you can just watch your team die. This means you have to somehow "guess" what your opponent is going to do, which is not always obvious.
/
The gameplay is very good, with some options I only saw in this game, like waiting time and ignore enemies (the first 2 that pop in my head). Planning path and actions for your team is easy, but sometimes the paths overlap and it's a bit confusing in my opinion.
The difficulty curve for single player is ok, introducing the different classes in a good pace and allowing you to understand their pros and cons.

Cons:

Only a few game modes and a handful of maps. Some overpowered weapons and gear. With packs purchased through steam better equipment can be obtained early. Content which can only be unlocked via purchase. No actual expansions, maps, weapons, anything added for years. Not many players nowadays.
Overall, after more than 2 years of my purchase I still cannot play the game smoothly. The performance only slightly improved. It is a shame that good ideas were ruined by incompetent optimization.

Atlas Reactor is a unique, fresh game that delivers on simultaneous turn-based play. Excellent execution and high-level design carry this game into a real cult hit.
Positives:
* Depth is there in spades, as the guessing game/prediction/yomi factor keeps the game from ever being solved in a real way. This adds a ton on the tail end and really rewards your skill and ability to fake each other out.
* Character kits are well designed and surprisingly well-balanced.
* The game plays out in a good time frame, 20ish minutes, allowing it to be fit in easily
* F2P model is pretty fair, allowing you to earn stuff with time or cash
Cons:
* Comp in solo queue can be all over the place, and without healing or any CC pressure it's hard to feel you can win unless the enemy team is dumb.
* Some turns feel hopeless when all your cooldowns are down. It's not unfair, but feelsbad.png
Overall a great and fresh game worth anyone's time who has wanted turn-based multiplayer to work.

Greatest game I ever done did play. Allow me to bring you point by point through my experience with this game.
I clicked play to start and the game booted up. I was met with the soothing sounds of a microwave engaging in passioante love with a hair dryer and from that moment I knew I was in for the greatest gaming experience of my life.
I looked at the menu and saw listed in the order I saw them, New Game, Loading, and Continue. You read that right dear reader, Loading. In my haste to begin my thrilling journey I clicked New Game without even CONSIDERING the possibility of what clicking Loading may do.
I was spawned in a room, dimly lit and possibly housed within the♥♥♥♥♥♥of Optimus Prime. After taking in my surroundings I utilized my W key to walk forward. To my delight I did in fact move in a very forwardly direction just as I had expected to do. By utilizing my mouse I was able to look around and properly observe the grey-silver room I had found myself in. The sensitivity for the mouse felt too high so I pressed the escape button to pause the game and change the options, but alas there was no options menu. That is when it dawned on me that who was I to tell the game how sensitive the mouse should be? T'was the game who dictated things and I was not to impede upon their vision!
From there I walked through several rooms, connected by short hallways, until I reached a room with three doors in it. Naturally I pressed the E button on one of the doors but I found that only caused me to lean to the right while standing in front of the door. I sytematically pressed every button on my keyboard but none of them seemed to do anything. I tried this in front of every door and none of them opened. I soon discovered that there was a door on the far side of the room which required a key. Excited to embark on my new quest to find a key, I departed back the way I came.
I searched and I searched to the best of my abilities but I was unable to locate the mysterious key. I walked around for literally minutes unable to find the key I needed to progress. I thought to myself "Is this what the game means when it says it is hard as hell? It must be." It was in that moment I realized. There is no key. This was the ultimate test. The key was truly my sanity and that was a threshold I was refused to cross willingly. Confident in my victory over the game, I closed it and came to write this review.
Writing (and reading probably) this review was more fun that SECTOR and you should never play it.

I just started playing CK2 and cannot believe how much I've been missing over the years.  I love history. I love strategy games.  And I love roleplaying.  This game scratches every itch that I have as a result of those fascinations.  And it's the only game that I have ever played that can do that.

Admittedly, due to the extensive amount of information provided, it requires a good bit of imagination to keep up with the story - but the game comes in at just the right level of abstraction so that new things can happen every game.  Paradox clearly understands emergent gameplay - which so many modern developers fail to understand.
I own the vast majority of DLC and do not mind purchasing it.  If this keeps the game relevant and growing, then keep it coming.  I do not expect developers to work for me for free after I buy their initial product.  (Plus, many of the free patches added so much to the game by themselves.  Negative reviews seem to ignore this fact.)
Anyways, I've been gaming for over 30 years and have not encountered a phenomenon like CK2 before.
Count me in for as long as the developers keep pushing this wonderful game forward.

Uplink is a game that simulates being a hacker. It is novel and superficially well-done, but after I played for an hour or so, the novelty wore off and I was left with a lot of flawed and confusing game mechanics.
Pros:
+ Very immersive. The game does a nice job of making you feel like the main character. In fact, it almost feels like you are a real hacker at times.
+ Good sense of gradually building yourself up from scratch. There is a certain satisfaction in upgrading your programs and computers step by step.
Cons:
- A lot of aspects of the game are very poorly explained. Once you get through the basics, you have to look everything up on the internet because what the different hacking programs do and how/when to use them is very unclear. Several times I literally didn't know what I was supposed to be attempting in a mission.
- Poor mission variety makes the game very repetitive. Add to this the fact that a given mission can be completed exactly the same way every time you get it. Mission are fun the first one or two times you get each one, but then just become a chore.
- The game mechanics are very susceptible to tricks, loopholes, and exploits. This is the type of game that seems very hard until you figure out a couple of little tricks that make it painfully easy. Then it just becomes a repetitive grind of using the same tricks over and over. I'm honestly not sure if several of the techniques I used were the intended mechanics of the game or were game-breaking oversights.

Another thing about this game at rank 16 and higher is that you have to think to much about one movement , in the lower ranks , you just run at people and hit them while you're spinning around like a helicopter , that's pretty fun. This is a translated version of a Japanese deckbuilder/boardgame.   It's worth mentioning the translation work is of excellent quality, as well as the artwork from the original developers.   Overall finish is very high, which isn't always the case with Japanese game ports/exports.
Graphics: Sadly the graphics are simplistic 2D/iso only, but the gameplay doesn't require particularly involved graphics anyway.   It's mostly forgiveable because the artwork is decent, but you would really need to be a manga fan for that to overcome the limitations.
Technical: The game is polished and smooth, but neglects resolutions higher than 1200p.   The game engine is extremely simplistic because it's just a 2D cardgame.  This really feels a bit like a tablet port and doesn't really belong well on the PC platform.  A lot of the gameplay elements could have been done in flash - no real need for this to be a PC game, and certainly no justification for asking to be paid for it on Steam.
Gameplay: The core gameplay mechanic is pretty good, but fairly random, as it's a cross between Risk and a card game and a dicerolling boardgame.  Not really the kind of stuff that warrants a PC.   Unfortunately very little effort was put into providing justification for fighting the NPCs in the game, and the game modes are limited too, so it's hard to find any compelling reason to get into the game and stick with it.

Would be more fun if it were better balanced. Unfortunately new characters are nearly always OP, not simply because they change the meta but for literal overpoweredness. Lately I have been playing one of the OP characters but even I can't do much against someone playing Gnaw who knows what they're doing, Gnaw inevitably becomes the highest level 'naut in every game I play because not only is he an effective melee fighter, but he has huge poison attacks, a huge AOE poison attack that sticks around, and he drops turrets which can be upgraded to be really annoying, and they don't even reward you when you die 3 times to clear them out of a corner under or above a lane. The turrets also allow Gnaw to dominate the entire jungle, constantly killing the neutral creeps as soon as they spawn or distracting the jungle bosses (the jungle bosses can't attack around corners, so they just stand there uselessly trying to kill the turrets that are next to them), giving Gnaw constant money and health. In short, his build isn't even very difficult to put together, his attacks require very little skill, and if you know even a little about jungling then you will wreck every game if you play Gnaw.
My favorite character, Lonestar, was nerfed a while back and I find him utterly useless to play now. It is nearly impossible for me to get good kills with him unless someone else is setting up ganks for me. On his own, he is terrible now.
I appreciate tremendously that the devs are constantly trying to add new things, but expect to pay for each new character or expansion. It is certainly not expensive, I've dropped maybe 30 or 40 dollars on the game for many hours of gameplay and I don't buy a lot of skins.
The matchmaking system is also quite frustrating, because I get a lot of kills as Raelynn, my OP 'naut of choice, I get put with teams of complete newbies very frequently. Doesn't matter if I get more kills than everyone else in the game put together, having a team of people who don't even fight the enemy or don't observe obvious opportunities to gank will mean I lose nearly every game despite my tremendous lead in levels and damage output. Also if you go into Quick games, expect it to constantly put you in the same group of people over and over, and even the same games over and over after you've quit them. I've quit a lot of games, I'll admit, because I can't stand the people flaming, trolling, or playing horrendously, and when I click into matchmaking it puts me back in the same game. It seems to me like matchmaking needs just a few small tweaks and I would be a lot less unhappy. When matchmaking screws me I end up quitting, without any other choice, really. I have to wait for some of those people in my region to stop playing or diffuse into other groups of players in matchmaking so that I don't constantly end up with the same 3 jackasses.
If you are just getting into the game and you know even a little about jungling and stuttering from other MOBA titles then you will probably appreciate the simplified, arcade-style gameplay in Awesomenauts. Games are fast, you don't spend a long time doing nothing as in other MOBAs, there are even maps that force you into direct combat before the creeps even spawn. Character powers are all quite varied, and can be customized so that they do completely different things, and there are a few characters that have different modes where they do a completely different array of actions, allowing you to walk into battle a harrasser-pusher and walk out if it having murdered everyone as a tank with a DPS aura. The varied nature of the characters means that every game is different, different combinations of characters obviously work well together compared to others but a lot of the time you won't know what your allies are going to be until you're already in the game, so you'll often end up trying to get creative to win a game against some people with a good combination of, for example, an assassin, a tank and a puller-AOE who set up ganks you can't avoid unless you never walk in front of your tower. The loadouts you pick before a game can also vary widely, and you can even put completely opposed upgrades in there so that during the game you can buy the items that make sense for a situation rather than adhering to a strict build, and you'll still do fine against people with an OP build sometimes, because you chose to be flexible.
Lastly, this game appeals to people familiar with youth TV of the 80s and 90s, and videogames of the past 20 years. You will enjoy this game a lot more if you understand all the oneliners (there are probably hundreds) and recognize all the visual references. Some gaming personalities voice some of the characters so if you are into the gaming segment of Youtube you may enjoy playing as your favorite Youtuber. Personally I like Jesse Cox and Totalbiscuit as well as Dodger but I don't really like playing their characters, I end up playing that Yogscast guy, Lewis I guess, but his character's humor is up my alley anyway.
If you queue up with a team you may have a better experience. But expect a much more classic arcade form of MOBA, and in my opinion more fun and still with a high skill ceiling (though arguably not nearly as high as DOTA).

The concept of Frozen Synapse is pretty solid, but the gameplay has too many problems to be an enjoyable experience. The map and unit placements are randomly generated, and much like Solitare, the deck is often stacked against you in such a manner as to make it impossible to win no matter what you do. Losing units at the start of the first turn before they are able to act is commonplace. Furthermore, the units themselves often inexplicably fail to do what they are ordered. Rockets and grenades are often launched at trajectories different from what was input, while some units simply don't engage an enemy directly in front of them (and yes, "Engage on Sight" was selected). I have also had instances where a unit glitched against a wall and became stuck in place as cannon fodder. The tutorial was largely useless; I learned more through trial and error in a few randomly-generated skirmishes.
All-in-all, I really want to like Frozen Synapse, but the frustration from bad spawns and glitches outweighs any enjoyment in the end.

Sonic Mania is a 2D platformer made in the spirit of the old Sega Genesis (and one Sega CD) games. Kinda a celebration of what Sonic was and what people liked him for.
Before I start, I should state that I played all of the 2D Sonic games to death as a kid, including Sonic CD. I loved the games, although playing through them again recently I can say they have a number of flaws (especially Sonic CD, which has really bizarre level and boss design and the time travel mechanics were finicky at best). Still, really great games that stand the test of time, some more than others.
Now for Sonic Mania. First thing about it is that it looks gorgeous. All of the spites are amazingly detailed, with a wide variety of fluid animations. The levels are colorful and full with personality and life, and are a blast to explore and look through. This is all to an amazing soundtrack composed of remixed themes of old Sonic levels, and brand new tracks that fit perfectly. Absolutely top notch soundtrack.
The level design is for the most part top notch. Each of the levels (even the ones you grew up playing!) have interesting gimmicks and plenty of paths to explore. You can play the same level multiple times and find multiple ways to get to the end, and maybe find a few new secrets! Many times my first time through, I came relatively close to hitting the time limit just because there's so much to explore and look at. 'Course, there's also plenty of ways to speed through the levels if that's more your fancy.
There's one or two instances where the level design was chaotic and confusing, though, mostly near the end. The last level in particular neared Sonic CD levels of confusing.
Most of the enemies are variants of old foes you've seen in the original games, although there's some new, interesting foes to fight. The bosses in particular will surprise even veterans of the Sonic series, playing on old mechanics with brand new twists, or flat out being brand new. A number of bosses require you to think a bit more than just jumping into them 6/8 times.
However, there are a number of bosses that feel they take too long to beat, and a number that are flat out no fun and frustrating. I can name two bosses I absolutely hated fighting throughout the game...But that's a vast minority. I enjoyed most of the boss battles, and loved a good handful of them. Overall, a blast to fight!
The brand new Special Stage (which is found via the Sonic 3 method of exploring and finding hidden giant rings) took some time to grow on me, but I ended up loving it after I got the hang of it. And you will need to get the hang of it: It's difficult to control until you understand how it works and you'll find yourself running into spikes or into pits a lot until you get it. It took me around 6-7 attempts to get the second Special Stage (out of seven) down, but then I cleared the one after like nothing.
If there is a real complaint, it's that finding the Giant Rings is really hard. In Sonic 3 & Knuckles, you were given a few gimmes and some were just in plain sight, but in Sonic Mania, they are hidden in far areas of the map and you really gotta search for them in these huge levels. That's good in a way, but I would strongly suggest not to think you can get all the Chaos Emeralds your first run without a guide.
One other complaint is the prevalence of Blue Sphere, which makes a triumphant return from Sonic 3. Blue Sphere replaces the mini games from the checkpoint lampposts, and only requires 25 rings to activate. This means you will likely activate the Blue Sphere portal every single checkpoint you reach. This means a
of Blue Sphere.
It takes levels from Sonic 3, Sonic & Knuckles, and even the Sonic 1 + Sonic & Knuckles combination, and there are 32 levels in total. You can clear these to earn coins that unlock extras and secrets, but if you take the time to clear every single one of these stages, you really ruin the pacing of the game. I ended up ignoring Blue Sphere entirely after getting around 10 coins because I wanted to actually play the game.
I would have prefered Blue Sphere just being a separate game mode, and put back the mini games that give you powerups like in Sonic 3. There's just...Too much Blue Sphere.
Overall, I really enjoyed Sonic Mania, and I'm looking forward to repeat playthroughs with all the extras and other things included. I also will eventually take the time to get everything in Blue Sphere. Eventually.
I would recommend this beyond people with nostalgia. If you like 2D platformers, you're sure to love Sonic Mania even if you're not a Sonic fan. I give it a hearty recommendation despite it's slight flaws.
