Tree of life is an yet another survival crafting sandbox but I feel it manages to differentiate itself in a few ways that make for a more fun and interesting game.
The graphics are cartoony and certainly could be better but the art style is colorful and fun. I could see some people hoping for grittier graphics in game about surviving but it helps make everything a little more light-hearted.
The music is pleasant and the sound design is satisfying and effective at conveying things.
The skill progression system is a fun, though I think it could use some more info on the progression for crafting. The progression reminds me of Oblivion, where almost every action is tied to a skill and you raise them by performing the action. There is a limited supply of skill advancement that is allowed (at least that's what the in-game tool tips seem to suggest), so you do have to specialize at a point.
Chat is area/distance based and can make wandering through the world frightning, you may have no idea if anyone who can help you is near by. It was really fun stumbling on to a small village of players after barely escaping some zombies and finally be able to talk to someone. I've seen some people complaining about this and I know I wished I had some way to communicate with players that I'm not nearby when I wandered away and got lost.
The game is still rather early and it's hard to tell if some of the things I don't like are intentional or just things that will be improved but I'll mention them anyway. There is very little introduction/tutorializing, you get dropped into the game and have to try to survive with no weapons, armor and only a little food and a bandage to heal. There is no in-game explanation of controls, I had to find a guide in order to figure out how to eat. You get dropped into a random point as far as I can tell and because this is an MMO, you can get dropped in when it's pitch black and have to wander in the dark avoid the dangerous creatures that come out at night.

It's a good game for the price. The original price in US was 5$, and that was reduced to 3$ later. On a sale it becomes extremely cheap.
It's a solid top down shooter. Personally i love the aesthetic of halo, and i feel that this game done the franchise justice, but there are some drawbacks.
Most of them are related to the game being also released on mobile. First of all, the structure of the levels. Levels themselves are very short. Basically, there are 6 missions in the game, and each mission has 5 levels in it. That makes for 30 levels that can take anywhere from a minute to a maximum of 5 minutes (that's the longest it takes). Altogether it took me 3 hours to finish the game.
I feel that dividing the game into smaller levels wasn't right. The game has a very mobile feel to it as i said. The 3 star rating for every level for example. I feel that smaller levels is related to that.
The game also gives you XP for every level you complete. During the start of each level you can use that XP to buy yourself items. You have 2 weapon slots, and you can fit them with a sniper rifle for 500 XP, laser rifle for 750 XP, rocket launcher for 1000 XP. There are also other slots for boosters (damage modifiers, shield increase) and special abilities. And all that only lasts for that level. You have to rebuy that for the next level if you want to use it, and all this is very overpowered. I feel that this is where microtransactions were on mobile.
That said there is really no reason to buy all that, because the game is fairly easy, ouside of a few levels. You can make the game harder for yourself by adding "skulls" to the level. There is a skull that disables HUD, a skull that makes your shield drain when you shoot, etc. There are 6 skulls and you can add up to 2 to a level, and that will give you more XP at the end of the level. But again you are stuck in a loop, because XP is useless.
There are also problems with the mechanics of the shooter itself. First of all, the scorpion (tank) controls are really bad. It's ironic, cause there is another tank on the alien side that you can use. In that tank, you use the mouse for direction and W key for acceleration. In the scorpion, you control only the turret with the mouse. The body of the tank is controlled with WASD. It becomes very hard to control a tank because of that, and in a lot of cases you can actually get stuck.
Second of all, there is no turn rate. You instantaneously turn to any direction, and that catches the eye.
Also, there is no coop if you are wondering. The xbox versions have an extra mission that has coop, but it's exclusive unfortunately.
What can I say Halo is Halo.

This is legit one of the best games I've ever played hands down. The amazing scope of freedom is unbelievable because you can do literally anything in the game and not be punished for it or break it in anyway. The writing for this game is simply phenomenal from the main story, lore, and the fantastic origin characters. I can't get enough of the characters in this game from the origin characters to the ones you're supposed to dislike or meet on the journey, each one of them is simply written with such care. Graphically the game is very good looking with the isometric layout and the world design is stunning to look at times. Quests in this game have so many different branching paths and ways to do them. The game offers insane amounts of replayability to play with new classes, play with other origin characters, or simply playout the story in a completely different way. Honestly, it would take me hours upon hours to write why this game is the one of the best games I've ever played so I'll just do pros and cons.
Pros:
-Fantastic worldbuilding and graphics
-Incredible writing (characters, story, and lore)
-Freedom to do anything and not be punished (You can kill everyone you meet and still have an ending)
-Really well-done branching side quests
-Some of the best side characters I've had in a game in ages to have a journey with
-No handholding whatsoever which really lets you explore and flesh out your own story instead of being told how to do it.
-Really innovative and fun combat system
-Looting and dialogue in this game is brilliant
-A metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of content
Cons (very little)
-Some occasional bugs here and there (like quests not ending when you've done everything)
-Some annoying quality of life thing that are improved with workshop mods
-Not really a negative but since this doesn't handhold it can be quite intidimating to newer players, especially when learning the combat early on
-Unfortuntely, there are parts in the final act that feel a bit rushed but nothing too serious
Overall, this is a MUST play experience for fans of Crpg's or rpgs at all. It will simply be one of the best of its kind and I seriously can't stress how much positive more things I could've said. Like i said earlier, if I was going to go on about the positives of this game, I'd be writing a college essay of 10 pages so I hope you catch the drift. Backed by an amazing developer studio with such care given to this game, this is without a doubt worth 45 dollars and a steal at anything less then that. Hell, it's a steal already at full price. Must own experience!

This is a 4v4 team deathmatch – first team to five kills or the highest after twenty turns wins. Ties go into overtime, and can become very tense as both teams maneuver to get that last kill. Players each pick a character/freelancer from one of the three categories: firepower, frontline, support. Teams are limited to one of each freelancer (although both teams can have the same freelancer fighting against the other.)
Matches are played out with simultaneous moves for all players, which is where the strategy comes in – green actions go first (mostly heals), then yellow (mostly dashes), then red (mostly the main offensive abilities), and finally player movement. That means that using a yellow ability can get you out of the line of fire from enemies using red abilities; so you need to decide what the best time is to use your yellow dashes (which are usually on a long timer.)
The individual freelancers are well balanced against others of their class and to a lesser extent against each other. I’ve had games as a support or frontline ‘lancer where I managed to inflict more damage than anyone else on either team.
It’s a great game, and honestly my only complaint is that although they’ve been good about supplying us with new ‘lancers, they’ve only introduced a single new map in the entire time I’ve been playing. Some people complain about low player counts, but I’ve never needed to wait more than a minute and a half to find a game, and it’s been very, very unlikely for me to play with or against the same players in a row.
It's free, so give it a try!

This game is a whole lot of fun. If you are good at programming this game will still challenge you.
I will go in more detail:
The whole game is based around a little computer called the TIS-100 (Tessellated Intelligence System). The computer consists out of multiple little "Modules" that can each be programmed to do specific tasks. These modules can transfer data back and forth and can be used for simple calculations. This can be anything from adding, subtracting to harder tasks like multiplying numbers (which is way harder than you might think). Each of the modules only has 2 pieces of memory, the ACC and BAK memory. Each can be used to store one number from -999 to 999. BAK data cannot be accessed directly and can only be swapped with the ACC memory or copied from the ACC memory by using SAV. This makes the game very challenging because if you want to store 2 numbers you have to swap the ACC and BAK memory back and forth all the time or use multiple modules as storage. This system makes for some very interesting cheesy workarounds.
The puzzles in the game are pretty challenging, which is a good thing. At first you will have quite a learning curve for the first few puzzles trying to figure everything out. After a while it starts making sense and you have to start thinking of ways to use the least lines of code. The timing in some puzzles may also be slightly off, every module can only do one calculation per "step", this means that if you have multiple inputs this might cause a delay making the different inputs not align properly. This adds a big challenge which I do like a lot.
All in all, this game would probably get a solid 9/10 from me :D

This being one of the first RPG i ever played, it blew me away. This game is just so well put together that it leaves me to want a remaster or something of the sort. However, the game isnt without its flaws. Specifically, the combat can seem dull and repetitive if you play it with an aggro mindset, not bothering to avoid attacks and spam health potions. Another flaw for me personally is the difficulty setting. Finding the perfect sweetspot varies from character to character. Enemies will either become total wimps getting one shot by any attack or be absolute tanks that drain your resources to nothing. What i would more prefer is something along the lines of fallout 4's survival mode damage, where you and enemies both have increased killing potential. That aside, this game has characteristics that far outweigh the cons. My personal favorite being the music. This game's soundtrack, in my honest opinion, is amazing. I feel myself getting lost in the harps, flutes, and violins when wandering the various cities. Ominous music kicking in when i enter an unexplored cave. But who could forget the epic tones of the games title screen. Another great thing about this game are the secrets hidden throughout the landscape. Perhaps a bow or chest that you would have never stumbled upon in a first playthrough. Another topic i wanted to touch on is how you play this game. If you are the type of person that loves getting to the end fast and wants instant gratification, maybe this isnt your game. I think you have to be the observant type, listen to the dialogue, read the books, dont rush through every quest like you are in a hurry like so many others do. You miss out on the little nuances the game so delicately hides. You can appreciate the game on another level. Though this game is very outdated, i feel it gives the game a certain charm that few others have. It was the RPG that paved the way for future games of its genre, and look where we are now. These are just my thoughts on the game, the may not be true or subjective, but i hope i can convince someone to experience this game the way i have. Much love and thank you for reading.

Actually I've played this game plenty and I have plenty of thoughts, I'm not exactly sure what to say about the game.There are plenty of reviews that go over basic mechanics and there are many more reviews that are just poking fun at the inevitable random number generator and the luck that goes into such a game. Or something about pudding/Poppo and trying to be funny.
So I guess I'll be giving my thoughts on the ingame community and some of the things about this game that some players tend to overlook. If you have any other concerns about the game before purchasing it, you can message myself or other players in the forums if you can't find an answer.
I have never opened or participated in a private lobby in this game, lobbies can hold four players and up to four spectators. I mention this because there have been some concerns and complaints about too many private lobbies. It's true, this game from the outside, you can't imagine that this game being very popular or populated after a couple of weeks or so. 100% Orange Juice has players on everyday, whether they be some of the more dedicated players or a bunch of newer players. At certain times there can be a lack of players for a game, as you wait, or it might seem that there are only private lobbies. That's just the nature of having such a playerbase, there are players on at different time zones and it can be difficult to get a game started. However in a public game, you can join midgame if there is a spot open and the host is willing to let you join in. After I bought this game I would've been concerned about the game's population, but now I think the game holds a very niche playerbase that keeps itself alive. Also evidenced by the numerous updates the game gets and DLC, players start to flock back to the game if they go on an extended break. I would not be concerned about the lack of games, unlike Orange_Juice's other game on Steam 200% Mixed Juice, this game has plenty of replayablity and players. If you don't see that many games you may be playing at a bad time, like at 3AM somewhere.
This is only about my in-game experience, as I have barely ventured into the Steam forums for this game, but from a distance I can tell there are discussions about balance, changes, and answering questions. The players I have met through 100% Orange Juice have almost always been nice. I've played many online games, off and on Steam, but 100% Orange Juice has one of the nicest community of players. From players being playing around like complete idiots, some serious ones, quiet types. You guys have put a smile on my face and I can never get stressed out playing Orange Juice when I play with such players. I can count on one hand the number of players I have disliked, and I'm hoping it was just a bad day for them. Players are really helpful, I try to answer any question as a player/spectator, when someone asks a question. That's not to say there won't be games where no one types a sentence to anybody except for the endgame, "gg", I am guilty of this myself. Sometimes I can't find anything to talk about or I'm really tired. All in all, it's the players that makes me play this game over and over. You can play with your friends in a private lobby, if you purchase the 4 pack, and that's fine too.
That being said, I can see the stress test for some players. Being completely serious, not poking fun like some of the other reviews, this game can and will pull off some of the incrediously odds in situations even after playing the game so often, I still have to take a deep breath. If you are someone who might be turned off because you like strategy and don't like luck playing too much of a factor, just hold on. For some players this seems like luck plays such a big factor, I can't argue that. Over a couple of frustrating months, I've learned to cope with the bad luck. I'm pretty observant of the luck that goes against anybody, but I won't go off on anybody for taking me down. This game has literally taught me to accept misfortune and be stronger for it, to do better inspite of your bad luck. I usually poke fun at my own demise, if I have anything to say about an unfortunate luck.
In multiplayer, no matter how much strategy you think you have, luck will come into effect. Some players might have more experience/levels but anybody can beat anybody and that's a good thing. You are no better than any other player if you decide to win with a mob character or otherwise. If you are strictly looking for a strategy boardgame I would look elsewhere. That isn't to say there is no strategy in the game. There is plenty of strategy, that often gets overlooked amid the complaints of rolling the only number that would've gotten you knocked out. Choosing the right moment to play a card, to keep opponents guessing about cards, choosing paths, building a deck and many more.
But if you aren't put off by that, there might be a few more concerns. The pacing of the game comes in 4 speeds, (1,2,3,4). When I first played this game, I purchased this for 3 other friends and I created a room at 2/3 speed with just 1 other friend. I kept the room public, and someone joined the match (it's been a very long time I don't remember who you are), and they joined us. They mentioned not many players play at such a speed and wondered why, I told the person that we were new and had almost little to no experience with any of the cards and effects. We were helped along, and after a few hours I played strictly on speed 4. To newer players this may seem very intimidating, especially if a lobby goes along smoothly, playing cards quickly and paying attention to the game (and not occupying their 60 seconds with something else). After my first hundred hours I sometimes wonder if the game could be just
. I enjoy how quickly games can go though, the longest game I've ever played was an hour+ with the worst field events on a map that punished every player for coming close to a base. On average games can last around 20-30 minutes, though I have had stretches where games end in 10 minutes or so.
If you are just getting started, you may want to familiarize yourself with the game through single player. 100% Orange Juice has been updated to give another difficulty option which I haven't bothered to touch, but the single player experience as evidenced by many other reviewers, can be very unforgiving. It's unfortunate that you need to play through single player just to unlock the rest of the characters, outside of the mobs/boss characters. Though I guess it's a way to get players to know the characters and some cards. The story is throwaway for the most part, it's cute, but don't look for intense character building, deep story etc.
Over time, you start developing a better understanding of the mechanics of the game. There are a lot of different interactions that can happen, and other players can help you along the way if you're new. Just ask, it's press enter for the text box, if you didn't know in lobbies. Field events keep every game different and chaos can happen very quickly.
A lot of players like the music and themes the characters are given, Personally I like the themes, but after my 200th hour, I muted the game, to put my own music on. I do on occasion like to put the music back on at times, which can be accessed through options.
Would I recommend this game? Yes, I want to play with so many other players. Every time I login to Orange Juice, I play with 1 new face at least. I'd avoid this game if you are, again, strictly looking for a hardcore strategy boardgame or a RPG type boardgame. I've always wished there was another boardgame like Dokapon Kingdom, but this is a great casual game  that I've enjoyed for the past 2 years. Even if you are just getting into the Orange Juice series of games, this would be one of the better ones to start with, as there's plenty of replayability.

TL;DR: This game has a ton of potential but needs some serious work. My recommendation is to wait at least a couple of months.
I don't believe I can recommend this product at this time. Perhaps, after a couple more months of patching and refining, I will be able to change my rating, but there is a lot to be done before then. Let me be perfectly honest here, I enjoyed this game thoroughly, for a while, at least. The following is my specific tale in this game so far:
The beginning of my play through started with me wandering one of the starter isles in the pitch black of night, bumping into murderously slap-happy zombies and skeletons. Armed only with my karate pokes of justice, I quickly learned that fleeing was the best strategy. One of my friends soon arrived on a stolen bull with a saddle and soon led me to a nearby encampment where i could steal one for myself. Now riding our trusty beeves, we rode off into the wilds looking for this base my friend assured me was safe for us.
We crossed many different terrains on our way to the promised lands, from mesas to geyser fields to forests to crevasses, the land certainly wasn't the same looking for very long. It is at this time that I encountered the first of many bugs: My friend started randomly and rapidly taking damage whilst riding his trusty mobile steak platform and soon died. He dropped all of his stuff and became a spooky ghosty. This was no big deal at that moment because there was no one else around to steal any of his stuff so he quickly repossessed his now slightly used corpse and we continued on our journey.
We finally reached the base after about 45 minutes of travelling in circles and around hills, mostly because my friend relied on his memory to guide us instead of the coordinates he had copied down. They welcomed us fully into their guild and we had a place to rest at last. We quickly started working for our keep in our own ways: I was a tree puncher and log hauler, while my friend worked on his tinkering and rapidly became the resident Batman, what with his useful gadgets that he whipped out like locks for houses and lanterns.
Night descends rapidly and rather frequently in this game, and it gets dark. As my least favorite Pyromancer in Game of Thrones says: "The Night is dark and full of Terrors." Zombies and skeletons are attracted to settlements and bases; the larger the base, the more they attack and it wasn't long before houses started to collapse from the undead onslaught. We would fight off the invaders as best we could, but the night is so dark and the torches so nearly useless at actually illuminating the surrounding area, we were usually too late to save anything.
Now there is a way to repair in this game, but that brings us to a significant problem in this game: Very poorly translated tool tips that offer no real insight into what an item does. Now, some items are rather self-explanatory, fishing rods allow the catching of fish and swords are for filleting the creatures of the night, but others are just a mystery. For example, hostile mobs drop bronze coins. These coins are not used for a currency system or bartering. Instead, you take these coins and place them on a damaged building and then just hammer them into the side of it. This has the magical effect of repairing the building... somehow. The description on the coins did not point to this, indeed, the only thing I could make out about them is that they "have goblin face" on them. Another hilarious mistranslation would be the lumber mill. I believe that it is called the "Snow-Shredder." Because wood chips fall like snowflakes I suppose?
And then there is the raiding aspect of the game. At this point in time, I see no reason to do much in the way of hard work when you can either steal all you need, or just have your stuff stolen. Yes there are locks in the game, however you can also pick those locks. If your big stuff like cabins or walls gets destroyed, you have a 24 hour grace period to repair it before it disappears, but most of the planning buildings and tables don't get this grace period and are flat out destroyed. People can parkour over walls and steal stuff inside the encampment, including mounts. You can also loot while mounted and be impossible to stop, since you cannot fight on the back of a mount and the only way to catch someone on a mount is to be mounted yourself, so you are kind of at an impasse, except the other guy has all your stuff.
Things like this kill the fun factor of this game for me. Why should I work hard at something when the next time I log on, my fields have been torched and all my livestock butchered? When our walls are dust and our resources drained?
If you are a marauder, this will probably be a dream game for you. Rapid, unpredictable attacks on resource rich areas on the back of meals on wheels will make you the richest in the land, until someone steals that from you in turn.
I suppose, what I'm finally getting at is this: This game has some amazing potential and I am prepared to love it to death, if only it gets more polish on it, someone hires a proper translator, and a serious look is taken at the crime system.

So, first off. This game has its issues, but it's pretty fantastic. The game is a bit grindy, seeing as it's Korean in origin, that didn't surprise me right off the bat. What did surprise me was an incredible early access game, that has had me playing for nearly 6-7+ hours a day since the minute I added it to my Steam Library. The game, at first glance, seems typical of most survival type early access games currently on the market, and you would think the only difference is it's choice in art style, well.. that's not quite the case. This game, is relatively similar to other survival games (ie. DEALBREAKER ALERT: Game uses Denovo and hid it until after launch.
Sonic Mania is pretty much everything that made the original Genesis/CD classics great 25 years ago distilled into one bombastic celebration of a game. Unlike Sonic Generations and Sonic 4, Mania is incredibly accurate to the original controls and physics of Classic Sonic and even improving them in some ways. There are are certainly a few missteps, but overall this is the best Sonic game to come out in ages if you enjoyed any part of the originals. Unlike some Sonic Team titles of late, Mania knows what kind of game it wants to be and absolutely nails it.
+Physics, controls, and gameplay are on point.
+lovely art and fluid animations.
+Level design vastly improved and expanded from the originals. Levels are big and sprawling.
+The music is up there with the best of Sonic. Especially the new level tracks.
+The New levels are the highlight. Old Levels take on a lot of elements that make them entirely fresh.
+Bosses are mostly great and a big step up from the classics.
+Special stages are the most fun in the series.
+super replayable with 3 characters, massive levels with tons of routes, unlockables, speedrunning, etc.
-Denovo. Certainly a dealbreaker for many.
-Not enough new levels. While the old levels are heavily remixed and are great, the highlights are the new stages.
-Bugs. There are certainly quite a few. Nothing major, but they exist
-Bonus stages: Blue Spheres, are neat to see again, but offer no in stage bonus and once you clear them there is no point to them.
-Some instances of unfair hazard placement/boss design.. They feel more like oversights than design choices.
-Big levels means stopping to smell the roses can punish you with a time over death. I feel this old mechanic could be done away with.
Overall, unless Denovo is a dealbreaker, I would heavily recommend the game to platformer enthusiast, Sonic fans, or anyone who likes a well crafted retro platformer.  Keep in mind to get the most out of the game, you need to replay it a few times with different characters in order to play all the stages and bosses.

After years and years of poor or mediocre Sonic games (apart from a few such as Generations) Sega finally released a TRUE sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles. From the fantastic animation, great colour palette, superb music and a well thought out choice of levels, this game has everything an old school Sonic fan could want.
Throughout this review I'll try not to give away too many spoilers and if I mention things from Sonic Mania I will only be dealing with early on in the game parts.
My favourite element of the game is how they implemented the original zones into this game. By giving Act 1 the style and play of the original zone with tweaks to the layouts, sort of combining both the original acts in one, it gives players of the original games a hit of nostalgia without making it too easy if you've played the original games. In Act 2 though, they expertly included new elements - both level design and new gimmicks to use that make the zones feel completely new and exciting while retaining the nostalgia hit in the process.
I was particularly happy to see so many small "you'll know it if you've played it" nods to the fans in this game. For instance enemies from old zones appear in different zones but they didn't just throw them in there, they thought carefully about which enemies would suit the particular zone. For example, the Catakiller, Jr.'s in Chemical Plant Zone - an enemy that didn't appear in the original zone but works well within it. Also there's a certain boss that will be familiar to those who played one of the more obscure Sonic titles - Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine (Spoiler:
).
Sound design is on point too, the new soundtrack for the levels is fantastic, sounding new but familiar. If you play the older Sonic games in the 2D series and then play this game, the music and sound captures the old Yamaha YM2612 sound chip sound but it goes beyond that, giving crisp clear sound effects, higher quality voice samples etc. The audio in this game truly pays homage to the series.
The unlockable content is terrific too. By playing through the Blue Sphere Bonus Stage and clearing it (with or without collecting all the rings) you'll start unlocking new extras like Debug Mode etc. I appreciate the fact that the unlocks are earned rather than purely given with unlock codes. While I love the old codes from the Sonic series (well apart from the hard-to-time Sonic 3 level select code) I really do enjoy that to get the bonus features you've got to do something for them. It adds a bit of replay value to the game and what you unlock actually adds to the playable content of the game rather than just being some art or a video.
Boss and level design wise, this game has an appropriate difficulty level curve, making the later zones challenging enough that you get a real sense of accomplishment while not making you want to rage quit (too much). I wanted to keep playing till I finally beat the game.
In terms of series evolution, this game does a terrific job improving on original concepts and implementing new ones. It feels very much like the incremental increase that we would have seen had Sega put out a new 2D Sonic game on the Sega Saturn or 32X. This game really does feel like it should be considered part of the original set of 2D Sonic games from the Mega Drive/Genesis era.
There are so many great things about this game and I really appreciate the level of detail in the graphics, gameplay and sound. It truly is the Sonic game that fans of the series from the Mega Drive/Genesis have been waiting for since Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
If you like smooth animation, toe tapping music, enough nostalgia that makes you feel like this is a real Sonic game but not too much that you feel like you're retreading the past too much, then this game is for you.
I definitely recommend this game and hope that the talented developers (Christian Whitehead, Headcannon and PagodaWest Games) get to create another 2D Sonic title in the future.

I am amazed how this has any good reviews.
The standard product is buying the game twice, so you can give it to a friend. Really it looks like it's trying to justify charging 23 bucks for a single sale.
Aside from all other critical thoughts I also had the displeasure of graphical and gameplay bugs in the first 2 hours of simple campaign play.
The game is paradoxical in almost every aspect:
It is a turn based game,
yet ultimately actions are done timebased.
It puts very little effort in the story telling,
yet it drowns the player in expositional dossiers, conversations and monologues. Luckily you can skip them all.
You need to micromanage and possibly run simulations of every nanosecond,
yet the choices you can make are very simple and gameplay lacks any depth.
Machine gunners are the "bread and butter" unit you control very precisely,
yet their aim is so horrendous that engagements outside of shotgun range feel completely luckbased.
Waist high objects give cover,
yet standing on the corner of a wall does not give sideways cover.
Standing behind waist-high cover is an advantage,
yet ducking(so you fit below waist-high cover) has no effect aside from hiding behind cover.
I mentioned gameplay lacking depth, let me go into more detail on that.
Your mindless drones have no inventory and never need to reload. You can not change weaponry, the drones you use or how they are distributed on the map at the start of a singleplayer mission.
The options available are wait, move, aim, duck, ignore all enemies, ignore a specific enemy and prioritze a specific enemy and reversals of these commands.
That's it.
If your guys are in♥♥♥♥♥♥positions, your enemy has to make a mistake. Your drones can not have more than object in their hands. So unless that object is a grenade thrower or rocket launcher, the only feasible "strategies" are
1. to be in a good position and aim, motionless, at the correct angle.
2. move, preferrably without line of sight, to a better position and do 1.
3. exploit positioning mistakes of the stupid AI and shoot them in the back. If even possible. If not possible, do 1.
If a drone is standing still and an opposed drone comes around the corner, both having the same weapon, equal cover and given all appropriate commands(aim at that direction, focus specific enemy), then the drone that stood still will always win.
There is no time to outmaneuver the enemy drone with your own drone in a single turn, either. Rewarding inaction with 100% chance to win an encounter is atrocious game design.
The graphical bug I encountered seceral times was hatched green neon lines connecting my selected units with my other units for no apparent reason
The gameplay bug I encountered after a particularly long processing time for the first turn, including 2 prompts to kill the program, because it didnt respond.
It changed a unit of mine from a sniper to a machine gunner. While no other downsides, it was an annoyance.
The music was nice, I guess.
In summary, a shallow and unresponsive tactical game that requires huge amounts of micromanaging miniscule movements.
It feels like playing counterstrike without grenades from the top down perspective, which is entirely the wrong perspective for that kind of gameplay and also lacks grenades.
Would not recommend.

Crusader Kings II is one of those hit-or-miss games. It will miss with 95% of the population. Hell... you probably only have this game because of a deal, received it for free, or purchased it in a bundle.
Amongst strategy lovers, 75% of you guys will consider it a miss. But... for those of you who are as stubborn as myself, this game will suck you right in.
Before we continue any further... I have attempted to play Crusader Kings II almost 5 times before I actually enjoyed it. I quit 5 times out of frustration and simply not getting this game. If you love strategy, you must keep trying. Once I did understand the complex mechanics, I fell in love... just not with my first wife Matilda that I may or may not have simply used for an alliance with the Duke of Flanders. If you're reading this... sorry dear...
My highest recommendation for beginners, start off at the bookmarked game and play as William the Conquerer. If he still holds the title, William the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you're a little behind. Move up a few months.
Playing as William the Conqueror definitely helped my learning. And once you get a feel, you'll want to play as one of the Kings of Spain. Poor King Sancho dies, leaving his kingdom divided amongst his 3 sons. They are respectively the Kings of Galicia, Leon, and Castile. Will you be the youngest King of Galicia, who struggles with his Portugese Duke who plots to overthrow him? Or the middle King of Leon, the plotter with high intrigue that holds the support of his two sisters and his mother in his realm... Or perhaps the brave King of Castile who has under him the legendary El Cid, the greatest military mind of his time.
Now, let's backtrack for a moment...
Crusader Kings II has an in-sane amount of roleplaying involved. There are even fantasy elements that are added with some DLCs that come about, some of which let you fall in love with a horse, seduce your sister, eat your vassal, sacrifice virgins to God, or blind and castrate your own father. If that's not good enough, create your own character and dynasty and destroy history as we know it.
Now here's a little example of something I normally do in a normal gameplay. Almost all my playthroughs, I hated the Holy Roman Empire. Solution? They give the pope a million reasons to hate them. Get enough money, piety, prestige, and the pope can grant you an invasion right. Net the right alliances, and you can storm into claim the Holy Roman Empire for your own. But suddenly expanding so massively will only get me overthrown... so why did I bother taking it? Simple. I destroy the title and grant everyone independence and watch all hell break loose in a nation that's magically divided into 100 country-states.
Now, that being said, Crusader Kings touches base with a variety of religions, cultures, different ethnicities, and government. There are many playstyles and no one way to go about winning. You may become the Emperor of a grand Empire, such as the Holy Roman Empire, or be a starting Count that aspires to become a Duke or even overthrow the King... If those don't work, become a Republic state and work on building your house and fleet to make money as the more notable factions of Venice or Milan.
With so many elements to this game, you may expand your influences and become Emperor through some basic means of marriage, alliances, marrying off your children and siblings, fabricating claims and fighting for claims. You can grow your power through military might and expand one county at a time. You may also save up and focus on wealth, expanding your land toward finances and heavy taxes, and putting that hard-earned gold to good use... and by good use... obviously we mean to kidnapping, assassinations of enemies, buying the pope's love, buying your liege's affection, heck, buying everyone's affection so that they may support you and elect you to becoming the new ruler. Oh... right... did I mention you could also just do the kidnapping, assassinations, and various other ploys yourself, start factions against your lord, and simply screw up anyone at your leisure? And if that isn't your thing... be pious and be with the Pope, and he will surely grant you invasion rights, which then may be called to action through alliances and simply declaring war. If that doesn't tickle your fancy, you could be the master of diplomacy, and let the people who love and support you do the plotting for you.
As a ruler, you will come across many random events that determine the path your kingdom and your character goes.
As a summary, Crusader Kings II is a must-play for strategy lovers, history lovers, roleplay lovers, and peoplewhosecretlylovedoingevilthings-lovers. You and I both know that you will all end up either castrating your own brother or sacrificing virgins somewhere along the line...
Crusader Kings II is the gateway to heaven and hell with immense replay value, amazing roleplaying elements, and most important of all... sleeping with your brother's wife and letting your brother raise your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child.
Did I mention you get to name your kids and any land you own...?

I got so frustrated at this game, that I developed a splitting headache by the end of my playthrough.  I played about 2 hours over the course of yesterday and today.  I played as much as I could complete and as much as I could stand.  Let's get into some details.
The gameplay is pretty generic, almost boring at times.  It feels slow and sluggish, even though you can "run".  The enemies in this game are much too difficult for this kind of game; they're sparse, but they're too accurate and too powerful.  I think the reason is because the developers didn't know how to make proper enemy AI that's neither overpowering nor simple-minded.
The gun selection is standard for a game like this.  Most of the weapons were pretty tough to use because most of them were pretty ineffectual.  The shotgun was the only weapon that was decent.  However, there are a lot of problems with the gun mechanics.  For example, there's a delay with switching guns.  Also, you can only switch guns while standing still.  However, I think the biggest problem is the ability to remove your ammo.  This function has no purpose, at least in the part of the game I played.  I don't know if this is a mechanic for another part of the game or a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥mechanic the developers never finished or even implemented.  All I know is that it's a completely useless "feature".  On a side note, everytime I would restart the game and reload my save, I would find a couple of ammo clips that reloaded near dead enemies.  I didn't complain, since I needed all of the ammo I could get, but in a good game, this would be considered a flaw in its coding.
Most of the controls were fine.  However, this isn't without its problems, either.  Some of the controls felt sticky and unresponsive.  Also, you don't have the ability to customize your controls.  Sometimes, this is fine, but for a game like this, I expect an option for custom controls.
The graphics weren't that bad.  Actually, the game looked alright.  The textures reminded me of Quake 2, which is a much better game than this.  Of course, this game can't go without problems in every department.  The texture and color choices for many parts of the game were abysmal.  Making the keys and floors a similar texture and color didn't help me get through the levels.  It also didn't help that the lighting only worked properly some of the time.  However, the models looked pretty good.  In fact, some of the design choices were aesthetically pleasing.  This game also had moving skeletons, which is always a plus.
I haven't even talked about the worst part of this game: the level design.  Starting a new game or a saved game was pretty simple.  Getting there took a seemingly inordinate amount of time.  When the game finally loaded, what did I get?  Floating guns, walls that I could go through, missing ceilings, etc.  It's not like this game was loading a lot of assets.  The levels are insultingly basic: boxes strung together by hallways.  This is amateur stuff.  Sure, there were a couple of halfway decent designs, like a stairway that wrapped around the room, but this design is thrown out the window when you have a stairway that's not complete and stops short of where you need to go.  This actually happened.  I couldn't complete this game because of this major design flaw.  It was such a tease.  It's as if the developers didn't test this game and wanted to♥♥♥♥♥♥it out of their asses as quickly as possible, so that they could get money as quickly as possible.  Doors in this game worked only if their properties were loaded in correctly.  At one point in the game, I thought you had to jump onto a chair and glitch through the ceiling in order to progress.  It turns out, there was a key hidden behind a couple of computer console assets in a space I thought you couldn't get through.  The only way to get this key is by accidently walking over to this area and grabbing the key.  Actually, I think that's how I got every single key in this game: by sheer luck and by total accident.  What a load of ♥♥♥♥ing garbage.  Getting lost in this game is probably what compounded the headache I got while playing this stupid game.
The physics in this game were pretty much♥♥♥♥♥♥  Everything wants to stick to the nearest surface, as if everything is made of ♥♥♥♥ing magnets.  Quake 2 had better physics than this game, and that was from 1997.  The difference is that Quake 2 was made by people who actually gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about their product.
The best thing about this game is probably the sound.  The ambiance was pretty chilling.  It reminded me of Quake 2.  Do you get the idea yet?  This game seems like it ripped off Quake 2, but did a really♥♥♥♥♥♥job at it.  The music that played in the background was decent, but it took me out of what little immersion this game put me into.  In other words, it was kinda out of place.  One thing that bothered me a lot was with the iron sights of the guns.  For example, when I used the iron sights for the water gun toy (the laser pistol), I would hear a mechanical moving sound.  Why?  Unless I'm a robot or unless there's a groan tube in my gun, that noise shouldn't be made.  This little tidbit sounds like me nitpicking, but it was something that bothered me.  In fact, it bothered me more than a lot of the other problems in this game.
This was a terrible game and a boring experience.  This is an ambitious first game that someone would post on IndieDB for FREE.  This isn't something you would expect people to pay 5 ♥♥♥♥ING DOLLARS FOR.  Luckily, much like the Grinch, the developers developed a heart and made this game free about a month before the writing of this review.  However, this doesn't justify the lack of quality put into this piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥
This is reccommended only to people who have a thing for♥♥♥♥♥♥games, just like how there are people who have a thing for♥♥♥♥♥♥movies.  Also, a final word to the developers: if you're going to have multiple save spaces for your game, test your game and make sure you can complete it with the least amount of problems as possible.  Shadow Warrior (1997) was a game where you likely had to use multiple save states for the extra tricky parts.  The difference is that Shadow Warrior was a classic, whereas this game was complete drivel and utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

SECTOR is apparently a FPS game that was released in mid 2015 from the folks at UD and published by Airys Software. After enjoying some hate and low sales, as well as publishers not being able to contact developers for some reason, it went Free To Play at early 2016. At least from what I understand. It was a game that got through Steam Greenlight and from what I heard uses FPS Creator engine and some assets. Well, that sure isn't a good start.
Technically, it's pure awfulness. No options. Never save while forced to crouch. You will get stuck. It will crash on loading. Keep few saves, sometimes you die by loading some savepoints. And look, this game is a glitch, so.
Upon learning that this game had only 9 levels, I started my quest by launching the game. Immeditly I was thrown into main menu, which had only New Game, Loading and Quit Game. No Options. Ever. Some ambient generator sound that looped horribly was playing. I clicked New Game and was thrown into first level. No plot. No music. No explanations. Dark. This world is dead. Level 1.
After walking through two big rooms, last one having skeleton resting against pipe, I picked up key without noticing it by just wandering around. As I would later find out, keys in general are black tiny pieces of turd that are almost impossible to see with the Doom-3-made-awful lighting that this game has. They are sure to be pain to find. After that, opening door with ENTER, I picked up pistol and in next big room I got to fight a single enemy.
Where I found out that combat in this game sucks. Your movement is clunky, the weapons are clunky, enemies are 100% accurate hitscan shooters who just charge at you. And they are clunky. And have no painstates. It's as primitive and unfun as it gets. There also was random NPC who had enemy skin on him, just standing there and shaking head in disbilief.
On level 2, having solved the puzzle-thing and crawling through the overly long shaft because staring at wall texture for minute is fun, I got out into room, with new sucky weapons. There were more enemies, shooting and skeletons. This is where I found out that you can lean around with Q and E. Or more exactly that most enemies don't awake if you lean around corner and shoot them, which is the way I beat most of the game without pain.
Until I went to level 3 and game crashed there. Sighing, I reloaded my save and sighed again, as I found myself outside of level geometry with no way in. Never save in shafts.
Level 3 was funky. One of the soldiers didn't attack me and instead yelled at my something like a commander when I came close. He was too adorable to shoot at in this dead world. I didn't find key, but I found place where I managed to activate switch through the wall. Or ceiling. I don't know by now. By the end of level I found a skeleton. Mr. Skeleton got tired of acting dead in this game. He was standing and chilling like NPC, his favourite drink was placed on a pipe nearby. Even he didn't care about this game anymore. He was drunk.
I don't remember where, but in level 3 or 4 I found shotgun. It's the only good weapon because it either kills instantly or at least knocks them back, stunning for a bit. It's also the only weapon where iron sight works, as it tightens the arc at which pellet spread up, defying the real life logic.
Level 4 had rooms with open ceiling, you could see the sky there. But it was grey, flat and the base was as dark as ever even under the sky. The whole universe was dead and had no soul. There was a room with BSOD computer, broom. It was room with open ceiling too, with useless air shaft nearby. I also saw stairs that I couldn't reach above. As it would later turn out, devs wanted me to build stairs out of wooden boxes, but I already destroyed them all. Never destroy boxes, they hold nothing. Thankfully, engine's player movement sucked and I was able to get there by ramming and jumping nearby fence.
Level 5 had water. And green light. And no one to listen to your whines. This is where I researched and found a way to grab boxes in FPS Creator engine. Right mouse click works, but you have to "pull away" weapon by pressing same slot number. Weapon will remain, but it will show "0/0" ammo. If you don't do it, then you can still hold the objects but game will glitch out and you will not be able to switch weapons. One reviewer said that it's impossible to get out from water. But with my experience of awful game, I bet on the awful player physics again and succeed by placing three boxes in corner of a room and spammed the jump button while ramming them.
Level 6 and level 7 mixed around in my memory. There was nothing good to talk about. Or nothing special. My brain already wants to block this. But I think that there was lab theme and skeletons. In one of them there was a shaft almost-maze section. And one of the side dead ends there had a skeleton with red lamp between his lovely legs. Upon recognising my buddy, I went to check if he has something and I got pushed on top of level geometry of the shaft by his collision. Thanks again, Mr Skeleton.
Level 8 was hospital-lab themed. There was a real human corpse on a single sit. Wandering more, I found a corridor. It wasn't textured like sci-fi. Instead it was more like a dungeon. I had a bad feeling about it. In next turn there was torture room, as evidenced by torture chair, human corpses hanging off the ceiling and skeleton in corner. I grabbed key, wondering what the game might show next, if it could go horribly wrong. A teleporter was awaiting me at the end of a level.
In best tradition of creepypasta, level 9 loading crashed. Maybe it wanted to keep me away from the horrible secret of the final level. But my curiousity got the best of me as I loaded it once again.
There was something behind me.
Yep, there certanly were two boxes stacked on top of each other behind me. It was both a sign and a warning.
And indeed, I kept meeting the boxes. And once I came to the big room it became clear that developers intented me to build boxes stairs to reach the second floor. Thankfully, I had experience of awful glitchy games and did it only with three boxes, placing two of them on top of climbable shelf thing.
Well, bolloks!
The door needed key.
After going down and finding key, I was less lucky at using same exploitish stairs, requiring me to do 30 loads of saved game as I kept ramming into boxes instead of jumping straight onto them.
After that there was no horror hidden futher. Just same corridors with new boring base textures. More enemies. At the end there was the last room. It had a sci-fi pedestal thing and there was spherical artifact placed on it. Neat asset. Was it the reward for our quest? I grabbed the item. Nothing happened. Then I went futher and the door in the middle turned out to be the exit.
There was a single splash screen with "Game Completed" message. Background was just another futurustic wall, no skeletons. As soundtrack you had another, even more awful generator sound.
Well, it sure was just like "classic hardcore shooter" as promised store page. Exactly how I remember Doom and Quake.
Now that I placed the order in that world, it's my turn to leave this game along with Mr Skeleton.
Or don't know, I beat the game so I could write this masterwreck. Read this and stuff this cashgrab game somewhere deep. It's awful. Thanks, Steam Greenlight.

Im put in a tough spot reviewing this because it's a really good RPG and the team obviously has come a LONG way since the older games (even Original Sin 1.) One one hand I think the game has glaring flaws that is keeping it from achieving true greatness but on the other, games are so bad now overrun with F2P trashware that it's hard to compare to anything else since there is no modern competition that cares as much about the end-product. I felt this way about Original Sin 1 as well, that it was kind of a oddball niche product that was at the same time incredible and even perfect in some aspects, amazing production yet very obtuse and weak in scope. Overhyped and yet simulntaneously somehow underrated at the same time. It's almost like they get credit for all the wrong things and are given no credit for the monumental feats that they achieved which go completely unsung.
I will try to outline my gripes and positives:
PROS:
-Amazing score, very memorable and serious soundtrack which is often underrated in importance for a game that tries to create an epic saga in a larger epic.
-Some awesome memorable fights that truly feel like you are part of a greater conflict of gods and demons, rather than incessantly pandering to the player and making it about you. Fights are messy, brutal, chaotic and unforgiving as they should be in a medieval setting of strong beings fighting against netherworld monstrosities, rather than sterile monotone and mechanical like in a JRPG for example.
-This game treats the player like an adult and expects you to read and have intelligence which is a nice change of pace from AAA titles like the Witcher that assume the player is a toddler and is aimed at toddlers.
-Old school rpg players will appreciate almost to a degree of guilty pleasure how easily you can become uber-god powerful and make the toughest bosses into a joke with even the most rudamentary amount of knowledge, the game really goes all the way with making you feel like a god in combat if you earn it and it's a pleasure to watch unintelligent players on streams and such to suffer through the easiest challenges and really sets a boundry between "divine" game masters and clownshoe plebs.
-Great to see that while slowly, they are putting a lot of work into fleshing out the world and making it more like a proper rpg setting rather than a Diablo-esque dungeon crawl with a tactical facade, which Original Sin 1 for example may seem like after player this game. There is a ton of atmosphere npcs, even enemies that have something to say or try to sway you to join them, even talking animals.
-Nice gritty, realistic dark euro-classical fantasy setting rather than the usual bubblegum anime fantasy that is so common these days. The drab world of Skyrim for example looks like a saturday morning cartoon compared to the brutal gory shades of gray world of Original Sin 2.
-Good graphics and very detailed enviornments, it's almost shocking to compare this game to screenshots of something like Divine Divinity. It doesn't even look like the same series.
-No bs DLC, 150$ for a game, this is a full fledged product and it is on a fairly short list of modern games that I did not regret paying for in any capacity.
------------------------------
CONS
-There is definitely some dated obtuse puzzles and UI/inventory quirks that existed in Original Sin 1 that are still present, for all the game does to focus on a feeling of old school gaming, there is plenty out of date mechanics and ideas it could let go of.
-Some bugs, I did notice more crashes especially 200 hours in and when installing some mods on a second play through, it becomes more and more noticeable (I skipped or didnt understand this quest at first, but second time I can see it's just bugged or whatever, things like that.) The engine I suppose is more fragile than it seems. There is an overall some lack of polish in spots, less like actual game flaws but things they simply didnt have time to finish. (For example there is a crypt that is actually labelled "Unfinished Tomb" or something of that sort. This could be perhaps the developers poking fun at modern AAA publishes releasing unfinished games, but at the same time they are somewhat guilty of this themselves, so the parts of dialogue branches or quests that seem unfinished or abrupt, may just simply be unfinished.) It's not nearly as pronounced as some reviews of this game will have you think, but it's very real.
-Turn based in general can be hard to get into for some, one thing is for sure this game will not convince you if you are on that side of the fence. It has it's specific demographic dead center in it's crosshairs and casualising the fundamental aspects would be a detrement overall. I can see how some people will at best suffer through it, but at the same time they are kind of deadlocked in their own design of how the game is.
-I really dislike the attempts at real time or platform elements within the rigid turn-based system, it's less common but it's still an annoyance. It's the Metal Gear Solid syndrome of a game using one engine trying to squeeze another type of gameplay that doesnt belong and the result is basically a bad version of that. Bad real time combat (like attacking enemies from stealth, let me pause and attack, its a turn based game,) or the teleportation puzzles. Original Sin 1 had actual puzzles related to teleportation pyramids, here it just feels like a holdover that at best sits in your inventory and at worst sequence breaks the event system in unintended ways. The source gathering mechanic is another example that falls in here, because the indended design is obviously to force you to use AP to restore your "Super Mana" to balance out your Super Abilities in combat, but out of combat it's a finnicky chore and you have to sit through the animation of each character individually (instead of every member gathering at the same time out of combat for example) because it's a turn based engine and a mechanic like that doesnt quite fit.

------------------------------
MIXED FEELINGS
-Story and writing. One one hand the writing itself is decent and sound, but the overall story is fairly standard and uninteresting/unengaging. I don't know why reviews are praising the story in this game, I guess the reviewers grew up under parents who never read a book and thought Final Fantasy VII had good writing, and it is just a game so the bar is really low. The quality of writing and the details in the writing of the side quests is actually higher than almost any game you see nowadays, but I just cant give them points for this because the grand epic is fairly disconnected from the core gameplay or immediate player decision so I have to put it under mixed. The pacing and phases of the story and progression is often very jarry, abrupt and confusing, which has an appeal of its own for immersion or roleplaying (a human at the mercy of greater powers perpetually confused,) but I dont know if it really adds to the whole. It's obviously not the intended effect and the story is supposed to be simple and clear, or maybe not, that kind of highlights the issue that there is a tone clash or something going on.
------------------------------
I think thats about it, I went on long enough, probably could say a lot more. Overall it's a very impressive entry, leagues better than Original Sin 1 which was already great and certainly nothing comes close to this on the market. Divinity Original Sin 2 comes to us from a time machine from a world where developers actually care about the product they are creating, hire actual artists and competent programmers and still have faith in PC gaming. A shining beacon of light in our post-apocalyptic wasteland of F2P mobile machine-generated/copy pasted anime trash and "indie pixel games" by people too lazy to do art and were not born yet when pixel graphics were common.
MUSIC A+
GAMEPLAY B+
STORY B-
DEPTH A
ART/GRAPHIC A
OVERALL A-

I'm not sure about this game.
Actually I've played this game plenty and I have plenty of thoughts, I'm not exactly sure what to say about the game.There are plenty of reviews that go over basic mechanics and there are many more reviews that are just poking fun at the inevitable random number generator and the luck that goes into such a game. Or something about pudding/Poppo and trying to be funny.
So I guess I'll be giving my thoughts on the ingame community and some of the things about this game that some players tend to overlook. If you have any other concerns about the game before purchasing it, you can message myself or other players in the forums if you can't find an answer.
I have never opened or participated in a private lobby in this game, lobbies can hold four players and up to four spectators. I mention this because there have been some concerns and complaints about too many private lobbies. It's true, this game from the outside, you can't imagine that this game being very popular or populated after a couple of weeks or so. 100% Orange Juice has players on everyday, whether they be some of the more dedicated players or a bunch of newer players. At certain times there can be a lack of players for a game, as you wait, or it might seem that there are only private lobbies. That's just the nature of having such a playerbase, there are players on at different time zones and it can be difficult to get a game started. However in a public game, you can join midgame if there is a spot open and the host is willing to let you join in. After I bought this game I would've been concerned about the game's population, but now I think the game holds a very niche playerbase that keeps itself alive. Also evidenced by the numerous updates the game gets and DLC, players start to flock back to the game if they go on an extended break. I would not be concerned about the lack of games, unlike Orange_Juice's other game on Steam 200% Mixed Juice, this game has plenty of replayablity and players. If you don't see that many games you may be playing at a bad time, like at 3AM somewhere.
This is only about my in-game experience, as I have barely ventured into the Steam forums for this game, but from a distance I can tell there are discussions about balance, changes, and answering questions. The players I have met through 100% Orange Juice have almost always been nice. I've played many online games, off and on Steam, but 100% Orange Juice has one of the nicest community of players. From players being playing around like complete idiots, some serious ones, quiet types. You guys have put a smile on my face and I can never get stressed out playing Orange Juice when I play with such players. I can count on one hand the number of players I have disliked, and I'm hoping it was just a bad day for them. Players are really helpful, I try to answer any question as a player/spectator, when someone asks a question. That's not to say there won't be games where no one types a sentence to anybody except for the endgame, "gg", I am guilty of this myself. Sometimes I can't find anything to talk about or I'm really tired. All in all, it's the players that makes me play this game over and over. You can play with your friends in a private lobby, if you purchase the 4 pack, and that's fine too.
That being said, I can see the stress test for some players. Being completely serious, not poking fun like some of the other reviews, this game can and will pull off some of the incrediously odds in situations even after playing the game so often, I still have to take a deep breath. If you are someone who might be turned off because you like strategy and don't like luck playing too much of a factor, just hold on. For some players this seems like luck plays such a big factor, I can't argue that. Over a couple of frustrating months, I've learned to cope with the bad luck. I'm pretty observant of the luck that goes against anybody, but I won't go off on anybody for taking me down. This game has literally taught me to accept misfortune and be stronger for it, to do better inspite of your bad luck. I usually poke fun at my own demise, if I have anything to say about an unfortunate luck.
In multiplayer, no matter how much strategy you think you have, luck will come into effect. Some players might have more experience/levels but anybody can beat anybody and that's a good thing. You are no better than any other player if you decide to win with a mob character or otherwise. If you are strictly looking for a strategy boardgame I would look elsewhere. That isn't to say there is no strategy in the game. There is plenty of strategy, that often gets overlooked amid the complaints of rolling the only number that would've gotten you knocked out. Choosing the right moment to play a card, to keep opponents guessing about cards, choosing paths, building a deck and many more.
But if you aren't put off by that, there might be a few more concerns. The pacing of the game comes in 4 speeds, (1,2,3,4). When I first played this game, I purchased this for 3 other friends and I created a room at 2/3 speed with just 1 other friend. I kept the room public, and someone joined the match (it's been a very long time I don't remember who you are), and they joined us. They mentioned not many players play at such a speed and wondered why, I told the person that we were new and had almost little to no experience with any of the cards and effects. We were helped along, and after a few hours I played strictly on speed 4. To newer players this may seem very intimidating, especially if a lobby goes along smoothly, playing cards quickly and paying attention to the game (and not occupying their 60 seconds with something else). After my first hundred hours I sometimes wonder if the game could be just
. I enjoy how quickly games can go though, the longest game I've ever played was an hour+ with the worst field events on a map that punished every player for coming close to a base. On average games can last around 20-30 minutes, though I have had stretches where games end in 10 minutes or so.
If you are just getting started, you may want to familiarize yourself with the game through single player. 100% Orange Juice has been updated to give another difficulty option which I haven't bothered to touch, but the single player experience as evidenced by many other reviewers, can be very unforgiving. It's unfortunate that you need to play through single player just to unlock the rest of the characters, outside of the mobs/boss characters. Though I guess it's a way to get players to know the characters and some cards. The story is throwaway for the most part, it's cute, but don't look for intense character building, deep story etc.
Over time, you start developing a better understanding of the mechanics of the game. There are a lot of different interactions that can happen, and other players can help you along the way if you're new. Just ask, it's press enter for the text box, if you didn't know in lobbies. Field events keep every game different and chaos can happen very quickly.
A lot of players like the music and themes the characters are given, Personally I like the themes, but after my 200th hour, I muted the game, to put my own music on. I do on occasion like to put the music back on at times, which can be accessed through options.
Would I recommend this game? Yes, I want to play with so many other players. Every time I login to Orange Juice, I play with 1 new face at least. I'd avoid this game if you are, again, strictly looking for a hardcore strategy boardgame or a RPG type boardgame. I've always wished there was another boardgame like Dokapon Kingdom, but this is a great casual game  that I've enjoyed for the past 2 years. Even if you are just getting into the Orange Juice series of games, this would be one of the better ones to start with, as there's plenty of replayability.

When Sonic Mania was announced, I had only ever played the original games for the Genesis. The last Sonic game I completed was Sonic 3+Knuckles back in...1995 maybe. I remember really enjoying those games as a kid, so I thought I'd give this one a shot, since it looked like a fun piece of nostalgia.
It is very nostalgic, but also new. 8 of the zones are from the original games, and each one is remixed to varying degrees. They usually will start out identical to the originals, but by the second act things start to change. New mechanics (like the bouncy goo in Chemical Plant) are introduced, the enemy placements and the layout start to change, and by the end of the second act it's a completely different level from what you remember.
There are also 4 new zones, which have the roller coaster layout from the originals (large and somewhat non-linear, like in Sonic 3 and Knuckles), and offer enough varying mechanics and challenges to stay on par with the original games.
The story is told through short scenes with no dialogue, and the only purpose they serve is to explain how Sonic and Tails move on to the next zone. This game focuses on the gameplay, which I prefer.
My only complaint about the game would probably be that it wasn't all new zones. This complaint is very small, as the remixing of the old levels makes them somewhat new.
I think this is a great game for people who enjoyed the original Sonic games, but were turned off by what the series became after the Genesis era.

I will say for the record that the Denuvo DRM is pretty scummy, regardless of who decided to put it on or how it was implimented. However, I give my thumbs up on the merits of the game itself, not the DRM. If you're a Sonic fan or a fan of platformers in general, you don't own a Switch, PS4, or Xbox One, and you don't care about the Denuvo DRM, I recommend Sonic Mania. It perfect in every way. However, if you do care about the DRM, I recommend either waiting for an eventual patch-out of it, get a non-DRM version that likely exists by now, or simply get it on any current gen console you own. Whatever the case, you won't regret it!
A lot of passion went into making this game and it shows. The devs deserve all the praise they can get. This is momentum physics based 2D platforming at it's best and I highly recommend it.

Aside from the two-week delay and the apparent Denuvo problems (I was able to play in offline mode anyways), I'll provide a substantive review.
First off, I thought the game was great, and for me, it lived up to the hype. I've played Sonic for what seems like forever now, and this truly felt like a sequel to Sonic 3 and Knuckles.
There is quite a bit of new material placed on top of the obviously recycled material. This can be found in revamped levels (no act of the same zone is identical) as well as the entirely new zones like Studiopolis Zone. There are plenty of new gimmicks, Badniks, and bosses that will almost definitely give you nostalgia while simultaneously keeping you excited and entertained as you progress through the game.
The level designs are fun and creative, and they certainly prove wrong yet again those who claim that Sonic games are beaten by "holding right and waiting." The special stages are reminiscent of previous games', yet they are completely new, and for me at least, they are fun.
There are also checkpoint Blue Sphere stages from S3&K that incorporate both old stages and new ones, and completing these unlock some cool features both in game and in a separate extras menu. I won't divulge what they unlock here, but I thought they were good unlockables (some better than others).
Aside from these points, I thought the story of the game was pretty interesting. Again, it's not like modern Sonic games with voice actors and such, but rather, you pick up the plot by various mini-cutscenes involving your character sprites--much like other classic Sonic games. There is a bit of rising difficulty as the game goes on, but it doesn't ever get too tough (or hard at all for a seasoned player).
There aren't many cons for the actual gameplay. I played the Switch version and was bombarded with various glitches, but I haven't encountered them on my playthrough of the PC version yet. Though, I did have a slight audio problem in game at one point after getting successive lives in some level. One thing I will say is that there are far more recycled levels than new levels, so if you're coming into this thinking it's going to be completely new material, think again.
The competitive mode is pretty useless on PC if you just have a singular keyboard to play it on. There's no online play as far as I can tell.

To say it in short: I love this game!
To say a bit more: It is a tactical turn based game where the turns are prepared simultaneously by the players. This game can be played online and offline, against the AI in skirmish mode or in a campaign as well as against other players from around the world. It can be nailbiting while you watch the outcome and realize all your awesome and unbeatable planning goes down the toilet as your opponent does exactly what you didn't think of. And on the other hand, the feeling is great when you watch your plan unfold and you stomp the opponent into the ground. But the best thing is, if things go awry and you lose, you always know it had nothing to do with luck but all with the mistakes you did. It is a bit like chess where you have to plan your moves into the future and adapt to the strategies of your opponent.
The units you (can) use range from machinegunners, to shotguns, rocket launcher and grenades to snipers and riot shilds. There are also differnt types of scenarios such as rescue hostages, secure a specific area or just plain extermination to name only a few.
The most important thing about this game is that you cannot just rush in and shoot blindly. You have to use a tactical approach and plan your moves carefully. Your units don't have many hitpoints as in classical shooters. One hit and they are dead biomass. Buildings and covers can be destroyed by rockets. So depending on the units there might be not a save spot to just sit and wait.
Another nice aspect of this game is, that you don't need to be permanently online. You can plan your moves offline. And soon as the turn result is there, you get notified of it and can prepare the next turn. So even for casual players who don't have much time, this is a good game to spend a few minutes for your turn and upload it.
I really hope this game gets more attention as it surly deserves it. The grafics in Tron style and the nice soundtrack are really catchy. Very nice is also, that when you buy a game, you also get a second one to send to a friend.
So would i recommend the game? Yes, definitely!

This is an early access game and nowhere near finished.  Fair enough.  The devs are promising more ships, missions, career mode and possibly free roam.
However, the game needs some very fundamental changes to the core.  The graphics are very amateurish and, in the case of the scenes at port where one is trying to choose a mission, the whole thing looks like something from the 1990's.  The NPC's look like something a child would create, the colours are all wrong and are too vibrant.  The port area is excrutiating to look at.
The ships exteriors are not too bad, but utter rubbish compared with European Ship Simulator (ESS) which this game is supposed to be replacing!  The bridges are nowhere near as good as ESS either and equally lacking in any interactivity with most of the controls not working.  The UI controls are too small and are tricky to grab with the mouse, especially the throttles.  The sea is not as good as ESS either and the water breaking over the bow looks rather like a poorly done snow storm.  The background pictures on the horizon are very poor as well.  It is nice that you can walk out of the bridge and around the ship, but why would you want to as there is nothing as yet to do, though this could be changed in the future as could interactive radio comms with the port authorities and other ships or interactive fully detailed bridge controls.  More ports are also promised.
However, I fear that all such improvements will come to nought if the devs do not do something drastic to change the quality of the graphics.  Ship sims, like non-combat flight sims should be all about beauty and something to behold.  If the graphics are not improved at least to the standard of say, ESS or Silent Hunter 5, then this game is going to be a flop.
Personally, I would dearly love to see this game developed to the standard of FSX with a full world to roam about (or time skip if the distances are too far on a particular voyage).  fully interactive bridges, interactive comms with ports and other ships.  Radio traffic from other ships and, like FSX, a system in place where other publishers can produce high quality detailed accurate real world ships and ports as addons whilst paying a percentage towards this game's publishers/devs.
However, such developments may eventually be achieved, but are pointless unless the graphics, colours, textures and animations are not significantly improved.  I will soldier on with this game and will be happy to revise this review in the future if things improve.
Update 11/12/17 - The Devs have abandoned this game without making any improvements.  It is utter rubbish.  DO NOT BUY.  YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.
