Hi! I may not recommend the game, but that doesn't necessarily mean it's a bad one.
The animation for one is absolutely gorgeous, as is the art direction. I also liked the lighthearted story before my gamepad died on me (gamepad required, so, wasn't able to experience more). However...As well made as various segments are, none of them felt cohesive during my time with the game and I didn't end up really enjoying more than a part here or there. Let me explain:
In Harold, you play as a guardian angel in training. You're at top of your class but through some cruel twist of fate, in the final exam needed to become a guardian, you're assigned to protect/guide a lovable klutz named Harold through a series of races. It's a simple, innocent story that provides a nice framework for your job of zapping Harold to make him go faster and launching opponents into pits of spikes.
Actual gameplay consists of going through a level a number of times in several modes. The first is "Practice" and can not be skipped. Ostensibly, you're supposed to be learning how to best navigate the actual race to come by making Harold collect stars in bite-sized stages. However by the time you're fifteen or twenty stages in you want to simply get things over with and it begins to feel like unnecessary padding.
After getting through Practice, you can enter "Race" mode (the meat of the game). In this, you attempt to, again, help Harold get through the level as efficiently as possible. This time, though, you also have to make sure Harold places third in a race against opponents more fit and smart than our reluctant hero. You do this by affecting his environment (bridges, platforms, obstacles, etc.) and "encouraging" him with bolts of lightning gained by using "Puff Power." You also directly control the timing of Harold's jumps. This is where the gamepad-based controls and animation come into play.
You always feel like you both 1) Never have enough control and 2) Have too much. This seems contradictory, but in practice this feeling dominated my time with the game. Every obstacle and platform, etc. can be used both to help Harold and hinder his opponents. So, despite Harold's sedate pace, you're constantly in a state of information overload unless relying on rote memorization based on constant failure.
You can't point at an object and affect it with a mouse--you have to use the triggers to switch between objects, and the analog stick to conduct whatever changes you will. However, in the midst of the lavish animation, the cues for what object you're affecting can get lost. Even as early as the second stage, that one lapsed second of attention can mean failure and a trip back to the starting line. The animation and focus on beautiful artwork also affect collision accuracy in a number of ways--a case of game design fitting art, rather than the other way around.
My typical thought process during a race:
"Okay, a pit. Need to move it so that dude falls in and Harold gets across. Just swing across the gap and..."
*Death*
"...Shoot. It LOOKED like I'd make that jump. Wait, why am I controlling his jumps and not just the environment?"
*Death*
"Dang, got distracted. Okay, encourage, encourage..."
*Death*
"Man, I was moving too fast and couldn't put down the bridge fast enough. Okay, what if I move slower and take out my opponent before going across myself..."
*Death*
"Wasn't able to move the bridge back correctly in time. Okay, what if I..."
*Death*
"Too fast."
*Death*
"Too slow."
*Death*
"Couldn't see."
*Death*
"Got confused."
*Death*
"Mistimed jump"
*Death*
"Mistimed environmental change."
*Death*
"Wrong."
*Death*
"Wrong again."
*Death*
*Death*
*Death*
You can get used to this over time and enjoy the game, sure. As I said, it's not necessarily bad, and there is significant content here including another mode focused on moving through an entire level perfectly, but without the pressure of opponents to race against. However, in a time where we're left with too many games and too little time to play them, to have to dig and dig for that kernel of fun is disappointing.

Harold is a very challenging, action-packed, platformer running/racing game which is currently available through Early Access on Steam. You take control of a guardian angel in training and you have to watch over Harold, the underdog of the competition, as he takes part in practices, races and challenges while making sure he stays ahead of the competition. Taking place across 12 stages you must first complete a practice mode where you familiarise yourself with the stage, then you take part in a race against five other competitors each controlled by another angel in training and after the race you can take part in an incredibly difficult challenge mode where you have to run the whole course without dying while collecting stars.
+Absolutely beautiful design, in particular the background scenery
+A very likeable main character (Harold) who is also well designed, as are the other competitors
+Despite only having 12 stages the different game modes, and the difficulty of the game, Harold provides hours of entertainment

+Entertaining cartoon style cutscenes
+Great humour, I laughed out loud a fair few times while playing
+Wonderful voice acting
+Interaction with the level itself is well thought out, fun and at times challenging
+You only need to finish in third place to unlock the next event which makes it great for all players
+Each stage introduces a new mechanic/obstacle
+Great animation
+Great soundtrack
+Very nice special effects
+/-You fail a lot in this game, personally I enjoyed retrying certain sections until I got it just right but some people may find it irritating, it really just depends on how much failing numerous times bothers you
-It doesn't have keyboard and mouse controls so the only way to play is with a controller which seems strange for a PC only game
-The controls for interacting with the environment are quite difficult to get used to in my opinion

Gabriel is a bit of a prankster and a jerk, but he’s also the best Angel at Guardian school. Everything comes naturally to Gabriel, so he doesn't even have to study for his tests. He’s basically been gliding his way through school without a single problem. That all changed when he learned that his final exam involves protecting humans in a series of races. As a lesson to Gabriel for being a bit too confident in his training, he is tasked with guarding a rather clumsy human named, Harold. Now Gabriel must help Harold place third in every race or he won’t obtain his scholarship to Archangel Academy.
High Points
Fun Story – Gabe is a brash and confident Angel-in-Training trying to get his wings. Saraphel Malakh has a rich family history to live up to, but she’s not in the same league as the rest of her family. She watches Gabe earning his accolades and gets bitten by the green eyed monster. Needless to say, watching the both of them come to terms with their own failings is worth helping the uncoordinated, Harold.
Great Animation – The cinematics are flash animated but they boast a nice art style and a Saturday morning cartoon aesthetics. The animations during the gameplay are astounding to say the least. It is fun to watch Harold go full sonic the hedgehog, or be wowed by the smooth transition of one of the many boost cinematics during a race. The backgrounds could be a bit more dynamic, but the shifting level scheme more than makes up for it.
Awesome Soundtrack – The music during a race escalates depending on what place Harold is in during the race. Since this game is all about heavenly miracles the music is filled with the gospel sung by a choir. As Harold advances in a race the hymn will begin and start a song about his exploits.
Hard And Fun – Harold is an endless runner with a few tricks up its sleeve. As a god like being you control the environment around Harold and his fellow racers. You’ll move objects so that he can continue at his pace, and strike down lightning with FURIOUS anger to bring out his inner speedster. It’s a challenging process to keep him dashing at optimal speed, and also sabotage his opponents by moving platforms out of their way.
That’s probably the best part of the game, sabotaging the other angel’s racers by trapping them or pulling the rug out from under their feet. Every stage is based on remembering where to jump, or what to move in a certain stage. This gradually makes the platforming more difficult as Harold proceeds through the various races. Like a game of Rock Band - you’ll have a chance to practice areas of the course so that Harold can move through it faster. The game is layered with alternate course routes and constant boosts to keep Harold moving act optimal speed. It’s a ton of fun if you get used to the control scheme.
Average Points
Controller Support Only – It makes sense that the game needs controller support, but only because some of the controls require rotations. I feel like some concessions could have been made for the keyboard crowd. Maybe changing the rotations to simple up and down movements with the keyboard.
Low Points
Convoluted Controls – Since Harold is a game about basically recalling every piece of a level. It’s weird that the controls are all over the place. Instead of a simple structure to dash, the player has to tap the top buttons on the controller. Flick the trigger buttons to change between platform sections, pull back and push forward to break items, or do the same to pull bridges. There is actually more to learn as the stages progress, but that’s a lot to memorize while sabotaging other humans and watching Harold.
Conclusion
Harold is a fun plat-former that clumsily steps on its own shoes with weird controls. If you’re into puzzle platforming you will have a blast directing Harold in and out of danger. Everyone else who isn't into punishingly difficult games based off memory and precision… well you’re just going to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot. If you do ever get used to the controls this can be a fantastic game for practicing speed running. I recommend you wait for a sale on Harold. It features splendid graphics but for a game that requires precision timing, it doesn't have a particularly functional control scheme.

This alone should determine whether or not this will be your type of game, if you're a fan of competitive PvP and Turn-based strategy games, then this game is for you. Its gameplay is unique and is similar
to games such as XCOM and SPACE HULK.
The main focus of the game is to eliminate as many opponents as possible before 20 turns have been made. Any team that scores their 5th kill, will win the match prematurely. However, should both teams score their 5th kill on the same round, or the 20 turn mark is hit and both teams have the same amount of kills, the game will go into Sudden Death. In Sudden Death, the team that scores the next kill, without losing one of their own, wins!
In conclusion, Atlas Reactor is an extremely fun and addictive game. However, bare in mind I am a fan on Strategy games, as well as competitive PvP games, therefore my review is semi-bias and is heavily opinionative.

Of the three TES games released on the Gamebryo/Creation Engine so far, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is the most well-rounded. The gameplay can be described as "one step forward, one step back" as not everything survived the transition from its predecessor. Judgment on whether the additions are a net positive will come down to each individual player familiar with the series.
TES4 also chooses a more traditional fantasy setting for its province as opposed to the imaginative, exotic land of Vvardenfell that was featured in TES3. Enemy types also seem more generic as a result. This is corrected in the Shivering Isles expansion where nothing is constrained by preestablished lore, allowing the developers to implement their wildest creations.
While it doesn't have the same depth in its lore and world-building as TES3, TES4's presentation and incredible questlines make it a contender for being the best in the series. With more modern gameplay mechanics and visuals, it's admittedly also one of the best starting points in the series for newcomers.

You know what makes chess the ultimate strategy game that has lasted for thousands of years? Its simplicity.
Frozen Synapse takes the turn-based strategy game genre to an extreme level of meticulousness. This is saying something in a genre that already resembles something like chess with more rules.
I am a long-time fan of turn-based strategy games, with the X-Com iterations holding a special place in my heart (well just the first two and the remake actually), so I am no stranger to intricate control over characters and exhaustive planning for each turn. However, there are two questions that must be answered in the affirmative for any TBS game to be considered "good":
First, are the controls efficient?
Second, is the game fun?
Unfortunately, Frozen Synapse fails on both accounts. The painstaking level of control over every minute movement of your troops is maddening and superfluous. You are the most anal-retentive military commander in all of history, and while the game provides a reasonable explanation for it, your troops are apparently mindless drones. Simply adding more controls over every little movement does not make a TBS game superior to others. Extraneous controls weaken a strategy game's enjoyability by obstructing its very purpose: strategy. Very often, you will find yourself losing rounds/games because you forgot to set a drone to look in a specific direction or to duck at the right moment, or walk quickly/slowly. Not because you didn't realize that those moves were necessary, no, because you FORGOT. There are so many options to set for each individual unit, that you can easily spend an hour just setting up a SINGLE TURN. I am not exaggerating, the multiplayer gives opponents a week to post their turn! This kind of burdening complexity removes the players ability to strategize and gives advantage to the player who is most able to memorize details. Strategy is about out-thinking your opponent's moves and countering them, or recovering from a weaker position with superior tactics, NOT micro-managing the user-interface.
So is it fun? Well, Frozen Synapse insists on you monitoring every sniffle and cough your troops make, so the majority of the time playing this game is spent staring at a screen of unmoving drones and identical walls, running simulation after simulation to determine the highest likely method of success. It would be just as fun to compare tax audits to determine which IRS agent was the most efficient!
Speaking of identical walls, the graphical quality of this game is terrible. I have never before claimed to need high quality graphics in a game, in fact in many ways the fight for ever greater graphics is ruining the industry, but if ever there was a game that needed better graphical design: this is it. The neon colors that honestly looked cool in the trailers and screencaps are horrendous to look at after only ten hours or so of gameplay. Every character looks the same, every wall is identical, you are a robot commander of a robot army killing other robots for no reason whatsoever.
Some of the positive reviews said the game was "easy to get into, but hard to master," and this is an outright lie. This game is hard to get into and hard to master. I will say it again: strategy games require simple controls so the only thing between you and victory is your tactics. Not fun.

Everything about Spartan Assault is mediocre. Spartan Assault is a tech demo designed to show off touchscreen Windows devices. As a result, the controls feel clunky when using a controller, maps are short and easy, and the game lacks replayability. If it weren’t for the Halo I.P., Spartan Assault would be neglected in favor of indie games like Helldivers or Assault Android Cactus.
Spartan Assault’s biggest sin is its tedium. The game’s missions are short set pieces that feel too long. The actual missions are extraordinarily short. Each mission doesn’t take more than ten or fifteen minutes to complete yet they feel longer. The game lacks variety. You’re usually just defending something (i.e. killing a few waves of enemies while protecting some dopes) or killing groups of enemies which is the same as defending except you only have to worry about yourself dying.
The enemies are standard Halo fare, however they’re a lot less intimidating this time around. Elites seem confused and somewhat stupid. They generally run around aimlessly, shoot and miss, or try to melee you which is the only threat you face. They’re easy to troll. One of the few times I had fun playing this game was when I spent a mission trying to bait Elites into smacking me only so I could dodge and smack them instead. This is what Spartan Assault reduced me to. The other major threat is the spam of Grunts suiciding into you and your squad with plasma grenades. Aiming with a controller is ludicrously hard at times both due to the insensitivity of movement as well as the fact that none of Halo’s weapons work well in a twin stick shooter setting. Melee is the only useful weapon. Even the Elites seemed to have realized that.
Spartan Assault is incredibly easy lest you enable Skulls. Skulls, just like in previous games, are basically mutators that can make enemies harder or remove your H.U.D. Spartan Assault’s Skulls aren’t fun. You don’t have exploding corpses, grenade spam, enemies who all wield heavy weapons, et cetera. Instead 343 bestows only the most obvious of Skulls such as the aforementioned enemy buff. The Skulls add a layer of artificial difficulty without making the game more fun. The worst part is that obtaining the best scores for achievements and the like is impossible without Skulls. I’ve stopped caring.
Oh, and Spartan Assault doesn’t even have co-op. The mass of Spartan Assault’s sales were in hopes of a true Halo F.P.S. port. Do yourselves a favor by buying a better game like Helldivers.

Tree of Life is a lighthearted survival game. It challenges the player to either make trustworthy friends to cooperate with, or go it alone with all the dangers of having no one to watch your back. Yes, there are raiders; some demand tribute, some just want anything not tied down to the ground, and some kill and destroy for fun -- but it doesn't rule your experience. You can store, lock up things, and repair easily. On the whole, if you're willing to be friendly and interact, life will reward you with the little awesome things that can happen between players.
As for PvE, there's an autotargeting system (the green outline) that lets you lock on, which is especially helpful for hitting monsters that look like they're running all over the place - or sheep who won't stay still! Gathering food, leathers, straps, ore, etc. is all exciting for me in particular because I get to have my home base, but am encouraged to travel the continent for different items I need. This spurs interactions, sometimes some stiff situations I have to talk myself out of. Sometimes I meet a nice person building a campfire and I stop to chat. The mapping of resources keeps players circulating.
This game is in Alpha. The developers are doing their best to find a nice balance for players from both walks of life: PvE and PvP. They read the discussion boards and suggestions and try to implement/try new things to see if they can please the farmers, the grinders, the tree choppers, and the raiders.
I don't suggest you play it if you're easily bothered by other players and their actions because
. I highly suggest working with a friend, at least in the beginning while you're working to raise skills and such. I split the work with a friend and it made life WAY easier - as far as I could read from other peoples' comments and complaints.

This is a little gem from 1997 and it's a really awesome and unique 3D first person action / RTS hybrid. I originally played the demo when I was growing up, which only had 2 maps (this version has 20), but the game was that good and innovative that I must have played those maps dozens of times each!
Major con: This game likes to crash. A lot. And if memory serves this was true in 1997 as well. I mean seriously, how did they ever release it like this? As a programmer I know that memory corruption bugs can be damn hard to track down, but jeez! Just make sure you save fairly often (at the very least after every mission) and you won't lose too much progress. Mostly I only lost a minute here or there, though I did lose an entire mission when it crashed right as I won :(
The single player campaign took me 17 hours to complete every mission, which is a pretty decent amount of content for it's time. It's possible to skip some missions or play them in a different order, so it could probably be done in less time if you rush. The difficulty curve is good - the earlier missions should ease you into the game, while some of the later missions really keep you on your toes and you really can't let your guard down. I tried doing one of the missions earlier than I should have, and was absolutely creamed as neither I nor my support units could take down any of the enemy turrets. Went back and did a few other missions to get some better tech and had a... less difficult time.
Since the game is pretty unique, I'll go over it's gameplay a little:
You directly control a one of a kind souped up Tank (The Wraith) on the battlefield, but you also call in support units as you need them. But, unlike other strategy games, most of the support units (except the Bomber) teleport directly to your location allowing you to instantly deploy a formidable army whenever you need it, and periodically reinforce it. When you've finished blasting whatever it was to smitherines, you simply recycle the units to recover their resources so you can deploy them again elsewhere (or not, if you would rather leave them to defend the area or just have plenty of resources to spare).
You capture Citadels in the game, which are huge towers with big guns that serve as your bases. They are capable of defending themselves, but you will often need to take direct control of them when they come under attack (which leavs your Wraith vaulnerable, but doing so automatically raises it's shields to maximum and it can take quite a beating). This also allows you to easily deploy more units and turrets around the Citadel to help defend it, even though you might be way over the other side of the map.
Given it's from 1997 you will have to spend some time rebinding the controls to modern best practices (and turn that damn mouse acceleration off and bump the sensitivity up to max), but that's all doable. The main changes I had to make was WASD for movement, TAB for overhead map, Q to control a Citadel, R to recycle a unit. Cycle power triangle is fine on C, but learn to use it effectively! I set my mouse wheel to generate [ and ] to switch secondary weapons, though you can use the number row for some of them as well. I left the unit deploy keys as F1-F7 even though they are a little awkward because I'm still used to them being that from 1997.
Minor con: This was one of the earliest 3D DirectX games and the draw distance sucks as a result. You can raise it in the settings a little, but even the max is still pretty low. I find this more annoying than the low resolution, especially when you know there is an enemy building just out of the draw distance from a Citadel and if only you could see where it was you could eliminate it from a distance...
That was a fast refund..game crashes after calling in the citadel. Way to go.

This game is an amalgamation of all the best parts of Sonic 1 - 3, Sonic CD,  Sonic Jam, Sonic and Knuckles. If there ever was a game to tell Sega, and through Sega to Sonic Team, that this is the way to go for Sonic games going forward, there couldn't be a better message. The Ai processing is much improved over previous games in the 2D series, the pacing of levels is perfects down to the hidden special stages and checkpoints, the replay value is through the rough, and the music is better than anything I've heard from the past games. If you like Sonic Games, you will enjoy this.

The levels are sprawling with a multitude of routes - often intersecting each other - that offer many hidden or creative ways to move through them. This is as important for Time Attack as it is for emerald-seeking; both of these activities will challenge the player's creativity and encourage exploration.
Exploration is a real pleasure, too. The levels are rich - like, Knuckles Chaotix +1 tiles & colors - with regular adjustments to color palettes between Acts of the same Zone. Unlike Chaotix, each section of a level is unique from the other sections. The music accentuates exploration with its own jazz influences: sprawling solos unraveling in parallel with the stage's twists & turns. While repising Zones maintain their traditional themes (remixed with care by Tee Lopes), the new compositions - and their respective stages! - are some of my favorite from a Sonic game so far.
"The Sonic game for the Saturn we never got." Pretty much sums it up.

Its bloody fantastic. (my opinion)
Why?
Based on my opinions
Because its the first game that made multiplayer turnbased bearable.
No flippen waiting for each other because every contender locks his/hers action in the span of 20 second at the same time. All actions will be played when the either everyone locks in or the time expires.
Prep-Dash-Blast-Move
Actions are categorized in Prep, Dash and blast.
Prep actions go first.
Things like heals, boosts, heals and traps are prep phased actions. these actions can NEVER deal direct damage. and rely soley on predict or support. Predict I did say? yes. This game is a mindgame. You try to predict your opponent actions.
Dash actions go second. these action moves your character before the move phase and can damage opponents.
these action are use to avoid potential blast phase Damage. but Dash phases can be countered by a well predicted Prep phase.
Blast actions are the third actions and also the one of the most devestating phases.
This phase is were the most Dmg will be dealt. if its not avoided by dashes or mitigated by shielding in the prep phase.
but in this phase you can also predict were you think your oponents are trying to dash to in still hit them in blast phase.
Move Final phase before it returns to Prep.
its as straight forward as it sounds. But there are a few simple rules.
If you do blast you can move 4 squares.
if you dont blast you can move 8 squares
If you Dash you cant move (except 3 lancers in the game)
If you are under haste status effect you can increase that by 50%
If you are under slowed status effect you can decrease that by 50%
If you are rooted or knocked down/back you aint moving.
these set of rules combine a very nice game of predict and trickery which can be very tense in the 20 seconds you and everyone else has to come awesome combo or completly negated because your opponent outsmarted you.
But its free to play you can see for yourself.

To go along with the review, Footage and First Impressions here:
Summary:
A game that does well in its basic concept of helping a runner win a race while being his guardian angel, but could have been a lot better if there were detailed that were shored up. While the experience was enjoyable, those little frustrations will wear on the player, but not enough to not have fun messing with other racers, and the concept in a whole. Pros:
-Interesting Gameplay design, and engaging.
-Varied paths in tracks, and interactive items sometimes are good not to use, which makes you question things.
-Background story is actually interesting. Like the idea of being a guardian angle.
-Controls are spot on.
-Smart use of practice mode to help the player in the races.
-Races are challenging yet fun.
Cons:
-No keyboard support: this is only controller gameplay. And no way to rebind (I hate using LB AND RB to hit the bumpers). Definitely shows its console roots.
-Challenge mode just doesn't change enough to make it feel different from the regular race.
-Lack of retry button on practice. This means if you screw up, you HAVE to finish the portion in order to retry, which is really really annoying. Some obstacles just slow you down, and with trying to go for speed, that's really freaking annoying.
-Sometimes, messing with other racers or jumping into a pit seems to be a benefit. While use lose a "puff", the spawn time really makes it so that sometimes it actually helps in terms of time to race. Which is annoying.
-Early on, protagonist is hard to relate to, in fact, he seems like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in question. On the other hand, they are setting up for a character building moment down the road, so only slight against it.
-No sound sliders. Really annoying in a modern PC release.

Harold is a 2d-sidescrolling runner, in which you have to manipulate obstacles to your advantage.
The video review can be found here:
The game is segmented into 4 zones with 3 levels each. It's a little bit lackluster when it comes to variety, in my opinion, but it's not too bad either.
Each level has a practice mode, a race and a challenge mode. Each mode has to be unlocked in that particular order.
In practice mode you play each obstacle combination on its own and the faster you are, the more stars you get.
You have to complete each practice level to unlock race mode and when you get the maximum amount of stars, which is 3 per segment, you get a bonus puff power.
A puff power can be used in a race to get a burst of speed for a short period of time. At the same time the amount of puff powers represents the amount of lives you have.
Puff powers can be regained by collecting two winged halos that are floating around in the level or by interfering with your opponent by manipulating obstacles to their dissatvantage.
After completing a race at third place or better, the challenge mode is unlocked. It is basically like race mode, but without opponents. You are also constantly running at max speed,
you have to collect stars and you are not allowed to die even once. Additionally all side paths are closed, which somewhat makes sense, since you can't really collect all the stars in one run.
One little thing I have to complain about gameplaywise is the fact that you are forced to complete everything at least once in practice mode, in order to unlock race mode.
I get it, each zone has its own hazards and obstacles, but forcing this linearity, especially when you are on the second level in the zone, is not so great in my opinion.
Another thing I'd like to point out is that in the game you have to do lot of flicking and twisting with the analog stick. So if you are not really used to playing with the controller a lot, the game might become difficult relatively fast.

In race mode each level has a secret shortcut that is somewhat required to be found when you want to get a good time. Getting a good time also ranks you higher on the global leaderboard, so there is some competition to be had.
Sound- and artdesignwise the game looks really good. The soundtrack is somewhat unique, and for some reason it reminds me of the Lion King, which was a bit confusing the first time I've heard it.
It might also be due to the fact that I don't hear a gospel choir singing in the background of a game that often.
The general art diretion of the game is inspired by disney movies and to me the game in terms of artdesign is somehow reminiscent of SNES games like Aladdin or Asterix and Obelix.
Conclusions: It has been a great experience so far(about 50% through the game) and there wasn't that much I had to complain about, so I'd recommend it.
However the game is 20€ or your regional equivalent. A little bit pricey, but worth the money, especially when it goes on a sale.

Harold is a challenging, high quality hand-drawn 2D platforming racing game where you play as a guardian angel in learning, trying to graduate from school into a prestige academy, you have to at least win 3rd place in all (I think all) races. The twist is, you mainly control the environment of the race, with only a jump action you can do with the character that's in the race.
The hand drawn graphics are really high quality, and it looks gorgeous along side the animations and the music too. At first glance one could say it's a game that came out of a Disney movie, the 2D classic kind, not the CGI kind.
The story is cheerful one, and the characters are nice and likable, accompanied with great voice acting. And just the whole presentation of the game is almost spotless, with the right fine touches being applied. The music is just damn awesome and 'magical' if one could say, it reminded me the awesome music from Lilo & Stitch.
The gameplay is you racing with having control mainly of the environment rather than the character, where you have to interact with certain parts of the environment, and little character control, which is only jumping and enabling a speed bost, to be able to finish a race.
The game itself is really challenging, even from the beginning, which is why they always have a practice session before every new race in a new level for you to get an idea of how you manage and finish the level. It was also a good thing for me that they didn't make it mandatory that you have to finish first place, and they made it where you have to finish at least at third place.
Along the way you will learn new techniques every now and then regarding a level, that will introduce something new you will have to cope with, in order to finish the level in most cases, or learn how to better use them and finishing the level in the fastest possible way at first place.
There's a decent amount of content for you to go through and finish, with a challenge mode for each level that's even changed up a bit in a different way where you have to finish the race with speed bost on and not failing once, and that mode helps add more replayability.
The bad thing is that it's sometimes it's hard to tell where the character you play as is standing, especially in speed mode, which results in fuzzy knowledge of when to jump. The other problem is on PC, there's no keyboard and mouse support, only controller support, and that's not a good thing. To those who say that it isn't a big deal, sure, but imagine for a moment that a game on console gets released, and it only has keyboard and mouse support, no controller support. Bad right?
The game's presentation is just spot on amazing, with the art, animations, special effects, voice acting, the beginning to the ending, the story, all of which one would think they developers hired a director from Disney movies. That plus the good challenging and different type of gameplay. I went to have another look, and actually the game is inspired by classic Disney animation, with Hollywood animation veterans that have worked on it, so no wonder this game looks great.

Don't expect a military strategy in the vein of Total War, as Crusader Kings 2 goes beyond the scope of any Total War game. some people may find the combat lacking compared to games like Total War etc. However these are completely different types of games, which some people just don't get. Combat comes down to size of force, composition of units, commander abilities, terrain and other modifiers. You don't get direct control like you would in Total War etc.

You have the Feudal system, where you're trying to please your vassals and build relationships with them, while you're trying to protect and enhance your dynasty, all the while stopping plots on you or your family, you're trying build claims on land to justify an invasion and you're setting up an Anti-Pope because the Pope excommunicated your uncle... Edit: Bought the Game 7th March 2017, by May 2nd 2017 I have 501 hours.

Crusader Kings II is a vast pretty map with an enormous database of historical figures and all their relations, titles and whatnot, that plays out as a giant real time spreadsheet. I've enjoyed many abstract games with minimal graphics (Dominions, Conquest of Elysium, Tales of Maj'eyal etc), each with large inventories of foes, items, locations and so on. But I cannot say that I even began to enjoy Crusader Kings II.
The learning curve is vertical, with tiny icons studding nearly every window. While there are tool tips to go with each view, because of the number of little buttons and icons, I had a difficult time figuring what each section of the tutorial window went with what controls. Even when I did digest what a tool tip might mean, I still had little idea what the described control did in the larger game.
About six minutes in, I was asked by the tutorial to pick an ambition for my King. Since he was single and there was already an alert about only having my brother (who doesn't like me one bit) as my sole heir, taking care of that seemed like the natural first order of business.
Forty-five minutes later I'd clicked on everything that I could find that had anything to do with anyone in the game getting married. Not only could I not marry my ruler to anyone, I had absolutely no idea WHY! While I noticed some contextual tooltips that listed out qualifiations required for a particular action, most of which were dense and had obtuse names, I couldn't find a anything that would tell me why my young King could marry no one.
The kicker for me was the tutorial telling me that my choice of getting my King married was a wise and sensible first ambition. There even came a tutorial window directing me back to the marriage window that I'd already discovered on my own and could (as near as I could tell) in no way afffect.
I could have perused the manual or searched for guides online, but spending nearly an hour on one step of a tutorial and getting nowhere made me feel decidedly unwelcome.
I'm sure there is a deep, rich game under all the very specific terminology, the family trees, under the byzantine UI screens and between the insane number of tiny buttons and icons, just waiting for someone wonky enough to sort it out. Normally, I feel like I'm that wonky person; not so with Crusader Kings II.
I found the game entirely unapproachable, so I've given it the thumbs down. I have no doubt that there are the patient few who have cracked the UI and are conversant in all the very specific terms for medieval succession and the associated ranks and whatnot. But if you're not willing to learn a whole set of antique jargon and navigate screens studded with damnable tiny buttons, and abstracted into meaninglessness icons, you're like me and this game isn't for you.
Probably one the funnest games I've ever played, but be prepared for the amount of DLC to destroy your wallet.

This review will be divised in two parts: for programmers and for non-programmers. But first, let me just answer quickly two questions: no, you don't need to know how to program to play this game (though it would help), and no, it won't teach you how to program (in assembly or otherwise).
For programmers:
You love programming? You don't program just as a job, but also as a hobby? You love writing useless yet challenging programs? You love doing competitive programming (Project Euler, Hackerrank, Codingame...)? You just couldn't get enough of this system hardware/assembly class? Then this is the game for you! However, don't be fooled; even though your skills will come handy, this game has little to do with assembly, and is even very different from programming. It's very "spatial": you have data going from one chip to the other, with each chip having its own code (that you write) that tells it how to deal with the data. There's one register by chip, and only a dozen of instructions. This has almost nothing to do with anything you've done before.
For non-programmers:
The game may look complicated and/or boring, but don't be afraid: fun comes from the solutions you find to the problems, it just doesn't need an elaborate presentation. Also, if you've never programmed before, it won't prevent you from enjoying it. Your learning curve will certainly be a little bit slower than a programmer's one, but if you're able to read, think logically and compute, you've got everything to succeed. There's a manual included in the game. It's a couple of pages and you have to read it carefully, but so would anyone since it's an invented programming language. If you have patience and enjoy mathematical or logical puzzles, this might be a very enjoyable experience for you! It will be very novel and hardcore, but if some people enjoy Dark Souls, I don't see why non-programmers (aka Muggles) wouldn't enjoy TIS-100 (not to say that this is anything comparable). However, I've said it before and I'll repeat it: this will NOT teach you how to code. At best, it will teach you how to think like a programmer, but there are better resources to do so (like Scratch, which is free and understandable for anyone, even a 6 years-old kid).
Extremely difficult, but very satisfying if you're okay with staring at the screen long enough until you figure out the solution.

Quite intriguing game!! This actually comes from the same mind that gifted us of that incredibly, absolute masterpiece called SpaceChem, and even though I see TIS-100 having less expectations than SpaceChem (startng from the price tag!), the game is no shallower, although quite shorter.
You have to actually program a weird node-structured computer in what resembles a partial assembly code. If you've played that great game called Human Resource Machine you'll find the two games have a lot in common, but where HRM tried to make a mouse-friendly assembly simulator, TIS-100 is entirely played on a keyboard in what looks completely like a virtual machine opened on an exotic hardware. There's even space for an intriguing storyline and hidden contents!
Compared to HRM, TIS-100 is less code-writing and more try-to-work-around-the-absurd-hardware-limitations: 12 nodes, each node has 15 lines of code available, no variables at all except for one variable per node with a backup function. no direct access to the other nodes' variable. given this structure, you have to abandon what you've learned in your programmer years about spaghetti code, about object programming, about functions and modules, and work around the nodes.
PRO
- a serious challenge for your mind
- impressively immersive in a 1980 machine!
- tiny storyline that is actually VERY intriguing!
CON
- the limitations of the nodes can be quite frustrating at times
Reccomended!! If you like smart puzzles, programming (no need to actually know a programming language, but it might help) and 80's!

Of the three TES games released on the Gamebryo/Creation Engine so far, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is the most well-rounded. The gameplay can be described as "one step forward, one step back" as not everything survived the transition from its predecessor. Judgment on whether the additions are a net positive will come down to each individual player familiar with the series.
TES4 also chooses a more traditional fantasy setting for its province as opposed to the imaginative, exotic land of Vvardenfell that was featured in TES3. Enemy types also seem more generic as a result. This is corrected in the Shivering Isles expansion where nothing is constrained by preestablished lore, allowing the developers to implement their wildest creations.
While it doesn't have the same depth in its lore and world-building as TES3, TES4's presentation and incredible questlines make it a contender for being the best in the series. With more modern gameplay mechanics and visuals, it's admittedly also one of the best starting points in the series for newcomers.

In my quest to find the
for me and my circle of friends to play, I stumbled upon this gem.
A very intimate medieval themed crafting system, with a unique world leads to this being a very deep and rewarding MMO. Your typical MMO stats (HP, MP, Energy) are increased through the leveling of your own personal skills. For example, every level of the Farming and Unarmed skill you rank up, you gain 1 CON(stitution) in turn which increase your health by one point. That may seem mundane but skills level up relativley fast in this MMO and you are rewarded a bonus stat of the same or different attribute every four levels.
Progression and technology is not an easy thing to obtain therefore requiring cooperation on small to massive scales, and because of the way these mechanics are set up, players are unusally friendly and helpful! Beware though, most will stop at nothing to take revenge if you steal from them, especially those with their own guild. You dont need ten people to start a succesful group in this game, infact with that many people it may be hard to start out, given that
is a serious requirment in this MMO. Yes, I know, an MMO that requires food? I realize that no one signed up to play farmville, but agriculture and hunting/foarging is another aspect of this game. Being hungry doesnt lead to you dying, rather it reduces your Stamina, chance to dodge and move speed. In a game as large and dangerous as this one, the loss of those three stats is crippling. On the bright side, food is not hard to come by in the least.
For the price of $22 Canadian Dollars, i feel like this game was a steal.

Hacker life simulator 101

Uplink is a hacking-sim in which you are an agent working for an underground corporation known as Uplink taking on certain jobs in order to get enough credits to tackle on bigger jobs. This game successfully captures the '80s style of hacking into a video game form.
What makes this game so brilliant is the 'tracing' that is performed whenever you attempt to hack a server. Using any form of brute-force technique or logging in as an admin starts an 'active trace'. This means that you have a limited amount of time before the server admin's find your ip and hit you with fines or jail time, so you must be quick enough to get in and out of the server before your time runs out. There is also what is known as 'passive tracing'. This starts after you have hacked a server, done what you needed to do, and have gotten out. The server admins will begin checking log files to check the ip through which you have connected, essentially meaning that the admins will be creeping up on you through these logs, so you mest never forget to delete them! One simple mistake in this game can cause you to be caught and you fill face jail time. The game is hardcore, in which if you get caught, your save will be deleted forcing you to restart the entire thing again from the beginning.
One of the things to be aware of is that this game can get repetetive. If you are caught and must restart from the beginning again, you will essentially be doing the same jobs again. If you can get past this, there is a lot to be enjoyed.
Some of the starting jobs will be simple things such as copying files from servers and sending them in an email to your contract employer or deleting certain files from a server. If you manage not to get caught in the beginning and make it to the later-game levels, there will be some interesting jobs such as framing people and wiping entire databases. Don't think that money will come to you easily either in this game, you will have to grind to get some of the better equipment (or you can hack a bank, try not to get caught doing that ;) ). And always never forget the simple things of hacking in this game. For example, forgetting to delete your logs just once will make you lose, so never forget to delete your logs!
The main story is about a company attempting to develop a virus and destory the internet. There are two sides that you may choose, to side with them and help develop the virus, or to side with another company and try to stop them. The choice is completely yours. Much of the story and campain is delivered through the news board in the Internal Services System and through emails that you receive, so make sure to read these.
Graphic wise, there isn't much to say. The game follows the same 'the graphics aren't good because it's old' rule. Most of it is text-based/gui-based, and it is black and blue, so try not to let it strain your eyes. If anything, there are community themes which can be found online with a quick google search to shake things up a bit.
The soundtrack, is nice and fits with the theme of this game perfectly. Again, not much to say.
Overall, this game is nice, and if you can get past it being very repetetive, it can prove to be very interesting and much fun.

I have been playing this game for a quite a while and maybe, only maybe, I'm starting to understand how it works right now (~200h). It is not a game for everyone and it's true: waiting times are everywhere. In theory, you can pay to reduce them but, apart becoming incredibly expensive pretty soon, removes part of the fun of the game and not all can be removed. This game is not one you sit and play for hours consecutively. You plan in advance. Even 8-24h before. What do you want to do? Where do you want to be? And when you gathered what you need and updated your main skills, it's time for a good ol' fight and go into a dungeon and try to get some more coins or rare materials.
Skills are increased by doing certain activities, for example woodcutting is raised by felling logs or transforming logs in planks. Every action has a level of difficulty (some time the activity has also a terrain level of difficulty). You must overcome them, to be able to do the action, with your base skill plus companions/tools/jewellery/etc. Doing those actions increases your skills (only when your base skill without the bonus is lower). So, when an action is mastered you have to move to the next action that still improves your skills. All over the world NPCs will give you quests, usual fetch or craft quests, but this gives you a direction of what next tasks you have to practice for.
Dungeons are different as you move on a board and every action can trigger a random fight. In this fight, each turn you can attack the enemy, defend or cover one character. Maximum 5 companions including the avatar can participate in a single fight. Each successful hit reduces one of the health bars (2 for companions and enemies, 6 for the avatar) chosen at random. Once one of the bars is depleted that character is out of the fight. If the avatar is eliminated you can’t fight any more and you must rest. If this happens in a dungeon you are automatically evicted. There is no perma-death, after resting enough all companions are back to normal.
My personal opinion is that this game is a little gem. Some waiting times are ridiculously high and they could improve on it. For example, every time you move on a dungeon you have to wait 5 second… why? Half of the world has not been finished yet, but the half that has been finished it’s already pretty intense. Took me 2 months playing solo to raise in my main trade skills to be able to produce something it’s actually worth selling. But I slowly started to understand that solo is not the correct way. The community is amazing, they helped me a lot, lending materials, under-selling products I needed or just with hints. There are plenty of guides and materials in Internet and even complex calculations already solved for you.
It’s not a game for everyone, but for who is searching a light-hearted RPG where you do what YOU want, WHEN YOU want it and is prepared to wait some time while planning his next move, then I would definitely recommend this game.

In general, I am not a PVP-focused player. Games which hinge on direct competitiveness really don't speak to me…
Except when they do.
Atlas Reactor is one of those rare games which combines timed, turn-based gameplay with exciting visuals, a DotA-style/League of Legends-like lineup of characters, and an almost old-school sensibility about turn-based tactical combat.
Each turn gives you 20 seconds to make your decision for one character, which feels frenetic when you start but after some practice feels positively comfortable. Combat doesn't hinge on random numbers; every skill does a static amount of damage or has a static amount of affect every time it's used – changed only by status affects which themselves have static values which they adjust things by.
Combat occurs within arenas, some of which are designed to show off the breadth of an area, some focused on controlling a much narrower channel, and some which provide a surprising amount of tactical flexibility in how the space can be divided up. Line of sight is important; some skills actively break line of sight. The phase of the turn that effects go off is also important; it is possible to – out of the way of an Ultimate skill and receive no damage at all.
At this point, AR is not a "pay to win" MOBA-like. It's free to play, giving you access to a rotating pool of characters every month, and for a flat $30 you can have access to all the characters, all the time, forever. All of the characters in game can be purchased for in game currency, which means that – in a technical sense – you don't have to pay for access to any of the characters. But you'll probably want to.
I find myself playing AR in waves. Every chapter sets new goals and challenges in order to "finish the chapter" and receive a relatively minor cosmetic award. Popping in and kicking a daily, maybe play a few extra games – that's fun. It's not a game that you have to throw hours upon hours of gameplay at every month to feel like you're involved. In my book, that's a total win.
If you'd like to check out AR, ask someone that you know plays for an invite code and you can play any of the characters in the game for a week for free. That's more than enough time to find out if this is the kind of game that will keep you involved and enthralled.
Give it a go. You might discover that it scratches an itch you never knew you had.

Frozen Synapse is an unforgiving turn-based strategic experience. Every turn, you must plan your moves or face almost certain death at the hands of your enemies.
Story missions hand you control of a small present squad. Every member of the squad can die from a single hit. Units are differentiated by the weapons they carry: shotguns, assualt rifles, sniper rifles, or rocket launchers. Shotguns dominate close-range, sniper-rifles dominate long range, and assualt rifles are useful at any range but will lose if too far from a sniper or too close to a shotgunner. Rocket-launchers will blow away walls and enemies, but must be set up in the right direction.
As in Chess, the simplistic nature underlying the game leads to surprising complexity in motion. Every turn, you must try and forsee what your opponent will do. Once you've planned your moves to the best of your ability, you submit your choices and wait for the game to work everything out. Waiting is the only downside to this game, as you will be forced to wait for surprisingly lengthy periods while everything gets worked out, and it can be frustrating to wait so long only to see all your units die at the start of the next turn. Nevertheless, the feeling of gratification when things go right is worth the experience. I highly recommend this game.

The developers of this game are also incredibly active, with someone often taking control of the server to make witty comments in the regional chat. They also stream developer updates each week, and push out new content very often.
There is an economy in this game, which allows you to purchase in-game stuff like weapon and warframe slots for the currency, Platinum, but it's tradeable and you don't
to spend any money if you aren't afraid of some grind.
I have over a thousand hours and still have yet to spend a single cent on this game, and I love that fact.

Pros:
Heavily sandbox
Charming visuals
Lots of freedom
Build fun buildings quickly
PVP is fun
Cons:
While buildings and 'towns' are easy to make, items are not
Some of the grind is outrageous even for the genre
Very little is implemented, many skills/items don't work
Red/Yellow criminal system is a joke
Jump in the game, punch some trees to make a paddle. Use the paddle to beat trees and rocks better. Start skilling up your first few points into crafting skills so you can make daggers and food -- you get the idea. ToL delivers the usual sandbox crafting routine, but with a somewhat unique pacing. A few people can very quickly set up a town complete with fences, walls, watchtowers, gates, farms, animal pens, and work stations. Oddly enough, making a simple set of clothes or a shield or sword is actually the difficult part. For example, several people have spent dozens of hours funneling resources to my guild's blacksmith, who just now was able to make his first spear. The way skills affect items though means if you create items you barely meet the skill requirements for, it will be almost worthless because of the low quality. The only way to be successful is to specialize and be a part of a large group.
ToL borrows its skill system from UO. You gain skill by doing things, and your skill level will determine how good you are at doing those things and which items you can make. For example, at lvl 5 tinkering you unlock crude axes. The quality level will be semi-random  between 1-5ish with maybe +3 attack. If you level your tinkering to 20, and go back and make the same crude axe, the quality may be as high as 15-30 with maybe +10 attack. This is great because it means leveling your skills directly pay off with better items, even if you haven't unlocked anything new. The severe downside is that newly unlocked items will be almost useless because of the low quality until you gain even more in the crafting skill.
In the current state of the game, there are some major bugs and game-breaking mechanics. No matter how much time you spend building walls, players can build a short building outside your fence and 'hop' in. If you attack them or their building you will turn into a criminal for hours and if you die players can fully loot you. Even if you decide to kill them and take the penalty, they can respawn inside your base every 3 minutes and continue to harass or destroy your town. If you kill them again, your penalty is extended. Griefing is a welcomed part of sandbox games, but one naked person can level an entire player town overnight.
Overall:
The game is fun and has a lot of potential. If you can front the $20 its worth checking out and securing yourself a copy.
Don't expect to even touch cool weapons or armor within days of grinding though. Expect to lose everything except your skill gains every time you log off unless you are in a huge active guild.

I've definitely lost a few hours playing this for only the last couple of days. I am enjoying my time by finding a group of people who were willing to let me join them. The game is okay to play alone but there are some aspects you're going to want a group for.
If you build something, make sure you break it down and put it into your inventory when you log off. This game suffers the big thing that most games suffer from, the community. If you're trying to play alone, I can guarantee someone is going to come by and destroy or steal just about everything you have. The good thing though is that unlike most of these other survival games around, when you log off, people can't kill your sleeping body and take your inventory and housing stays broken for quite a long time so if someone breaks your house, you can easily log on the next day, break it down and get your loot.
Your character will not have enough points to distribute into every skill of the game, which is fine but limits solo play if that's what you're looking for. It seems best to take up 1-2 weapon skills and the rest be put into crafting of some kind. You're going to have to rely on a guild if you want a good defensible land, good armor, weapons and items.
The mobs/monsters will break your defenses down really quickly and don't even think about fighting anything when you first start out. Except rats and livestock, you're good there. It's hard enough to keep a couple of people on at all times to have to worry about players but the mobs can just let them inside of your fort within a couple of minutes. I haven't gotten to stone walls yet, just the wooden ones so I'm assuming that will help with this issue.
The game controls very easily, it's easy to learn and it is pretty easy so far as I have found to find a group of people who will be willing to run around with as long as you pull your own weight. Even if you were to be wiped out, it's easy enough to build your stock back up with a couple of hours of gameplay.
All in all. I would suggest getting this game. It's easy to play, there is plenty to do and there will only be more content added at this point and mostly, it's fun. Just get some friends if you plan on playing heavily.

Crusader Kings II is a vast pretty map with an enormous database of historical figures and all their relations, titles and whatnot, that plays out as a giant real time spreadsheet. I've enjoyed many abstract games with minimal graphics (Dominions, Conquest of Elysium, Tales of Maj'eyal etc), each with large inventories of foes, items, locations and so on. But I cannot say that I even began to enjoy Crusader Kings II.
The learning curve is vertical, with tiny icons studding nearly every window. While there are tool tips to go with each view, because of the number of little buttons and icons, I had a difficult time figuring what each section of the tutorial window went with what controls. Even when I did digest what a tool tip might mean, I still had little idea what the described control did in the larger game.
About six minutes in, I was asked by the tutorial to pick an ambition for my King. Since he was single and there was already an alert about only having my brother (who doesn't like me one bit) as my sole heir, taking care of that seemed like the natural first order of business.
Forty-five minutes later I'd clicked on everything that I could find that had anything to do with anyone in the game getting married. Not only could I not marry my ruler to anyone, I had absolutely no idea WHY! While I noticed some contextual tooltips that listed out qualifiations required for a particular action, most of which were dense and had obtuse names, I couldn't find a anything that would tell me why my young King could marry no one.
The kicker for me was the tutorial telling me that my choice of getting my King married was a wise and sensible first ambition. There even came a tutorial window directing me back to the marriage window that I'd already discovered on my own and could (as near as I could tell) in no way afffect.
I could have perused the manual or searched for guides online, but spending nearly an hour on one step of a tutorial and getting nowhere made me feel decidedly unwelcome.
I'm sure there is a deep, rich game under all the very specific terminology, the family trees, under the byzantine UI screens and between the insane number of tiny buttons and icons, just waiting for someone wonky enough to sort it out. Normally, I feel like I'm that wonky person; not so with Crusader Kings II.
I found the game entirely unapproachable, so I've given it the thumbs down. I have no doubt that there are the patient few who have cracked the UI and are conversant in all the very specific terms for medieval succession and the associated ranks and whatnot. But if you're not willing to learn a whole set of antique jargon and navigate screens studded with damnable tiny buttons, and abstracted into meaninglessness icons, you're like me and this game isn't for you.
Probably one the funnest games I've ever played, but be prepared for the amount of DLC to destroy your wallet.

What to say about this lovely game?
TL:DR Its the best hack and slash game out there, the best combat system and great class selection with extensive customisation and if you stick with it and aquire some level of aptitude you will grow to love the game. I got the game for free and have subsequently bought a copy for everyone who has joined my (very small) gaming circle. The voice commands are great. The taunts are great. YOUR WIFE WAS A HOBBY HORSE.
I got this game free from a friend, I played 20 or so hours and uninstalled. The player base was already advanced when I recieved the game and I was basically getting kicked pillar to post and rage uninstalled it. I thought that there was no way I would be able to actually /play/ the game because of high ranked players kicking everyones♥♥♥♥♥all the time. How wrong I was.
After some goading by my friend (yes I have one) I reinstalled and haven't looked back since. Im nearly at 1000 hours. I should probably kms. It atleast deserves a review, considering Torn Banner's recent (and regrettably unfortunate) misfire with Mirage.
The graphics are still acceptable today, the combat system still has not been surpassed (this game will possibly make you stop playing any other like-for-like hack and slash; simply because there is nothing that currently rivals its combat system). Mount and Blade (though I have played it since you had to purchase it on "that turkish site" circa 0.7 - possibly even prior to that) pails in comparison for PvP combat. Weapon choice is excellent with lots of varied (without getting into technical detail) cutty, smashy, stabby weapons that you can adopt to fit your playstyle.
Which brings me to perhaps the best part of the game; the fact you can adopt any play style you like and that each player has their own style of fighting. Me? I prefer Javs, trollhammer, thrillhook as mains and for secondary (or dessert as I like to say) Dane hAxe, Norse and Short Sword (with that lovely Sax skin). There are literally tens of other weapons you can choose from - right the way from the heavy and devestating Maul down to your grandfathers old pocket knife (the Hunting Dagger). The game has a variety of ranged weaponry from Slings to Throwing Axes, from Pilum (ok /Pila/ nerdicus) to Crossbows. This allows for creativity in adapting a style; whether you like to charge in swinging a huge maul and crushing everyone in your path or prefer to sit on a nice quiet hill sniping at unwitting melee classes (everyone hates archers - I have no idea why). Everyone has the opportunity to aquire, use and master each weapon - limited only to the class chosen.
Classes are: Knight (Attack speed: Slowest) - which have access to hardest armour and perhaps the most killy of weapons (maul/messer) and 3 types of shield; Vanguard (Attack speed: Slow) - which has access to a special Vanguard Charge which deals a great deal of damage, access to decent armour and some very killy weapons (Zweihander/Polehammer); Man At Arms (Attack speed: Fast) - which has access to some fast, upredictable (like my spelling) and niché weapons (im talking Quarterstaff, firepot, daggers, one handed axes and swords) as well as shields; Archer (Attack speed: Fastest- which has access to some lovely mid and long range weapons such as Javelins, Bows, Crossbows and sling, you trade off your range damage for melee damage (you only get small side arm weapons which on the whole do small amounts of damage to heavier classes) and survivability (IE you will get 1 shot killed by Knights and Vanguards regularly).
Side note to veterans: I know that attack speed is relative to the weapon you choose (and there is a lot of crossover in the side arm across the classes) but this is to give an overview of the overall game to players who do not own the game and therefore are not aware of drags etc.
Side note to everyone: I can't believe I wrote this much.
Maps are generally of good quality and mostly well balanced - though to be /very/ picky sometimes you can get hung up on crappy bits of terrain perhaps only 1% of the times you are killed but its still irksome. The game modes are great, Last Team Standing, Team Deathmatch, Deathmatch, Team Objective (fantastically put together i might add) and duels for you loners out there. There is/are co-op modes but I have never explored them. There are mods, skins (weapons/armour) and expansions for the game of varying quality and worth (except the expansion theres only one of them and I personally loved Deadliest Warrior). The customisation of your avatar is expansive in colour, symbols, designs and armour types and you may purchase/be rewarded with unlockable armour peices/colours.
The cons - I personally can't think of many genuine and game breaking issues myself so for the sake of objectivity I will air what I have witnessed others say annoy them;
I know people whine about archers a lot, but I personally think that they are a welcome and integral part of the game and add diversity to the battlefield. They are annoying but I couldn't imagine a medieval battlefield game not including longbows, crossbows, slings (ok maybe) and throwing weapons. Take a shield if it bothers you. Protip: The heater shield is best 1.
Draggers/ballerinas can be annoying to newer players as it seems like you cant get close enough to kill them without your torso being parted from your head. However the more you play the more you can adapt and overcome. This is probably the biggest frustration of the game for newer players because it is a total immersion breaker, arguably a distortion of the physics engine and unfortunately for most - entirely devestating. Though it can not be avoided, it may be overcome, it is up to the individual player to find out what style or approach suits them. Also take a shield.
Smurfs? There are a lot of them about, they seem to enjoy lower ranked servers and trolling higher ranks by farming them. Take a shield thrice.
Voice Chat spammers? Hilarious. Take a shield. It probably wont save you but he can't see the terror on your face as the Man At Arms jumps and slithers round you poking holes in you laughing all the while.
Javelins? Im sorry man, it's not personal. Shield?
So yea. Thats Chiv. Good old chiv. You should buy it, learn some techniques, stick with it and then when you're ready unleash the sword-song or Maul-moo?

They use to make us play Oregon Trail growing up in school and it's this sort of style of play. It's a long and drawn out game, but it has progression, even if it moves like a snail along the trail. And it does. Move like a snail.
You just play in micro-movements. Let it ride. Come back in due-time, after about thirty or fourty-mins, sometimes longer, hour and a half to two-hours, and then assign more tasks, back-and-forth, back-and-forth, and then, like magic, you've grown a little-bit stronger.
You'll want to play it more and more, more than it'll let you, but think about it like this: This game gives you a lot to look forward to, which is why I give it a 10/10.
You'll wake up thinking about it. I've got to login and multi-task more functions, you'll think. To grow stronger, you'll think. You'll sit and watch your screen as you play and your playtimes will continually grow longer and longer, and just think about it, one day you'll be able to last long enough to just let it all hang out while you sleep, dreaming about Therian Saga at night in your sleep.
All you're ever going to want to do with your life is play this game. You're going to quit at life to be in this game fulltime. And trust me. It'll happen. Just like magic.

Briefly: A very pleasant online game that can drag you on for a long time.
I'll begin my review with the fact that I do not really like the genre of "strategy", in other, I do not like to think in videogames.
Going into this game at first everything seemed very simple - here is the map, here you are, here's the enemy. Go and kill. You kill a lot - you win. But after 5-10 sessions you start to wonder: what if i use this ability after this one? And can try to drive the enemy into the ally's trap?
Gradually, you start to think up some tactics, see what allies are doing, analyze the game of opponents. It takes very little time - and you have already spent 50 hours in the game.
It's time to tell you about the gameplay part.
First of all, the game has an interesting system of rounds: each round is divided into three stages, which adds many variations in the course of events. There are a lot of characters, "Freelancers", with their unique features and skillsets. Several battlefields differ from each other quite drastically. There is a system of levels for each freelancer and for the player; Increasing the level of the game will encourage you in every way buns such as in-game currency and cases with characters looks, emoticons, backgrounds and other cosmetic nonsense. Well, once they started talking about cases, let's talk about the donations. Donations in the game is, but he absolutely does not affect the gameplay, but gives you all the same cosmetic nonsense.
I can not say anything specific about the graphics. It is rather pleasant to look at and does not cause pain in the eyes. And this game is not about the graphics at all.
There are, of course, a few shortcomings, but they are not critical. Online is quite low, which is sad, but for a comfortable game it is quite enough. On my old non-gaming machine (Intel HD 4000 and i5 1.7 GHz), the game produces 25-30 fps, which is quite enough for a comfortable game.
Time to draw a conclusion. I SINGLEALLY recommend the game. Atlas Reactor is one of the most interesting projects I've played in recent times.

This is the Sonic game you've been waiting for since Sonic games came on cartridges. The level design, graphics, music and overall feel of the game will give you the same feeling of familiarity combined with innovation that you got when you first played Sonic 2 after the original or Sonic 3 after Sonic 2. The dev team has handled the nostalgia element of the game perfectly, hooking you in with recognisable levels, music and mechanics before reinventing, remixing and tweaking them to provide a new and exciting experience from start to finish.
One way this has been achieved is by making the first 30 seconds or so of Act 1 of the 'classic' maps essentially carbon copies of the original, before taking it in a new direction, either through a new or repurposed mechanic taken from another map or game or literally allowing you to go left, up and down instead of perpetually to the right. The entirely new maps are refreshing and innovative, one even adding literal depth through a second background layer.
The music is outstanding. Remixes are crisp reworkings of the 16 bit classics like Chemical Plant, Hydrocity and Flying Battery, and new tracks like Studiopolis and Press Battery (omg Press Battery) are worthy compositions to sit alongside these greats. The rest of the sound design is instantly recognisable as a Sonic game, leaving virtually nothing changed from the originals.
Bosses are also a combination of old and new, with former Robotnik/Eggman contraptions trying to thwart you in new environments, plus some new foes adding alternatives to the 'avoid spikes and hit 8 times' standard. The blue spheres special stage of S3/S&K returns, acting as a way to unlock bonus content through collecting enough silver and gold medals for successful completions. Chaos Emeralds are earned through a brand new 'pursuit' type minigame, which is challenging and satisfying enough but feels bland in the midst of the excellence that is the rest of the game.
The price point is spot on for a new release, and once the next few Steam sales push it even lower, this is going to be a must buy game for anyone who has ever got some enjoyment out of a 16 bit Sonic game. For fans of the Sonic classics hungry for more, don't wait - you won't regret it.

Have you ever wanted to play a game where your tactical thinking was rewarded without having too much hassle or any difficult  mechanics to grasp? Yes? Then this is the game for you.
Frozen Synapse is an absolute wonderful tactical battlefield commander game. You are able to control several of your soldiers on a randomly generated map against either a human or AI player and lead them, showing whether they should duck or stand up, engage or continue on sight, time their actions, etc., all in hopes to out-think your opponent and guess what they will do. You are given planning phases which, although they may be lengthy, give you the chance to test every possible scenerio to your liking, giving you the ultimate think session of your life every turn.
Frozen Synapse also has great co-op in it's expansion pack, which gives you the same tactical fun with a friend. I highly recommend you get it - it's called Red Mode, or something like that. Another great feature this game has is the ability to play multiple games at a time. You get popup invites from other people, which you can either accept or deny, into their games, which allows you to play however many games you want to play over any period of time you like, which leads to the bad parts  about this game.
I'm not going to lie, this game isn't perfect. There's no punishing system for abandoning games, which happens a little too often with bad mannered players who don't want to finish a losing game. Not only that, but It does have two or more glitches (you can plan to move your soldier through a wall, but the game says that you can't do that, and an extra move when trying to walk beside a wall, really nothing that major or game-breaking) which can annoy you a little, but it won't consistantly happen to you.
My final verdict for Frozen Synapse is this - if you are a fan of thinking games, especially chess, GET THIS GAME IMMEDIATELY. If you are not, wait for a sale, because you very well might enjoy this game for it's easy-to-understand, but hard-to-master mechanics. A solid NINE out of TEN from me on this wonderful game.

This is a game with enormous potential that was effectively squandered due to lack of imagination or courage from the developers.  While there's a lot of whimsy to be found in soaring through the air on a glider, spotting hostiles via tech goggles or using the terrain to your advantage, these are merely the frosting on a Call of Duty-based cake.  Almost all of the meat of the game boils down to bog-standard COD style machine guns blazing murder, never mind how poorly that juxtaposes with the silliness inherent in this comedic take on the Gotham setting.
Along with its derivative gameplay, GCI also boasts an almost dead community.  You'll never find players for any mode other than deathmatch.  What players you do find will only be found after excessively long queu times.
Its Pay 2 Win aspirations, which involve speeding up the enormously tedious grind to get better gear and perks, are severely outdated in a universe of TF2, Path of Exile and Dota 2 style 'vanity only' models.
Not recommended unless you really love COD style gameplay or are absolutely desperate for a lighter take on Batman, no matter how flawed the implementation.
