TL;DR:
Oblivion is my favorite game of all time. You should defiently buy it and never play any other game, ever. I'll give it a 10/10 for what it is. The game is just amazing, though bethesda REALLY seems to have a thing for tracking down sons/famiy members or people in their games.
(Martin, "Dad", Shaun, the blade guy in Morrowind).
P.S. This game is better than Skyrim in a lot of ways.
------------
You start as a prisoner in the Imperial City Prison. Sentenced for unknown crimes (Great for having an RP backstory). The Emperor comes down into the dungeons, it turns out your jail cell just happens to have a badass escape route out of the city. You end up escaping the city with the emperor, along the way you find out a little about what's going on.
The Emperor has the "Amulet of Kings" which is used to create a barrier between your realm and Oblivion (hell).
Mehrunes Dagon (main antagonist), god of Oblivon, wants to invade your realm. His little idiotic cult followers called the "Mythic Dawn" help him do that. They assassinated the Emperors sons and now have came for the Emperor himself.
Now it's your destiny to take the Amulet of Kings and locate the Emperors b*stard son, kept in secret, hidden away & make him Emperor and "Shut close the jaws of Oblivion".
The story is awesome really, though the game lacks as a choice-based RPG. There's no choices (There's a few in the Dark Brotherhood (Assassin Guild)). The storytelling is amazing,
Oh boy, this is where the game really shines. Bethesda is known as MASTERS of world development & Oblivion is no different. The game is set in Cyrodiil. The world is a bright, beautiful & vibrant place. It's very diverse (The game is set in the center of the continent, so has bits of everything).
From Anvil, a port town on the west coast, to Bruma, a city of the Nords, far to the north in the mountains near Skyrim, to Leyawiin, a city far to the south, mostly inhabited by the Argonians and Khajits (Lizard and Cat people, beast races) a dark, swampy-like town.
Or even the Imperial City itself, the largest city on the continent, filled with all the races and culture from everyone. Also the arena where you can pay to watch people beat eachother to death.
It's not a choice-based RPG. You can't choose sides and nothing conflics, but honestly it's not a bad thing & i'm sure there's mods for it anyway. It's more of an RPG that expresses a sense of freedom for the player. You can literally walk anywhere and interact with things, drag objects in the world around using the game physics, kill almost anyone you see and just take in the world. Anywhere at anytime.
If you do NEED a choice-based RPG for your library, i'd definetly reccomend Dragon Age Origins (probably my second favorite game).
(Same music composer too, Inon Zur, known for The Elder Scrolls, Fallout, Star Trek, Pirates of the Carribean, Prince of Persia and more)
Cyrodiil, being set in the center of the continent, is home to all races, it has a large feeling of diversity, each city generally has a larger population of the race that the city is closest to their home province. The voice acting is great for ever race and there's a large amount of culture to it too. You'll here ambient dialog from characters in the street talking about things around the world & all NPC's wander around openly, they all have their scripts that they follow daily, at certain times they'll do certain things. Counts and Countesses will sleep at night, then attend their courtroom during the day. Places open and shut and scripted times and everything acts like a real world.
-------
Overall I LOVE this game, it's a MUST have for any RPG/Open-World/Fantasy lover. If there's anything more to say I might add more to this review later.

If you're looking for a hacking game, then this is it. Nothing else even comes close!
You get to ruin people's lives, destroy mainframes, penetrate high security networks, use voice analyzers and chat to strangers online! What more could you want? An open-world sandbox and smartphones? Pff.
Really though. Uplink is Hollywood-style hacking (Think of the 1995 movie, Hackers, but a little bit more true to reality) at its best, compressed into a game and far more addictive and immersive than you would expect. The entire game is quite fast paced, and there is always something to do. There are missions you can accept from clients, or you can simply go rogue and do your own thing. Regardless of your choice, tension and stress will be prominent, and are a mechnic that is used very effectively. One small mistake can lead to you being caught and disavowed, meaning that you'll need to take extra precaution before initiating a hack, during a hack and even after successfully completing a hack. All of this creates a tense atmosphere during an attack, and while some may find it offputting, I found it to be incredibly immersive and enjoyable.
If you're at all interested in network security, fictional or non-fictional representations of hacking, then you're going to love Uplink!

After a little more than an hour with this game, I have to say that I'm impressed. If you like puzzles, programming, retro-tech, and/or mysteries then this is a gem. This is a game that doesn't hold your hand and it is all the better for that.
The game may look minimalistic (it is) and complicated (which it also is, to a degree), but try not to write it off as boring because of that--it's far from it. The basic premise here is that your uncle has died and you've inherited his last pet project:  cleaning up the mysterious TIS-100 computer that he found at a flea market. Your uncle has stored some of his thoughts and notes in the computer itself, and these show up as corrupted files within the game's interface. Each time you reach a new puzzle you get a little more of the story, which is definitely worthwhile from what I've seen so far.
The puzzles aren't terribly difficult at first, but things ramp up after you make a few programs (or solutions, if you'd prefer). The tasks at hand - like transfering a piece of data to a specific point - might seem simple, but you're stuck with an assembly language, which means that all the comforts of high-level languages like C++ have been stripped away to leave you with the basics. The real meat of the game is solving problems with such a simple language, and it's very satisfying when you finally write just the right code to get past the final series of checks that each program has to go through before you can move on.
This is as far from a casual game as can be. The whole "read the manual" joke that gets thrown around about video games is entirely literal here, as the game is essentially unplayable without doing so. This might normally be a negative, but considering that TIS-100 goes out of its way to acheieve immersion, I think that delivering the instructions via the facade of a "real" TIS-100 manual is brilliant. Though, that means that you can't really pick up and play the game. You need to sit down for 15 minutes and learn about how the game does assembly programming before you can start your first real puzzle.
Fun game, easy to learn, hard to master. Not a game you should buy if you play games to rest your mind.
TIS-100 is a unique and challenging puzzle game.

Eve Online meets Final Fantasy XI, by way of graphic MUD.
The game is a class-less RPG that's heavy on crafting. And all skills are trained primarily through use.
These two elements alone make it worth checking if you want a game that rewards you for what you actually do.
It also borrows from Eve Online timed actions, where most activities are done by selecting an action and after a set amount of time the results are given. You can also set up actions for a few hours and then come back later, as the world continues to exist after you log out.
Exploration also plays a big part in the game as almost all the areas are hidden until you discover them either by exploring or through questing for NPCs.
As for skills, you obviously have your combat and defense abilities, modified by armor, weapons and training (experience), but also pretty much every conceivable trade skill imaginable from leatherworking and jewelry-making to mining and taming/breeding animals.
And there's the expected auction house/market to buy and sale goods and materials with other players.
Very in-depth and well-polished.

I play in my browser, therefore it shows 0 hours played.
If you are interested in trying out, here are the key points:
1) Progression is entirely based on perpetually increasing numeric skill stats. There are no overaching stories or epic pvp combat. You can pick up all skills on one character like in wurm or eve. You improve stats by doing related activities repeatedly. There exist many fetch quests. UI is mostly functional. Every panels have fixed locations and are unresizable. Text is tiny making quests even more boring.
2) It requires silverlight and thus IE 11 or lower to run because silverlight is not supported in any up-to-date browsers, not even Edge. It might expose you to unknown and never-patched security issues.
3) BOTH energy and timer are applied with extreme prejudice. For the most parts you need to perform a sleep action which takes over 2 hours to completely recove energy
This is how bad the timers are: In runescape, you click on a tin node, your avatar does some quirky animation and you get tin within a few seconds. In Therian Saga you click on a tin node -> you wait for the client to communicate with the server (takes a few seconds) for the interaction panel to show up so you can select the amount of attempts you want to make and to authorize the action -> you wait for the client to communicate with the server (takes a few seconds) -> finally you wait exactly 13 minutes 53 seconds for each mining attempts to complete, yielding you 1-3 units of tin, animation free. And that's tin, the absolutely lowest tier resource. Eventually you'd encouter activites that take so long to complete that the developers break it down to multiple actions that build up a progress bar, so you can complete like 1-2% for every 24 hours dumped on it. You'll find players with dozens of alts because that's the only way to make it actively engaging.
4) About 1% of the times, when you happen to see the crafting interface, it becomes mildly interesting. Each activities (crafting included) has a few stat checks you must overcome such as terrain difficulty, thermal resistance, etc. Each crafting ingredients has an assortment of fancifully named stats such as lightness, density, calming, etc. Each recipes makes use of some of those stats to determine the stats of the final items so different ingredients have different strength. Generally, to reach a specific amount of stat, easier-to-obtain ingredients are more difficult to work with. Hence in crafting you must balance between the difficulty of the crafting action (limited by your avatar skill), the stat goal of item to be crafted (set by the activities it is used for) and the time needed to craft it (set by the type of ingredients you use and the time needed to collect said ingredients)
Note that they apply this golden formula to every crafting skills. There are many of them but they are essentially the same with zero varieties.
5) You might have noticed that I dont use the word "game" anywhere else in this review.
Complicated game not for the impatient gamer.

Hands down, my most favorite game of all time on Steam!
It's not comparable to any other FPS game out there. You can't beat the fact that it's free but even if it cost $30, I would pay it. I've never enjoyed a game as much as I do GCI.
If you've never been big into FPS games, like myself, there's likely quite a bit of a learning curve. You'll probably die like crazy in the beginning, get teamed against a level 1000 and want to throw your mouse across the room while screaming profanities about how they had to be a hacker.
PROS:
- This game is fun!
Hands down, this is the most entertaining game I've played in YEARS. Especially considering it's a FPS. I literally play this around 20 hours a week (sometimes more, sometimes less) and it's always my go to game even after this long.
- Customizing everything to fit your play style
A lot of FPS games just give you the options of various weapons which really only fall into a few categories of long range (sniper), short range (shotgun, SMG) or medium range (assault, rpg/rockets, grenades)
This game lets you customize not only your Body Types (Each have different amounts of hit points, speed, agility, etc.) Outfits (which are purely cosmetic), Weapon types, support weapons and support "passive" abilities.
- The weapons / support items are hilarious
Parrot Launcher: You literally shoot a parrot out of a gun and it gnaws on people's faces so they can't see anything
Ice Gun: You shoot beams of ice that can freeze people into a block of ice and upon taking any damage, EXPLODE!
Hatchet: Pretty straight forward axe but you can throw this damn thing across a map. With good accuracy or luck, insta-kill some noob just standing there. Fun to be had
Jetpack: Rain DEATH from above upon everyone
Inflatable Insoles: Beach ball shoes that let you double jump
Toxic Gas: A can of beans, when used you fart a stench cloud that impairs and hurts enemies. What more is there to say?
- It's FREE!
Seriously, there is no reason to at least give this game a try and play it for a few hours to get the hang of it. Sure you'll probably lose a bunch like I did and swear people are somehow cheating. There are spots you'd never think of hiding, there will be lag spikes and you learn how to play with them and still do decent. Overall, I LOVE this game and I seriously cannot suggest it more to people, even if you hate games like Call of Duty. This may be a FPS but it's nothing like CoD.
CONS:
- The game has basically been abandoned
There won't be any new maps, any updates, etc. This game is what it is and is likely staying that way. Makes me sad because I love it but doesn't have an affect on the game really, just makes me sad about it's future.
- No dedicated servers
The game is peer to peer and of course, people will horrible connections don't lower their connection settings because they either A) Don't realize they need to or B) Think it will affect their performance (It won't). So there are times you'll get a crappy host and can't do much of anything. So if you know you have a bad connection, go into the settings and lower your connection settings to 1.5mb. It just makes you less likely to host a game.
- Matchmaking
I wouldn't exactly call this a CON but there are times when your opposing team can be a level 1000, 300, 200 and some lowbies and your team is all under level 50. It sucks but it's all part of the game. Honestly, getting my butt kicked when I was a low leveler helped to teach me some tricks. Sometimes I would just follow them around and watch what they were doing. It taught me some vantage points, hiding spots, etc. There are some groups of top levelers that get together and form a team. That's not really my style, I prefer to just play by myself and let the teams fall how they will.
- Not a ton of players

From great level design to amazing music (as most of the time), this official fan project was made for the fans. Even those who haven’t played a Sonic game before may enjoy this.
Some quirks were brought back from previous classic games, but they won’t bother you as you adapt.
And the bosses, are possibly my favorites in the entire classic series.
All in all, you could say Sonic had a considerably better year.

I don't usually play Turn Based games; when it comes to RPGs, I'm more of an free actions kind of guy (Gothic, Dragon Age, Witcher etc).
However, a colleague told me about Original Sin and I've purchased D:OS EE and had a blast with it.
Unfortunately, I arrived late to the party and didn't get a chance to help Larian with their kickstarter for D:OS2, but I did pre-order it (which I almost never do).
And I'm glad I did.
There are some good changes to the first game:
- you can choose your companion's class when you recruit them
- you can respec your character and your companions at almost any time!
- if you respec, you don't lose your learned spells/skills
- you now have a skill bar with many slots at the bottom of the screen
- summoning, hands-down one of the best class in the game; summons can really turn the tides of battles, especially since they can be infused with different elements
- full voice acting (I know EE also has that, but the original D:OS didn't)
There are also some changes, let's call them neutral; some I've learned to like, while others not so much:
- physical and magic armor: you first have to tear through your opponent's armor before you can apply any CC to them; this bothered me a lot at first, when I didn't have the means to get rid of their armors easily, but, as you gain more skills and spells, it becomes less of a problem; there are still some weird things about this system, like you fight an attack dog and it has physical armor for no reason (I mean, I understand when a human enemy has physical armor because he has a breastplate, but a naked dog?)
- you have to spend skill points on Memory, which increases your skill slots; I didn't like this at first, because I'd want to spend my points on other attributes; however, it isn't as bad, as you receive free Memory slots when leveling up at certain levels
- Source Points; I still don't like this mechanic as some of the best abilities are now locked behind the need of source; these good abilities already had the disadvantage of using more than 1 Memory Slot, but you also need Source to cast them; of course, you can steal source from enemies or corpses, but enemies can also steal you source
- a bit of spoiler ahead:
- your party members can leave you permanently late in the game, depending on dialog choices, even though you had a good relationship with them (high attitude) until then; I was shocked when this happened, because I don't understand what the point of companion attitude is
- new game modes: PvP and Game Master; I haven't tried these yet, so I don't know if they're good, but they're there
- it also comes with a free Map Editor
The game also has some bad parts, of course:
- I didn't play it when it launched because I was sure there were going to be bugs. I've waited for a week or two and a few patches and played it without major technical issues (though I did have a 100% crash in an area that had a lot of lava around, but lowering the graphical settings resolved that).
- on the gameplay side, as many have pointed out, the last part (Arx) isn't as good as the rest of the game, but it's not really that bad. There are some weird fights with respawning enemies in a certain embassy, but those can be avoided by sneaking.
P.S.: When writing this review, I'm just before the last fight, so I'm not sure what that's like.

What little I can play in this game without forgetting to quicksave and then blowing up, I can honestly say it's been fun.
However, there's been that issue of blowing up. A lot. Near planets, on planets, into asteroids...there's a lot of blowing up in this game if you're not careful about your actions.
I can understand that these are somewhat expected of games like this, but at the same time, they're somewhat off-putting. And I say this having owned Evochron Mercenary before Elite: Dangerous was a thing. This game is insanely strict about certain things and you will blow up with the slightest provocation when starting out. And you will lose progress many times if you're used to games made in the last decade and a half using autosaves.
That said, it's probably one of the biggest spaceflight sims I've played, with the widest range of options in terms of gameplay. It doesn't ever really shift out of space, either, into transitions or loading screens or anything. It's just space, end of story. And that's nice, because it's rare that you can literally fly, freestyle, between sectors. I don't know why you would, because they're huge, but this is one of the rare places where this is actually possible, and I feel like that's worth merit in itself. The world never limits your ability to travel within it, and you can seamlessly exit a station, pop over to a planet, fly around in the atmosphere, and then be back out in space and out to an asteroid belt without a single moment of pause.
So while the game is hilariously heavy-handed with its smackdown if you make even a small mistake, it makes up for it by having a huge world that seems to go on forever, and without a single loading screen or transition...except for the one between the game and the menu. That one, however, we can ignore. I'll take one loading screen to a series of "jump gates" any day.

Therian is, at it's heart, a crafting game. A lot like old school Runescape (in a good way), the game has an intricate interconnected system of skills for producing better tools, armor, weapons. No one skill seems to outshine any of the others (although I recommend Fauna as a starting skill for the pets) which makes for a lot of flexibility in how you play. The cash shop features a mix of account wide unlocks and quality of life consumables that speed up activities or give convenience.
My experience is a modest expense (10 dollars US) gives a good portion of the unlocks. The game is fully free to play, you can play with no money spent, however you will have to switch tools more often, and won't be able to que up as many actions.
Therian uses a lot of queues. You choose activites which often take from 10 minutes to an hour. This gives the game a sort of idle feel to it. I compared it to Runescape, Therian replaces the mindless repetitive clicking of that game with blocked out amounts of time. I greatly prefer this to that.
Surprisingly well put together. Abit of a time sink unless you have the $$ to keep pushing ahead, but I enjoy it.

Oh, hey, a new MMORPG. With a... heavy bent towards mathematical systems, crafting, and the ability to set up actions while offline. Huh. Sounds interesting.
(After two hours) OK, this system is ... weird, but I think I can manage it. It revolves around Energy points and real time - chopping this type of tree takes this much effort and lasts for this long. So I can set this up to run while I'm asleep tonight and have stuff to do when I come back tomorrow. OK.
(After one day) Man. I really wish I had better stuff and gear.. I know I've got all these different items. Do they stack?... No, you use the best item, the best companion, and best skill you've got, nothing stacks. So there's not a big reason to go into the ingame shop unless you want to carry around more companions, or set up super complex multiple-day job queues, or maybe link multiple characters together in one house, saving time and energy. Well, maybe a few bucks sometime down the road, but I think I can play just fine without it. It's just a little more complex.
(After two days) Huh. I've scraped together some gear, I'm enjoying the ability to travel to different places and do things and being able to tackle every job skill in the game, as long as I have the time investment and gold pieces for it, gold which I am sorely lacking. Let's go poke my nose into the first dungeon.
(After two days and one hour) Ow. What the hell is 'mutilated?' How did a snake mutilate me? ...Oh, everything takes twice as long and I can't fight anymore. It's this game's version of 'unconscious/dead'. I'll... take a 15 minute nap, restore my health, and not go in that cave again until I'm healed up. It was fun, at least.
(After a week) I've learned to make decent starting clothing and armors, I've got a handle on the herbalism tree which lets me make my own healing potions, and I've clobbered the cave. Everything takes time to do, but you can either pick little actions to do one thing at a time, or big resource gathering/sleeping extravaganzas. Wait. They want me to leave the kingdom to go somewhere? Wait. Lemme scroll out and look at the map. HOLY CRAP. And I don't know where anything is! I gotta explore to find it all!
(After three weeks) why do I have two hundred hours in this game, it is eating my life and I'm enjoying the hell out of it, send help.
Really, though, If I have to single out one aspect of the game I don't like, it's some of the other players. But for a free to play game, that's to be expected. If you go into the game thinking of it as something like a cross between EVE, WOW, and a phone game, you'll have a good grasp on it. It's at least worth downloading and seeing if you like it - you can't beat the free price. If you do try it out, look for me on the new Loucantar realm - now's a great time to get into it while it's still young!

This'll be a short review because I got a lot of turns pending :D
Frozen Synapse is a turn-based strategy-game similar to Breach&Clear but with a more intense focus on multiplayer.
Overview:
The game is set in a future world in the city Markov Geist. The reality has become divided into the real world, controlled by humans, and the shape, something like a second reality that can be accessed through the widespread wireless network that has been established over the years. It's home of so called shapeforms which I won't explain in detail.
The setting is somewhat similar to that of the Shadowrun Universe (Cyberpunk).
Gameplay:
As there are so many other reviewers out there who already explained the gameplay in detail, I will just sum up my impressions. The game easy to learn but hard as f*** to master. You are given a small tutorial which explains the basic commands and teaches you how to chain them and plan your turn. Then you're on your own to figure out what to do with that information. I suggest playing the campaign a little before jumping into multiplayer.
The mechanics are fair although sometimes frustrating since who kills who depends on a list of factors you have to be aware of and at times they are not that easy to assess.
But that's what makes this game great. It really forces you to THINK about what to do next!
The graphics speak for themselves. Simple yet stylish. You get a good overview of the map and there are no irrelevant objects. If you can see it, it has a function -> Good guys, bad guys, cover, walls. That's it.
Summing up I did not regret paying 7€ for this. If you also want to play Coop, buy the Red DLC. Only one of the Coop-Players needs it for coop to work which I think is really well done!

TL; DR: Uplink is an enjoyable hacking sim that anyone can enjoy. 9/10. Would recommend to my Grandpa
So, I don’t really like amoral companies that are out to make a profit at the expense of customer happiness or even human life. So it comes no surprise to me that I really like a game that lets me f**k them so badly by destroying their mainframes and stealing user account data. I even get to wait a few days and then see the news story about what I did break, with multi-million dollar losses on their part. Ahh. Bliss.
In case you did not read any previous reviews for the game, or take a cursory glance around the store page, Uplink is a hacking simulator. More precisely, it is a TV-hacking simulator. Unlike many hacking sims, you don’t spend that much time messing with IPs and command prompts. Those are there, but they are light references to reality, grounding the rest of the game to our reality. Instead you spend your time launching programs. There is a program for just about everything from breaking a password, the most common thing you will do besides click, to log modifiers that are used to either protect your identity or frame other hackers. There is also a program to nuke your computer in case the Feds show up. The Feds showing up is something that you might have to get used to, as the game can be difficult. It follows a pretty fair difficulty curve, but getting caught (the only true fail state) results in having to start over. This may sound annoying as hell, but in truth I would say that it is a fair system once you accept it. Uplink reminds me of Dark Souls, or DayZ in the sense that every time you play, you learn more and get better. When I first started the game, it took me about an hour and a few retries to hack the International Academic Database to alter someone's qualifications, a pretty normal job. Now, 25 hours of gameplay later I can get there in about 10 minutes.
Along with starting fresh every time you fail, Uplink changes the names of the people assigned to the various positions within the numerous corporations you interact with. As I previously mentioned, screwing with these corporations can be quite an enjoyable aspect of the game, and also completely user-generated fun. One the most enjoyable moments with the game happened when I figured out how to, after completing a mission to race a balance transfer, and receiving payment for the job, siphoning the 1.2 million dollars into my bank account, then deleting the logs to prevent a trace. However, I found out shortly after that doing this specific action was kind of the wrong way to play Uplink. Without the need for funds to upgrade your computer and software, the challenge of the game falls apart, and after upgrading my machine to a pointless degree, I decided to start fresh simply because the journey was more fun than the reward. Otherwise, the only thing to keep me playing that playthrough was the story missions.
The story of the game is a simple hacker story about a corporation developing a virus to take down the internet (cuz their marketing department was just full of 60+ has-beens that didn’t understand it). Funnily enough, if you hack their server you can find out that they are actually a cult devoted to destroying the internet, to which I can only say LOL.
Uplink’s basic concept breaks the 4th wall in an interesting manner. When you boot up the game, there are no logos, just a login screen, prompting you to make a new user. This user you create is an online avatar for your Uplink corporation profile, and the Uplink corp is used as a way to hire hackers for jobs. This is all framing of course, but when you are caught, a message along the lines of “A major corporation has discovered your broke into their systems. We disavowed all knowledge of your actions, however your Gateway (the computer that you “link” into from your computer running Uplink) was seized by the authorities after all data was wiped from it”, then it prompts you to make a new user. Basically, the game pretends it isn’t a game, and that is rather quite clever in my mind, because unlike many attempts in other games to do the same, in Uplink I am most accepting of this. One could argue it is a borderline ARG. Also, there is a IRC client that you can “buy” for 4000 in game credits, a relatively small amount of money in the grand scheme of things. From here you can connect to the Uplink Corp server and talk to other hackers that are other players.
This leads me to the community, which is sadly kind of hard to gauge. The game is
10 years old according to Steam, but was originally released via a strange piece of technology called a “box” that stored a “CD-ROM”, a finicky and lightweight method of data storage pre USB thumb drive. Apparently the console peasants use these still, but their corporate overlords wish them to switch to Digital Downloads. Anyways, the boxed copies were released in 2001, so the game is technically 14 years old at time of writing, and there is about 1000 reviews on Steam, so the community is pretty small by this point, but it is a dedicated one. I mentioned the IRC chat about 727 characters ago, and there is usually 21 folks on it (pop in and say hello, my nik is Moose). You can also find celebrities such as Icepick, the fellow who made the Ultimate Uplink Guide, and apparently Introversion guy pop in occasionally, but I have yet to be on to see them.
To conclude, Uplink is a unique and very interesting example for its genre with a high skill ceiling, but low skill floor. It requires no understanding of how computers work or how software works, or what the hell and IRC chat channel is or even what an IP address is, so theoretically you could install it, take it to your Grandpa's place, and the two of you could have a merry time breaking into a bank.
9/10

Pick it up full price, or if you are not sure, get the $5 tablet version

Divinity: original Sin 2 is a strong contender to "Game of the Year"  and with few meaningful tweaks it could easily compete to rank among the best RPGs of all time.
Like for its predecessor, its strong points are the massive amount of player agency permitted, one of the best turn-based combat systems in the business, a great degree of environmental interaction and very solid encounter design.
Disappointingly enough, this sequel fails mostly in the same area that hindered its predecessor: itemization and stat bloat.
Larian's stubbornness with randomized loot over unique and hand-placed items means you'll never get rewards that are meaningful, just generic items that can drop anywhere or pop in any merchant's inventory at any given time.
That kills a lot of incentives to bring down strong enemies, solve quests and explore for hidden treasures: when every action can potentially get the same outcome, it doesn't really feel like accomplishments matter that much.
On top of that, the problem with stat bloat emerges few hours into the game. While the problem presents itself from the beginning (by the time you'll get all the pieces of the first armor set in the starting area they'll be completely obsolete), it becomes genuinely grating past level 14-15, as you'll quickly get to the point where the jump in values at each level will be so ridiculous you'll literally double your HP/damage/armor values, etc.
This essentially forces (well, strongly encourages) the players to replace ALL the equipment for his entire party at every level up.
That's not just annoying and a bit pace-breaking, but it also has the not irrelevant side effect to make you feel like no piece of equipment you'll find, no matter how strong at that given moment, gives you any long-term value.
There were surely better ways to handle these aspects, even just looking at the past.
This game with the Baldur's Gate 2 itemization could have been a all-times classic.
Hands down THE best tactical RPG of this year. Maybe ever.

I get that Denuvo is controversial, but this review is about the game rather than the DRM.
This is the Sonic game you've been waiting for since Sonic games came on cartridges. The level design, graphics, music and overall feel of the game will give you the same feeling of familiarity combined with innovation that you got when you first played Sonic 2 after the original or Sonic 3 after Sonic 2. The dev team has handled the nostalgia element of the game perfectly, hooking you in with recognisable levels, music and mechanics before reinventing, remixing and tweaking them to provide a new and exciting experience from start to finish.
One way this has been achieved is by making the first 30 seconds or so of Act 1 of the 'classic' maps essentially carbon copies of the original, before taking it in a new direction, either through a new or repurposed mechanic taken from another map or game or literally allowing you to go left, up and down instead of perpetually to the right. The entirely new maps are refreshing and innovative, one even adding literal depth through a second background layer.
The music is outstanding. Remixes are crisp reworkings of the 16 bit classics like Chemical Plant, Hydrocity and Flying Battery, and new tracks like Studiopolis and Press Battery (omg Press Battery) are worthy compositions to sit alongside these greats. The rest of the sound design is instantly recognisable as a Sonic game, leaving virtually nothing changed from the originals.
Bosses are also a combination of old and new, with former Robotnik/Eggman contraptions trying to thwart you in new environments, plus some new foes adding alternatives to the 'avoid spikes and hit 8 times' standard. The blue spheres special stage of S3/S&K returns, acting as a way to unlock bonus content through collecting enough silver and gold medals for successful completions. Chaos Emeralds are earned through a brand new 'pursuit' type minigame, which is challenging and satisfying enough but feels bland in the midst of the excellence that is the rest of the game.
The price point is spot on for a new release, and once the next few Steam sales push it even lower, this is going to be a must buy game for anyone who has ever got some enjoyment out of a 16 bit Sonic game. For fans of the Sonic classics hungry for more, don't wait - you won't regret it.

I think the description for the game is missing one important thing - it's an idle game (well, it does say it's "asynchronous", maybe a mistake in translation?). Most of the time the game is about queuing some tasks and coming back couple hours later. And I'm fine with that - that's the kind of game where you pop in once or twice a day, issue some orders within couple of minutes and then just watch as your character and wealth grow over weeks and months. It doesn't take much of your time and attention - it's an idle game after all, a nice thing that you do in the background.
I understand many people do not like it, but I must say I prefer to queue some actions and go offline rather than having to spend hours in the game and mindlessly repeating the same action to progress (like in Wurm or Runescape). In a way it reminds me of games like "Castle Age" or "Dawn of the Dragons", except that it's more about crafting and economy rather than combat. Or "Big Farm", but more complex, with more freedom and not having to click every 5 minutes.
Also, the game isn't really free-to-play. The free version is more like a demo. Microtransactions let you unlock some permanent bonuses which make the game a lot more enjoyable - for example free players can only queue up to around 10h of actions, while paid players can queue 20h or more. And yes, the game is somewhat pay to win, as in you can sell premium currency for in-game-gold or buy premium consumables and bonuses so the free players cannot really compete. But then again the game is not about competing or winning - just chill out, build your home, improve your skills, explore and don't bother yourself with the fact that other players might be more advanced.
But apart for that the game is what it says - you will harvest materials and craft stuff, improve your skills and explore.
As for the tutorials and introducing new players - it could indeed make it better. Current tutorial introduces some basic concepts like exploration, combat and questing. But explanations on, for example, housing or how skills are calculated seems to be missing. I disagree, however, that the game should teach the player where particular components can be bought / obtained - I find a lot of joy in exploring the continent and checking every settlement to see what can I find there.
To sum up - if you don't like idle games or energy mechanic - you won't like this game.
If you are looking for action - you won't find it here.
But if you like idle games AND crafting, like me, then this game should be great for you.

This is a nice little time killer.
Let me start by saying this game is not for everyone.
The game is timer based so when you first start out you are going things that take 10-15 seconds to complete in real time.  As you progress the timers become longer and longer until you end up Queueing up several hours of tasks for your characters to perform.
Pros:
The playerbase is very helpful
The game is extremly casual.  You play for a little bit once or twice a day and set your character up doing things to raise skills.
The world is huge.  RIght now there is two or three lands but thatcovers about 30% of the map.  The potential is huge.
The game is NOT P2W but really F2P (A very very rare thing)
Simple graphics
Cons:
Simple graphics (sometimes they are pretty hard to see things.
Excessive timers (yeah mos things at even my low level take a minimum of an hour to do)
Gold Spammers (Although most of the time they get muted by the Mods)
The game is Polish and even on the "English" servers people speak Polish in the global chat.
The UI is severly lacking - things get buried in your backpack.  No way to control which quest chain (objecitves) you are working on. Unmoveable windows.  Needs more polish
Large gaps in crafting and little to no explanation on the next step
Overall I really enjoy the time I spend in the game.  Soon I shall move on to the second land area.
As for the Gold Spammers I have little to no doubt these are just hackers trying to get malware on your PC.  The in game currency is called Blue Crowns.  They can be bought with real cash to buy things in the in game shop.  You can also sell them on the in game marketplace for Gold Coins.  So why attempt to buy gold from a hacker when you can buy BC and sell to players for Gold.
This is NOT a game you sit down and play for a few hours.  This is played in short spurts.
Here is my suggestions.
Buy a few BC to spend in the marketplace.
Buy the account upgrades like more slots for everything (except the marketplace).
Get more queues and compainion slots (You will need leadership though to fill those slots so work on that).
Maybe buy a few of the things that take a hour from your queued items.
Sell a few BC on the Market for some fast gold to pay for supplies and grab a second character.  This way you have one person making things for your other who gathers things for the one making things.
I am enjoying this so far.

This is a game you'll either love or hate.  It's true that it uses timers and waiting for hours for tasks to be completed but if you could skip all the waiting (such as by using premium currency) the game would be woefully boring and done in a few hours.  The fact that it takes time to explore, time to build, time to gather all emphasizes that you want to figure out the optiimal progression routes to shorten your time spent playing.  It also allows players to show their skill by letting you raise or lower your wealth based on your own DECISIONS.
I find myself drawn to its simple appearance yet complex skill system.  Sometimes you'll be trying to do something like recruit a companion and you'll notice you're 1-2 points shy of the requirements.  Which means somewhere else there's a companion you can recruit to raise your skill rating.  So much of the game is about exploring, reading hints, and figuring out where you're supposed to go and in what order to raise those skills.  It puts a huge emphasis on exploration and discovery and the wealthiest players will know the best secrets to making fortunes.
Give it a try if it sounds good to you and drop it if it isn't your cup of tea.  But personally, I'm loving every minute of it and it's easy to play around anyone's schedule since you only need to assign tasks and then check back later when they're completed.

I have spend quite a handful of hours on this game. What I will say about the game is that had you asked me a few months back, or even at the beginning of this year, what I felt about this game. I'd say it is polarizing at best. As it stands now I enjoy coming back to the game every now and then. I can't really get myself to play this religiously anymore and spend 4+ hours on it every day. But I usually come back just to mess around a lot. I'll structure my thoughts a bit more now to give you an overview of the game.
TL; DR.
Pros:
-Beautiful Visuals
-Fast-paced combat
-Tons of acrobatic and responive controls
-Large arsenal of weapons and warframes
-Microtransactions that aren't necessary to play the game
-[DE]Steve is Bae
Cons:
-A lot of grinding
-Some mission rewards are really questionable
-Cats and Dogs are vastly inferior to Sentinels because of Vaccum
-Archwing mode is highly uncontrollable and generally not very fun
-While you can craft almost any weapon in the game, the cost for some is unforgiving (Just google Hema)
-The boss fights are a joke. Either they go down too fast or they're ball bustingly frustrating
-[DE]Steve's beard is better than mine.
Story:
Already in the description of the game. Second of all, the speculation and tidbits of lore are pretty intriguing. Personally back in 2015 there were a lot more mysteries running around than I have seen today. Question like who are the Tenno? Are we people inside suits? Or are we the suits themselves? Is the Stalker a warframe? Are we robots or biological creatures.
While many of these old questions have been answered some new mysteries arose with the new ship design and doors appearing inside of it, with eople speculating the purposes of these new rooms. Overall though, I don't play Warframe for the story.
Gameplay
By far the most important element don't you agree?
Warframe is what I would classify as: Third-Person Hack and Slash/Shooter.
One of the most appealing elements of Warframe is the fastpaced action. I rarely struggle with the controls with some very few things that don't happen all that often. You can do all sorts of acrobatic manuevers to move around the map faster, close in on enemies and finish them off at range with one of the 100's of firearms in the game, or over 100 different melee weapons.
Warframe sees you take control of a Warframe (There I go), with 4 unique activated abilities and a passive. At the beginning you get 3 warframes to choose from, but all other warframes can be attained in the game without spending a dime. You can also find or buy weapon blueprints to craft new weapons. Your weapons and warframes can be upgraded with mods that you obtain by playing, these mods can increase your weapons fire rate, damage, or even their chance to inflict status effects. Your warframe can be upgraded with faster sprints, more health, stronger abilities, more duration on abilities or less ability costs and much more.
While there are not many in-game ressources to help you out with what to go for next. You don't know exactly what planet to move unto afterwards, nor what weapons are good unless you happen to join up with either a good player with a weapon and warframe you want real bad and you google it. Or someone is friendly enough to offer their help to you. Granted there is the Region chat, but if you take to the subreddit for Warframe you might quickly find that it is a rather... Interesting place.
I absolutely love the gameplay in Warframe, fast paced action with a large arsenal of weapons and warframes to add to your collection.
Missions
You have a variety of mission types to choose from. Some are known as endless missions, in this category you will find 4 common ones: Defense, Survival,Excavation and Interception. These missions quite literally can go on forever. You are however given the option to extract from these missions after either 5 waves of enemies (Defense), 5 minutes (Survival), 1 wave (Interception) or 1 Excavator drill (Excavation). Other endless missions do exist but they haven't always been around. Those missions are Infested Salvage & Defection. Infested Salvage has you repair data consoles, creating decontamination zones around them so data can be extracted from these consoles. Whilst you avoid your warframe from dying from the heavy infestation in the air.
Defection has you escort VIP's through an infested ship to safety, and avoiding them dying due to the toxins in the air.
Other mission types include: Spy, Rescue, Capture, Extermination and Sabotage.
Spy and rescue missions are stealthbased. Luckily stealth is optional throughout not only a mjaority of the level but also around the main objectives. Albeit it does make things go a lot smoother if you stay quiet. Spy has you extract valuable data from databanks or datavaults while avoiding secuirty measures. Rescue has you saving a Tenno operative or ally from prison. Should you be spotted on your way to these key location you will not be failed for not keeping it stealthy. Being stealthy is mainly in the rooms with objectives. Setting of the alarm in these rooms gives you a timer, in which you can still complete the objective. Fail all 3 vaults in spy and you get a mission failed. Fail rescuing the prisoner and you are failed as well.
Capture has you hunt down and detain a person with valuable information the Tenno can use. Exterminate has you flatout kill x amount of enemies. And Sabotage has you going in and sabotaging things from mining drills, computers and even reactors.
There is also Archwing. But for the most part Archwing reuses the same gamemodes. Plus everyone in general agrees that Archwing sucks. Myself included unfortunately.
Visuals
On the lowest graphics setting which I used to play with, I never thought Warframe was worth writing home about. I liked the designs of the warframes and some of the weapons.
Finally getting a stronger PC and allowing myself to playing at higher graphics all I can say is that the visuals are impressive for a game that is F2P. The lighting effects while they can be a bit distracting are awesome and gorgeous. The models are very well designed with the polys and vertices not easily visible.
Some of the grand levels such as Plains of Eidolon can be stunning to look at, set against the sun. Definitely a beautiful game.
Platinum
The premium currency of warframe. You can buy this for real money. BUT unlike other companies I won't name (But one rhymes with Balafronic Farts). The premium currency is first of all available to you even if you do not spend a dime on the game. Should you happen to acquire pieces for weapons or warframes that happen to Prime. These parts alongside mods and some other unique weapons, can be sold to other players in exchange for platinum. A couple of external websites provide you with the tools to view the typical asking price for these items and some even set up a market place where you can see what people are selling or put things up for sale yourself.
New players may think: But can I really make that much plat from selling things?
The answer is: Yes. I have made over 3-4k platinum on sales through my playtime. And I'll be honest, i could have made a lot more if I wasn't as lazy as I am.
Final Verdict
As I wrote this review I more or less realized the things that made Warframe polarizing for me is not there anymore with the exception of the grindy element of the game. (I still dread farming for relics due to how boring it is). Aside from that one element annoying me, the game has actually made things better. My main complaint was the design of the recent PoE update. But I am glad to see it has been largely changed for the better.
I have rambled on for long enough. While it is not a game for everyone. I do encourage you to try it out. Preferably with a friend who has more experience with the game. You can always go to the subreddit, the community in general tends to be very friendly.

Not a review REVIEW but more of just my opinion on the game,here goes:
This is an absolute love/hate case, the game has flaws, but the strong points of it are very good. so low lows,high highs.
Mind that all that i'm saying comes as my opinion afterplaying a total of almost 700 hours, 300 of wich were back in 2013 on it's early versions,400 just recently as of the last few months.
First of all it's easily one of the fairest F2P games i've played to this day,in the sense that you're not paying to win,you're paying for convenience. every piece of equipment,warframe,mod,item can be acquired for free, and outside items and equipment locked behind events you can get them at any time,if you want something from an event not currently active in the game,you can use the trade chat and trade item for item,or use the premium currency to buy said items/equipment from other players,and people are always looking for not just event locked things,but just things you can get any day,and they will pay you premium currency for it,as such you're able to attain the premium currency that can be used for the only thing it's absolutely needed to: equipment slots and cosmetics.
With that said,both the grind and attaining premium currency feels like it has a snowball effect of "I don't have this weapon,so let me grind for it > now i have this weapon,in case i get the parts to craft it,i can sell it off to another player". this goes on up to a point you have so much equipment it will be rare for you to not have X or Y,so you'll have more things available to sell to other players for premium currency.
That said, once again, while you can use the premium currency to purchase equipment(limited to regular equipment in the shop) it's almost always a waste to do so,as everything is easily crafted. with the player market turning towards selling rare mods and prime equipment,wich,once again,are not an horrible grind,and there are many ways to manipulate the RNG in your favor.
That out of the way,let me go into the elephant in the room,the gameplay and the gameplay loop.
Do you like meaningful grind? the journey is what it's about and not the destination kinda thing? then warframe is for you. howrever,if you'd just like to keep going foward constantly without stopping to play the same content much,then it's gonna be an horrible experience.
The game is very repetitive, and you're in a constant grind for X,and on the road for X you'll get Y and Z,and play around with equipments Y and Z,so in a way even if you aim too high you'll constantly get new weapons in between the start and end of a grind for a specific new weapon, the enemies are separated in 3 main factions,with some smaller factions in between for unique enemies,so expect to see a lot of the same enemies within the same faction.
You have incredible maneuverability, it feels like Gunz:The Duel 1 but with much more freedom and that takes less to master, the combat itself feels great and works togheter with that maneuverability to make an unique experience,this makes the shooting so much more fun when you're constantly in movement,in the air jumping like a no-grav acrobat and shooting down whole squads of enemies before touching the ground.
As far as melee goes,it feels like it's "better than your average TPS but not amazing" at first,but the further you go you will find both the amazing variety in weapons,mods and things like stances,wich will give you entire new movesets and change completely how you approach melee combat,be something focused for hit'n' run tatics,specific combos for crowd control,specific combos for taking out single targets,specific combos made just to increase a combo counter that multiplies damage,etc.
Plus the further you'll go,alongside a great story on story quests(some of wich can be co-oped but some later ones can only be played solo,full of cutscenes and moments that only make sense if you are alone) you'll be introduced to many new mechanics that open up more customization options alongside maybe making you rethink your playstyle to suit the new mechanics as they are introduced.
that's where the best part of the game comes from,it's about experimenting with all the tools you're given,a shame it's on a lot of occasion on very repetitive scenarios,and that may turn off people from the game,howrever the sheer variety of weapons,warframes with different powers and special mechanics on later bosses and stages wich feel much more amazing than the rest of the game is good enough to keep me going.
So it all comes down to,do you enjoy being a "space ninja" ? because that's what you're getting and that's what you should expect,everything else is a bonus,it's all about the "rule of cool" and finding cooler♥♥♥♥♥♥as you go on.
If you don't then it's not for you,but if you do,it will be an amazing experience.

You are Shay Patrick Cormac, a colonial Irishman trying to find his place in the war between the Assassins and Templars. Proving to be a skillful Assassin, Shay must overcome his habits and doubts in order to become the Assassin he always wanted to be. However, his doubts still haunt him, often having disputes with fellow Assassins and his Mentor’s guidance and judgement. He wanted to fight for humanity’s freewill, but feels that the Brotherhood has been distracted by the race for the pieces of Eden. When Shay embarked on a mission to retrieve a piece of Eden, he mistakenly mishandles the artifact triggering a devastating natural disaster that leaves thousands of innocents dead. Shay blames those who sent him in the first place, and tries to convince his Mentor that this pursuit for more artifacts would only doom more to die. However, his words fall ignored, leaving Shay no choice but to betray those he once loved in order to stop them from repeating his mistake. He no longer is an Assassin, but an Assassin-Hunter, a Templar.
I don’t care if fans consider this AC game nothing more than AC Black Flag 2.0, or that this is the shortest AC game. It is definitely one of the most unique and compelling AC story in this franchise. You finally get to play as a Templar until the story ends. Really drawing out that nothing is black and white in the AC series. There are Templar agents that have noble intentions and there are Assassins who are ruthless and corrupt. The story sets in the Ohio River Valley and the North Atlantic during the French and Indian War and covers the events between AC BF and AC III. Yes, the gameplay and graphics are very identical with Black Flag, there are few new gadgets and a tweaked economy system that still can give Rogue it’s own identity.
There are familiar faces that are welcoming, such as Achilles, Adewale, and Haytham Kenway, and the story gives off rather a very engaging experience. Definitely not one that a fan of this series should pass. I enjoyed it very much.

This game was NOT what I was promised. I was told that the Denuvo DRM would preventing me from enjoying the game, that it would ruin my SSD, that the game would lag every 20 minutes as at phones home, as one review attests, written by a user on a state-of-the-art Tandy 1000 computer. And so far, it's done NONE of those things.
I mean, I thought we might be on our way to a bad time when the game wouldn't recognize my Dualshock 4, but it turns out my 3rd party drivers weren't configured correctly. I want to blame it on Denuvo so bad, because I have no awareness of my own confirmation bias, but I'm afraid I can't do that. The controller worked fine with no configuration required within the game itself, so the promise of broken controller support is... broken.
The game runs at a smooth and consistent framerate (probably 60 frames per second, though I didn't count them), so the promise of poor performance was not kept. The game did not attempt to access the internet once it started, so doesn't even phone home constantly like I was promised.
But here's the worst part. After quitting the game, exiting Steam, disabling my network adapter, loading Steam in Offline mode, and attempting to run the game... IT STARTED UP JUST FINE! Holy f**king s**tcakes are you s**ting me?! That was the biggest promise the community made, broken like my dreams of moving out of dad's basement. I was promised a terrible time, and I didn't get what I was promised.
What's that? How's the game itself? Oh, it's absolutely fantastic, are you kidding? I haven't had such a nostalgia rush since... well yesterday when I bought Starcraft: Remastered, but I digress.
Realtalk: The DRM concerns are overblown. I won't blame you if you want to avoid this one for philosophical reasons, but as a practical matter, I wouldn't have known the DRM was there if you hadn't told me, and you'd be missing out on the best Sonic game since S3&K. (Edit: And after 3.5 hours, that still holds.)

Where to start with Therian Saga... well its a very unique game that really stands out with a friendly and tightly knit community. It starts rather slow but I quickly found myself playing 5 characters with weeks invested in its gameplay. It's certainly not everyones cup of tea as it does have timers and the ability to rush these timers without a cooldown on the premium items, which is basically my only complaint. This would typically turn me off of a game very quickly, however the craftable machines and items along with a complex skill system adds a deep and compelling layer to the gameplay. The game rewards players for perserverance and dedication over the long haul much like Ultima Online or other MUD games of the past. Over a period of time you can become a mogul within its resource system cutting out your own little niche for yourself as you wheel and deal with real players instead of using NPC shops.
There are far more positives then negatives but It's not for people with low patience or subpar intelligence, as they would just get lost within the vast economy that is Therian Saga, I'd suggest you try it out! If you find yourself playing a lot and longing for more then drop the devs some cash for the premium account upgrades which make the game even more enjoyable which really are not any more expensive then a triple A title.
You can argue its pay to advance which some consider pay to win and you would have a pretty valid argument... however there is absolutley no win condition and it's more about long term goals then it is short ones, it can be played completley free and still be able to accumulate your own empire. This makes it very unlike facebook and mobile games that it often gets compared to.
If you have played a MUD before in the past then I urge you to try out something different in todays market of flashy graphics and twitch gameplay you may be pleasantly surprised at the change of pace.

Ah Therian Saga; what can I say without coming off as a total fanboy?
Well let's start honest; do NOT play this game if you're looking for anything fastpaced because it's anything but that. However, if you like games that have a more than friendly community or games that have a treacherous amount of depth in them and don't mind spending hours or even days to build something you can really be proud of you really SHOULD check this game out.
Therian Saga is an adventure-RPG of an asynchronous nature; a semi-idler if you will. You start off by creating a character get through a small tutorial that shows you the most basic of mechanics and at the end reach the Kingdom of Hawkoria....what you want to do after that is up to you. Want to dungeon-delve and get all the goodies; then there's plenty of dungeons for you to discover and explore. Fancy yourself a trader? Well with over 10 disciplines and 3 crafts within that discipline (MOST of which intertwine to boot) you wouldn't be the first player who would spend their days crafting clothes to sell to others (either directly or via an AH). No; you look like more of the landbaron type; well why not build as many homes as you wish in the far corners of the map; maybe add some labour-farms to that so you can sell your ores, cloths, gems to that trader? Want to do it ALL? Well there's no stopping THAT either.
In short Therian Saga is much like any MMORPG out there, just asynchronous.
Pro's
* Huge amount of depth in the game.
* Freemium (you CAN buy preemium currency but it's more convenience than needed to "win" this game)
* Asychronous the game goes on while you leave meaning workkers keep working, timers keep running; stuff gets done. Ideal for people who have a life on the side
* Extremely friendly and helpfull community
* Vigilant and present Mod/Dev (support)
* Great story
* nice Graphics (if you're into the handdrawn style that is)
Con's
- Waiting games aren't for everyone and expect to wait....a lot...and then some
- Lack of a more advanced tutorial (you WILL need a guide for this one; it's too big without)
- no Party-up mechanic
- Hardly any PvP
my verdict 10/10 would chop cedar to provide for my guild's festival days again; party up people

This game is something I've been looking for ever since I played a little indy flash game somewhere on the internet when I was 14. It had interesting lore, trading and combat in unique space mercenary environment made by someone who had a great idea and new how to code. The map is massive but divided into indivdual systems to make it easier to handle, each system tracks your reputation and has every odd job to military contract you could want. You can customize your ship and change out and upgrade equipment to tailor your ship to the jobs you want to have. The game is meduim paced from starting out, I upgraded my ship's size about 5 hours in for the first time. I've barely scratched the surface of this game but I have played plenty to give it a good recomendation; that being said I recomend getting a key mapping chart due to the complexity. It is a game that makes you think and feel like you are immersed in this world, added with a backdrop of stunning nebulae and planets with a swelling orchestral sci-fi soundtrack.

Probably the most tactical game I know of.  The tactical control of your units and the ability to test out scenarios with the enemy units at the same time as you try to counter your opponent is just perfect.  The units are balanced well and the additional Red DLC with those units also provide an even deeper level of strategy in the game (along with it's own campaign as well).  The controls are mainly all done via mouse and are really easy to pick up, the tutorial is straight forward and explains everything very well.  You learn tactics and the various strengths and weaknesses of each unit as you play and advance through campaign or online matches.
The campaign is huge and difficult, the ai will destroy you if you do not try to counter it in your own moves, and the sheer number of levels in the campaign make this totally worth any price it is set at, definitely worth full price and then some.  The missions you play are beautifully made and the story is intrigueing and thought provoking, keeping you guessing and wanting to play more and more.  The levels are randomly generated every time you start a new mission or fail the one you are on, adding to the difficulty and replayability, though you will probably take a serious amount of time to beat the huge campaign.  The various game modes are integrated into the campaign as different mission scenarios, like basically killing everyone, defending a position or key person, infiltrating a base and assassinating a key person, etc. etc.
The soundtrack is also great for transitions between different situations, in-between levels and on the menu screen.  I would buy it again just for the soundtrack alone, I think it is that good.
The online is still just as active as it was on day one when I bought it, with just as many people and game modes being played.  The huge number of online game modes that you can play online are also available in skirmish offline for practice against the ai, and help you to better understand the different game modes that you will come to play online.
While there is the secondary account for loggin in, you just enter it once and it keeps all of your online stats and games synced so you can login from anywhere and keep playing, not intrusive or painful like origin or other third party drm's.  The account you use is tied to your steam name so you just click login when you start the game and it literally only takes one extra second to do.
Has a replay feature after finishing an online match or campaign mission that allows you to upload directly to youtube, after logging in through their menu, and share your amazing victories or glorious defeats with the world, or just save for reviewing strategy later, whatever suits your fancy.
*     The only problem I have is that sometimes when I try to set chains of commands for a particular unit using the timeline aspect (I don't remember the exact name for the button) it can be difficult to get orders to work in the sequence I want them to, but I then just try out scenarios before making my moves final anyway and it usually does not cause a problem.

A fun, fast and cheap alternative to Mario Party and Dokapon Kingdom. Luck is a huge component in this game, and while randomness can change the flow of a game immediately, there actually is a lot of subtle strategy that goes into deciding what cards to put in your characters' decks, and because the game is so heavily based on luck, swaying the game in your favor takes a lot of practice.
For example, if you unlock the playable version of the board monsters, your advantage is that if someone KOs you they get less wins than they would normally get for KOing a player. It's fun trying to think of ways to use cards that can take advantage of such a weird ability like that. There are many such playable characters in this game, re-playability is very high, and the developers have been making updates and releasing new characters at a steady pace since the game came out three years ago. The music is also quite good and the game is adorable and just makes you feel happy, despite the rage that this game does tend to induce.
I highly recommend picking this game up to play with friends. You will all be screaming at each other, and have a good time.

Ups:
The controls are spot on and easy to use.
Some missions make the game exceedingly fun.
This game lets you have fun, but be serious at the exact same time.
Remember the Focus Rifle in Halo Reach? They upgraded it to max, and they will drain your shield in no time.
Downs:
The AI could be harder, it's real easy to kill an elite as you need to melee it two times.

But here, let's talk specifically about the AI.
The setting is a little weird actually, it's in Halo 4, but, correct me if I'm wrong, but there were no brutes in Halo 4 right? Because they are in here.
The Elites are very easy to kill, 2-3 melee attacks and they're dead.
Grunts, easy as always, really no con there.
Jackals, medium, I mean they have shields and they are very hard to avoid for me, so I'd give them a medium because when their shields are down they are very easy to kill.
Drones, for people who don't know what drones are, look in the link below this sentence, anyway, they're somewhat hard, as you can't melee them so they can be a little difficult.
Brutes, complicated, they swarm into battle on jetpacks so you can't kill them instantly, they take a few hits to hit and are a little hard.

In Halo 4, there were spartans that would help you in battle, same as a marine that has shields and a little more health. Torn Banner, the devs of this game, have either completely forgotten how to patch simple things, or are simply too lazy to fix them. I'm seeing nothing but negative reviews for this game and it breaks my heart. After nothing but Sonic Boom and similar nonsense from the Sonic franchise, this is more than a breath of fresh air--it's a mainline shot of pure nostalgia.
Personally, I grew up on such games as Sonic CD, Sonic the Hedgehog 3 and Knuckles, and even (oh horror) Sonic R Racing. This game throws in new levels, new mechanics, new characters, in the midst of recalling what was best about those games, and drops like a hot potato what irritated us about them (When's the last time you played an honest-to-goodness FUN water level in a 2-d platformer? And yet Sonic Mania brings back 3's Hydrocity Zone and makes it FUN, rather than a hunt-for-the-oxygen-bubbles panic-fest.)
I don't know what the modern gamer expects from the rebirth of retro Sonic gaming, but as a young man who grew up loving and raging at the old games in equal measure, and has since grown very accustomed to the conventions of modern gaming, this game is exactly what it's supposed to be, and it SHINES. Five out of five stars from this reviewer.

Sonic Mania as a game is more polished and better designed in many ways than the original Genesis Sonic games. Sonic Mania plays like the Genesis games and yet fixes most of the problems that the older games had. There are no levels that are tedious to artificially lengthen game time (ergo Sandopolis or Marble Zones). Many of the repeat zones in Sonic Mania are actually more fun than their original counterparts such as Oil Ocean and Metallic Madness. These traits make Sonic Mania stand out as the game is created as if the creators had many more years of experience than they did when the original Genesis Trilogy was created.
The only issue Sonic Mania has is that not enough of the game is original. 2/3s of the game is filled with older zones which is dissapointing because the four new zones are great and stand out. Sonic Mania could've shined even brighter if it didn't cling so much to the Genesis days (i.e. having only local multiplayer even though online multiplayer would've been fun to have).
I encourage the return of the classic style of gameplay for Sonic The Hedgehog and I hope succesive games come out with more new and improved content.

I do play Therian for quite some time now (off steam) and i wanted to address some issues i see in the reviews:
It is an idle game:
Well yes and no. It is a game for patient people, everything takes time, but it is supposed to be played both on and offline. When you are online, you usually do quests, run dungeons and kill bosses, when offline you harvest, craft and try to improve your skills. Actually the more of the bosses and dungeons you have unlocked, the more online time it takes you to run them, so much so that at the end game ppl usually just do the run on the top bosses, set their queues and that's most of their online play - and even that takes them quite a long time. Personally it takes me way too much time online to even do the bosses :(.
It is pay to win:
Definitely not. You can pay to go faster, you can pay to be first to reach some milestone, but that's about it. Having a good guild actually takes you a lot further than paying money. There is no PvP except for the arena (which is used mostly to improve combat skills) so paying will not help you there. You could say that paying can get you to be the first to be able to craft some item and "corner the market" but that does last usually for like 1 week, then other ppl get there. Demand actually far exceeds offer (on older servers), since most of ppl don't spend time to make items to sell and what they make they use themselves, for alts and guilds. In Therian there is actually constant need for huge amounts of even the lowest level materials and crafts, for guild projects or as a consumable "fuel" (blades and chisels in particular) so even new player can contribute a lot.
Is Therian completely free to play?
Well actually it is not. While you don't need any consumables from the shop if you are patient, to do the high end content you need to buy more weapon/tool slots and usually ppl usually also buy more companion/queue slots. Also you have to pay if you want to make alts. But those are pretty much one time payments that are imo quite inexpensive compared to amount of content the game offers.
I don't know what to do, the game doesn't give me enough information:
Therian is more or less a MMORPG, it is meant to be played with interactions with other players. Ask questions, find a guild to join. Players in Therian are mostly very helpful when it comes to advice, or even material help for new players on old servers.
Honestly, the biggest problem I personally have with the game are the random rolls. If you are unlucky, you can fail to gain skill up on the craft that gives you 95% chance of skill up and takes weeks to get all materials for it, or you can do the task that has 10% chance of giving you something 50 times in a row and not get it. But then again there are people who are lucky, that's the unfortunate way the random works.
The most fun in the game in my opinion comes from interacting with your guild mates and from sense of accomplishment you get when some long guild project is finished.

Therian Saga is the very definition of an idle MMO. Unfortunately, because of how it is built and executed, everything takes ages to complete. Want to mine/gather this? You need to mine/gather this to improve your skill. Can't grind out this task anymore to improve your skill? Find an item that raises it. Can't find an item to raise a stat? Hire an underling to add to your skill level. Can't hire an underling? Sleep for 10 real-time hours to replenish all of that energy you spent trying to train your skills.
The game also has a shop, with a ton of time-saving items and convience items. They require in-game paid currency to buy. It just isn't worth playing.
