Game is special in its own way and can be not for everyone. But i find it to be a hidden gem.
Many activity types are timer based and game is meant to be played at that pace but there are active gameplay as well and one can easily spend 2+ hours a day on dungeoneering and planning stuff for passive tasks or learning how to do something.
So its good for those kind of players who dont rush and like a slow and steady type of games. Think kind of adventure with building strategy(especially on guild scale) with infuse of personal action. With stylish picture, lots of different skills to master and new approach in many things compared to most games out there.
What is game about - i would say its mostly about exploration and planning stuff to do and reap what you ve planned, while enjoying story, quests and new possibilities you will unlock. The only PvP is arena (and probably we will get some guild vs guild later), so game is mostly about pve and exploring new lands and story. And its not as easy or fast as it seems to - there are a lot of quests or hidden places to discover and new zones are usualy locked behind some storyline quest chains.
Active part of gameplay is about dungeoneering, questing, traveling and exploring for new sites on map.
Passive part is about setting up tasks and harvesting/hunting/resource obtaining or crafting activity or recruiting new companions/taming wild bests. any tasks you ve planned will continue even if you log off.
In actual game you will have to combine both types of gameplay but it depends on player what he will focus more. Most actions require to spend some amount of energy and you can set "sleep" action to restore it back.
Game provide really deep and intresting to explore crafting and building system with lots of material combinations and ways to experiment. Things might look confusing at start but people in general chat will be able to help and guide you most of the time - so dont be afraid to ask for advice.
There is ingame housing system for both players and guilds. And is not cosmetic thing but actually VERY important part of gameplay and ingame progression. You will need to buy concession papers (look around in Military District in capital city of Hawkoria) to get your own homeland spot. Homes are used as storage space for both materials and companions you dont need for current activity, as a base for different buildings from crafting stations of all sorts to mines or hunting grounds, or resting buildings where you can recruit new companions.
There is a player trading system - you need to visit and access market district in city to put items on sell or get whatever you bought. One can use mail to send items/money but need to be at location with mailbox to do that.
- I think main fault of new pplayers is getting stuck at basic tasks like chopping the wood or hunting hares at starting locations for days - you wont see what game has to offer this way and will find it boring in a week. Go explore and do quests - to adventure! This way you will see new things faster and find how much is there to discover and feel game overal perspective.
- you can zoom map out too see continent and zones names
- many tasks will require you to have certain level of both activity related skill AND land skill depending on place.
- use equipment / companion bonus / tools / jewelry / potions to rise your skill if needed.
- knowledge and undestanding of game is a skill of its own and you will need to master it
- There is a browser map which may really help (different languages included)
- use Therian Saga official guide page to see where is what or which craft skills you need to get something.
- use general chat if you feel lost, this game might seems complex and confusing at start.
- use "sleep" action to restore energy, you can do it in wild camp or at Inns providing some additional bonus energy for a little cost.
- buy any amount of Blue Crowns (game currency) with real money to get "readiness" buff so you will be able to set tasks after sleep task and energy restored from sleep will be counted in.
Give it a try it definetly deserves it. I find its a hidden gem of semi-idle games, while not perfect but really good with with its own style and ingame depth. If you will find its your cap of tea it can become your small game for months or even more and game is expanding slow but constantly as dev add new territories and content. Community is great as well and ready to help.

I bought this game, because I wanted to customize my ship and then have a "sandbox" environment to kick around in. After half an hour of playing, I realized I'd bitten off way more than I'd ever wanted to chew, so I put the game away for months. I came back at it with the intent of finally mastering the thing. After spending an hour and a half beating my head against the control options, I finally learned how to toggle inertial flying and began to work my way through the first few frankly boring missions and got to the race against the AI ship. After half a dozen frustrating goes of bouncing helplessly around and then out of the course "rings", I had my fill of the Evo after 4 hours of playing.
I really wanted to give this game a positive recommendation, I really did, but it all comes down to the game trying too hard to be too much. Yes, the hardcore space simulator enthusiast looking for perfect immersion will LOVINGLY CARESS this game all night long (so if that's you, I TOTALLY recommend this game), but if you are a more casual gamer looking for a fun sandbox space combat game you can jump into and start kicking around in immediately? This is the exact opposite of that.
The controls are designed for a high level of investment in both time and energy in learning how to play. Ultimately, to get the best experience, a full function joystick and throttle are NOT OPTIONAL. Don't even buy the game unless you have a very robust controller. You'll have to devote yourself to memorizing dozens of key commands and unfortunately the opposite of intuitive control options, which is the only serious knock I have against the game from a critical standpoint. The control options desperately need better laying out (IE: movement controls need to be separate from head swivel controls need to be separate from combat controls, etc.)
Compared to other space themed games (ie: Wing Commander, X-Wing, Freelancer, Colony Wars, etc.), Evo is orders of magnitude more difficult to play, being marketted as a "game" (which it is technically), but it's more accurate to call it a space simulator with game elements bootstrapped on. So I simply can't recommend this game to anyone that isn't a hardcore space simulator enthusiast.
Unfortunately, my search for a nice middle ground space combat sim continues.

TIS-100 is a great game by Zachtronics of SpaceChem fame.
It's probably the ugliest looking game I've played in decades. I mean Pong ugly. But the game itself is so brilliant, you get so absorbed in it, that you stop even noticing the aesthetics.
On the surface, TIS-100 is about assembly programming. On each level you are given a programming task: read this sequence and find the max; read these two numbers and divide one by the other, finding the quotient and remainder; etc. Most of these tasks would be trivial in any modern programming language.
The challenge comes from the computational model. What you have to work with is some number of processing nodes, some of which are connected to each other, which allows primitive message passing. Each node is extremely limited: it only has two registers, and can't even work with both at the same time; one is a backup register and can't be the source or target of arithmetic operations. This means that even simple tasks take ingenuity to perform. On top of that, each node only fits 15 lines of code, which means you have to squeeze computation out of every command.
In most levels you only have some network of processing nodes, so in effect what you have is a deterministic finite automaton (although with a huge number of states). In some you have one "stack memory" node, i.e. a pushdown automaton. In only a few do you have two stack nodes, which makes for a Turing-complete system. (And, appropriately, one programming task in such a level is sorting. It is well-known that pushdown automata can't do general sorting.) Actually what I just said doesn't exactly capture the computer science at play, since the very limited instruction set makes for additional restrictions. It's an interesting theory problem to model and understand the TIS-100 computers more fully!
I don't think someone totally untrained in CS can finish this game. But if you do know some of the standard ideas and/or are used to modern programming languages, TIS-100 is an excellent way to think outside the usual patterns and explore how surprisingly powerful even very weak models of computation can be.
There's a story in the background too which I thought was well done.

I'm seeing nothing but negative reviews for this game and it breaks my heart. After nothing but Sonic Boom and similar nonsense from the Sonic franchise, this is more than a breath of fresh air--it's a mainline shot of pure nostalgia.
Personally, I grew up on such games as Sonic CD, Sonic the Hedgehog 3 and Knuckles, and even (oh horror) Sonic R Racing. This game throws in new levels, new mechanics, new characters, in the midst of recalling what was best about those games, and drops like a hot potato what irritated us about them (When's the last time you played an honest-to-goodness FUN water level in a 2-d platformer? And yet Sonic Mania brings back 3's Hydrocity Zone and makes it FUN, rather than a hunt-for-the-oxygen-bubbles panic-fest.)
I don't know what the modern gamer expects from the rebirth of retro Sonic gaming, but as a young man who grew up loving and raging at the old games in equal measure, and has since grown very accustomed to the conventions of modern gaming, this game is exactly what it's supposed to be, and it SHINES. Five out of five stars from this reviewer.

Sonic Mania as a game is more polished and better designed in many ways than the original Genesis Sonic games. Sonic Mania plays like the Genesis games and yet fixes most of the problems that the older games had. There are no levels that are tedious to artificially lengthen game time (ergo Sandopolis or Marble Zones). Many of the repeat zones in Sonic Mania are actually more fun than their original counterparts such as Oil Ocean and Metallic Madness. These traits make Sonic Mania stand out as the game is created as if the creators had many more years of experience than they did when the original Genesis Trilogy was created.
The only issue Sonic Mania has is that not enough of the game is original. 2/3s of the game is filled with older zones which is dissapointing because the four new zones are great and stand out. Sonic Mania could've shined even brighter if it didn't cling so much to the Genesis days (i.e. having only local multiplayer even though online multiplayer would've been fun to have).
I encourage the return of the classic style of gameplay for Sonic The Hedgehog and I hope succesive games come out with more new and improved content.

Energy bar, limited task queue size, spend real money to speed up tasks/add more tasks to queue....  It's a facebook game in disguise.  A nice facebook game, but definitely a facebook game.
If you LIKE Facebook games, then you'll love this.  You play for 10-15 minutes at a time, just long enough to queue up some quests/whatever.  You queue 8 hours of stuff at a time, so the game has the default 3-check-ins-per-day you expect from a facebook game.
Roughly 25% of your time is burned "refilling energy", unless you spend real money for energy refills.  This makes the game pay to win, since anyone paying will progress 25% more quickly than those not paying.  Real money can also buy you better equipment, personal/guild NPC stores, to insta-finish queued quests, etc....
Basically this game is just like any facebook game where you have to build stuff, and queue up building upgrades/new buildings/research.  Just replace buildings/research with "quests".
It IS possible to buy the "premium currency" for gold on the auction house, just as long as someone pays real money for the premium currency and is willing to sell it.  Of course, this cripples your in-game currency income, while the pay-to-winner leaps forward through the game at the speed of money.
All in all, it's good for a Facebook game, but again, still a Facebook game being disguised as an MMO.  If you THINK this qualifies as an MMORPG, then every idle game with chat qualifies as an MMORPG.
tl;dr This is a pay-to-win game written in silverlight, exactly like every other pay-to-win Facebook game claiming to be an MMO.

Let's Review Assassin's Creed Rogue!
Like the title says, you join the adventure of Shay Cormac, one of the Assassin's that turns on them, siding with the Templars, and if you are aware of the Assassins/Templars War, this is a big deal.
- Shows you the other side, the Templar side while still having that lifeline to the Assassin's.
- A storyline that tells you a different side of the same coin, well written and well executed in this game.
- Brings back the open world and naval warfare that made this Franchise great.
- Serves as a stepping stone to Assassins creed 3 and a connection to Assassins Creed Unity.
- Beautiful graphics like always, and yet some improvements.
- Big variety of activities,  environments and mission types.
- Some graphical glitches but nothing that's game breaking.
- Uplay connection that sometimes interferes with the game, but it's a rare ocasion ( thank god ).
- Lack of Multiplayer.
: Assassin's Creed Rogue, let's you experience the other side, the side you've fought so many times, introducing new mechanics blended with old ones. Its a good game, but can at sometimes feel like an extension of Black Flag, but if you enjoyed that one, you'll enjoy this one without a doubt. I give it a 7.2 out of 10.

This game is really cool! Unfortunately, it's nigh unplayable. After poking around for a bit, doing some mining and contracts, I've realized that I really don't want to play, any more. Flying around an open world universe in your own pile of space scrap is a good feeling, one that deserves an interface worthy of its task. Unfortunately, it's just abysmal. Your starting ship starts out with one cargo hold. Sounds ok, right? You can only put one type of item in each hold, even though it'll hold 25 of that item. When mining, each asteroid gives three ore, which means you're missing out on two-thirds of the ore, since they're not compatible with each other.
Ok, you can upgrade your ship to five cargo holds. Fine, but the miner stacks to the lowest cargo hold that isn't full, so if you have 1 platinum ore each in holds 2 through 5, it'll still put any new platinum in hold 1, meaning that if you actually wanted to get some diamond ore from the same asteroid, you'll have to trash one of the platinums to make room for it, instead of (logically) moving it to one of the holds that already has that same item in it.
One time, I got a contract to mine 25 platinum. As it works out, I ended up with about 32. Unfortunately, about half was in hold 2, and the other half was in hold 3. When I got back to the station, it said "contract failed". O.o My best guess is that the game is too dumb to figure out that 16 + 16 = 32, which is more than enough for the contract. Another mining contract flew me right into a planet as soon as I jumped to the waypoint it gave me. Yet another didn't give me a waypoint at all, so I flew to an asteroid field and saw, yet again, "contract failed". I failed a mining contract by flying to an asteroid field?!?
Ok, that's most of my experience. I also happened to run into a hostile ship. He decided to engage me, and I gladly took the challenge. Unfortunately, the starter ship couldn't even dent his shields... Guess I won't be roaming around, looking for fights to get into. There are a lot of other problems, mostly with the interface. Variety is also sorely lacking. Sure, there's a few ships you can buy, but no one ship or weapon is particularly different from any other. Their stats aren't all that different, either.
Meh, 4/10. A great idea, implemented very badly.

Each player can draw cards that can influence the game in various ways.
When two players meet they can battle which consists of both players throwing dice one for attack one for defense or evasion.  The combat results in someone's health reaching zero they K.O. and have half their stars taken and the winning player is awarded 2 wins. The aim the game is to collect 200 stars or 14 wins and then land on your or another player's home base.  As the game is dice based and pretty much decided entirely by chance it can create some rage inducing moments like Mario Party. however, overall the game is very enjoyable and keeps bringing me back even after I leave in a swamp of frustration.

A lot like Hero Clix table top. The fastest characters (i.e- the characters who can dash the most often) have a severe advantage. Combat works in 4 phases. Simplified it's 1-Traps/some buffs, 2-Dash (before combat movement), 3-Combat/primary buffing and 4-Normal Movement. The flaw is step 2. Some characters seem to be able to dash almost every other turn, not just giving them greater mobility but ensuring whoever attacks them wastes the attack entirely for their turn. This gives them a big advantage AND ruins the play experience for the one getting screwed out of their attack. I"m sure there are a good amount of people who like this type of game, my guess is the majority of people who really enjoy this title are also the same ones who have spent money buying better characters. Otherwise it looks fine, plays smooth and has good match making. I just can't recommened, I wish steam had a 10 point scale instead of a yes or no, because it's not awful or horrible. I've just been playing table top games long enough to know the 'dash' phase as they call it, is pretty flawed when there are characters built around dashing abilities. Anyone that can move more often than another before attacks are made in a turn based game have a serious advantage mathematically, and this advantage will ALWAYS be abused by players who are aware of this advantage.

Quick, tactical PvP with Classes.
Heard it before? But don't be too quick to judge, Atlas Reactor twist is that the actions are set in a phases and happens simultaneously. Which opens opportunities too those that can predict his/her opponent actions.
Phases are divided into: Prep/Dash/Blast & Move
Prep involves Buffs/Debuffs/Heals from skills
Dash involves jump/dash to another place, a dash is used as a repositioning tool to dodge damage.
Blast involves just about everything that is doing damage.
Then there are catalysts and mods.
Mods are different bonuses and/or behaviour of the skill.
While catalysts are a:  1/game "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥/Imma gonna get you!" button/phase (excl. Move)
Is it for everyone? No. But it might be for you if you want a more tactical and intelligent PvP experience to the kin of
X-Com but against humans, in a lore-filled universe.
Can you predict my next move? There is only one way to find out, in Atlas Reactor.

Therian Saga is an interesting take on idle games. I don't mind waiting for tasks to complete, but Therian Saga takes the idea of Sandbox to a whole new level -- and this isn't necessarily a good thing.
I appreciate a good bit of freedom in games, I honestly do. The issue is, Therian Saga is 1) not translated THAT greatly and 2) impactless.
The lack of visual animations means that text is going to be your biggest helper in envisioning the world of Therian Saga. Since the game isn't translated too well, lots of things are fumbled and sometimes plot points are missed. For example, in the tutorial island it extrapolates that it's a happy, fun island full of people. When you get on the boat to leave, they suddenly make you swallow some kind of elixir to cure you from your "disease" so you can leave the "contaminated island." Huh???
The lack of direction is also a problem. You're greeted with TONS of skills and tasks (Runescape-esque) such as Masonry, stonecutting, botany, and other things. Unfortunately, you're not told what these skills can do for you as a player. There's a whole questline towards getting a pickaxe, but just learning how to mine your first few ores is going to take upwards of an hour. What's the point of it? What can you do with these ores? What is marl, and what can I do with it (other than turn it in for quests)? The way the game is set up, there needs to be more of an initial shove with players getting ideas on WHAT they want to do before they're unleashed on this big open world. There's a freaking skill for travelling for god's sake, WHAT IN THE HELL DOES LEVELLING UP TRAVELLING DO? It never tells you! There's skill checks for crafting, but you're not told what the skillchecks are until you've found the items! So I could essentially get my stonecutting up to level 99 and still have no freaking idea what the hell stonecutting does for me UNTIL I FIND SAID USE. That's awful! Even Runescape had guides which told you what you unlocked at which levels, which incentivized progressing in skill trees!
The UI is also wonky, but I'm gonna make this really short: The game defaults to windowed-fullscreen. In this mode, all the text is so uncomfortably tiny that I have to strain my eyes to read the text. In a game where reading is literally the majority of your worldbuilding, that's a fatal flaw. There's an option to not-scale the UI to your screen size, but that breaks way too many menus to use. It makes buttons go off-screen, some buttons shrink to the size of an ant, and the resolution just looks ugly at that point.
It really is unfortunate. I like the concept, but I just don't like the execution of Therian Saga. It might be more apt for players who don't mind slogging through the initial few hours, but trust me: it really is a grind to work through. I really liked the game for the first half hour, but after that I just couldn't stand it. I'd just queue up tasks for up to an hour in the future, leave and come back for 5 minutes just to get the next set of tasks queue'd. I was so confused and unguided during the whole ordeal I just said "♥♥♥♥ it," wrote this review, and decided to call it quits.

It's the best Sonic game to come out in a long while. A love letter to every Sonic game made in the Genesis era, it's full of inspired remixes of ideas from everything that came before it to make something entirely new and original. The more time you spent with those first five Sonic games in your youth, the more you'll appreciate all the ridiculous little references, both visual and mechanical, scattered throughout.

I've been playing all kinds of Sonic games since I was a little kid and the classical style is something that I've missed for quite a while, although various ROM Hacks from the Sonic Retro community helped to fill that void, some of them achieving incredible level of quality just out of pure passion.
What I love about Sonic Mania is that it's the result of SEGA giving this passion of some of the best people from the community a green light and support to develop it into a new, well polished game and it really shows. The attention to detail and faithfulness to what made classic Sonic games so good in terms of gameplay, level design and gimmicks, art style and music is incredible, even more so that Sonic Mania actually pushes all those to the next level.
While I hope that any potential sequel will feature a lot more original levels, the remixed levels surprised me in many ways, that now I actually want to see at least a few more in future - it seems that the team just had so much fun with them and finding ways to expand or twist them in unexpected ways.
And while the inclusion of Denuvo DRM is very unfortunate business decision, this review focuses on reviewing the game itself, not SEGA's business practices. I hope it'll be removed as soon as possible as it's only punishing paying customers and represents strong anti-consumer tactics, but at the same time the game itself is so incredible that I can only recommend supporting it and voicing complaints using other channels.

This game seems to give me what I've been looking for in a space sim game for a long time.  The atmosphere, the feel, the freedom and sense of scale - really succeeds in giving the feel of a lone wolf mercenary with the vastness of space just outside his cockpit.
I started slow; some mining, some trading, some exploring, some simple contracts - and have only in the last session or two had a taste of combat.  That's part of what's great about this game: you do what you want to do.  And even after just scratching the surface I can see there is a LOT to do in this big chunk of space.  Love the mood (or moods) of the game; relaxing one moment frantic the next depending on what you want; where you go, what you do.
I'll admit to being personally shallow enough that I needed to get a cockpit and UI mod before really being able to get immersed - made a huge difference and there's tons to choose from.  Don't let the first few seconds of the game throw you.  There is a LOT of beauty in this game (I've taken a ton of screenshots already), and the feel is top notch.
I've only played singleplayer so far, but the multiplayer sounds great - enough to convince a die-hard singleplayer to be very tempted to dip in.. soon.  The community seems active and friendly, and the dev (yes, a single individual is behind this!) deeply involved and interested and responsive.  And it would seem he is currently working hard on the next iteration - which seems like it will only make this very good thing even better, much better.  Can't wait.. but in the meantime I've a huge chunk of space to explore, so back to it..!

For an alpha game, It's remarkably stable, with minimal hiccups when compared to other early access games. Now granted it does have a few flaws.
First off let's start with the bad.
Notably the game is a bit grindy, but think about it, what games aren't nowadays? anyway the night times are also waaaay to dark as you cant really see much of anything and with the lack of brightness and gamma options you're stuck with it unless you change your monitors settings. In my opinion the worst part of the grind is that some animals, and some materials are waaaay too rare. for example Iron is extremely rare in every part of the map or just non existent in that area. Flax also. Wolfs and rats (sources of small leather) are extremely rare considering how often small leather is needed. Also tin which comes from sailor corpses. For a game that encourages settling down with a village/town/guild to progress and expand, there's way too much of having to trek halfway across the map for materials. I've spent so much time just looking for tin, flax, wolfs/rats and iron its probably been about 5 of my 20 hours of gameplay atleast. also as other people have probably mentioned the morale system, it works and discourages KoS and stealing but it only works if you have a lock on what you dont want peolpe stealing from. now moving on the game has an arguably brilliant way of cleaning the map up as people quit, or move on, the zombies and skeletons that spawn at night attack structures and if they arent repaired within 24 hours of being destroyed? Poof. however I think it needs alot of tweaking as It's annoying having to spennd 30 minutes everytime I log on replacing and repairing everything thats broken as well as defending it all at night time. also the game desperately NEEDS permanent light sources, it has street lamps but like everything else they require fuel and its just not resource efficient. there NEEDS NEEDS NEEDS to be some sort of permanent lightsource that can be put around towns. now they obviously cant be actually permanent. but say lasting a few hours or a day/night cycle and just needing to be relit would be fine. alternatively make charcoal and coal last significantly longer than it does as to be honest the rate that fuel items such as twigs, firewood, coal, charcoal, etc is used is abyssmal and needs tweaking to be atleast 5 times longer likely more like 10 times. maybe not in fireplaces, but for furnaces and lamps its necessary.  Also while I do enjoy how it favours community building, I do wish it would remove the 400 point limit system, its a bit arbitrary and honestly communities are forming before the limit is even becoming an issue. It's not needed. and some people just prefer to play solo, but they cant because of this arbitrary limit. it seriously isn't needed. the time it takes to level up is enough to inspire communities. and  depending on your community, people will cooperate, or they wont, arbitrary limits like that wont make it happen. and on that topic, Guild size limits, need to be expanded. Badly. and lastly the Quality and Durability systems... well starting off, durabilities are way too low they need to be about doubled and theyd be just right I think. And as for the quality system which is basically how good this item is at what it does, It needs a rework, its very inconsistent on what qualities youll get. I still get quality 3 crude axes at level 14ish tinkering, but sometimes as high as 24?! thats so inconsistent the range I can get at my level should be lower, or atleast pick up the minimum qualities I get, its really frusterating spending 30 minutes crafting to make a bow that youve been excited to get and to have the first one you make be quality 1 even when you have 24 carpentry and it requires 15. also theres some issues with logging out and quiting the game while its fullscreened that are a bit frusterating and there is a bug (the only bug Ive really seen so far) where theres essentially ghost items on the floor that aren't really there. there's also some syncing issues but hey the servers are pretty loaded. Lastly the combat. Now what to say about the combat, the targeting and hitbox systems need alot of work staying still and slamming my left mouse button is not an exciting prospect for combat, the game needs to make it either as hard for AI to hit you as it is to hit them, or just add an actual targeting system like press tab and your targetting something, although I prefer the former.
Anyway on to positives,
#1 the atmosphere. the game has an extremely pleasant and relaxing atmosphere and I love it it reminds me of an old MMO I used to play that had an awesome community and wonderful atmosphere. the feeling of the game world just couldnt be much better in my opinion. this is partly due to the soundtrack as the soundtrack is very soothing, calming relaxing whatever you wanna call it. secondly, like I stated earlier, the game has excellent communities and cooperation.
thirdly, the game does a good job of discouraging KoS and stealing, even if a bit questionable. 4th for an early access game, like I already said its more stable and bug free than alot of actual full releases *cough Assassin's Creed unity cough Skyrim cough* 5th, the price normally Id think 20 dollars is a high asking price for an alpha survival sandbox game ive never even heard of until now but its fairly modest considering how fun the game is.
The positives honestly out way the negatives but if the negatives where to be fixed this game would be borderline perfect in my opinion. The level limits, fuel burn rate, and darkness are the biggest issues I think if those were fixed i'd enjoy the game so very much more. but anyway If you're on the fence about it, my advice is to buy it. I was on the fence just like you were once. and now I think I have a compulsion/addiction for it

Previous to AC Rogue, I have finished only AC Black Flag and enjoyed it immensely. As a result of that title, I bought several other AC games, including Syndicate, AC II, as well as AC Rogue. I tried to play AC II first as it was perhaps the most acclaimed AC title there is, but found the control rather clunky without a controller (also in part due to my getting used to playing Black Flag in my 40-hr playthrough). Consequently, I turned to Rogue. In this short review, I will discuss what I think of Rogue over its World-building effort and its narrative.
Rogue, in many senses, is very similar to black flag. However, as a stand-alone title, I found AC Rogue rather disappointing in comparison to Black Flag. The world that Rogue renders is fragmented and lacks the depth that an open-world game should have. The entire world map is divided into 3 sections, one for the River Valey, one for New York, and another for the Atlantic and the player is forced to travel through way points between these different mini "worlds". The seafaring that Black Flag was known for becomes almost a nuisance as player often time is forced through narrow channels of water, having to navigate through icerbergs and reefs for no good reason. The only feature that I can applaud was its effort in creating a sense of historicity as along the River Valley there scattered many British/French settlements, yet even these seem to suffer from a gross, generic, simplification. All of the settlements are mere side missions with no real consequences in which the Templars can help the British army to get rid of the French "Gangsters". There doesn't seem to be any real historicity built in, while the repetitive form that it presents itself actually undermines the immersive nature of the story. Most of these sites of interest remains unvisited after I've completed the entire game, while the game doesn't seem to provide any real incentive for the player to visit them anyway. The only benefit for the player in completing these side quests are a measely sum of reward that can easily be gained through other revenue and some collectibles, useful only if you are aiming to get an 100% completion. They are just there to fill the empty space on the map so that the title can hide its linear structure under the "open-world" catergory. Despite all these, I do wish to acknowledge that the devs did a great job in recreating models for cities such as the historical New York and Lisbon. The visuals were absolutely stunning, although they suffer the same lack of depths.
The story-telling of Rogue are perhaps even more lackluster: In short, it doesn't make any f-ing sense. The idea behind the story is brilliant! It's basically trying to break from the Genre's single view point of the assassins and have a fresh take of the Templar's perspective, yet the execution of this idea can only be said to be sub-par at best. I understand that a major constraint to the story-telling might very well be the length of the game -  in a mere ~15hr game, one has to expound on the dynamic between ideas such as "order" and "freedom" while conveying it through the life story of Cormac, the assassin-turned-rogue. Yet the entire story just came out as utter nonsense, failed in both its intricacy and its consistency. There are way too many loopholes in the story, and the gameplay around the story just came off as lazy. The entire political dynamic between the Templar and the Assassin are simplified as such: the Templars are (connections with) British army (whom, mind you, will still come after you even if you are doing their Colonel's bidding), and the Assassins are basically French Gangster that terrorize local citizens for god-knows-what reasons, despite the fact that both organizations are by nature GLOBAL. The Templars depicted in the game are no Templars from AC Black flag, whom supposedly controls all levels of the government in secret. They really are just batmans, whom try to fight lowlifes that hides in bushes. Accompanying this confusing dynamic between the Templar and the Assassins were extremely unsatisfying filler quests, such as the like of this:
"Benjamin Franklin's Lightning Rod got confiscated by the British Army, go and steal it back so he can perform scientific magic over this ancient artifact!"
*The next paragraph contains minor spoiler for the story, albeit a pretty darn bad story*
The centerpiece of the story is the transformation of Master Cormac, and this transformation is done terribly, in an extremely inconsistent manner. We learnt from the start of the game that Cormac was a great guy that most people in the Assassin's group like. He respects his mentor, although he doesn't quite like one of the older assassins. The reason that he left Assassin is therefore not personal (not because of any grudges towards any specific individual), but rather, due to his particular notions of ethics. He found it despicable to assassinate an old man who cannot fight back, although this old man supposedly wishes to change/destroy the known world. Once he found out that the Assassins were responsible for the destruction of 2 cities due to their ignorance of the power of the artifacts, he practically flipped out with his mentor and decided to take the matter into his own hand (to steal the map and destroy it), instead of trying to reason with the persons that supposedly he trusted the most. A characteristic that we see from Cormac during this period is that he doesn't take authority kindly, whether it is from the old, reverend Assassin or his mentor; yet after his becoming a Templar, he seems to have absolutely no qualms with taking orders from anyone. The transformation from an assassin to a templar happens when Cormac believed that the templars saved his life (and thus becomes his friend) while the assassins betrayed him (noted this is completely personal), instead of the moralistic "I am doing what is right and I am saving the world" reason. We also never really see the true idea behind the Templar's cuase, as it is always in the form of "the Assassins are bad bad people, and they are wrong."So the picture painted here is one of mixed signals: on the one hand, Cormac loved his assassins friends and broke off due to moral commitment of not killing innoncent citizens; on the other hand, we never really see moral commitment of the Templars' (except perhaps the one moment of "let's take care of the thugs that threatens the local villagers!"), instead we see a wierd friendship between the templar Colonel and strayed assassin, a friendship that's almost miraculous. The supposedly spirited, moralistic assassin Cormac, when turned into a Templar, is also somehow perfectly Okay with sacking French Colonies and stealing from the treasury (not to mention all those other atrocities that a player might commit). These wierd inconsistencies, coupled with the generic assassin's creed quests made the game a lot less convincing than it could have been.
I will not recommend the game on the ground of its story. It really should have taken the form of a Black Flag dlc, but as the matter stands, buy it if you just want another 15 hour or so of Black Flag experience.

Assassin's Creed Rogue was the first AC game I played since AC3 which massively disappointed me, I didn't came with great expectations for this game, but was honestly surprise. I didn't like the Ship's fights at sea at all in AC3 but somehow
however, this time around I really loved it.

Without these activities, by my estimation this game takes about 6-8 hours to complete if you rush through it, unlike the former AC games, which are quite longer than this.
The Verdict:
Honestly a great game, Absolutely worth the money I paid for. I thoroughly enjoyed the plot, the characters, the huge vast open world, it is a splender to behold. If only this game was 5-10 hours longer I'd love it even more.
Gameplay: 8/10 same as AC3 with a few new improvements, but overall movements and climbing is the same, same as for the combat. You are however given a grenade launcher, which I found hilarious to bombazle 4 enemies at ones then hiding and doing the same to the next group of enemies who appear to help their comrades.
Graphics: 8.5/10 Great, but could be better. Overall It's not a breathtaking game, but we have to remember that this game was optimized for the last gen consoles. And that my friends, is a solid reason.
Storyline/Plot: 9/10 I found being in a Templar shoes for once can be interesting, to see the Templars idealism and convictions.

Imho the best game of the whole Assassins Creed franchise. Let me tell you why:
It didn't try to reinvent the wheel. Instead, the devs took the skeleton of AC4 (which was nice by itself), put in more relatable characters and a more interesting story and set it all in a colder environment. And they fixed all the bugs and optimized performance. All in all a really nice game.
One of the most important aspects of a game is that you can play it without being annoyed by bugs or frame drops. AC Rogue manages that awesomely: It runs on my notebook (3d gen i7, GTX660M, win 8.1) on near max settings and it runs smoothly (neither AC3 nor AC4 had constant high frame rate). I did not encounter any mentionable bugs nor any frame rate drops that went below 30fps. It also runs perfectly fine on my gaming PC (6th gen i7, GTX1070, win 10) with no compatibility issues whatsoever (unlike AC2 of AC Brotherhood). All in all 10/10
The story line isn't very long (i guess just playing through the story would be 20 to 30 h) but it is interesting. AC Rogue tells a tale of redemption, which is a nice change from the classic "arrogant young boy grows up to be a decent killer" - schematic the other AC games posess. The caracters are diverse and unlike so often not either 100% good or 100% bad, which makes them much more relatable.
It is no epic quest like the Ezio-story but it's a solid fresh standalone story. Oh and did I mention that the out-of-the-animus part is really short and has some nice puzzle elements? Thumbs up for that!
All in all 8/10 - it was a bit short after all.
One word for that: perfected.
The game lets you choose your own approach to the missions: you can decide yourself whether you want to sneak past anyone, stealth kill everyone or slowly walk in and slaughter any attacker (why hide? wou are a templar after all). There are no necessary mission goals like "don't be detected, even if you kill the guy before he can get help". All those goals are optional and just needed for 100% sync or a bit of extra cash.
The Parkour is quite smooth but relatively easy. A HUGE plus is that from the beginning there are no restricted areas - everything you can reach after finishing the story is also reachable at the very beginning of the game.
There is a nice variety of weapons and tools at your disposal and switching them is quick and immersive. Personally, I kind of miss the dagger from the first games, but the rifle (yes, you have a pistol AND a rifle) more than makes up for that.

Atlas Reactor is a turn based "tactical MOBA" (I will come back to that later)
You pick any "freelancer" (hero) of your choice (DPS,TANK or SUPPORT).
There are around 10 of each class to choose (it's in early development, they release a new freelancer every month).
All freelancers look pretty balanced, each one haves 3 abilities and an ultimate.
You can play Practice to test any hero, Coop against bots with different levels of AI (easy, medium, hard), PvP and Ranked.
You get better rewards (exp and season's boxes) from PvP or playing against hard bots. You level up seasons and unlock new chapters related to the lore of the game as you level up. Each time you lvl up your season level, you get a box with loot.
There are 2 type of matches, deathmatch or "support" roulette, both are 4vs4. In deathmatch wins the team that reaches 5 kills before turn 20 (or the team with most kills until turn 20). Support roulette is the same but you are limited to play only support heroes.
Combat approach is similar to XCOM, you play per turn, and each turn haves three phases (PRE phase where you can use only support or trap abilities, DASH phase-> you can use abilities that move you away to escape or ambush an enemy and BASH phase where most damage abilities are being casted).
PROS
+F2P
+Not P2W
+Original "tactical" combat
+Balanced heroes
+Balanced matchmaking
+You can customize any hero as you level up (skins, taunts, abilities)
+You can taunt your enemy before using an ability
CONS
+It can be frustrating at first if you are not familiarized with this type of approach in combat (strategic positioning, moving per turn, tactical abilities, phases)
+There are no many heroes to pick (remember its in beta)
+There's no ingame communication besides chat and pinging with alt (you can download discord and it will serve as voice comm for any ongoing match)
+Special kind of game in this genre (it may be fun if you like strategy turn combat mixed with a moba, or a con if that's not your thing)

"Crusader Kings II" is an unfortunate name for a game that is SO much more than the title indicates. CK2 is a history simulator that takes place during various times in the Middle Ages (700-1400 AD). It is also a Medieval role playing game, with clear elements of Dungeons and Dragons implemented throughout.
I have never played a deeper, more intricate, and more sophisticated grand strategy game than CK2. Every time period represented has (an ever-growing) map of the "world" (Europe, N. Africa, India, C. Asia). The map is incredibly detailed and full of different cultures, and even better... you can pick just about ANY ruler you wish (ranging in influence from Emperor to lowly Vassal). Some favorites are Charlemagne (esp. for the detailed, historically accurate drama that plays out during his life), Rurik (viking founder of Rus/Kiev) and King Alfonso VI of Leon (the Tutorial character!).
At the moment, there are ~8 "time bookmarks" that one can select when starting a custom game. It is stunning to see the world map change so much between each interval. What this means for you is an almost endless amount of variety. And you will undoubtedly learn a lot about history in the process (I know I did).
As if this isn't already enough, CK2 takes things one step further by being an RPG as well. It's kind of like "Civilization meets Dungeons and Dragons." In CK2 you ROLEPLAY your chosen ruler... while still managing and expanding your realm (and techs) like you would in Civilization.
Every character in the game has a set of D&D-like base stats: Diplomacy, Martial, Stewardship, Intrigue and Learning. On top of this - and also like in D&D - every character has a number of personality traits (like Genius, Cynical, Ambitious), as well as personal ambitions (have a child, see kingdom prosper) and a personal focus (War, Carousing, Seduction). The  secondary traits I mentioned (of which there are MANY) are of course linked to your core D&D stats (e.g. Martial determines how good you are at War, Learning ability comes with Genius, Diplomacy is needed to be an affective Carouser).
Some character traits are set in stone from birth. Others can be earned/loss through how you RP your character. Or through luck. Or questing. Or by precious relics in your inventory/vault.
And let me just say... that there many, many opportunities for RPing. You can always go looking for it yourself... say by starting your OWN crusade... or by making one of your Dukes the Court Jester so he tries to break away from your kingdom... or by secretly joining a Satanic cult that gives you superpowers (like Summon Familiar). This last part is where CK2 diverges from history/reality a bit... but who cares! Mideival history is more fun with D&D superpowers!
Look, I could write a more lenghty review of this product... and feel like it deserves one... but the simple take-home message here is: if you are a fan of games like Civilization and like RPGs set in Medieval times.... THEN JUST BUY CRUSADER KINGS 2.
Oh and get most of the DLC as well...
Yeah that's the only downside to how this works. Vanilla CK2 is lacking some of the things I mentioned (like joining cults). Paradox is constantly expanding the depth, breadth and replayability of this game by slowly releasing DLC. Ok, whatever. Just accept this. Then go ahead and load up on DLC. It's frequently on sale for 50-75% off.

Wraith Tanks and Grunts patrolling the streets below the bridge I was on, while Hornet gunships wizz passed followed closely by the wale of the Banshee fighter aircraft furiously firing their plasma guns. Warframe is a game you'll either enjoy or hate, due to the fact that it is a MASSIVE TIME SINK. Either you'll enjoy the endless grind becuase you always have something (usually several things) to be working towards, or you'll have it becuase you don't enjoy grinding I guess. Personally I like it because, as I said, there's always something for me to be working towards but all the goals still feel attainable instead of being an MMO-style 1/500,000 grind bar that increments by one every four hours of playtime.
The customization is nice. You start off with fairly limited colour options, but the colour palletes are cheap to get and once you buy one you can use it as much as you like as long as you play the game (I can't believe I have to praise that, but that's modern gaming for you). Basicly every piece of gear you have can be completely recoloured, and it's a popular feature in the playerbase.
The premium currency (platinum, usually shortened to plat) is only exclusively used for cosmetics with one excpetion: inventory slots. The inventory slots are fairly cheap and it's advised you use your starting platinum to purchase a few. Platinum can be used to buy weapons and gear, but every warframe, weapon, and other gear can be attained purely through gameplay. It's fairly common to get coupons for reduced price platinum as a login reward (usually 20% or 50% off, but 75% off isn't exceedingly rare) and you can trade several types of in-game items to other players in exchange for platinum.
The gameplay is fun; the movement system encourages speed and allows for easy movement through the maps, most of the guns feel generally effective and fun to use, and while the enemy AI isn't particularly clever you usually mince through so many of them so quickly it doesn't matter. This paragraphs is pretty short because I'm not very good at describing gameplay. Warframe shows up on livestreams sometimes, so check it out there. If you check out youtube videos, make sure they're fairly recent as Warframe is still in development and a video from three years ago won't bear much resemblance to the game today.
The new player experience is probably the game's weakest point. There is a tutorial, but you have to find it and it doesn't explain a lot. However, there are plenty of updated new player guides available online and the in-game community is one of the most friendly and helpful I've ever encountered.
Warframe isn't getting out of here without a recommendation (I've played more than a thousand hours, I'd look pretty stupid is I said it's bad), but this reccomendation has a qualification. Warframe is not going to be everyone's sort of game. It's entirely possible the grind will turn you off the game, or it might be your sort of thing. While the early game is unfortunately the weakest part of the game, it's free to give it a try and see if it's something you enjoy.

Summary
In short, Frozen Synapse is a turn based counter strike with focus on tactics rather than action in a cyper-punk setting.
You get thrown right into the action from your first match with little introduction which may put off some people. I did not find it too bad though.
When playing against other players online, it feels very rewarding to win a match. Seeing a carefully planned out plan work feels great! However losing also feels as progress as you gain experience points for your actions rather then just the outcome.
Gameplay
You control a team of units armed with different weapons (either shotgun, grenade, machine-gun, sniper or rocket) in a battlefield against opponent units. Orders are given to a single unit as a path of nodes to travel along and you can assign actions along the path such as "crouch", "ignore at sight",  "shoot at sight", "wait" and "look in this direction". You can order units to take cover, make distractions, flank enemies, flush out enemies and many other tactics that make use of the randomly generated environment. You can also simulate the enemy units to test out your plans and make sure you covered all outcomes. It is hard to describe the feeling of seing enemies fall into your traps or pressured into defeat other than "Just as planned...".
The game was slightly intimidating in the beginning as there are many things to get used to and most of it is presented without much introduction. There is a single player campaign which presents all actions from the first mission and the tutorial only teaches a few basic tactics. Generally the overall focus seemed to be on playing online and learning by doing and failing.
Multi-player
Online works overall well. You can play any number of matches you want at once as the game does not progress until both players have submitted your plans. Once both players have submitted their plans, the outcome is played out. You can also choose to have the game notify you by email or through Steam when your next turn is ready.
Theme
Lastly I really like the overall style of the game. The music is very fitting and the sparse visuals keeps focus on the gameplay.
An amazing game that everyone should get it.

A simple to pick up, yet hard to master strategic game.
The variety of units and game modes increases the game's replay factor, and the ability to plan and play a turn whether or not your partner is online or not is fantastic!
The single player is good enough, however the amount of text boxes to click though in order to gain any form of narrative could be re-worked.
Overall an entertaining and often stresssful game which is perfect for play amongst good friends.

Before I bought this game, I was so ♥♥♥♥ing hype, because this is the first Assassin's Creed games that we can play as Templar. Then I bought it..and you only need 10 hours to complete the main missions...

Whilst painfully short, Rogue is a great example of the AC Canon being read in such a way that blends both the Assassin and Templar stories, and makes you question truly who is right and who is wrong.
The story bridges the gaps between Black Flag and III, respectively before and during the American Civil war. Its very interesting to see how the characters developed, and with the obvious set up to Unity. It is slightly rushed at the beginning, Shay could have used more time to develop his motivations but its enjoyable nevertheless.
Essentially Black Flag 2.0, the gameplay mechanics such as naval combat, warehouse raids, hunting etc are carried over with a few new additions. These additions are fun, but I personally would have preferred a longer main story arc as sometimes the map screen is full to bursting with collectibles.
I am an unashamed fan boy of the series, but not a fan of the direction it has headed. Rogue is what the series could have been heading towards, with the creative department, not the financial department, leading the helm.

Assassin's Creed Rogue was announced a few months after Unity, however it was only a couple of months before its release in 2014. Was this a spin-off game like Assassin's Creed 3: Liberation? no... this was a main series game, tying in the story of Black Flag and AC3 and even Unity together. It seemed like it was going to be just as important as Revelations was when that game tied in Altair's story to Ezio's with Desmond's. But from all the gameplay footage, it just looked like Black Flag except... winter. But who knows, it might be good, well after playing it and completing it in 7 hours... errr....
The story begins with Shay, our new protagonist, working with the Assassins. Achilles recieves news from Adewale that the artifact they're looking for is capable of destroying cities, but they must stop the Templars from reaching it, so Shay is sent to collect it. Shay travels to Lisbon to retrieve it, but activates the artifact and destroys the entire city. Its fine, but...
God does it get repetitive after a while.
I don't know if it has to do with the pacing, the way that the game introduces its missions, and side activities, or if it simply has to do with the fact that the game fails in creating the illusion of "diversity" whilst keeping the player repeating the same actions, over, and over again.
After a while it's as if all just blends together, and I just couldn't stand it after a while.
It does have some brillant moments tho, for starters, I love the combat system in this game, I understand completely why some people always held Assassins Creed combat, as a whole, as one of the biggest issues in the series, but I always enjoy it, even if it was "trivial" at that.
All you do its counter, watch an entretaining animation of the player murdering in a brutal way your enemies, and then you can chain those executions together.
It incorporates several different elements of all the other Assassins Creed, and I enjoy that, I don't remember if the air rifle was ever present in any of the past entries in the franchise tho, so maybe that's new.
Essentially, it's a silent rifle that allows you to shoot darts that produce different effects to your enemies, it's quite enjoyable to put a soldier to sleep, only to wake him up with a massive stomp in his stomach.
Brutal, but enjoyabe, quite fun.
However the flow of the combat, and exploration gets...
"Burst" by the incredibly annoying sailing that you need to repeat, wherever you go to.
It would be understandable to have a multitude of activities that you can complete while sailing, but besides being able to pick up certain things, and attacking other ships, there really isn't that much to do, which I resent, because it can get quite boring to just sail across the seas, at first it was quite relaxing, eventually it just became jarring.
I ended up fast travelling to most of the places I needed to go to for this.
Then the other issue that I have it's in regards to the multitude of objectives, upgrades, and crafting, mechanics, and systems, that the developers incorporated in the game.
I can't tell you how redundant, and unnecessary this are, in the hours that i've spended in this game i've yet to use any of the crafting systems, or even the act of just hunting animals around islands, I used it once during the tutorial mission, after that another time, and that was it.
There's just no incentive whatsoever to keep you doing this things, it's as if you can carry just enough to get you through your journey, without pinning you against any real challenges, or situations in which you need to use any of those particular type of upgrades.
Then there are the upgrades of the ship, and of your equipment, with the equiment, being the weapons that you can carry, like the pistols, and your trusty knife, and sword.
Probably the last one of which it's among the simplest to obtain, given you only need money, which you can get in a multitude of ways, with the ones from the ship being tedious to get, for the simple reason besides money you also need materials that you can find whilst attacking other ships.
Which are hard to come by...
To me, it's as if Ubisoft has this checklist for every game, it is insane to me that just because say, something like the crafting system, worked wonders in Far Cry, they add it to this game.
But they do it in such a blunt, and dumb way, to me is as if they took that system, and "stapled" it on top of their actual idea of the game they wanted to make.
When this game is its own game, then it shines, and it provide me with an experience that I can relate only to the unique, and very special one I had with Assassins Creed 2, but for the most part, sadly, it suffers from a lot of the "syndromes" that current Ubisoft titles have...
When I started this "review" I planned to recommend the game, and in a way I do, frankly if I could vote in a "mixed" way, I would, but since I can't, and really, in retrospective, the negative aspects of the game seem to be the ones that resonate the most.
I have to lean to not recommend it...
If anything, do buy it, but on a deep, deep discount.
The story is fantastic, and maybe the one in years, that has truly surprised me, the "turn" at the end of sequence 2, and at the start of 3, was presented, and handled, masterfully.
Really the only negative thing about the narrative for me, where the completely unnecessary and annoying "Animus" sequences, I really don't understand where that aspect of this games lies anymore, of what's trying to tell me, if anything at all, to me it's a completely unnecessary "slog" in an otherwise fantastic story.

Atlas Reactor is truly one of a kind! There are of course other games like this; isometric MOBA's with unique characters and abilities, but with an added twist. The game is turn based and fast paced. Turns happen simutaneously as you and your team engage in a battle of wits against your opponents.
The best way to describe Atlas Reactor is that it's like Chess With Guns and a Rock, Paper, Scissors guessing game. (Yeah stole that straight from a trailer.) Everyone gets the same 20 seconds to decide what abilities they want their lancer to use, and once the time is up the game goes into resolution mode, which has three different phases that go in this order.
Prep phase is for healing,  shielding, and buffing/debuffing, as well as setting traps.
Dash phase is for dashing out of the action and into safety.
Blast phase is where all the attacks happen.
Every ability you use happens within this order so it's important to know how you set up not only your lancer's actions, but also communicating with your team on how to plan the next turn. Don't wanna chat on Discord or in the text chat? No problem! A very neat feature in this game is the visual language it offers as you can see the abilities your teammates are about to use, and where they will move at the end of the turn. You can even set up combos between your party like if one of you sets a trap in a space, and teammate uses a knockback ability to throw your enemy into that trap.
Now that's just the gameplay. Another great aspect of this game is the character design. They look like highly detailed action figures constantly taking epic actions no matter what you command them to do. All the lancers, as they are called, have not only unique looks and sounds to all of them, but their abilities are also vastly different from each other making every team composition and conflict possibilities almost endless.
With new lancers being introduced every once in a while, a decent community, Atlas Reactor is a fast and growing game that I hope more and more people LIKE YOU THE READER decide to download COMPLETELY FOR FREE! You can pay to unlock all the lancers along with some skins, or you can grind the hell out of the game to earn in game currency to unlock stuff. Sounds like a chore at first until you realize that this game is so immersive that you forget to keep track of time.
I surely have. As of writing this review I've only played for 2 weeks and have clocked in 118.6 hours!

Tree of Life is an engaging and fun sandbox game, the game is in early access, however the content and progression is paced enough that people are not finished within a day. The game has a strong focus on casual, relaxed game play with music that reinforces that point.
The early game is without a tutorial at the time of writing, but the game is easy and simple to pick up for most basic skills. Resource distribution for most resources is ideal; however ores are too rare for the difficulty in levelling mining up. Resources change based on the zone you are in, making a list of where to locate resources is really important for later in the game when you are missing, for example, braided straps.
The mid game is where the game is still being fleshed out, with some mechanics still unknown to the wider community, such as ranching. Defending your settlement is impossible without walls, and the player should focus on skilling and logging out with everything they want when they have had enough for the time being, either players will destroy settlements or the night time mobs will erase most abandoned settlements in short order (a very nice mechanic for getting rid of abandoned buildings). This mechanic allows the map to feel not so settled.
PvP in the game is a mixed bag, with the system in the early stages with no current claim system in place, the only way to protect your belongings is to group together so that there is constant activity in your town, or work on locks as quickly as possible and hope nobody thinks you are worth lockpicking.
All in all, for a freshly released game, it is enjoyable and engaging to play, combat can be intense and fun and updates that balance the game seem to be frequent, the developers react to elements of the game that may be too hard (a good example was iron ingots, which require 25 mining, were used in wooden gates, which put walls outside everyone’s capabilities to place, were nerfed to requiring just 10 sculptures)

You're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Hi Guys.
First things first. It's not full review because i played only something about 10h. Second thing, probably you can find here some language mistakes because i didn't use english for long time and it's my way to improve it. Last thing: At the bottom is TL;DR version.
The game stands somwhere between MOBA and XCOM which is nice idea. So the game is turn based arena where we have to kill our enemies. You have to choose one character from 3 classes (DMG dealer, frontline and support), every char have own abilieties (4 +1 ULTIMATE) and playstale. There are not too many characters but i believe that developers will add new ones (someone remember LOL beta? ;) ). THe main downsaid here is that you cannot buy items for your char during the game so you are not able to customize character to your game style. You are able to add some small upgrades to abilities before game starts but i think they dont have too much game impact, just a little addition which is nice but cannot change the playstayle of character- you will not be able to figure out "super own build" cuz you don't have option to do this. You also can choose catalysts- utility abilieties usable once per match, they can save your♥♥♥♥♥so choose wisely.
The game is 4vs4 and it's really based on teamplay so you cannot carry whole team if they are not able to cooperate. This had to be said because if u don't have team then sometimes you can be frustrated because of your random teammates. On the other hand matches are not too long, so you are not prisoned with bad teammates for 40 mins or more. Match lasts max 25 min.
Game is TURN BASED, BUT YOU DONT HAVE WHOLE DAY FOR THININKING. You have something about 10-15  sec. for decision. If you didnt make it you char will be watching action and do nothing. It's nice because it's force you to fast analyzing and decision making in stresfull conditions. Sometimes it's funny when you are hitting your ultimate and didn't noticed that everyone on other team has dash which allow them to run away before you hit them.
Graphics: Nice comic book style (you can drop or buy some animations in comic style for example before attack which gives even more comic book feeling). I really like the graphic style and even potato computer will handle it! My laptop i-5 2410 with GF 540M 1gb is able to handle it really well.
Maps: There are not too many areas but they have unique style. The downside here is that they are similar in tactical/ strategical sense. You have only 1 height lvl and even objects like walls or covers are placed in similar way in every map it really sucks. I think that there is a place for improvement here.
Pay to win? I think that there is a lot of champions in rotation and after 5 hour you will gain 1 free character (you can choose it). There are daily quest so at all you can farm new characters but it will take some time. There is not content which affect gameplay (abilities, catalyst etc.) which is locked only for ppl who paid money. It's not pay to win but probably you will not be able to unlock every character. Model is similar to Smite or LoL.
TL;DR
Pros:
- Low spec. PC will handle it
-Matches are fast
-Graphic is nice
-You have to do a lot of important decision during match
-Teamplay is important
-Characters have unique playstayles. You can customize some abilities...
Cons:
- ...but this customization is cosmetic. :(
- Maps are similiar in tactical sense
- Sometimes you are waiting for game even 5 mins (WE NEED MORE PLAYERS!)
OVERALL: TRY IT, IT'S FREE AND IT'S GOOD (but im not sure for how long the game will be interesting for me).

I'm not against games with energy systems and wait timers when they are done well and still provide a player with things to do while queue timers are up. This game does not achieve that, it only achieves at making you wait. Playing this game is waiting.
Simple tasks take hours to complete, and what the game has to offer is locked behind massive queue times. YOu won't even get a chance to scatch the surface of this one without needing to find another source of entertainment while this "plays" in the background.
Another major red flag is the game is 3 years old yet you can't find any informational videos or guides. I have to assume that is because ppl quickly move on to other games after just a few simple tasks end up taking 12+ hours.
The community will also tell you the game is not p2w, but like usual, one has to do some mental gymnastics with the definition of "win" to claim this is not p2w. You can pay cash money to speed up all timers in the game. Just because there is no "win" condition does not mean paying for progression is anything but p2w.

Therian Saga, if you are ok with games using real time timers to progress, this is probably one of the better made games that have a lot o timers. It just feels more polished and less full of pay to win advertisements than the slew of mobile game ports we get that use timers.
This is going to be one of those games where the opinions are going to be pretty divided so the best advice I can give you as a potential player is to try it your self, its a mixed bag.

Once I noticed that Steam didn't actually "install" Therian Saga and merely downloaded the game-setup, which used the default installation folder for applications in C:\Program Files (x86)\ with no way to change that, I was about to uninstall it again. Seeing that it's quietly installing the deprecated Microsoft Silverlight plugin on top of it, there was no reason to keep the game. Too bad, but what do you expect when a three year old game gets added to Steam? The integration in the service is just bad and there was no word (read: warning) about Silverlight anywhere I could see.
Note: these were "merely" technical issues I have with the game, I can't speak to the in-game experience cause I only kept the game open long enough to write this review. It wouldn't be fair to write a complete critique without having experienced enough of it.
Edit: and just when you think it can't get worse, it happens anyway. Removing the game from steam does not uninstall it from the system, you have to do that manually. I'm surprised that Steam even lets that pile of incompetence through, massive disappointment!

Easy to learn, very, very hard to master. In this realistic hacking game (yes, that exists), you will probably lose at least three or four times before you even reach the top-10 list (you start at 20-something). Then you'll lose again because you forgot to delete you logs properly that *one* time.
This game's fun is not about the excitment of hacking into secure systems and performing movie-geek-like feats. Most of the hacking is done by automated scripts, and your sole job is to make sure you don't get caught.
That's where the fun lies. Being methodical, precise and never allowing yourself to make a single mistake. Give the feds a single opening, and they'll be on you faster than you can say &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥ did I forget to erase my logs?"
My most recent run ended when I stole one million (a lot!) credits from a bank. I did everything with scalpel precision: I erased my logs, deleted the transaction from the target account... And I lost as soon as I realized I'd forgotten to delete the transaction from my own account.
So if you're wondering about buying this game, yes. If you're not against slightly repetitive gameplay and the fact that you will die, Get this game and enjoy it as I am.
Stay vigilant, don't breathe until after your tracks are fully covered and, whatever you do, never get sloppy.

Uplink is a heart attack inducing hacking game about just that,  hacking. You take jobs from various clients, negotiate prices, and utilize various programs to hack through security systems and perform your objectives before a trace can be performed on your computer. All from the safety of your own home! Figuratively and literally. There's no overworld. Or anything similar. The entire game takes place on an emulation of a custom OS designed for hacking. You can use money from jobs to upgrade and customize your computer, which you use to tackle bigger and bigger jobs. Outside of a simple plot, that's all that there really is to it. It's a simple, stressful, fast paced game about using your CPU's power as efficently as possible to manage your various hacking programs to slow traces, crack passwords, copy and delete files.
For it's price,  the gameplay is solid, and it's definitely worth the buy. However, Uplink is a one trick pony. If you don't enjoy resource management, have a poor memory, or can't think quickly, this isn't the game for you.

A fun halo-themed arcade shooter. It's nothing complex and can be mindless shooting, but the medal and scoring system adds a suprising amount of depth to the game as you try to string together kills and perform special actions to maximize your score and get the best rating on each stage.
You also get simple, short intro movies to each operation (chapters basically) that are a fun reward for advancing in the game. If you enjoy Halo and the occasional arcadey game, you should play this game.

Really good game. A very good mobile to PC port. The controls were tight, gameplay was fun and reactive to what you have done via medals. The plot was decent, there was enough context there to create a meaningful story. The base mechanics are inherent of the twin-stick shooter.
You can manipulate the game's challenge/diffuiculty level via skulls that modify the play style of the game. E.g. The player only has a shield and when that is destroyed then the player dies or dropped weapons have lesser ammo. A nice twist that offers a chance for some replayability and allowing the player to get better at the game.
The enemies come in all different forms and are taken straight out of the Halo games. Watch out for the Brute Chieftan, one-hit-kill. The best enemy is the kamikaze grunt, kill him and it'll drop it's plasma grenades (hopefully raining explody plasma death on it's allies!).
For a Halo game it was really good. Of course it been a small game it was easy to get immersed into the Halo universe. I've played the original Halo trilogy on the Original Xbox and they were a stand out title. I'm very surprised Microsoft haven't released the Halo games on Steam. A FPS like Halo was meant for PC.
Also the regenerating shield makes a return, so it is possible to cower behind some rocks and suck your thumb until your shield becomes active.
I don't really like giving numbered ratings (kinda cliched) but I would reccomend getting this game, especially on sale. You can play through the campaign in a few hours.
