I want to like this game, I really do, but sadly it’s riddled with all kinds of perplexing and probably unsolvable problems. The game has a very immature community of which is comprised of toxic players which makes the game extremely exhausting to play and devoid of fun. This supposed “competitive” attitude players give is very obnoxious and irritating to say the least. Also, because of its “competitive style” many people will kick and scream and rage quit a game if things aren’t going their way (to be fair though the game is quite imbalanced so I could understand some frustration on that front). Basically, this game suffers from a very unsportsmanlike community.
The game itself is surprisingly unbalanced and this is my main problem with the game. Some characters are very over powered while many others are severely under powered. This leads to either extremely easy victories or crushing defeats. On top of already unbalanced characters we also have unbalanced game play as well. If everyone on your team goes with one type of class character, say everyone goes a tank class, then you will more than likely lose to a team with evenly spread classes over each character. This should sound extremely obvious but the problem is the game will not stop anyone from picking a character of the same class or with the same functions and features as other characters already chosen by other players. This makes joining random teams dangerous and almost makes it a requirement to be playing with friends who already know who’s going to be whom and how they’re going to play.
Speaking of unbalanced game play, the games mechanics are also extremely screwed. The objective of the game is to take down enough enemy Turrets in order to reach their Base and destroy their Solar Drill, after that your team wins the game. There are 4 Turrets for each team (two Turrets on the top of the map and two on the bottom) and each team has a Solar Drill and a small army of Robots to help them defend or destroy enemy Robots, Turrets, or Solar Drills. The problem here is that, for the most part, after a Turret is destroyed by one of the teams that team now has a major upper hand in the game. While you can comeback from just one turret being destroyed if 2 or more are destroyed you will very likely lose the game. Also, when one of your Turrets is destroyed the enemy team will receive a big robot with a rocket launcher who has a great deal of health and power (think rewards for killing sprees in Call of Duty). While a Big Robot might help a struggling team at times it normally only helps an already overpowered team do even more damage. Defending you Base or Turrets in this game is impossible and is punished by the game itself. Once the enemy team has made a path to your Solar Drill/Base the game is over. You can defend it, but only if you wish to prolong the game. This game could greatly benefit from a timer of some sort to make defending a more viable option and not seem like a hopeless, prolonging last resort.
I have not played massive amounts of this game but I have been able to experiment with it in the short amount of time that I have played it. The main reason I did not play it more is because of the glaring problems stated above. I hope my two cents as well as the two cents of others here on Steam help you make a wise and beneficial choice as to whether or not you should purchase this game. In my humble opinion this game is not worth your money.

This game is a puzzle stylised as an assembly language simulator. Like many before have already stated: if you're a programmer in some way you'll probably love this game, if not - you should probably look the other way. TIS-100 can be extremely tedious at some points, but those that are familiar with working with code will recognise the rush of excitement and happiness that comes when you find the solution(and the inevitable feeling of stupidity that it took you so long to think of it).
I think this game is the closest I have ever seen to the core idea of "hacking" - finding out how something works, tinkering with it, experimenting, trying to break it and to fix it. Usually, this is a very slow process and you'll only get results through tiny increments - and the game nicely balances this so that you still feel the frustration but it doesn't get so overwhelming that it feels like a job and not a game.
However, whilst the core game is great, albeit frustrating at times, it doesn't end there! You can also try yourself at editing the game files to make your own custom levels implemented through Lua, which is very "meta", and can bring hours upon hours of fun if you have the inclination for that kind of stuff. You can even draw pictures in the console if you can figure out how the damn IMAGE_OUTPUT input array works. And I'm sure there are more things to discover in the game engine that I haven't got around to yet. If you manage to find something new and cool don't forget to share it on the TIS-100 subreddit so you can get your well-deserved tips of the fedoras in your direction from fellow 1337 haxX0rs.
All in all, a great game with a healthy dose of frustration with small periods of accomplishment! If grinding your face on sandpaper all weekend to impress your friends(haha, read: "disinterested acquaintances") with how much of the sandpaper you managed to smoothen out with your face sounds like great fun to you - then get this game!

Like most negative reviewers, I can't say that I didn't enjoy the game... The game is fun. However, there are a few glaring issues.
First of all, the game is a "casual" MOBA, which means that there are a lot of lax component. You can be matchmade 3v1 if things go wrong (2 bots with you), and that will spell inevitable doom for you and whoever is unlucky enough to get into your game. There is also only 1 queue, which you could consider "ranked" since there is a visible ranking (tier-based).
Next, as everyone mentionned, there are no servers, every games are P2P, this means that your games will lag based on the host's (chosen at "random") internet.
Otherwise, the balance direction is totally stupid and a disaster. The expansion came out recently, 2 out of the 4 new nauts I saw seems to be flat out better then 80% of the roster. I say 80% because there are still iabilities in the base game. For instance, Gnaw has a kit that makes it so he will inevitably get ahead (can kill "jungle camps" on spawn), and his kit also allows him to stay ahead when he's ahead (he can spew acid on the ground, which inflicts a DoT when stepped on, and has plants for insane sieging/defense)... So unless Gnaw or his teammates are bad, you're spiraling down to the ground. And even if we keep those aberrant data out of the calculations, it's a "casual" game with extreme champions (you will see quite often people 1-shot you or present you with very little interaction, like flinging for half the map).
If you got friends, you can buy it during a deal, it'll probably be a blast... but seriously, the game is not a "good MOBA".

Sonic Mania. Quite the addicting, frustrating, fun, somic game out of them all. Really reccomend it to the "classic sonic" fans that like games Like Sonic 1, 2, 3, & Knuckles & Knuckles. I couldnt stop playing this at my school, that ive been called out for it about 3 times now. This game will kill time like a mofo.
Sonic Mania. Its a M A S T E R P I E C E. But with only one downfall. Yep, you know. The DRM.
I cant play Sonic Mania when im at the airport, i cant play Sonic Mania while in a car, I cant play some Sonic Mania offline PERIOD. End of story. Because theyre "scared of hackers and exploiters" is a pretty understandable situation, but ruining a game that is made to be played offline is quite the bad descision.
I love this game so much because of its fluid animation, and amazing soundtrack. This is the game to play if you absolutely love classic platformers. Sonic Mania is the game to play, BUT you have to play with an internet connection. It might not be a problem for some people, but for people with laptops and other such things are very enraged that they cant play their favorite game in certain situations.
Some might say, "stop exaggerating the graphics dude, Call of Duty easily surpasses them by a landslide" and your right, but Sonic Mania isnt a game that relies on graphics. It is a game that relies on PURE ENJOYMENT. You dont play Sonic Mania to study the graphics quality, you play to fufill your nostalgia meter to the highest point. You play to have fun. Even though the graphics and fluid animation is top notch, i only bought this game for the pure fun. Go wait till Sonic Forces if you want graphics. I cant contain the pure excitement and marvel when sonic runs on one of the new obstacles and you get to see that fluid animation of him doing backflips, running in a loop-de-loop, running inside one of the new loop-de-loops, bouncing on one of the springs and doing a little sideflip, its just so great from what sonic used to be.
Also, you might just say "oh its just a lame port with enhanced graphics, its the same game" But there, your wrong. Sonic Mania not only brings the sides and main course to the table, but the dessert and beverages too (see that nice analogy i made) to make it the best possible dinner you will ever eat. It re-imagines the classics, from enemies to the soundtrack, and from remixed levels to new mechanics, Sonic Mania isnt just "classic sonic". Its improved sonic. Sonic games over the years have been VERY disappointing, like the Sonic Boom franchise, it was pure recycled bull. Its safe to say that sonic is back, baby.
Dont get me riled up, i could write a whole entire story with a sequel about this game. Just trust me. Buy it. Give Sega your money. You will be satisfied. In the whole 4.9 hours i played on the first day of getting this game i can say with confidence that Sonic Mania is not only a great game, but an amazing one.

Updated Review: May 2016
Current Recommendation: Still should hold off on purchasing this game. Changes from past review and reasons below.
+ The Criminal system has been worked on and seems a lot better. A huge plus from the original review.
+ The random damage over time from absolutely nothing bug has been addressed and no longer present.
+ Tower issues seem to be fixed and the ability to "lock" your animals is now present.
+/- Most skills are in the game, still no magic though.
- The company still ignores the English speaking users on the forums and support tickets, which is a major major issue as there are...or were a lot more active English players than any other languages.
- Players from locations that are far from the servers with high pings still are glitchy as hell in combat situations.  This makes them very hard to connect an attack on them.  Kind of a game breaking issue, seeing that there is a lot of PvP in the game when people get their bases built up.
- The server wipes to introduce the new and bigger map did not include character wipes.  Yes, the game does have a slow leveling process, but it gives the game better replay value if you have to earn your levels.  Granted, there are those who have earned their levels by grinding before, but this is a game in development and wipes happen in developing MMO games.  A lot of the people interested in buying this game at this current stage are going to be met with a lot of PvP trolls with decked out gear and decent sized groups that will not take in new players who just purchased the game.  Basically, they will be thrown to the wolves and most will not keep playing for longer than a week, if that because of this decision.
Original Review: May 2015
I hate to do this, but I have to edit my review and change it to a not recommended.  At least in it's current state.
The Bad:
There are many issues with the game's criminal system, what I call a Karma system, after many games with an open PK system with a punishment. Criminal acts give the player a red name tag and a criminal debuff that runs on a timer based on the act(s) commited and how many times they were commited. During this time players will drop all of their loot on the ground upon being killed by the environment or other players.  The problem lies in that there are ways to work around getting flagged by committing crimes that are flagable by simply only doing up to 3 hits within a 10 second period then back off for a bit and come back to do some more damage.  This has led to a major abuse by many troll-like players in the community and has already pushed a good number of players out within the week the game h as been out.
Just like any game in development, there are bugs in this game.  However, some that are halts progress in the game. Taking damage every second by an unseen force until your death has personally caused me to lose 3 mounts and full bags of loot (because I was red named at the time) 2 times.  While dead you are a ghost and have to wait about 3 mins, or collect soul pieces that may or may not be near, to cut that time by 30 seconds each piece.  Within that time, any animals/tree/stone you were carring, cart yo were pushing, mount you were riding or all your loot (if you were red named at the time of death) is being picked up by random players just strolling along and seeing them just on the ground.
In addition to the invisible death bug there are bugs in the towers where they do not always attack threats to your base, whether they are undead monsters or red named players.  Because of this bug, your base will never be safe from thefts, because you will always have holes in your walls.  Unless you have a member of your guild online AND standing in your base doing a nightly wall check (every 20 mins real time) a section of your wall will eventually go down and players can just jump in.  Now you can lock your goods inside buildings and personal cabins with personal or guild locks.  However, any animals, carts or mounts are fair game at this time and loss of these can set you back.
If you are playing on the American or European server there is very poor support for them.  As this company tends to cater to their Asia (Hong Kong based) server. The Asia server will go down for an hour for fixes, and the American and European server can end up going down for 17 hours for the same exact fixes.  When the Asia server goes down, they will quickly post a news update about it within 10 minns.  When the American and European servers go down it will be about 2 hours, if any news update at all about what is going on.
Combat is screwy as heck.  Players are not sync'd together on the server.  You'll see those who are right in front of you and you are swinging your weapon right threw them, but they are taking no damage.  Then you sprint ahead of them about 2 strides ahead of them and keep swinging and you are doing damage to them, watching the numbers popping up over their head...behind you. The PvE threats are not much of a threat either.  You can get them stuck by any building corner, tree, fence, even sapplings on the ground.  Your attack range, as a player, is longer than the npc monsters in the world, even if you are using a dagger and the ogre has longer arms and a huge hammer.
The Good:
Despite me truly hating the over use of the phrase, it is true, "This game has great potential." The skills system is great. The different job specialities are great, much like Life is Feudal (on a MMO standard server where don't have unlimited skill points). The gathering basic resources like rock/stone carvings or logs/firewood is perfect.  The metals/coal farming isn't that great though with the number of people playing the game, but very minor bad point and I don't feel it deserves to be listed above.
Games this compares to (in my opinion/experiences):
Life is Feudal - pretty much 95% likeness
7 Days to Die - Environment threats like this game, just no roaming hordes
Any “survival”/builder game (GRAV, Minecraft, Planet Explorers, StarForge, etc) - having to go gather resources to crafting and building.
Harvest Moon/Farmville - Farming and feeding animals to gather their animal specific goods.

It's early, but it's got potential.
The game has some rough edges, the UI and customization, but if you're looking for something like RUST, or DayZ but with more of an RPG emphasis, this is definitely a  game to look at.
The crafting is more indepth than many games, but falls very short of titles such as SWG or Wurm online.
The combat is very simplistic, and the ping is a little unreliable but it depends on the time of day.
That being said, it is a huge sandbox, you can kill people, break/take their stuff and run away.

As you may have heard or read in the abundance of negative reviews, this game has Denuvo DRM. Now, no matter what people might say, Denuvo does not ruin your hard drive,  it does not cause latency or dropped frames, and it is not malware. On release there was an issue where the game could only be played online but this was patched out after the first day.
The only concerns with Denuvo are if you plan to go somewhere for an extended amount of time with no internet, or if you make a hardware change to your PC and won't have internet access for some time. The other thing is if you have Norton or McAfee antivirus software, it will prevent the game from launching. There is a relatively easy way to fix this and it does not happen for most other AV softwares.
The game was delayed by 2 weeks on PC for what SEGA claimed to be bug fixes. Before the release there was no mention of DRM being linked to the game, and it was not even listed on the store page until a few days after it released on PC. Among other things that made it difficult for users to rightfully refund the game, the publishers did some shady business with the PC release.
If you wish to not support SEGA's actions or the implimentation of game specific DRM, these are legitimate reasons to consider not getting the game. If none of this bothers you and you want the game, you should not let it stop you.

One word of warning to casual gamer: the difficulty will jump up on you quickly.
Some answers to FAQs:
Q) Do I need to know how to program to play this game?
A: If you're planning on beating it in a reasonable amount of time, yes.
You can still enjoy the game, or at least the beginning of it, but things will get difficult quickly.
Q) Will this game teach me how to program?
Unless you plan to become an assembly developer, no, not really.
The programming you do in this game won't translate into any modern language effectively.
If you are planning on writing some assembly in the future, this game will get you used to the syntax and "flow" of working in assembly, for sure. Real assembly is a lot easier to work with though.
Q) Will this game make me a better developer?
Maybe.
It will certainly help you get an workout in the "algorithms with ridiculous restrictions" category but chances are if your work is highly algorithmic and/or optimized at the assembly level, then you already know what you're doing it.
If your work isn't the above (i.e. you're a web developer) then trying to bring your new TIS-100 skills to your next JavaScript implementation of "iterating over data fields" will most likely do more harm than good.
Q) Will this game help me understand computers?
A: Yes, definitely. Having to do something like reverse a sequence and sort one at the assembly level will give you a glimpse at what is really going on under the hood when you call "List.sort()".
It also gives some good exposure to the difficulties of mult-threaded and parallel development.
If I was the Dean of a CS school, this game would part of the curriculum; "back in my day" we had contests on whose regex could parse a huge log the fastest.
How times have changed.

Frozen Synapse is a turn-based overhead urban-combat strategy game, where you input a chain of commands to coordinate your military squad each turn.  The visuals have a cool VR aesthetic and the game uses impressive procedurally-generated maps.
There are no lifebars and no damage in Frozen Synapse, only alive and dead.  The battle system is deterministic and skill-based, movement speed and a couple other factors deciding which player makes the faster killshot.  The rules behind the killshot timer are simple, but the game never details its combat mechanics (the tutorial is a brief how-to), so new players should read the wiki to gain a better understanding.
I barely played the single-player campaign as this game is all about multiplayer.  There are a number of different game modes, including a football analog where you bid on how far your squad can gain a foothold, and a mode where your team must capture and return more resources than the opposing force.
My favorite by far is Secure mode.  Each player proposes a defensive zone, and then the player proposing the largest area defends it from the other player's attack.  Secure is such an elegant blend of strategy, risk and objective it almost deserves its own game.  The procedural setup leads to wildly different plans.

AC Rogue is a stripped down version of Black Flag, a much shorter game (which is why it gets a 7 and not an 8 or 9), with a few unique little twists that still make it worthwhile. In addition to the ship upgrades and battles, looting warehouses and conquering forts/gang HQs are a different experience. It offers a few things reminiscent of previous AC versions.
For example, lightning assassin strikes like in Revelations, the usual search for items to unlock a native and Templar outfit, renovating buildings to get income like in AC II, Brotherhood and Unity, etc. My least favorite activity were the assassin interventions, it was the same thing over and over and way too frantic. Unlocking the computers at the Abstergo office was much easier. I did miss the underwater exploration with the beautiful color offered by Black Flag.
Overall, I think it’s an OK Assassin’s Creed game, but it certainly does not take the place of AC II or Black Flag. I didn’t think I could side with the Templars but the reason for doing so was valid. However, the main plot, in my opinion, is weak, and just not captivating. There was not a great buildup to the ending. There are times when the camera movements are very “wonky” such as in the bar fights to unlock taverns and in defending the ship. Using the pucklegun is awkward. The scenery is not as pretty as in Black Flag, but the icebergs are a new twist. It’s interesting enough to buy the game (although when it goes on sale it would be a much better value).
I enjoy replaying great AC games, and have played AC II, Brotherhood and Black Flag numerous times. Will I replay Rogue? Like Unity, which also had a weak plot and other problems, not likely for quite some time. I'm still loyal to the AC franchise though, and I hope we get another epic one like AC II, Brotherhood and Black Flag and yes, even Revelations, which offered a great plot.

For anyone who is curious about programming, this is the perfect game. It teaches you how to machine code with a simple environment, with no prior knowledge required. Machine coding is often a challenge because you have to achieve certain things with limited resources which often makes the objective seem impossible, but it's a fantastic puzzle. High level languages (anything that's not machine code) have all these challenges solved already which takes away the pure programming element and a lot of the fun, in the name of getting a program written more simply and quickly. This game is startling for providing a destination, the means to get there via these machine coding puzzles, which aren't puzzles at all but just simple programming. The game shields you from knowledge required of machine specifics. You just get the key 'learning to machine code' experience without all the unecessary fluff. If you have ever messed around with an 8-bit computer back in the day, if you want to program, if you want to teach your kids to program, if you want to know what it is to machine code, if you want the purest puzzle game, if you want to understand the fundamentals of software, if any of these things appeal at all then this is an essential game for you.
Helped me learn assembaly! Also, play on your laptop in public to make people think you are way smarter than you actually are.

This game did the impossible
It made coding tedious tasks with assembly in a limited-resource environment not annoying.
Gameplay:
The puzzles are made up of a 4x3 grid of 'nodes' which are self-contained processor cores with no RAM and enough ROM for about 15 instructions. Each one has 1 internal register, a 'backup' register which you can't directly use but you can swap the primary register with, and 4 'directional' registers which basically act as busses between the nodes, performing a blocking operation when you attempt to use them. There is also a simple FIFO stack node, as well as a [citation needed] RAM node.
10/10 Would code again

I've been playing this game for 4 years. I used to play it on and off during the first two years. The graphics are great and the lore is fantastic. I love the second dream quest, and the lore behind the void. I had my share of fun with this game, but I'm burnt out from all the grinding. You don't have to buy plat. You can grind for pieces and sell them in trade chat. Most newer players get frustrated with the game because DE is terrible at explaining stuff for newer players. It took me a while to get into Warframe because I didn't know what the hell to do. It may also be frustrating to have to wait 12 hours to craft a weapon or 3 days to craft a warframe. DE has gotten slightly better at explaining the game ever since the Plains update, but it is still pretty bad. But once you know what to do, it becomes really fun up to a certain point. You will spend most of your time grinding for prime parts, rare mods, and if there is an event, the event items. The fun slowly started to die again. It started to feel like a chore. DE release new content quite frequently. I tend to dread it because it means more grinding. I have a problem with the missions. They aren't a challenge anymore.  Most of the content have enemies from lvl 5-60, 100 if it is a sortie. There are only a few weapons that are strong. The rest are weak in comparsion. DE has responded by nerfing some of them like the Tonkor and Synoid Simulor making them basically useless. Rather than fix the dmg system, they nerf some good weapons rather than giving their weapons more personality. I also don't see the point of having weapons lvl up if it only provides polarity slots. You may have put and Orkin Catalyst on your weapon and forma it a certain amount of time. But as you lvl up in mastery rank, you gain polarity points. The weapons get no addition stats, so you can have an Orkin Catalyst on a weapon with 3 forma, and you can basically can fit all the mods you want on it-- depending on how much polarity the weapon have ( some weapons have zero polarity slots, so you have to lvl grind the weapon even more to put the mods you want on it). I feel like the weapons should have addition stats much like the Warframes. That way it doesn't fill like you are using a weapon just to lvl it up and never use it again. I hate that. Make the weapons useful. Some weapons are so weak that they barely do damage to a lvl 60  Grineer Heavy Gunner with an Orkin Catalyst on fully formaed. While others weapons can kill enemies past lvl 120 with Orkin Catalyst and fully Formaed. Some weapons I really like, but they are so useless that there is no point in using them. I thought Riven mods was suppose to counter this, but it just makes the stronger weapons stronger. Most people use a pool of weapons that used because they are so damn good. I also have a problem with the game in the sense that there is no endgame content. The sorties and the Trail missions are suppose to be end game. But one is so boring and easy that it gets boring and the other requires a good team otherwise it becomes annoying. I never did much of LOR or The Jordas Verdict, but I have completed them, but they just weren't fun to me, mainly because of the grind and repetition. The sorties are just boring to me. They aren't a challenge unless if I purposely make them a challenge. Plus, the sorties rewards are pretty horrible. I enjoy seeing how far a certain build will take me. I don't mean going to the simulacrum and test weapons on enemies. It would be nice to have missions that start past 120 or more. I technically can do that by playing endless missions but do I really want to play for 1 hour plus? I can go on and on but alas I am tired of typing. Warframe is a fun game when you start playing. It may get frustrating because the game doesn't provide much guidance to newer players. To have the most fun with this game play with friends, like I have. Talk to people. It will make Warframe 100 times more enjoyable. It's amazing how much content there is for a free to play game. You don't have to pay a dime unless if you want some cosmetics.But even then, you still can make your Warframe look sexy just by buying the hundreds of other comsmetics available. UPDATED: 4-11-2015
Facts: Before I start the review I want to state a fact, so that this review is not entirely based on my opinions. The player base went from 228,886 players in season 5 (Sep. 2013) to its current player base of 24,889 (4-11-2015) for a reason. That is a 920% decrease in the number of players. Also not all of the 24,889 players actually play the game on a regular basis, that is just the number of players that have played at least one match. If you check the reviews on steam most of the negative reviews are written by people who have 200-1000+ hours in the game and used to love playing it. Just keep that in mind before you buy this game.
Credentials: I have put over 580 hours into the game as of this review. I am a fairly high tier player and go back and forth between leagues 2 and 3, this means I have a good amount of experience in higher tier matches.
First I will list the pros then the cons and then additional information. I do not consider the additional information to be a pro nor a con, I am just providing it for those who are still considering getting this game.
PROS:
-The graphic art and animations are great, and work well with the side-scrolling nature of this game.
-The characters are very unique and have cool abilities that give each character their own personality.
-The fighting in this game is very fun, it feels alot like smite had a baby with super mario bros.
-The abilities (upgrades) menu is very well done, and allows the player to counterbuild the enemy team.
-The leveling in this game is extremely simple. It is based off of collecting solar (currency) for player kills, turret kills, etc. and spending the solar in order to by abilities. This makes the game good for players that are new to this genre of game, and also provides enough complexity to entertain veterans to this genre.
-The maps are well made. Each map has a unique feature in its center. For example one map has reduced gravity, one has a giant worm that can kill you, one has an invisibility orb, and one has fire that turns on and off throughout the match.
CONS:
-The matchmaking system is terrible. As a league 2 player I was frequently matched against players that were league 6-7. There is a huge skill difference between leagues 6/7 and league 2, this made matches boring for me and frustrating for new players. Also the matchmaking system frequently puts players in matches that have already started. It is no fun to join a match in which your team is already loosing by a huge margine.
-The game is P2P. Players will constantly get matched against people with bad internet connection. This causes high latency and frequent packet loss. Since some characters do a ton of burst damage, if the player you are fighting has high latency, you can often be killed from 2-3 hit boxes away. The devs have talked about starting dedicated servers; however, they have been talking about it for over a year and still have not done it.
-Some characters are inherently better than other characters. This means that you will often play against the same characters over and over again until the next patch makes a different set characters better than the others.
-Players can die their way to victory. They do this by attacking the turret until they die, respawning and repeating over and over again. This is able to happen because certian characters do more damage to turrets than other characters. Also the abilities that these characters need to accomplish this are cheaper to get than other abilities.
Additional Information:
-Matches can last anywhere from 15-45 minutes.
-Each character has 4 rows of abilities with 6 abilities in each row. When you buy abilities in the match, you can have a maximum of 3 unique abilities in each row (only 3 out of the 6 for each row of abilities).
-The game is 3v3. This is the only option, there is no 2v2 or 5v5 like in some other MOBAs.
-You have to aim your abilities with your cursor (or controller), they do not auto hit on click (much like smite).
-The prestige system is optional. If you prestige, you loose all of your abilities and have to earn them back again. Some players will love this feature and some will hate it.
I hope that this review has been helpful, and has given you a better understanding of what the game is like. I love what this game used to be and it is still very good in some ways; however, until the matchmaking is fixed, dedicated servers are added, and the game is balanced more, I simply cannot recomend this game. If you find this game on sale for $2 or less then it cannot hurt to pick it up. I would love to see the player base go back up and the game to be restored to its past glory.

An excellent space combat simulator that has all the bells and whistles of most AAA titles; except it's made by one person.  Don't blow this off as some clone or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt; this will give everyone who enjoys space combat sims plenty of entertainment. It may not be as polished or in-depth as games like Elite Dangerous or Star Citizen; but it is
, and works 100%.
The star system is vast, mostly contained within our own Milkyway galaxy. I don't think any person has enough time to completely explore the whole area; as it would take thousands and thousands of hours to do so. There are many unexplored areas that are left for the player to find on their own; but there are plenty of "inhabited" planets and sectors in between to keep you busy.
There are planets with terrain, atmosphere, bases, vegetation, and resources that you will also need to explore, either by ship or on foot. You can customize your vessel almost however you want; from re-arranging the chassis and different sections, to customizing weapon platforms and even your character/crew.
The only "cons" that I have is the small (but active) community, and slow (but consistant) progress to perfection. However, these are easily forgivable since they are mostly my opinion, and theres still 1000x more to this game than just multiplayer and eye-candy.
There's really too much to write about, and I have barely scratched the surface. It's best to support a great and dedicated developer and see for yourself! It's cheap, and even goes on sale from time to time.  Check out the official forums and SeeJay's www site for starcharts, information, and mods.

I would have preferred a better reviewing system that would allow me to moderate my point, but this will have to do. If I had to give an honest opinion of whether or not you should get the game, I would say that it depends of what you're looking for, as well as how patient you are. This game actually came pretty close to a good recommendation for me : you're relatively free to do what you want, you can customize your ship on several aspects, you have multiplayer, if you're into that stuff... It doesn't look half bad either, the menus are clear and precise, the gameplay is pretty good, and the combat in particular is quite involving.
The game does suffer from a few flaws, though, one of them being fatal in my eyes. The first one is that even though you can customize you ship, the different modules you get are nothing more than upgraded versions of what you already have. What I mean is that you don't have the choice between a shield that's very strong and one that's less strong, but recharges quickly, that sort of thing. You just have "small shield that's not great but will fit on small frames", and it gets bigger from that.
Another flaw, this one more important : ennemies aren't all that smart, and seem to have access to an unlimited supply of missiles, or at least that's the impression I get. Combat isn't bad in itself, but make one mistake and you're likely to get blown up, so it encourages a sort of "jousting" pattern that can get repetitive. Your fights will be pretty much the same every time.
Last problem I have with this game, and this one is what made me give it a negative recommendation : the reputation system is absolute garbage. So, you have several factions in this game, and doing contracts for them or destroying their ships will impact it. Okay. But your reputation in a sector won't carry over to another, it's just for THAT sector. That means that you can (WILL, if you're following the plot) stumble on sectors where the Navy don't like you. At all. They don't know you, they don't know where you're from, or what you want, but boy do they know they want you dead. And we're not talking about pirates, we're talking about the NAVY. So pretty much every ship you'll come across here are hostiles. You'll want to bribe them, but they won't answer your trade requests. And here comes the REALLY dumb part : you'll want to do a few contracts for them, but for that, you'll have to dock in the station while everyone is trying to kill you, then pay a fee to even be able to bring up the contracts menu, then leave the station without getting shot down on the way out, then reach the mission waypoint. And do you think they'll stop shooting you just because you accepted to do their work ? ♥♥♥♥ no, don't be insane. Good luck trying to do your mission while having to fend off unlimited waves of hostiles and their flood of missiles. And good luck trying to get a good rep with those guys if you have to blow their ships up while doing THEIR job that THEY gave you. Not that you really CAN, since you won't last long against 15 bad guys and their unlimited reinforcements...
I really wanted to like that game, it had so much potential... But as you can see, despite the apparent choice you have to decide what you'll want to be, you'll get shoehorned into investing in weapons and strong shields to even have a chance. That, or ignore the sectors where everyone and their mother will try to kill you for no reason, but that's just really, really dumb...

This is an often overlooked gem of a space sim. Known for a very steep learning curve, especially with the flight model within a newtonian physics engine. Amazing but challenging.

Vice (the creator) is an amazing individual. I've purchased the last two titles as well, playing the hell out of them learning as I go. The Evochron series has been a solid space sim series for those that want the pilot experience. So much has been accomplished with Mercenary, just been amazing to be a part of.
I play this and Elite Dangerous (currently Gamma 1.05) a lot, and if you're good in one, you'll do well in the other. Evochron has a lot to offer the person that doesn't need led by a carrot on a stick, especially if you go online (seamless online/offline experience btw, along with seamless world and seamless planetary landings) as there is plenty of fellow pilots looking to help you become a skilled ace.

Upgrading and designing your ship is awesome, the community is among the best without an elitist attitude towards newcomers, very welcoming.
If you want an amazing space sim that doesn't break the bank or your PC, but offers one of the best piloting experiences period, you cannot look past Evochron Mercenary. As I said before often overlooked, but appreciated by most that give it a chance. Anyone that has enjoyed space sims in the past, arcade or realistic, easy or challenging, will find something to like here.

In honor of the release of Star Breaker: The Force Awakens, directed by J.J. Abrams, I will be reviewing the entire Star Wars franchise.
Now the original movies were nothing particularly 'new', but George Lucas brought something to the sci-fi concept that no one had before - anime style graphics and a predominantly female cast that would run around a board bonking eachother for resources that tallied up towards victory. These characters had personality - they had something they were good at, yet with all their flaws they felt very human. Couple that with bad decision making and you had a space opera in which anyone could win, even Jabba the Hutt. All of this meshed together into a franchise that would win the hearts of millions for decades to come.
Some odd decade and a half ago, George Lucas decided to unleash movies 1-3 to predate the struggles of Mark Hamill and Harrison Ford in the form of DLC. While these DLCs featured better visual effects and 'different' characters, the need to make the game children friendly meant that most of the RNG was thrown out the window and what you had were just upgraded analogues of previously seen characters, spread across different DLC as to trick you into thinking it was something new when it really wasn't. The story was pretty cut and dry, Liam Neeson failed to kill anyone within the first 3 seconds of the first movie, and everything was pretty two dimensional in an obvious attempt to rake in the money.
The worst displays of this came with the two recent superhero movies Ryan Reynolds did - the Green Lantern and Deadpool. DC has always been a failure in the box office, and QP Dangerous was just that: it was an unoriginal and groan-worthy game tapping into an overdone genre, overwhelmingly outclassed by the superior Disney produced Touhou films. Reynolds felt pretty uncomfortable in the role of QP (Dangerous), and the game was a failure as it failed to sell to 100% OJ fans based on getting this new character who was just absolutely terrible.
This was reversed with the release of Deadpool. In it, Reynolds was far more comfortable in his role as Sora (M), destroying everything in his path like the complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ he is. It was a box office success, raking in plenty of dough as Sora was a far more original game than QP Dangerous, and everyone loved the character Reynolds breathed life into.
And now, keeping that in mind, the much delayed Star Breaker: The Force Awaken DLC has arrived.
J.J. Abrams decided to tap into what made the original 100% OJ good, and update it for a new generation. Learning from what the old DLC had done, he introduced characters descended from others - Starbreaker from Yuki and Tomomo, and Sweetbreaker from QP and Peat. While somewhat fresh, it still went along a dangerous precedent of nothing really new while removing the flaws of the previous characters, ensuring that you were obligated to buy into these new ones or risk being left behind.
Up for debate is the storyline, which paralleled the original completely. Once again, it was nothing new, but designed to drag in a new generation of fans and their money. Because of the addition of a campaign mode for either character you are paying $1 extra compared to the other DLC, but this is laughably diminished by the inclusion of a fourth difficulty even lower than easy, so that you can just hold the skip button for five minutes and get to a dialogue sequence shorter than this review. This is on par with the spinoff card set DLC, which added in cards that no one really plays because they were awful.
Long story short, everyone is allowed to enjoy the original game, especially when it's on sale at 70% off or something comparable. It is well worth the laughs, the tears, the curses, and gets you good mileage in a simplistic format.
Just stay away from all the sequels. Even the ones with Liam Neeson.

There are quite a few reviews comparing Movie Studio Boss to Lionhead's The Movies. If you're looking for anything similar to The Movies, I recommend you to stay away from this game.
It is more comparable to the german game Der Produzent published in 1996 by Silver Style Entertainment. That being said, it seems to be a more watered-down version of it, reduced to mere number crunching. All the interesting aspects like calling actors and directors, negotiating with them, building up a kind of relationship, appearing in talk shows to promote your movies by choosing appropriate dialogue options without♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the crowd and all kinds of bargaining, award ceremonies, writing and reading scripts to find out who would be the perfect actors and actresses to star in your movie, all that is missing, alongside a multiplayer mode to compete against your friends.
What's left is the rather repetitive actions of choosing a script or having one written, waiting for it to be good enough, choosing all the people involved, waiting for the shooting to be done, choosing pre-production crews, waiting for them to finish and then gamble about with a marketing system that's not at all covered in the tutorial despite being the most complicated part of the game. I'm not even sure whether it's working correctly, with some amounts set back to zero when you switch between US market, international market and DVD/Bluray sales. I had to google how it's supposed to work, but am not entirely convinced the marketing plan does what it was designed to do.
There seems to have been an effort trying to simplify the game in general, with the different stations (script writing, pre-production, shooting, post-production, marketing) happening one after another, but that actually has a counterproductive feeling to it, taking away a lot of realism. Having to wait for the Postpro to finish instead of giving them a deadline they have to finish by, or being able to start the marketing process no sooner than when the movie is done, just seems rather weird.
Also, in terms of repetition, I'd like to add that I had 15 out of the 17 available achievements for this game after playing for only two hours, not helping my motivation go on much longer.
Apart from above mentioned criticisms, it's a nice time filler if you have a few hours to kill and happen to receive the game at a highly reduced price.

Sonic the Hedgehog 2 was one of the--if not the--first video game I ever owned. I recall Sonic 3 and Sonic & Knuckles. I remember the disappointment that was Sonic Adventure and the decade-long schadenfreude that followed. I've seen the horrors that is the Sonic fandom evolve in the grimy corners of the visible internet. I've watched the Errant Signal and Super Bunnyhop videos on what went wrong with Sonic as a franchise.
And despite all that history and nostalgia I never felt the Genesis Sonic games were that great. They were above-average to be sure, and had moments of greatness, but there was this intangible *something* that never put them into the same league as Mario or Mega Man or Castlevania. Even the decent Game Boy Advance/Nintendo DS games never really "got there."
Well.... that has finally changed.
Sonic Mania is the game that realizes the potential of 2D Sonic. The levels are long and varied. Chemical Plant Zones 1 and 2 run a clinic on this-- Zone 1 remains frustrating as ever, and it morphs into this glorious menage of new gimmicks for Zone 2. It is everything short of the developers showving a text crawl into the game saying: "We played the games too; we get it. Here's how we're going to make them fun." Then it throws you a great boss fight and sends you to Studiopolis Zone as a reward.
The rest is... well it's all good. The graphics, the music, the aesthetics, the feel of the controls it all works exactly as you'd expect a good game should. There isn't more to be said about it than that, and that's a very good thing.
----------
Tl;dr: Give this game a shot no matter where your opinion on Sonic the Hedgehog games lie. It is a great 2D Platformer--the best I've played since Shovel Knight--and worth full price.

This is my first writing a review, but Therian Saga earns it. It just released here on Steam, but it's been available for a while, and I've been playing quite some time. I gave up on it because the server population was dwindling, and I hope this Steam launch will bring back the masses.
I'm also writing this because I see some reviewers yelling "just another freemium facebook game!" and "p2w!" Don't believe them. They probably launched the game, saw the energy bar and the premium shop, and couldn't look past that. The premium shop sells some quality of life stuff, but it's not really p2w, and the energy system isn't all that limited, it's mostly to prevent fully idle play. (although some degree of idling is achieved trough automated settlements.)
The combat system is a pretty solid turn-based affair, complex enough to be entertaining, but not too complicated. Where Therian Saga really shines for me though, is the crafting. A robust player-based economy, where most resources are gathered and processed by other players? Check. Custom settlement building anywhere on the map, both player- and guild- owned? Check. Automated settlements that gather or process stuff while you're away? Check. Skill training that requires some actual thought, and not "make this worthless recipe a million times"? Check. Really, it's nearing Eve Online in complexity and depth.
Example? I started out chopping logs in a forest. To make these logs into lumber, I needed sufficiently strong enough blades. These were quite expensive, so I raised my carpenter skills slowly, and custom build some equipment to lower the requirements for those blades. Soon I was able to use lower quality (and thus cheaper) blades to process the logs. Still not satisfied, I branched out into mining and blacksmithing to make my own cheap blades. This required some firewood (lowest quality wood) so I could chop that myself. I even started making more money by selling those blades in bulk, and after a while I could afford to establish a settlement. I found a nice spot in a forest near a mountain, bought and gathered more materials there untill I was able to build some huts and hire a couple of lumberjacks and miners, each needing a specific building in the settlement (a lumberyard and a mine, each needing several components bought on the player market, and influencing the quality of the building) After that, my main char was travelling back and forth between my settlement and a nearby town with a public forge, where I could set up 8-hour queues of first ingot-melting, and then blade-smithing, when I wasn't playing actively. The money I made with that, allowed me to get some better equipment for combat, and better tools and machines to improve my crafting skills. Soon I was making steel equipment in my own private forge in my own settlement!
TLDR: Like old-skool rpg's? Like complex crafting and skilling? Like theorycraft? Play Therian Saga!

"I saw a distant planet with rings like saturn, as i flew closer i could see the rings were made of tiny particles of water as i drifted through them in my starship" - 8.5/10
EM is a sandbox space pilot simulator. It provides you with all the tools you need to live the life of an intrepid space explorer as you blast around an (almost) infinite galaxy filled with collossal space stations, glittering nebula, astroid belts, and planets.
How you choose to use this sandbox is very much up to you. Want to be a fighter pilot? No problem. Want to mine and trade precious minerals? You got it. Feel the need to build a fleet and have your own armada? Ok. Wanna explore the farthest reaches of the universe either by jumpgate or just pointing your ships nose at a distant star and pushing on the throttle? Oh yes! Fancy visiting the surface of that giant blue planet over there? Yep. Maybe cruise across mountains and dock at the local trade city for repairs and fuel? Sure.
Whatever you want to do EM has you covered.
However, despite the fact that it is probably obvious by now that I am impressed with this game it is only fair that I point out a few low points and niggles.
Firstly, the graphics. They are pretty dated. Still, what is here is all done pretty well. Distant stars flare light across your cockpit, nebula and gas clouds sparkle and shimmer as electrical storms rage, and giant space transporters lumber across the sky. On the downside the textures are all pretty bland up close. This is not so bad in space but it is on the planet surfaces that this really lowers the immersion. The actual concept of being able to fly from outer space, into the planet's atmosphere, and right down to the tree line is brilliant and the mechanics of it work really well. Unfortunately when you get there you see that the surface is just barren and featureless. A few sparodic trees and one or two cities is not enough to save this part of the game. A real shame as the actual descending to, and launching back up from, the planets is a lovely experience. Its just annoying that there is nothing to do when you get there.
Secondly, this is no hand holder. You will need to use the forums and wiki's to get to grips with this game. My six and a half hours playtime probably equates to about half of that as actual 'game' time. Still, nothing worth having is easy and  i found the learning quite fun.
Lastly, the quests are pretty generic. You will make more money in ten mins of mining than by doing a dozen starter quests. Also there is a very limited amount of detail at times as so far as the living, breathing galaxy goes. There are lots of other ships, constant radio chatter, and dozens of busy space ports, but i'm yet to see anything along the lines of real faction interactions. Still, not been playing long so we'll see
Don't let these points put you off, there are a few mods available for graphical tweaks and the community is still pretty active and helpful for the learning side of things.
EM is a wonderful opportunity to just grab a spaceship and jet off to the stars. You'll be glad that you did.

Being a fan of tactical shooters, I'd picked up Frozen Synapse the second I'd heard of it. I'd gone in expecting the same levels of awesomeness I'd experienced in titles such as Ghost Recon and Rainbow Six.
I wasn't disappointed.
As I'm sure you've gathered by now, Frozen Synapse is a turn-based strategy game. Both teams piece together their plans, press the start button, and watch as the battle unfolds.
The planning phase makes up the vast majority of the game, with most of your time spent fiddling with aiming directions, movement, testing the layout of your troops against every possible scenario and so on and so forth. It takes an incredible amount of time to plan out a turn that effectively lasts five seconds- but you'd better believe that they're some of the tensest five seconds I've ever experienced in gaming.
Beyond its brilliant core gameplay, Frozen Synapse boasts an intriguing storyline and setting that's vague in all the right places along with an absolutely fantastic soundtrack.
I'd fully recommend this to anybody with a love for tactical squad based combat and strategy. It's a great game.

The mastery level is what prevents this, people cant buy their way to the top and get all the best gear, when they need to level up for it first. When leveing up your mastery, you have to gain XP by using weapons that are not already max level, this means you must progress by changing up your weapons and warframes. This is not forced on you however, you may use only one new item that is not fully maxed out, this means less XP. It is a very well done balancing act that keeps the game fresh at all times.
Trading for the paid currency also is what many of games should allow people to do for ingame items. This means that the buying end can get a cheaper deal than off the market, and the free player who does not spend money also gets to enjoy the premium customisation stuff. It's a win win.
Combat is fluent and the controls feel right, once you get the jumping combos down to move around a map super quickly feels super awesome and so does melee attacking enemies from out of mid-air. This game aims to make you feel like a god and succeeds in doing so on a massive scale.
With the hundreds of different weapons and warframes to to choose from, you can find your perfect way of playing this game.

At 16 hours I had had enough: I HATED this game and logged in to write a scathing review. And yet, 160+ hours later, I’m on my second playthrough, purchased the previous DOS, and am writing a positive review while listening to the OST. What happened?! This whole misunderstanding started with an impulse purchase and a single, overlooked, very tiny, yet crucial word.
I had finished a turn based RPG and was in the mood for another, when I saw that DOS2 had just been released. I almost never buy a game at launch, but the trailer looked great, Metacritic boasted a ludicrously high score along with dozens of tasty blurbs, and the whole game had that tantalizing sheen that anything
has. The only negative thing I found at the time was a single review that ranted about rage-quitting the game. Who rage-quits a RPG, I thought at the time?
I took a risk, and was immediately entranced: the character creation was complex and intriguing, the opening story and fight sequences were engaging, everything seemed so promising that I hardly noticed the dreaded word I had overlooked earlier. After a while, however, things took a dark turn for the worse. I kept getting beaten, and beaten badly; my frustration mounted; the world was turning against me; nothing was helping; I felt completely powerless…and then…rage quit.
Amidst the guilt, confusion and shame, I decided to sit down and actually read through all those glowing reviews; what was I missing here? And then I finally noticed it, that dreaded word:
. I do not play tactical RPG’s, never have, assumed I never would, and was unprepared for what I was experiencing here. It’s not that I don’t play tactical games, but I like to keep my genres separate, and was clearly not expecting this.
I play games for different reasons. Some for immersion, others for adrenaline, mental stimulation, relaxation, storytelling, etc. For me, RPG’s equal immersion; that’s what I expect, why I play them. The acts of becoming a character, building them up, leading them through decisions and adventures, customizing them, engaging in their world, these are creative acts. Tactics, on the other hand, are left-brained; strategy; detached, clinical, chess-like, requiring a different mindset. When I crave that, I’ll play a strategy game. But to combine the two is counter to what I want from a role playing experience.
So, after hours of trying really hard to like this game, only to die repeatedly in the process, I had officially given up. This simply wasn’t for me. Just as I was about to uninstall, though, something happened, and to this day I still don’t know what it was. For some mysterious reason, I decided to launch DOS2 one last time. I began to play, I mean
play. By the time I finally escaped Fort Joy, I realized something: this game is getting better; a LOT better. And my negative review? Well, suddenly it was becoming a positive one.
It was still no cake-walk, but my feelings began to change when I altered my play style. Up to then I had been approaching it as any other RPG; and it finally sunk in that I simply can’t do that. I couldn’t run blindly into battles, dash wildly about the landscape, race through dialogue; instead I had to slow down, take nothing for granted, become obsessed with details. I also had to redefine what it meant to lose. I had to go into each fight knowing my characters wouldn’t survive, instead using the chance to study the enemies, how they play, how I react, and how it all unfolds, so when I reload, I can play the fight “for real” and have a plan in mind. This meant that I had to play most battles upwards of half a dozen times before I got it right; but when things did click into place, it was a beautiful feeling.
Still, I do have a few remaining criticisms, the biggest being the quest and map design. Confusing, unforgiving, unhelpful, oblique, unfair…are but a few of the words I’d use to describe them. Simply put, it’s just way too easy to stumble into things you’re not ready for. As for the quests, dialogues and journal entries are misleading, key information is frequently given out of order, or omitted altogether, way too may red-herrings, and the supposed freedom to tackle a quest multiple ways doesn’t work if you dare to do things out of order. If you’re looking for guidance, look to Google, for you will find none in-game. People might tout this as a feature: it doesn’t hold your hand, they cheer. Indeed. There is no hand-holding, which would be fine if the quest design didn’t keep tripping over its own two feet.
The map layout is so cluttered and dense that basically each and every pixel is trying to kill you. At first I felt this was infuriatingly random; after a while I did start to pick up on the clues, and was able to avoid such missteps, but it was a lesson learned the hard way. There’s nothing wrong with this, but I’m used to other games which balance the levels with your current abilities; you can freely wander where you’re likely to survive, and prevented from getting in over your head. But DOS2 is more than happy to let you get in over your head. The key is to recognize your own limits, knowing the game won’t do it for you.
As far as audio/visual design, this is single-handedly some of the best art-direction I’ve seen in a game. The detail given to the environments is so rich that the world feels alive in ways that other games could only dream of. Rivellon is LIVED IN; it exists, it’s lush, and rich in the most unexpected ways. By comparison, all other RPG worlds feel dead, like stage sets populated by mere mannequins. Every square inch of DOS2 is simply bursting with life. The audio is top notch too. I just love the soundtrack. Works brilliantly in game, and is great outside as well. The voices are an absolute treat, too. I don’t know where they found these actors, but their delivery is infectious. The dialogue is already good, but you can tell how much they really dug their characters, the way they rolled the words around and added such flavor to the lines, making each and every one, from the biggest hero down to the lowest fish monger, feel 100% unique. Seriously, is there an award for best video game ensemble performance?
Regarding immersion, even after coming to terms with a tactical RPG, I was never able to feel that I was part of the world of Rivellon, or that the character I was playing was really me, or that the decisions I made mattered. The story didn’t haunt me between gaming sessions, I can barely remember most of it now, to be honest. And yet, I’ve had so many
experiences, so many moments that feel were hand-crafted just for me, so many surprises (both by what I could get away with, and just how flexible the game mechanics really are), that I do feel an emotional, as well as intellectual, connection. This game has given me memories of frustration, true, but also memories of joy, surprise, amazement, wonderment, suspense, excitement, and mischievousness. Above all the miraculous small accomplishments that make this game possible, it is for these memories that I thank Larian the most.
So now we’ve arrived. That’s how a sternly negative review, over the course of a few hundred unexpected hours of play, morphed into a shout of praise for what very well might be one of the best RPG’s ever…even if it is tactical.
But one question remains: what on earth possessed me to keep playing, after I had given up for what I thought was the final time? Was it that I felt goaded into continuing by reading all the other glowing reviews? Perhaps. Was it guilt, that somehow I was missing out on something great? Maybe. Was it stubbornness, since I paid full price, I might as well force myself to enjoy the darn thing? Possibly. All of these things could be true, and could be what drew me back in to the world of Rivellon. It could be. But really…really, I think I did it for the cat.

Sonic the Hedgehog 2 was one of the--if not the--first video game I ever owned. I recall Sonic 3 and Sonic & Knuckles. I remember the disappointment that was Sonic Adventure and the decade-long schadenfreude that followed. I've seen the horrors that is the Sonic fandom evolve in the grimy corners of the visible internet. I've watched the Errant Signal and Super Bunnyhop videos on what went wrong with Sonic as a franchise.
And despite all that history and nostalgia I never felt the Genesis Sonic games were that great. They were above-average to be sure, and had moments of greatness, but there was this intangible *something* that never put them into the same league as Mario or Mega Man or Castlevania. Even the decent Game Boy Advance/Nintendo DS games never really "got there."
Well.... that has finally changed.
Sonic Mania is the game that realizes the potential of 2D Sonic. The levels are long and varied. Chemical Plant Zones 1 and 2 run a clinic on this-- Zone 1 remains frustrating as ever, and it morphs into this glorious menage of new gimmicks for Zone 2. It is everything short of the developers showving a text crawl into the game saying: "We played the games too; we get it. Here's how we're going to make them fun." Then it throws you a great boss fight and sends you to Studiopolis Zone as a reward.
The rest is... well it's all good. The graphics, the music, the aesthetics, the feel of the controls it all works exactly as you'd expect a good game should. There isn't more to be said about it than that, and that's a very good thing.
----------
Tl;dr: Give this game a shot no matter where your opinion on Sonic the Hedgehog games lie. It is a great 2D Platformer--the best I've played since Shovel Knight--and worth full price.

+ Border lines help to navigate differing territories, plan new settlements with a more informed approach, and investigate spheres of control; the restrictive aspect of this feature also serves to deter early rush tactics and general griefing
+ Zoom feature helps to navigate terrain and keep track of movement over large swathes of territory
+ The diplomacy options play out as more than a gimmicky feature, and are both simple on paper and functional in practice
+ Time restrictions during campaigns add to the challenge in a way that is rewarding if successful
+ Have seen some before and after stills, it's clear that the visuals and textures are noticeably improved; this should further appeal to veterans of the franchise
+ The re-release now supports Twitch integration; I don't use the feature myself, but this is still a significant boon for the streaming community
+ Features a satisfying variety of playable cultures, each with their own defining traits
+ The trategic overview map is a nice feature, and consists of a simple, turn-based Risk-style map; some notable features include: bonus cards you can apply, resource bonuses, diplomacy, and varying types of battles that hinge on several factors
+ Impressive array of options and game-modes available for multiplayer, many of them quite novel for an RTS game (although they're not quite as alien for other strategy sub-genres)
+ Attrition and supply features are a nice addition, and do well to keep one prepared and on their toes during offensive engagements
+ Excellent sense of balance in all aspects
+ Special units are presented well in the game and don't feel overpowered or cheap in their use
- The overworld strategy part of the game feels a bit watered down compared to other staples of the genre; it isn't necessarily bad, but it's also clear that this feature was never meant to be the bread-and-butter of the franchise
- The AI feels a bit underwhelming, and I had expected more of an improvement for the re-release

I really wanted to like this game, but I just couldn't. For an open-world game set in space, there is surprisingly very little to do, and the learning curve is so steep that it isn't really a curve at all. And unlike other games with harsh barriers to entry, there isn't enough of a userbase for new players to be able to rely on generous veterans showing them the ropes.
In all honesty, I might even be able to deal with all that if it weren't for the in-game economy being completely broken. That is by far my biggest complaint: that the player is forced to spend 90% of their time worrying about making enough money for fuel, and because of that, barely gets to experience any of the actually entertaining and worthwhile aspects of the game. The jobs available to pilots simply don't pay nearly well enough to sustain fuel usage and other mundane expenses, all too often leaving players stranded in the void of outer space. And no, there's no space tow truck; if you get stuck, you can only pray that some nearby player is compassionate enough to risk their own ship to save you (which, while realistic, is pretty unlikely to happen considering how expensive it would be for them to do this, and how few players there are to begin with).
Additionally, apart from avoiding becoming stranded and possibly losing their character, there really isn't much positive incentive for players to make money at all. In stark contrast to comparable space-simulator-MMOs such as Eve, there is an incredibly small selection of upgrades, most of which aren't even much better than the starting equipment when you think about how much work it is to acquire them.
Sure, it's probably one of the most depressingly realistic space simulators out there, and captures wonderfully the all-too-real feelings of futility one might conceivably experience as an actual space pilot attempting to tackle the cosmic abyss all by himself. But there's a point where realism just isn't fun, and this game has clearly passed it. All things considered, while it is a beautiful game and would've been excellent if it were released about 10 years ago, it's just not exciting enough to warrant its pricetag.
Money aside, I really wouldn't have half as much to complain about if it weren't for the fact that it was advertised as more of an MMORPG than it actually is. Evochron Mercenary is basically 100% simulator, so whether it was intentional or not, the way it was presented was misleading for many buyers, including myself.
tl;dr: If you're absolutely in love with retro space sims and are ready to tackle one of the most grisly learning curves you've ever experienced in your days as a gamer, then by all means, get this game; you'll love it. But if you're anyone else, give it a miss--or at least do a little research into the gameplay before deciding to buy it.

This game has so many different narratives it's amazing, it's essentially a book where you're the author yet you're also the reader. What follows is a pretty epic series of events, I'm not the greatest writer but I love this story.
Through much  political intrigue and disease alike, Queen Cumman of Eire (Ireland) sat on the throne. She had four children.
Her eldest daughter, Muirne, married a king of Scotland who shortly after died in battle against the English. The king's brother inherited the throne and offered his hand in marriage to Muirne. Her Ambition made the choice for her. Five children later, she died in childbirth at 32.
Her youngest daughter, Tuathflaith, was born Ugly and through her upbringing, became Deceitful and Gluttonous. No man desired her and so she resides in her mother's court. Through her many pleas to be married to have a family, Queen Cumman is considering one of her many courtiers for an arranged marriage.
Her eldest son, Cathal, the twin of Muirne, was taught as a child by Tressach, the Marshal of Eire, a Brawny man who none could equal in tournaments. He grew up to replace his mentor as Eire's Marshal but not for long. The Queen named him as the Duke of Ulaidh, a territory of four provinces including the county of Ulaidh.
Her youngest son, Aedgen, wasn't taught in hand to hand combat yet excelled his siblin on the battlefield as a  Brilliant Strategist. Through his desire for land, the Queen entitled him to the county of Ulaidh, essentially the capital of the duchy of Ulaidh.
Cathal had declared independence from his mother to create the Kingdom of Ulaidh, to the Queen's surprise. Although not on his own terms, Aedgen joined him. However their relationship with their mother did not change such was their loving relationships.
Years passed and King Cathal became consumed by his power. He was now known as Cathal the Tyrant. Having enough and seeking reformation, Prince Aedgen had declared a revolution against his brother. The timing was perfect as Cathal's troops were abroad in Wales attempting to expand his territory. However he had not anticipated Cathal sending a crow to the Queen of Eire who came to stop the rebellion. She had turned a blind eye to Cathal's method of reign, he was her eldest son and heir after all. Although the Queen was old she was a warrior at heart and so met Aedgen on the battlefield.  The rebellion was destroyed in an instant.
King Cathal had thrown his brother in the dungeon for a few years despite his mother's pleas to release him. Eventually Cathal had offered to ransom Aedgen for 46 gold to his mother. A ransom for his brother to his own mother. She accepted immediately although not as fast as she realized King Cathal wasn't the same Cathal she had raised. Previouslly unbenknownst to her, she discovered that he had even renounced the Lord, following instead the cult of Waldensian who were heretics of the Church. Queen Cumman made a heavy decision that very same day. She declared war in the name of not only Christianity or her Kingdom, but for her own family.
She had petitioned the King of Scotland (the same one, who had now married one of the Queen's kinswomen) for aid to which they accepted without question. Cathal the Tyrant's men were raised. The Queen ordered only her own men to gather, leaving her vassal's men to defend their territories. The Scottish were rallying but it would take them months to arrive.
King Cathal the Tyrant marched from their capital, leading 4300 men, half of which were heavy infantry. He was accompanied by a Waldensian priest.
The Queen's men of 4458 also marched. Queen Cumman decied there was only one man who, in every right, should lead her army. Prince Aedgen. Her faithful commanders, Mugron and Tressach (the very same man who mentored Cathal), secured his flanks.
The two armies met on the plains in Bréifne. This clash would decide the dynasty of Eire. The battle of Ceann Lios was about to begin.

100% Orange Juice is the 5 year anniversary game of Japanese Indie game developer Orange_Juice, starring some of their hit characters from Suguri, Sora, QP Shooting, and Flying Red Barrel - Diary of a Little Aviator. Now, you might be asking "WHAT THE HELL ARE THESE GAMES!?" and to that I answer that they're Indie and Japanese, and you need to know nothing about the characters to enjoy this game. If anything, this game is the gateway game to try out the rest of Orage_Juice's catalogue here on Steam!
Before each game, you can choose a character and what cards you want in the deck each game. At the start of each game, everyone starts at their own home, with a single star and card. You play by completing Norma, which are objectives. Each game starts with every player needing to collect 10 stars, but you can choose to change it after you get 10 stars. You can choose to collect stars or battle for wins to achieve the set Norma. Once you collect the number of stars or wins, you must land on a home, which you can stop at whenever you pass it, or land on someone else's home in order to achieve the Norma. The first player to complete 5 Norma wins. In addition, the cards you choose can be randomly drawn out the deck at certain times, such as landing on a green space. There are many different types of cards, though for the sake of time, I'll say that you need a certain level to use each, and some cost a certain amount of stars, and the types are Trap, Boost, Event, Combat, Gift and Hyper, Hyper being the card exclusive to the character you are currently playing as. Though it sounds like there is a huge learning curve, it's quick and easy to learn it all.
- A very pleasing artstyle

Sonic the Hedgehog 2 was one of the--if not the--first video game I ever owned. I recall Sonic 3 and Sonic & Knuckles. I remember the disappointment that was Sonic Adventure and the decade-long schadenfreude that followed. I've seen the horrors that is the Sonic fandom evolve in the grimy corners of the visible internet. I've watched the Errant Signal and Super Bunnyhop videos on what went wrong with Sonic as a franchise.
And despite all that history and nostalgia I never felt the Genesis Sonic games were that great. They were above-average to be sure, and had moments of greatness, but there was this intangible *something* that never put them into the same league as Mario or Mega Man or Castlevania. Even the decent Game Boy Advance/Nintendo DS games never really "got there."
Well.... that has finally changed.
Sonic Mania is the game that realizes the potential of 2D Sonic. The levels are long and varied. Chemical Plant Zones 1 and 2 run a clinic on this-- Zone 1 remains frustrating as ever, and it morphs into this glorious menage of new gimmicks for Zone 2. It is everything short of the developers showving a text crawl into the game saying: "We played the games too; we get it. Here's how we're going to make them fun." Then it throws you a great boss fight and sends you to Studiopolis Zone as a reward.
The rest is... well it's all good. The graphics, the music, the aesthetics, the feel of the controls it all works exactly as you'd expect a good game should. There isn't more to be said about it than that, and that's a very good thing.
----------
Tl;dr: Give this game a shot no matter where your opinion on Sonic the Hedgehog games lie. It is a great 2D Platformer--the best I've played since Shovel Knight--and worth full price.
